sections.title: Values, effects, and the confidence to change old code
sections.deck: Simon Peyton Jones explains Haskell’s functional experiment, its compiler and type system, and why human understanding still matters when AI generates code.

blocks.question: What is functional programming, and why should an imperative programmer care?
answer: Peyton Jones begins with values rather than changing memory. An imperative running total updates a cell repeatedly; a mathematical expression or spreadsheet formula describes relationships between values. Evaluation can calculate an answer without a programmer-visible sequence of mutations. Learning that distinction after machine-code programming changed his assumption that mutation was intrinsic to computation.

The lambda calculus and Turing machines have equivalent computational power despite their different mechanisms. His research asks what becomes easier to write, maintain, and reason about when unrestricted side effects are removed from the default model. He is not asking programmers to exclude imperative techniques from every task: Haskell has developed ways to combine them with a functional foundation.

followups.question: Why call functional programming the underlying granite?
answer: It supplies an executable mathematical basis for reasoning, and has been a laboratory for ideas that spread into mainstream languages, including garbage collection, lambdas, polymorphism, and stronger types. His preferred default is functional, introducing imperative behavior where necessary. Shared mutable state creates invisible dependencies: changing one part can disturb another because execution order matters. Explicit value dependencies make it easier to reason about whether two components interact.

blocks.question: What becomes harder when side effects are restricted?
answer: A deeply nested function that suddenly needs the current time cannot silently perform that operation while retaining the meaning of an ordinary pure function: equal arguments would no longer imply the same result. Effects have to be represented and threaded through the program. Haskell has an escape called unsafePerformIO, but its deliberately alarming name transfers responsibility to the programmer to justify its use. That is an escape hatch rather than the standard way to make input and output convenient.

blocks.question: Could hardware itself be designed for functional programming?
answer: There have been serious attempts. Peyton Jones recalls Backus’s proposal, Lisp machines, MIT dataflow machines such as Monsoon, and the British SKIM combinator machine. A dataflow machine fires nodes as their inputs arrive, while SKIM rewrites expressions made from a tiny set of combinators.

His retrospective judgment is that these were inspiring but often put an interpreter into hardware. A compiler can remove much of that interpretive work and then exploit the investment in conventional ARM or x86 processors. Targeted hardware support, such as assistance for garbage-collection barriers, can still help; a wholly new execution architecture has a much larger burden. He regards the work as a productive intellectual adventure whose practical lesson favored better compilation.

followups.question: What are the SK combinators?
answer: They form a tiny expression language: I returns its argument; K takes two arguments and returns the first; S distributes an argument to two functions and combines their results. Lambda expressions can be translated into trees of such applications and evaluated through rewriting. He mentions Lennart Augustsson’s microHS as a contemporary software demonstration of this approach. The appeal was reducing a large language to a few operations; the performance problem was leaving too much interpretation for execution.

blocks.question: Does functional programming unlock parallelism?
answer: Independent pure expressions can be evaluated in parallel without ordering mutable side effects. The difficulty is granularity: a million tiny computations can create more allocation, memory traffic, and synchronization than useful work. The dataflow research moved from individual instructions toward compiler-grouped chunks for that reason. GHC offers programmers hints to spark parallel work, rather than automatically forking every expression. Purity makes independence easier to establish; choosing profitable parallel work remains a separate problem.

blocks.question: Why did your language chart place C on the dangerous side?
answer: He points to unchecked memory access and pointer manipulation as foundations for buffer-overflow exploits. Continually patching vulnerable applications can resemble trying to strengthen a boat built from paperclips. His claim that using Haskell, OCaml, or ML would remove an overwhelming share of such vulnerabilities is a forcefully expressed estimate, not a measured result supplied in the interview. The argument concerns removing classes of memory errors at the language foundation.

followups.question: Can a Haskell application still contain vulnerabilities?
answer: Absolutely. It may expose confidential database information, deadlock, or implement the wrong high-level behavior. No language guarantees a correct application. A safer foundation removes some error classes and makes further verification easier; it does not establish total security.

followups.question: Where does Rust fit?
answer: He welcomes Rust as an effort to retain usefulness while improving safety. The goal is broader than functional programming. He explicitly says he does not know the precise details of Rust’s bounds machinery, so his endorsement is of its direction rather than an implementation comparison.

blocks.question: What would it take to reach the useful-and-safe quadrant?
answer: C-family approaches start with usefulness and move toward safety. Early Haskell started with an austere safe model: a program could effectively transform a string into a string but could not perform general input and output. A no-op language illustrates the absurd extreme of safety without usefulness. Haskell had to gain controlled effects and richer facilities without abandoning its foundation. The chart describes two journeys toward a shared goal, not a ranking that requires one community to lose.

blocks.question: How should someone compare Haskell with OCaml?
answer: OCaml evaluates arguments eagerly; Haskell ordinarily passes unevaluated expressions that are computed if needed. A defined evaluation order makes conventional side effects easier to accommodate. In a lazy language, printing placed inside ordinary arguments could occur in a surprising order or never occur at all, depending on how the callee uses them. Laziness therefore pushed Haskell toward keeping ordinary evaluation pure and handling effects separately.

The languages share a family history and exchange ideas. Haskell developed monadic effects; OCaml has developed powerful type facilities and, in his account, an active effect-system research and implementation community. He describes them as siblings with distinct defaults rather than declaring one the universal winner.

blocks.question: What benefit justifies lazy evaluation?
answer: His example, from John Hughes’s discussion of functional programming, is separating chess-move generation from search. A program can describe a huge, even conceptually unbounded, tree while a separate explorer visits and prunes only the required portion. Laziness supplies glue between independently written producer and consumer. The practical gain is modular composition without first materializing the complete result.

followups.question: Is that like a Python generator?
answer: Yes. Strict languages also offer generators, iterators, or other lazy facilities, and OCaml is included in that observation. Conversely, Haskell provides strictness annotations. Both approaches need a mixture; their default changes what is effortless and culturally familiar. Asked whether he would redesign Haskell as strict by default, he says that is attractive after implementing laziness, but suspects he would eventually miss the opposite default. His hypothetical strict version would still be pure.

blocks.question: What is a monad doing for input, output, and ordering?
answer: He explains the usable mechanism before abstract algebra. A value of type IO Char describes a computation that can perform input and output and yield a character; it differs from a plain Char. The do notation combines such computations and specifies their sequence. Reading a character and then printing it becomes a single computation of type IO (), meaning an effectful action whose result carries no interesting value.

These computations are first-class values: they can be named, stored, passed as arguments, or returned. A named read-and-print computation can be composed with itself to perform two read-and-print actions. The distinction between describing a computation and running it is central to the explanation.

followups.question: How does an effectful computation keep the language pure?
answer: The type records the difference. Int → Int promises an ordinary pure function; Int → IO Int exposes that the result is an effectful computation. The coarse IO boundary permits many effects, so he also describes finer effect systems that specify file reading, exceptions, thread creation, or other capabilities. Bluefin, designed by Tom Ellis, is his suggested Haskell example in the interview.

followups.question: What tax does that separation impose?
answer: Mapping an effectful function over a list produces a list of described actions, rather than silently performing them. Another operation must sequence those actions into an action returning a list of results. This requires the programmer to choose an order. He accepts that extra work as part of Haskell’s experiment and notes that monad-like composition also appears in impure languages, including F# workflows and Scala.

blocks.question: What is a type system, and what makes one powerful?
answer: A static type system rejects certain programs before they run, such as supplying a non-list to a list-reversal function. But a weak system can also reject useful programs. A reversal written only for integer lists should not need a duplicate implementation for character lists.

Parametric polymorphism expresses the stronger promise: for every element type A, reversing a list of A yields another list of A. It permits reuse while preserving information about the result. His lesson is to ask which type system a criticism concerns. A restrictive simple system and a richer one impose different costs. He traces parametric polymorphism through ML and its eventual mainstream forms such as generics.

followups.question: How does that compare with object-oriented polymorphism?
answer: Subtype polymorphism lets operations defined for a vehicle apply to a suitable car subtype. Parametric polymorphism works uniformly over a type variable. Both reuse code across types, but combining generics, subtyping, and mutable state creates a more intricate system. He avoids settling those interactions with a slogan; richer types aim to retain good programs while excluding bad ones.

followups.question: What is the largest benefit of static types?
answer: For him it is maintainability, followed by design. He contrasts old untyped programs that nobody dares change with GHC’s decades-old Haskell code. Changing a representation or a type and recompiling sends a wave of errors through the affected uses, helping him refactor systematically. He supports tests, but sees types as an additional source of confidence and a way to express the design before filling in code.

blocks.question: Is there redeeming value in C-style permissive typing?
answer: His preference is to strengthen the type system rather than celebrate unchecked reinterpretation. The host correctly observes that some programs rejected by a type checker would run successfully. Peyton Jones agrees: the ambition is to admit more useful programs without admitting the unwanted failures. This is why type-system expressiveness matters, rather than equating strictness with arbitrary restriction.

followups.question: What if the useful program cannot be expressed statically?
answer: He gives a contrived tree whose node types change at every seventeenth depth. When static types cannot conveniently represent such a structure, a dynamic value can pair data with a runtime type representation, checking it when a specific type is requested. Failure then becomes an explicit runtime possibility. Static typing can avoid pervasive tags where the type is known; Haskell can still offer dynamic typing where needed.

blocks.question: How does the GHC compiler work at a high level?
answer: The front end parses, resolves names, checks types, and desugars a large Haskell syntax into a small lambda-calculus-based intermediate language called Core. He is proud that this boundary has remained remarkably stable while the source language evolved. Repeated Core-to-Core optimization passes improve the program before it is lowered to C--, a portable assembly-like language, and then to machine code through a native backend or LLVM.

Core itself is statically typed. A checker can detect an optimization that transforms a valid Core program into an invalid one, locating a compiler bug near the pass that introduced it. Otherwise the symptom might be a distant runtime crash requiring a difficult search backward through the pipeline. He connects Core to System F and sees this as a successful transfer from theoretical computer science to a production compiler. His statement that he knows no other production compiler with the same property is explicitly a report of his knowledge, not a surveyed universal fact.

followups.question: Why not go directly from lambda calculus to assembly?
answer: Most lowering work should be shared between architectures. Generating x86 directly and separately generating another architecture would duplicate the common steps. C-- describes a generic machine with operations, control flow, and a stack; the final backend handles the smaller processor-specific portion.

blocks.question: Why is Haskell discussed more than it is used?
answer: It demands a change in how programmers think: programming with values and maintaining a principled restriction on effects. Early versions were academic and inconvenient, and the community tolerated disruptive changes. The language, types, compilation, and attention to users have improved over time, but the core experiment remains. He accepts that some programmers do not want that change. Enjoyment among those who do is one of his most rewarding signals.

followups.question: Did the compiler really delete a file that failed type checking?
answer: An old bug did, under a narrow combination of Windows and compiling a module outside the current directory. It was accidental, not a principled punishment for ill-typed code. A user’s extraordinary workaround was copying files before compilation. He emphasizes that those days are gone and the project now invests far more in users and continuous integration.

blocks.question: What does “avoid success at all costs” mean?
answer: The phrase has two readings. Avoid succeeding by sacrificing the central design principles; also recognize, jokingly, that a large successful user base makes experimentation harder. He now spends far more time on compatibility. He describes substantial work toward allowing a package that compiles with one GHC release to compile unchanged with the next. The interview’s illustrative version numbers describe the goal, not proof that the property was already delivered.

blocks.question: How should language design respond when LLMs generate much of the code?
answer: He predicts that static types will benefit because a model can run the compiler, see an invalid program, and revise it before asking a human to assess it. This narrows the space of plausible-looking but ill-formed output and shortens feedback. That is his outlook on language design and tooling, rather than evidence that every type-correct model output behaves correctly.

blocks.question: Which languages have the strongest type systems?
answer: He initially names Haskell, then qualifies the comparison. OCaml and the ML family explore module and functor systems more deeply. Scala combines many functional facilities with object orientation and subtyping, gaining expressiveness and complexity. He ends by grouping Haskell, Scala, and OCaml as difficult to compare: each is stronger in some dimensions. The answer does not establish a single linear ranking.

blocks.question: What future language problems interest you?
answer: Rather than nominate one definitive unsolved problem, he points to a new part of the design space. His work at Epic Games on Verse explores a functional logic language with a very different static type system. He compares its strangeness to the early reception of functional programming: exploration can be worthwhile before practical value is obvious. Epic supplies resources that early academic functional-language research lacked. This is an intellectual direction, not a promise of adoption or product success.

blocks.question: Should students still learn programming now that AI can write code?
answer: Yes, while taking employment disruption seriously. He hopes AI becomes a productivity tool like compilers, but acknowledges that a transition can hurt people even if a later economy improves. His metaphor is that copilots still need pilots: people must understand, review, and maintain the code they accept.

A disposable visualization and a long-lived compiler or safety-critical system demand different levels of confidence. He would not incorporate an AI-generated patch into GHC without competent review because future maintainers must understand it. Tests that happened to pass do not turn an opaque incantation into maintainable software.

He also argues that every child should understand bits, the mechanical execution of instructions, and the basic computational nature of neural networks. These form civic understanding of the surrounding technological world, much as atoms underpin understanding matter. His broad numerical sketch of a language model is an explanatory simplification, not an architecture specification. He is less attached to memorizing thousands of arcane framework APIs if tools can supply them.

blocks.question: Why was Excel your second-favorite programming language?
answer: He sees the spreadsheet formula language as widely used functional programming: users compose values without ordinary side effects. At Microsoft he wanted to bring functional-language ideas to the much larger population of spreadsheet domain experts. Adding lambda took a long time in his account but made formulas reusable as user-defined functions. He describes computational completeness as interesting, while the practical win is replacing repeated pasted formulas with a reusable abstraction. His adoption magnitudes are rhetorical estimates from the interview, not statistics established here.

blocks.question: What advice would you give yourself at graduation?
answer: People who appear successful often remain uncertain and are making decisions as they go. Their projected confidence does not mean they possessed a complete career plan. He would reassure his younger self that uncertainty is normal and that luck contributes. To encounter useful accidents, however, one has to enter situations where they can happen, which entails some risk. He acknowledges a balance rather than advising indiscriminate risk-taking.

parts.title: Building systems that survive reality
parts.introduction: Large systems test more than a design on paper. Follow the choices around architecture, data movement, reliability, integration, and the responsibility to end a project that no longer works.

sections.title: A technically successful framework can still be the wrong project
sections.deck: A Meta distinguished engineer recounts building, canceling, and fully removing ComponentScript.

blocks.text: The guest spent roughly two years building ComponentScript to reduce duplicated UI work across iOS and Android. Existing applications used ComponentKit and Litho. He says React Native did not fit the needed pattern at that time: a large native application embedding small cross-platform pieces in several places. He explicitly allows that React Native’s architecture has changed since then; his criticism describes the situation his team faced, not a current universal limitation.
blocks.heading: The requirement was integration, not just cross-platform rendering

blocks.text: An initial attempt to support the full React implementation proved too difficult. He then designed a smaller React-like API on top of the existing native frameworks. It worked: teams shipped features, full screens and small units could interoperate, and nested native/cross-platform embeddings were possible. Yet the framework did not gain the adoption he expected. The lesson is that satisfying technical requirements does not by itself make a platform successful; he had overlooked other factors that determined whether people would use it.
blocks.heading: Working code was only part of the outcome

blocks.question: How did the failed project affect performance reviews, and should an engineer fear canceling a project?
answer: The guest describes negative performance feedback as the signal that forced him to face the problem. A new manager saw the work with fresh eyes and told him it was not working. Rather than protect the framework indefinitely, he took responsibility for ending it.

That meant helping teams migrate their existing products and features to native code, React Native, or another chosen approach, and deleting the framework entirely. He did not leave a permanent remnant that someone else would need to maintain or clean up. He also shared the lessons. In his account, this responsible closure earned goodwill and helped his standing in the immediate aftermath. It does not mean every failed project improves a review; the point is what accountable cleanup looked like in this case.
blocks.speaker: Meta distinguished engineer

blocks.question: Looking back, what signals should you have acted on sooner?
answer: He says he knew during the project’s last year that it was not going well. His instinct as a prolific coder was to write more code and convert more features until adoption took off. That response avoided the harder conclusion that the project itself might be wrong. He wishes he had acted on the unease sooner and found another useful way to contribute.
blocks.speaker: Meta distinguished engineer

blocks.title: Close a failed platform responsibly

steps.title: Recognize the mismatch
steps.text: Treat adoption and outcome as evidence, not just technical elegance.

steps.title: Help dependent teams move
steps.text: Make a practical migration path available.

steps.title: Remove the leftover burden
steps.text: Delete the abandoned framework rather than preserve a permanent orphan.

steps.title: Share the lesson
steps.text: Explain what failed and what the organization learned.

blocks.caption: Arrows show an editorial reconstruction of the guest’s cleanup sequence.

sections.title: Build tooling around real pain, then earn adoption
sections.deck: The Bento story links a staff-level technical vision with onboarding, legacy support, team creation, and explicitly agreed exploration.

blocks.question: What was the work behind your senior-staff-equivalent promotion?
answer: The guest began on a project estimating usage of a Facebook property around 2015. Moving between separate data-pipeline and machine-learning systems was cumbersome, so he built helper scripts that let pipeline work live within the orchestration environment. Sensible defaults removed repeated boilerplate, with an escape hatch for advanced configuration. He estimates that a task needing roughly 300 lines in the older system could need about 20 in his library.

That experience redirected his interest from a single analysis to helping analysts and machine-learning engineers work faster. Notebook setup was another repeated pain: people used outdated wikis to install Jupyter or RStudio manually. With his manager’s agreement, he spent an initial two or three months exploring an automated setup, then recruited others. The earliest Bento was just a setup script; the larger vision was a browser-accessible environment integrated with internal libraries and eventually other languages.

Over roughly a year, the team built the platform and on-demand instances that users could request and release without maintaining their own server. He also assembled a team of six to eight people by inviting engineers who already loved building tools on the side to do it full time. He moved into a tech-lead-manager role and says his TLM2 promotion depended largely on his individual technical work and the Bento vision. The host explains that level as senior-manager or senior-staff equivalent.
blocks.speaker: Guest

blocks.question: How did you turn a useful internal tool into something widely adopted?
answer: Bento did not initially require converting everybody’s existing workflow. The team targeted onboarding programs, where new data users had no attachment to legacy setup. In a fast-growing company, that supplied many users; existing employees then saw more colleagues on the new system.

For people who remained on legacy notebooks, the team provided maintenance and support in previously underserved channels. That created trust before a migration request. When someone needed an awkward setup, the team could offer either a long manual recipe or the simpler supported Bento path.

The team also spoke with analytics leaders about concrete pain in their groups. Those conversations revealed a larger backlog of data-tooling needs. Because no dedicated team served that area, the guest moved from core data science into developer infrastructure to create one. Adoption was therefore a mix of a convenient entry point, service to existing users, leadership relationships, and a fitting organizational home.
blocks.speaker: Guest

blocks.title: A tool earns adoption

steps.title: Remove a recurring pain
steps.text: Reduce boilerplate and setup work in a real workflow.

steps.title: Meet new users at onboarding
steps.text: Offer a simpler default before habits form.

steps.title: Support existing users
steps.text: Help with legacy systems and earn trust.

steps.title: Expand with the needs
steps.text: Integrate the environment and create a dedicated team.

blocks.caption: Editorial synthesis. Arrows show the order of emphasis in this account, not a universal adoption formula.

blocks.question: How do you take a promising risk when short-term performance expectations are strict?
answer: The guest thinks underperformance has greater consequences than it did a decade earlier, but the key practice is the same: agree on expectations before departing from normal work. He was assigned to data consulting, while the proposed work was infrastructure, so he asked his manager and skip to make a bounded exploration part of his job.

If the tool succeeded, the team benefited; if it failed, completing an agreed exploration was still the expectation. He sees that as much safer than disappearing for three months and returning with work nobody knew had displaced his normal obligations.

Over-communicate and be prepared to hear no. He credits a manager who supported this experiment and remembers later proposals that leadership rejected. The story does not promise that every risk can be negotiated away or that an exploratory project guarantees a promotion.
blocks.speaker: Guest

sections.title: Match the database architecture to the workload
sections.deck: Mike Stonebraker connects specialization, GPU constraints, and the difficulty of building a database.

blocks.question: Does one database architecture serve every workload well?
answer: Stonebraker explains the argument behind his “one size fits none” position through three designs: a stream-processing engine, a column store for analytical warehouses, and a conventional row-oriented relational system. He says their implementations look fundamentally different, and that using a design poorly suited to the workload can give up an order of magnitude in performance. This is his characterization of the systems and comparisons discussed, not a benchmark supplied by the transcript.

He still sees value in a common parser above different implementations. He points to specialized column and vector systems as examples of why specialization persists, and criticizes the PostgreSQL capabilities he describes for very large analytical workloads. Those observations belong to the interview’s context; they should not be treated as a current feature inventory for every product or extension.

At the same time, he recommends PostgreSQL as a practical starting point: it is free, has a large community, supports many data-type implementations, and makes experienced developers comparatively easy to find. His distinction is between a useful general-purpose default and requirements at the extreme end, such as the transaction or warehouse scales he uses as examples. Those figures illustrate his argument rather than define universal migration thresholds.
blocks.speaker: Mike Stonebraker

blocks.question: Do GPUs create new opportunities for database optimization?
answer: Probably, Stonebraker says, but the work must fit the hardware. He contrasts the same-operation, many-data style of GPU computation with indexing, and warns that the path from storage through a CPU to a GPU can become the limiting bandwidth bottleneck. Attaching an accelerator does not remove the need to design the surrounding data movement.

followups.question: Why is an index traversal a poor fit for this kind of parallelism?
answer: A B-tree lookup for one person’s salary follows a pointer at each level before it can determine the next access. Those dependent memory reads do not parallelize in the same way as independent operations across many data elements. Stonebraker uses this concrete lookup to explain why the workload, not the presence of a GPU, determines the opportunity.
followups.speaker: Mike Stonebraker

blocks.speaker: Mike Stonebraker

blocks.question: Was the original Ingres implementation written from scratch?
answer: Yes. Stonebraker says the original version was written from scratch, including the components the host is asking about. The short answer does not provide further implementation details.
blocks.speaker: Mike Stonebraker

blocks.question: What was the hardest component to implement?
answer: The query optimizer. Stonebraker answers directly rather than telling a longer development story.

followups.question: Why was query optimization especially hard?
answer: He characterizes it as algorithmically difficult. The clip does not unpack a particular optimization algorithm or failure case.
followups.speaker: Mike Stonebraker

blocks.speaker: Mike Stonebraker

blocks.title: Keep the design questions separate
rows: What workload dominates?
Streaming, analytical scans, and indexed lookups can favor different designs.
What is the whole data path?
Storage and CPU–GPU bandwidth may limit acceleration.
What is the pragmatic default?
A community and available talent can make a general-purpose database valuable.
When is specialization worth it?
Judge the actual scale and workload rather than assume one architecture always wins.

sections.title: Owning storage means owning its failure modes
sections.deck: James Cowling explains why Dropbox built Magic Pocket and how workload specialization, predictable memory, and an elastic fallback made it viable.

blocks.question: Why did Dropbox migrate away from S3?
answer: Cowling describes a longstanding strategic desire to control the company’s storage destiny, especially when Dropbox’s central business was file synchronization and sharing. Building its own storage system also produced major cost savings before the company went public.

Hard technical work helped attract a strong, small engineering team whose members later contributed elsewhere, including synchronization and distributed databases. But ownership creates continuing obligations: after building the system, the company must keep maintaining and investing in it. He considers the project difficult to reproduce without enormous investment and does not recommend that other companies casually follow it.

blocks.question: Could Amazon negotiate a deal that would keep Dropbox on S3?
answer: Dropbox already received deeply discounted rates. Cowling says the new system ultimately had cost advantages that Amazon could not match: experimental shingled magnetic recording disks and a design tightly optimized for Dropbox’s known workload. S3 had to serve many different workloads. He emphasizes that the historical choice made sense for this company at that time, rather than advising every company to build storage today.

followups.question: What did knowing the workload let you optimize?
answer: Files were often accessed soon after upload for sharing or preview generation, then became colder. Dropbox could write first to storage optimized for inexpensive reads and writes, then move data in bulk to a more storage-efficient, static system. Taking the cold write path offline temporarily did not interrupt the live upload path.

Knowledge of block sizes, access frequency, deletion patterns, and even rack power consumption supported further tuning. Failures could alter that power budget: a bad disk batch increased re-replication, making racks run hotter. The optimization reached physical infrastructure at multi-exabyte and roughly million-drive scale.

blocks.question: Why did the storage nodes move from Python to Go and then Rust?
answer: The prototype was Python, which he considers reasonable for I/O-bound work but problematic here for concurrency, memory control, and safe refactoring. Go worked well for the larger system’s concurrent servers and data movement. The problem was unpredictable memory consumption on the storage nodes.

An out-of-memory restart resembled disk failure and triggered recovery. A sudden load spike on a small set of files could restart nodes, then force much more expensive reconstruction from replicas. He recalls that one incoming stream could become roughly seven streams of recovery load. More load caused more failures, creating congestion collapse.

Rewriting the storage-node component in Rust coincided with removing the conventional filesystem and controlling the new disks through their draft interfaces. He does not reliably recall the exact interface name. The combined project improved reliability and shifted spending toward disks rather than RAM, compute, network, and other overhead. This account identifies the behavior the rewrite needed to control, rather than treating a language switch as a magic solution.

followups.question: Did a postmortem reveal the failure mechanism?
answer: He says the mechanism was evident during the incident. Physical infrastructure made the fix difficult: adding RAM meant dispatching people to installed machines. He uses that constraint as an argument for appreciating cloud flexibility even while explaining Dropbox’s decision to own hardware.

followups.question: What other unknowns did the system need to survive?
answer: Two server-delivery trucks crashed in one week, delaying capacity for weeks even though their drivers were safe. Customers still needed to store data. The team therefore planned capacity buffers, guarded against memory spikes and congestion collapse, and used a structured failure-mode exercise listing possible problems and their consequences before designing protections.

blocks.question: Did you use emergency settings that reduced durability?
answer: Never for user-data durability, Cowling says. That guarantee was nonnegotiable. Emergency controls could stop background tasks or test loads to relieve CPU and memory pressure.

A system called Trampoline provided another escape: near a capacity threshold, Dropbox could write new data to S3 and move it back later. Access to elastic external capacity let it run owned capacity nearer the edge without weakening durability. He gives thirty petabytes as an illustrative large fallback volume and says the path was exercised in tests, even though actual emergency use was uncommon.

blocks.title: The congestion-collapse feedback loop

steps.title: Hot-file load rises
steps.text: A small set of files creates concentrated demand.

steps.title: Nodes exhaust memory
steps.text: Restarts look like storage failures.

steps.title: Recovery multiplies work
steps.text: Reconstruction loads additional replicas.

steps.title: Pressure spreads
steps.text: Additional load can trigger further node failures.

blocks.caption: Editorial synthesis. Arrows show how one failure increases the load that can cause the next; the last step can feed back into more memory exhaustion.

sections.title: Database architecture follows the workload
sections.deck: Mike Stonebraker traces relational databases, argues for specialized implementations, and examines the transactional demands of production AI.

blocks.question: How did you begin building database systems?
answer: After arriving at Berkeley, Stonebraker realized that continuing his doctoral work would not give him a promising research direction. A mentor, Gene Wong, proposed exploring databases shortly after the publication of the relational model. Stonebraker describes this mentorship and timing as consequential accidents, rather than a fully planned career.

Existing network and hierarchical systems tied programs closely to physical organization. Pointer-following made programs difficult to debug and schema changes could force extensive rewriting; hierarchical trees required awkward additions to represent more general relationships. The relational proposal offered a cleaner separation, so the team began Ingres in 1972. It became his main tenure project.

He distinguishes a demonstrable university prototype from a system others could actually run. The team invested the additional effort to make Ingres reliable, and roughly a hundred universities adopted the free Unix implementation. Commercial adoption exposed another obstacle: Arizona State could tolerate unsupported Unix and an unsupported database, but its COBOL shop could not proceed without COBOL on Unix. A company, formed in 1980, supplied support and a port to a commercial operating system. Technical quality alone had not supplied the surrounding ecosystem customers needed.

blocks.question: How could Oracle compete with a technically stronger Ingres offering?
answer: Stonebraker attributes Oracle’s competitive success to Larry Ellison’s sales ability, while making strongly critical allegations about the accuracy of its promises. These are his recollections and judgments, rather than independently established findings. His example is referential integrity: he says Ingres implemented it while Oracle documented the standard definition with a note that it was not yet implemented.

The host brings up customers’ concerns after Oracle acquired MySQL. Stonebraker credits that concern with helping PostgreSQL become a preferred open-source relational database. His account connects adoption to trust and business behavior as well as engineering.

blocks.question: What could PostgreSQL do that Ingres could not?
answer: The original academic Ingres project was supposed to support geographic information. Its fixed set of integers, floating-point values, and strings did not efficiently represent points, lines, polygons, and groups of lines. Although successful as a general database, it failed at this motivating application.

A later commercial customer revealed the same limitation from a different direction. Bond calculations treated each month as thirty days; subtracting two Gregorian dates therefore produced the wrong financial interval. The customer had to retrieve dates into application code, calculate there, and write the answer back, at an estimated two- or threefold efficiency cost. He wanted to overload subtraction with the semantics of his own domain.

PostgreSQL’s central response was an extensible type system: users could introduce useful domain types and their operations inside the database. Other experiments included inheritance and time travel. Stonebraker explicitly says the time-travel implementation was poor and was eventually removed, so extensibility should not be mistaken for a claim that every original feature succeeded.

blocks.question: How do you identify extraordinary engineers?
answer: Stonebraker judges accomplishment against his understanding of the difficulty of the work. A student who completes roughly three times what he considers a reasonable amount is conspicuous. This is a personal screening heuristic, dependent on an informed evaluator’s technical judgment.

blocks.question: How do you evaluate whether someone understands technical work deeply?
answer: He asks progressively specific questions about a candidate’s own thesis or project: what was built, exactly how it worked, how errors were handled, how many processes were used, and why threads were not chosen. The useful method beneath his blunt language is to test understanding through implementation choices and failure conditions, rather than accept impressive project labels.

blocks.question: Does one database architecture fit every workload?
answer: His argument began with three very different architectures: conventional relational row storage, stream processing, and column storage for warehouses. Each specialized implementation could be an order of magnitude faster for its intended workload. He maintains that this distinction still matters, including for vector workloads.

A common parser can sit above multiple physical implementations. He criticizes PostgreSQL’s lack of a built-in column store and multinode warehouse support in the context of very large analytical systems. These are his assessments of the offerings discussed in the interview, not a current product survey.

He nevertheless recommends PostgreSQL as a practical starting point for many ordinary applications: it is free, has a large community, offers many extensions, and makes hiring easier. His boundary is scale and workload fit: the ease of starting with a general-purpose system does not prove it remains the best design for a million transactions per second or a petabyte warehouse.

blocks.title: Different database requirements imply different architectures
rows: Ordinary application development
PostgreSQL offers a practical ecosystem and easy starting point.
Large analytical warehouse
Column storage and multinode execution may matter more than general-purpose convenience.
Uniform accelerator-friendly work
GPU parallelism helps only when dependencies and transfer bandwidth permit it.
Nonnegative inventory or coordinated money transfer
Atomic transactions preserve constraints that asynchronous reconciliation can violate.

blocks.question: Do GPUs create new opportunities for databases?
answer: Probably, but Stonebraker sees important architectural constraints. A GPU’s single-instruction, multiple-data execution fits uniform parallel work better than dependent pointer traversals. Storage bandwidth and the CPU-to-GPU connection can also become the bottleneck, so simply attaching an accelerator does not ensure useful speedup.

followups.question: Why does indexing fit SIMD poorly?
answer: Finding a person’s salary in a B-tree requires choosing a branch at the root, following a pointer, and repeating the process several times. Each next step depends on a preceding memory access. That dependency chain does not expose the broad, uniform parallel work that a GPU needs.

blocks.question: Was the original Ingres implementation written from scratch?
answer: Yes. Stonebraker says the original system was implemented from scratch, including its underlying structures.

followups.question: What was the hardest component, and why?
answer: The query optimizer was the hardest component. He calls it algorithmically difficult and says experienced database engineers would still commonly give the same answer. The interview does not develop a more detailed optimizer explanation.

blocks.question: Why did you object to MapReduce’s popularity?
answer: Stonebraker believes many adopters inferred quality from Google’s reputation instead of comparing architectures. He and collaborators already understood distributed database systems and argued that they could greatly outperform Hadoop; he points to their 2011 comparison as the basis for this criticism.

He extends that criticism to enthusiasm for eventual consistency. In his view, the approach addresses a narrower set of application requirements than its advocates implied. This is a forceful participant’s evaluation, and the section preserves it as such.

followups.question: What problem was eventual consistency intended to solve?
answer: Synchronously committing a transaction across distant replicas requires network round trips. Asynchronous updates avoid that immediate coordination cost: each coast updates locally and sends messages that eventually reconcile the replicas. The difficulty appears when both sell the last item at the same time. The eventual state may be negative stock, and one buyer cannot receive the promised item. Applications that permit overselling can accept this; systems that require stock to remain nonnegative cannot. He cites Spanner’s use of conventional transactions as evidence that stronger guarantees remain valuable.

followups.question: Did you discuss these disagreements with Google?
answer: Before the 2011 paper, his group proposed working together, but Google declined. The interview supplies no account of Google’s reasoning beyond that refusal.

blocks.question: Do you disagree with other large companies’ database strategies?
answer: He says he told Amazon that maintaining approximately fifteen database systems was excessive—about twelve too many—and that they had not retired them by the time of the interview. He sees this as a consequence of company culture and portfolio decisions.

followups.question: Why should fifteen systems become roughly three?
answer: His criterion is whether a system is sufficiently performant in a sufficiently large market to justify maintenance. He regards dedicated graph storage as rarely the best performer and suggests presenting nodes and edges through a layer above a relational implementation. This is his design judgment, not a universally demonstrated result for every graph workload.

blocks.question: Why influence industry from academia rather than work at a large company?
answer: An industry role brings a boss, company rules, publication restrictions, and reduced access to information competitors might share with an academic. He values the freedom to investigate and criticize across organizations.

He also prefers startups. After the commercial PostgreSQL effort was acquired by Informix, he worked part time in a company of about two thousand people and felt unable to make much difference. Bureaucracy and executive authority frustrated him. He openly acknowledges that corporate politics and interacting with people he does not respect are personal weaknesses.

blocks.question: What is DBOS, and how did its operating-system idea become a company?
answer: The academic project began around 2019–2020 with a scheduling problem at Databricks. At very large scale, existing operating-system schedulers did not meet the requirement. Storing scheduling data in PostgreSQL suggested a broader hypothesis: much of an operating system is managing state at scale, and database technology could provide that state management.

The research explored replacing the upper part of Linux while keeping device drivers. A language interface then made programs inherit database properties by keeping application state in the database: durability, transactions, and failover. Venture investors doubted that a startup could displace Linux but liked the programming model, so the 2023 company focused on that opportunity.

He describes integrations for TypeScript, Java, Go, and Python and a workflow model whose steps are transactional and whose completed progress is durable. Whole-workflow atomicity is described as something the system could support if there were market demand, not as an unqualified existing feature. He says customers include startups and increasingly larger organizations, and that roughly two thirds were working on agentic AI.

followups.question: Why would agents need stronger workflow guarantees?
answer: Many early agents produce read-only recommendations. Stonebraker expects applications that change real state to require database guarantees. Transferring one hundred dollars between two accounts requires the debit and credit to commit together or be rolled back together; separate agents do not remove that requirement. He presents growing read-write agent use as a forecast and a business opportunity for DBOS.

blocks.question: What tradeoffs appear when an operating system’s state lives in a database?
answer: Stonebraker claims that the research file system outperformed Linux’s, that scheduling was competitive, and that database-based state made failover available across the system. He argues there is no inherent downside in replacing the upper operating-system components while retaining device-driver code. The interview does not provide benchmark details or investigate counterexamples, so these remain his claims about the research.

followups.question: How did operating-system researchers respond?
answer: He recalls researchers feeling that database specialists were encroaching on their territory, and similar reactions from programming-language researchers to database-backed runtimes. He also cautions that adoption can be slow, using Java’s roughly decade-long path to broad acceptance as an analogy.

blocks.question: Which unsolved database problems interest you now?
answer: His first focus is text-to-SQL on production warehouses. His group obtained actual workloads from four warehouses and reconstructed the natural-language requests behind them. He contrasts those tests with Spider and BIRD, on which he says leading systems scored around eighty to eighty-five percent.

On his group’s benchmarks, the tested language models scored zero percent; retrieval and other additions raised that to about ten percent. Giving the actual FROM tables and join clauses raised accuracy to roughly thirty-five percent. These are the results he reports for the systems and benchmarks in this interview, not timeless capabilities of all language models.

He identifies four differences: proprietary warehouse data is absent from general training material; real queries can reach about a hundred SQL lines rather than ten or twenty; production schemas have cryptic names and redundant materialized views; and business concepts can be idiosyncratic, such as MIT’s January term. Together, these make clean demonstration benchmarks misleading for his target problem.

His group released the anonymized BEAVER benchmark and is exploring simpler retrieval units containing table and join information. For requests spanning structured databases, he prefers preserving tables and using SQL joins rather than asking an LLM to execute the joins. A Munich transportation example combines schedules, traffic-light sequencing, intersection CAD, and national and city regulations. Their research direction is to turn these into tables and use query optimization to join them. His second focus is transactionally correct read-write agents.

followups.question: What does text-to-SQL mean here?
answer: The user asks a question in ordinary language, such as identifying professors at MIT who won the Turing Award, and a model constructs the SQL needed to answer it. The important comparison is whether it can do this over a real production schema, not merely generate plausible SQL syntax.

followups.question: How well would a human perform on the difficult benchmark?
answer: Once the natural-language request is disambiguated, a knowledgeable SQL programmer with the schema should achieve very high accuracy, Stonebraker says. The host suggests ninety percent or more, but the guest does not supply a measured human benchmark score.

blocks.question: What should someone study to understand databases deeply?
answer: He recommends Readings in Database Systems, the Red Book he edited with Joseph Hellerstein, followed by influential research papers. He notes that the edition discussed was about eight years old, so the later literature matters for newer developments.

blocks.question: What advice would you give your younger self?
answer: Beginning a database system without knowing much about databases or implementation was, in retrospect, a very ambitious gamble. He encourages unusual ideas and learning by making them work, rather than assuming useful projects must follow prevailing fashion.

He distinguishes this from advice to students choosing a field now. He speculates that computer science may cease to be a growth industry, regards health care and building trades as safer, and is unsure he would recommend the same degree choice. Those are his predictions, not established labor-market facts.

For a new PhD graduate, he recommends the most prestigious available role, a willing mentor, and a research direction outside the main flow. He also acknowledges a tension in telling children to follow their passion while doubting that money necessarily takes care of itself.

followups.question: If money may not work out, why still encourage passion?
answer: His wife wanted to teach children, but her parents urged a better-paid path and she studied computer science. He says she continued to regret abandoning teaching. His point is about satisfaction: passion may not make someone wealthy, but work that feels like more than a trade can improve life. He enjoys his own work regardless of whether it pays a great deal.

sections.title: Leslie Lamport: Concurrency, Paxos, Byzantine Generals, and Thinking by Writing
sections.deck: Lamport explains how algorithms, invariants, and written proofs shaped his work on concurrent and distributed systems, from the bakery algorithm to Paxos.

blocks.text: Lamport argues that the reliable way to understand a concurrent or distributed system is to state an algorithm, name an invariant about its state, and write the proof down. He says informal code hides the issues that matter for synchronization. The conversation follows his key work in order: the bakery algorithm, the paper on ordering events, Byzantine faults, Paxos and Raft, then writing as a thinking tool, LaTeX, and his view of his own abilities. The host introduces Lamport as a Turing Award winner.
blocks.heading: Lamport's view: write the algorithm down, state the invariant, and prove it

blocks.question: What problem does the bakery algorithm solve, and how did Lamport first come across it?
answer: Lamport says Edsger Dijkstra introduced the problem in a 1965 paper, which Lamport treats as the start of concurrent programming theory. Dijkstra structured a program as semi-independent tasks that must synchronize. Time-sharing made this urgent, since a shared printer could produce garbled output if two programs used it at once. Dijkstra's answer was a critical section, a piece of code arranged so that at most one process runs it at a time.
Lamport says he first learned of the problem in 1972, from a Communications of the ACM article that gave a solution.

followups.question: How did the bakery idea develop after Lamport's first attempt?
answer: Lamport's simple two-process algorithm had a bug, which the editor pointed out in a letter. The lesson was that concurrent programs are hard to get right and need a proof of correctness. The bakery idea came from a deli counter, where customers take numbered tickets. Dijkstra's version had no central server, so each process had to choose its own number.
followups.speaker: Leslie Lamport

followups.question: Why was the bakery algorithm notable, and who doubted it?
answer: Lamport says its proof showed a surprising property. Mutual exclusion was assumed to need atomic reads and writes of shared registers. Bakery did not need that, because each shared value had one writer. A reader overlapping a write could see any value, and the algorithm still worked.
His colleague Anatol Holt found the result so remarkable that he did not believe it. Lamport wrote the proof on a whiteboard, and Holt went home convinced it must be wrong. He never found a flaw.
followups.speaker: Leslie Lamport

blocks.speaker: Leslie Lamport

blocks.question: What was unsatisfactory about Dijkstra's solution, and why was bakery different?
answer: Lamport says Dijkstra's original solution allowed starvation. If many processes kept trying to enter the critical section, one might never get in. Lamport recalls that the next solution, by Donald Knuth, measured efficiency by how long a process might wait. He believes bakery was the first with first-come, first-served order: if one process picked its number before another, it entered first. He also thinks bakery was simpler than the alternatives.
blocks.speaker: Leslie Lamport

blocks.question: What was the month in the Netherlands with Dijkstra, in 1976, like?
answer: Lamport says Dijkstra wrote short papers, called EWDs, and sent them to colleagues. One described the first concurrent garbage collection algorithm, by Dijkstra and associates. Lamport saw that the free list could be part of the regular data structure instead of needing its own coordination. That simplified the algorithm, and Dijkstra made him an author on the next version.

Lamport says the idea seemed obvious to him but was not obvious to most people. Dijkstra told him he had a remarkable ability at abstraction, which Lamport says he only came to appreciate in recent years.

followups.question: What came out of the visit?
answer: Lamport says the month produced one published result, a variant of the bakery algorithm. It came from weekly discussions with Dijkstra and a colleague.
followups.speaker: Leslie Lamport

blocks.speaker: Leslie Lamport

blocks.question: What is the story behind the paper on time, clocks, and the ordering of events in distributed systems?
answer: Lamport says a paper on distributed databases executed operations as if they occurred in a sequence that could differ from their actual order. He drew on special relativity, where one event can influence another only if a signal could travel between them below light speed. He applied the same idea to messages: one event happens before another if the first could have affected the second through messages actually sent.

Lamport says this happens-before definition surprised people, and it was the first of his papers he would call a scientific result about distributed systems. He admits it broke a rule he had been warned about, since it put two ideas in one paper.

followups.question: Why did the state machine idea matter, and why did readers miss it?
answer: Lamport says the paper's ordering algorithm let any distributed system be described as a state machine, where each command changes the state and produces a value. He calls this the practical idea in the paper, yet readers ignored it. Twice people told him the paper said nothing about state machines, so he reread it to be sure.
followups.speaker: Leslie Lamport

followups.question: Why does Lamport prefer invariants to reasoning about sequences of events?
answer: Lamport says a concurrent program is best understood through an invariant, a Boolean property of the state that holds at each point and guarantees the right answer. Reasoning about sequences is hard, because the number of possible executions grows exponentially with the number of processes. Lamport says the work in an invariant proof grows roughly quadratically, so invariant proofs are easier to get right.
He says much distributed-systems theory spent years on partial orderings. That approach produced many papers but is not the practical method, apart from exceptions such as bakery.
followups.speaker: Leslie Lamport

blocks.speaker: Leslie Lamport

blocks.question: What is the story behind the Byzantine generals problem?
answer: Lamport says his ordering work assumed no failures, but a distributed system should keep running when a computer fails. He assumed the worst case, that a failed process might do anything. His algorithm implemented a state machine under that assumption, using digital signatures so a faulty process could relay messages but not forge another's signature.

When Lamport joined SRI, colleagues were working on the same problem. Few people knew of digital signatures in 1975, but Lamport knew of them through Whit Diffie, a friend and co-author of the Diffie-Hellman paper. He says Diffie called building them an open problem, and he sketched a first signature algorithm on a napkin. By his rough estimate it needed about 128 bits to sign one bit, but signing a hash of the document made it workable.

followups.question: How did the SRI approach differ, and why did it need four processes?
answer: Lamport says the SRI group framed the problem as agreement on one command, repeated for each command, which he found a nicer abstraction. Without signatures, their algorithm needed four processes to tolerate one fault, against three with signatures. The original paper contained both algorithms, and Lamport co-authored it. Marshall Pease wrote the general algorithm, which Lamport calls brilliant and nearly incomprehensible.
followups.speaker: Leslie Lamport

followups.question: Why was the algorithm largely ignored?
answer: Lamport says the SRI group had a contract to build a multiprocess computer for flying airplanes, so they took malicious failures seriously. Each three-process design could be defeated by some plausible sequence of failures. Lamport adds that digital signatures were expensive at the time, which is why the algorithm was largely ignored.
followups.speaker: Leslie Lamport

followups.question: Why did Lamport choose a story about generals?
answer: Lamport says Dijkstra's dining philosophers problem was not especially interesting in itself, but its story made it popular. Lamport decided his result needed a story too. In his version, four generals must agree on whether to attack or retreat, and one of them might be a traitor.
followups.speaker: Leslie Lamport

blocks.speaker: Leslie Lamport

blocks.question: Was there an earlier version of the problem, called the Chinese generals problem?
answer: Lamport says Jim Gray had described a related problem as an impossibility result, which gave Lamport the idea of using generals. He first thought of Albanian generals, since Albania was largely closed to the outside world. His boss pointed out that Albanians exist, so Lamport chose Byzantine, since there are no Byzantines around.
blocks.speaker: Leslie Lamport

blocks.question: What made the Byzantine problem worth extra work?
answer: Lamport says the problem mattered because computers would fly airplanes. In the 1970s oil crisis, designers wanted fuel-efficient planes with smaller control surfaces, which were aerodynamically unstable. A pilot could not make the constant adjustments needed, but a computer could. People assumed three computers could tolerate one fault, without realizing that arbitrary faults needed four. Lamport believes that result needed to be well known.
blocks.speaker: Leslie Lamport

blocks.question: How does Lamport choose problems, given that most of his work was in private companies?
answer: Lamport says he worked for private companies, not in academia or government. Some problems came to him when an engineer had a need. Paxos was one such case, because someone actually wanted an algorithm that did what it did.
blocks.speaker: Leslie Lamport

blocks.question: What is the story behind Paxos?
answer: Lamport says Paxos addressed the same problem as the Byzantine work, building a fault-tolerant state machine. By then, industry cared most about failures in which a computer simply stopped, and Paxos handles that class of faults. Lamport joined Digital Equipment's Systems Research Center in 1985. Its group had come from Xerox PARC, had built one of the first distributed operating systems, and had invented Ethernet.

The group's system kept shared storage consistent across computers. Lamport did not believe that was possible, and he tried to write an impossibility proof. He eventually concluded that the group's code was itself an algorithm that worked. The group had code that did the job, but no algorithm written down.

followups.question: What did Lamport mean by code versus an algorithm?
answer: Lamport says most programmers start by writing code, but he thinks in algorithms. An algorithm is more abstract than a program and can be implemented in any code. Since about 2000, much of his work has been persuading people who build concurrent systems to write an algorithm for the synchronizing core first. Code mixes many concerns unrelated to concurrency, which makes the synchronizing part hard to get right.
followups.speaker: Leslie Lamport

followups.question: Why did the Paxos paper take about eight years to publish?
answer: Lamport says the referees found the paper acceptable but not terribly important, and he was in no hurry to publish. A new editor later decided to publish it, since it had been accepted but needed revision. Keith Marzullo wrote the interim update and a preface that kept the framing of an ancient system. Lamport says Butler Lampson recognized the algorithm's importance and promoted building systems with Paxos as state machines.
followups.speaker: Leslie Lamport

followups.question: How was the Paxos paper presented, and who understood it?
answer: The host recalls Lamport dressing as an Indiana Jones-style archaeologist for the talk. Lamport says the lecture may have gone well, but almost nobody understood the algorithm's significance. Butler Lampson was the exception. Lamport says Lampson understood building systems and was one of the original people at Xerox PARC who built distributed personal computing.
followups.speaker: Leslie Lamport

blocks.speaker: Leslie Lamport

blocks.question: What did Lamport think of the Raft paper, which seems to solve the same problem as Paxos?
answer: Lamport says the Raft authors sent him a draft, and he replied to send it back with either an algorithm or a proof, though he does not recall which. He says he never read the later versions. Someone whose judgment he values read them and said Raft was basically the Paxos paper, with some of Paxos's unfinished tales filled in and described differently.

Lamport explains Paxos in two phases. The first phase elects a leader, and it can be done once for a whole run of decisions, as long as the leader stays the same. The second phase repeats for each decision. Engineers usually describe it in the opposite order, repeating the second phase until the leader fails. Starting fresh, Lamport says, the first phase's work could be built into the initial state.

followups.question: Is Raft easier to understand than Paxos?
answer: Lamport says many people find Paxos hard, and he does not see why. He has explained it to some people in five minutes. The Raft authors taught Paxos to one class and Raft to another, and students found Raft easier. Lamport says a bug was later found and fixed in Raft, and he believes the version students found easier was the one with the bug.

For Lamport, understanding means being able to write a proof. For most people, he says, it is a warm, fuzzy feeling, and Raft gave them more of that feeling because it follows the order programmers already think in.
followups.speaker: Leslie Lamport

blocks.speaker: Leslie Lamport

blocks.question: What is the story behind LaTeX?
answer: Lamport says he was starting to write a book, and TeX was the basic typesetting system he had to use. He needed macros to make TeX do what he wanted, and he figured a little extra effort could make them usable by others. Before TeX he had used Scribe, which let authors describe a document's logical structure and left formatting to the system. Scribe did not format well, but Lamport liked the idea that the ideas matter more than the typesetting.

followups.question: How did the book with Addison-Wesley come about?
answer: Lamport says Peter Gordon, an Addison-Wesley editor, convinced him to write a book. At the time, Lamport did not expect people would pay for a book about software. The publisher introduced him to a typographic designer whose work became the typography of the standard LaTeX styles. Lamport says he did most of the work in his spare time, over six to nine months.
followups.speaker: Leslie Lamport

blocks.speaker: Leslie Lamport

blocks.question: What did Lamport mean by 'thinking without writing'?
answer: Lamport says the remark was meant for people building computer systems. Write a description of an idea before trusting it. He recalls a maxim to write the instruction manual before the program. He did not follow that advice with LaTeX, but while writing the book he found some things hard to explain and changed them.

followups.question: Why is writing good for thinking?
answer: Lamport says it is easy to fool yourself. When his algorithms grew complicated, his usual proof style broke down, because too many details had to be tracked. He devised a hierarchical proof, a sequence of steps where each step has its own proof, which can be a paragraph or a further sequence of steps. A step that does not follow from the stated steps shows the proof is wrong, even if the theorem is true.

When he presented this to roughly 20 mathematicians in a small seminar, their reaction was angry, and he thought they might physically attack him. He believes the fear was that they would have to write proofs for a computer, though he says the method needs only organization, not formalism. Writing a proof exposes steps the author left unstated. Lamport says thinking you know something you have not written down only feels like knowing it, and that is where errors enter.
followups.speaker: Leslie Lamport

blocks.speaker: Leslie Lamport

blocks.question: Why did Lamport's career stay in industry rather than academia?
answer: Lamport says he started out programming and took jobs that led him into what is now called computer science. He did not realize until the mid-to-late 1970s that computer science was a field in its own right. At one point he had to choose between computer science and teaching math at a university. He chose computer science for fairly random reasons. Until about the mid-1980s he did not think computer science was something people needed a university to learn, and he did not think teaching it would be fun.
blocks.speaker: Leslie Lamport

blocks.question: Did Lamport feel like a failure for not finding a grand theory of concurrency?
answer: Lamport says many people doing this work looked for a Turing machine of concurrency, an abstraction that would capture concurrent computing. Nobody has found one, though some think they have. Petri nets were a big topic in the 1970s, and a community still works on them, but they were language-based, and Lamport was never interested in languages.

He now thinks the Turing machine of concurrency is the state machine, described only by a state and a next-state relation, with no commands. A Turing machine describes what is possible. A state machine can also describe things that are not possible.

followups.question: Why are infinite values useful in state machines?
answer: Lamport says that when he describes an algorithm, he lets a variable take any integer, although a real program would use bounded integers. People often assume that because something is infinite, it is more complicated. Lamport says they have it backwards: infinity simplifies arithmetic, which is far messier on a finite set of integers. He says mathematics is the most powerful way to describe a state machine.
followups.speaker: Leslie Lamport

followups.question: Why are programming languages the wrong tool for concurrency?
answer: Lamport says many programmers and computer scientists are hung up on languages, and they keep inventing new ones. A semantics for any of them would be given in terms of a state machine. Code has real advantages, mainly efficiency. For understanding, though, Lamport says you cannot beat mathematics, and language-based attempts to reason about concurrency are the wrong approach.
followups.speaker: Leslie Lamport

blocks.speaker: Leslie Lamport

blocks.question: How can someone who does not consider himself smart achieve so much?
answer: Lamport says psychologists have observed that people who are good at something often do not notice it, because it seems simple to them. The reverse also holds: people who are bad at something tend to overrate themselves. He says the gift he has is not raw intelligence but abstraction. He realized only in the last ten or so years how much better he is at abstraction than most people.
blocks.speaker: Leslie Lamport

blocks.question: Looking back, what would Lamport tell himself just after college?
answer: Lamport says he learned early not to waste time on questions he does not have to answer. He does not dwell on what he should have done, because that is a question he does not have to answer.
blocks.speaker: Leslie Lamport
