parts.title: Engineering in the AI era
parts.introduction: The guests disagree about speed, autonomy, and the future of programming. Their distinct arguments remain separate, with the assumptions and conditions that make each useful to examine.

sections.title: AI adoption should move with demonstrated capability
sections.deck: Casey Muratori frames his concern about generated software as a race between tool reliability and uncritical deployment.

blocks.question: Was your warning that “vibecoding” could make software worse an accurate prediction?
answer: Muratori immediately qualifies the warning: the bad outcome depends on a pattern that may not become dominant. His concern is people describing a desired product, generating it, and sending it into production without competent review. He distinguishes that from a trained engineer using AI while understanding and checking its output.

The resulting risk depends on two moving forces. One is how quickly AI becomes capable of making better decisions autonomously; the other is how widely it is adopted, by whom, and with how much scrutiny. If capabilities stay adequate for the uses people adopt, he would not expect a major deterioration. If adoption outruns the tools and the users’ ability to judge them, he expects trouble.

He explicitly says he does not know where the situation will be a year later. Although he is personally skeptical of AI, he hopes the tools improve because many people are already using them. In his account, freezing their capability at the current level would leave existing adoption in a worse position. These are conditional judgments in the interview, not a forecast supplied by this book.
blocks.speaker: Casey Muratori

blocks.question: Is your criticism of corporate AI mandates that they push adoption ahead of capability?
answer: Muratori says the joke about Shopify was partly a pun, but his substantive concern is organizational fear of being late. He thinks some companies act as if immediate adoption is compulsory before they have established whether the tools solve their actual problems or improve outcomes.

His proposed alternative is familiar technology evaluation: measure what a tool can do, test it against the organization’s problems, compare the workflow with the previous approach, and adopt when it demonstrates a net benefit. Dedicated teams can run aggressive experiments; that does not mean every team should be required to consume large amounts of AI capacity.

He ends by resisting a comforting story about the past. Software quality was already poor before the AI era, he says. AI can make particular things worse without being responsible for the industry’s preexisting failures. The criticism is therefore about how to improve the quality of the work, not about preserving an idealized earlier industry.
blocks.speaker: Casey Muratori

blocks.title: The two questions in Muratori’s argument
rows: Can the tool reliably perform this work?
Is it being used for tasks beyond that capability?
Can it make appropriate decisions without intervention?
Who reviews the output, and how much do they understand?
Has the workflow produced a measured benefit?
Is adoption being required before that benefit is known?

sections.title: The percentage of code generated is less useful than the work humans still own
sections.deck: Anders Hejlsberg distinguishes growing code volume from the responsibility to understand a real system.

blocks.question: Will AI soon write more than 90 percent of code?
answer: Hejlsberg asks what the percentage measures. Some generated applications already consist entirely of AI-written code, and generation itself greatly increases the total volume. A large share of that expanding denominator is different from a large share of high-quality, novel software. He is skeptical of treating those claims as equivalent.
He expects AI to do impressive things, but does not assume that increasing success on familiar patterns establishes that it can perform every kind of engineering work.

followups.question: What is an example of code that does not fit the optimistic claim?
answer: He says his team tried using AI for their TypeScript compiler work and found it unable to reproduce that particular implementation. His explanation is that the unusual concepts and structure are not a typical match for learned patterns. He treats this as a limitation of the tools he tested, while acknowledging that they are improving. It is not a timeless claim about every future model or compiler.
followups.speaker: Anders Hejlsberg

blocks.speaker: Anders Hejlsberg

blocks.question: Could engineers stop reading the code or using an IDE?
answer: Hejlsberg worries about the point where prompting no longer fixes a bug or implements the next feature. Someone must then understand the system underneath. He also emphasizes responsibility for the application’s effects: the person or organization deploying it cannot treat AI as a substitute for understanding what they are vouching for. His hypothetical harm example illustrates that responsibility; it is not a legal determination made by this book.

followups.question: Why does your view differ from the more sweeping claims made by some AI developers?
answer: He distinguishes admiration for AI from extrapolating its contribution to complete human irrelevance. Even if generation handles a larger percentage of code, people still need to connect the system to the business problem and the organization around it. That larger context is what a simple generation percentage leaves out.
followups.speaker: Anders Hejlsberg

blocks.speaker: Anders Hejlsberg

blocks.question: Will AI replace junior engineering work?
answer: He questions how senior engineers would be developed if junior participation disappeared entirely. He thinks the entry-level pyramid may narrow for some work and people may be expected to move toward supervision more quickly. The craft can shift from typing code toward reviewing agents’ work, but he still sees programmers as part of the process. These are his expectations in the interview rather than a current employment forecast.
blocks.speaker: Anders Hejlsberg

blocks.question: Would a future with less manual coding make the work less enjoyable for you?
answer: Hejlsberg still enjoys writing code after decades of doing it, but is happy to delegate parts he finds tedious, including testing-framework boilerplate. Reviewing other people’s code has often felt harder to him than writing his own. He hopes tools can make review more understandable and ergonomic by explaining changes rather than merely displaying file lists and diffs. The transition can change the craft without making every part equally attractive to every programmer.
blocks.speaker: Anders Hejlsberg

sections.title: Use types and capabilities to make delegated work inspectable
sections.deck: Martin Odersky argues that generated implementation needs concise contracts and explicit limits on authority.

blocks.question: How might AI-generated code change programming-language design?
answer: Odersky sees a control problem: a human asked to review a mountain of generated implementation can lose a practical understanding of what the system will do. He also worries about tools that can discover or exploit vulnerabilities. Programming languages are only part of the response, but he believes they can make the critical guarantees easier to inspect.

He expects attention to shift toward interfaces, types, requirements, and higher-level specifications. A precise type or interface can become a contract between a human and the code-generating system—something concise enough to review and strong enough to constrain the implementation. In his view, this requires closing escape hatches that undermine the claimed guarantees, rather than merely adding advisory annotations.

He also proposes capabilities: explicit, fine-grained authority over resources and effects. An agent should be given the particular read, write, or secret-access permissions it needs, so there are meaningful things it cannot do. He treats memory safety as a necessary starting point, while emphasizing that control over files, data, and secrets involves more than memory alone.

Odersky says Scala work in this direction was available experimentally in the context of the interview. He does not present it as a completed universal solution. He also hopes AI could help migrate existing software when the target design is clear. That is a proposed path toward safer systems, not evidence that a wholesale migration has already happened.

followups.question: What would a capability guarantee look like in practice?
answer: He gives a file-lifetime example. A program receives access to a file for a limited scope and should not keep using it after returning control to the environment. Without a constraint, it might save the file in a variable or hide access inside a returned closure or stream.

In the type-system approach he describes, a value that retains access to the file must expose that capability in its type. The environment can then require a returned type that holds no such capability. This makes retained access visible and gives the system a way to reject an escape. He relates the idea to ensuring that pointers do not outlive an arena and to controlling which secrets a component can access: the recurring question is what authority can remain beyond an allowed scope.
followups.speaker: Martin Odersky

blocks.speaker: Martin Odersky

blocks.title: A contract for delegated implementation

steps.title: Specify the task
steps.text: State the requirements and interface.

steps.title: Limit the authority
steps.text: Give access only to defined resources and effects.

steps.title: Expose retained access
steps.text: Make capabilities visible in the values and types.

steps.title: Check the boundary
steps.text: Reject capabilities that escape the permitted scope.

blocks.caption: Arrows show an editorial arrangement of Odersky’s proposed control model. The discussion describes a direction and experimental work, not a guarantee for every existing agent system.

sections.title: Fast tools, cheap drafts, and expensive review
sections.deck: Charlie Marsh describes building Ruff, uv, and ty, then examines how agent use changes optimization, open-source participation, review, and the experience of founding Astral.

blocks.question: Why did you think Python developer tools could be better?
answer: At a computational-biology company, Marsh was a software engineer serving scientists and machine-learning researchers. A small team needed leverage from type checking, linting, and package management as its code grew. Working across Python, Go, Rust, and web tools exposed a contrast: native JavaScript tooling was experimenting aggressively with performance, while much Python tooling remained implemented in Python. Ruff began as a concrete test of the hypothesis that Python tools could become much faster.

followups.question: Did the proof of concept take only the nine days between two blog posts?
answer: He had not noticed the dates were so close. After writing about type checking at scale, he chose a linter as the smaller experiment. A small core plus a useful subset of rules can deliver value immediately and grow iteratively alongside existing tools. A partly complete type checker or package manager is harder to make useful, although he explicitly qualifies that generalization. He wanted users to receive value quickly and establish a feedback loop.

blocks.question: How was the first public release received?
answer: Hacker News and social attention brought initial users, but he sees that exposure as partly luck and neither necessary nor sufficient for success. He responded aggressively to issues, aiming to acknowledge, fix, and release within a day. When an influential potential user expressed interest, he asked what was needed for adoption and worked through those requirements.

He also takes developer marketing seriously. Excellent technical work can remain undiscovered if its purpose is unclear. A landing page, README, or article may have only seconds to convey why someone should care. He wants a skimmer to understand the main result without requiring the whole article, while still making every sentence accurate for the readers who do study it.

followups.question: What was the concrete hook for Ruff?
answer: A benchmark graph made the performance difference visible, paired with a simple compatibility-and-speed promise. He notes that benchmarks are imperfect; the hook should communicate a real advantage quickly rather than substitute attention for truth.

followups.question: How do you balance a provocative headline with honesty?
answer: He opposes misleading clickbait. The aim is communicating the most interesting true parts effectively. Lying can attract attention but destroys the basis for a useful relationship with users.

followups.question: What about charts with a truncated axis?
answer: He rejects deceptive chart presentation and then emphasizes the real benchmark difficulty: caches, project selection, and unrelated native builds can change the observed result. No single graph captures every situation. That does not remove the obligation to give users an honest sense of performance; he admits his own team may sometimes get the balance wrong.

blocks.question: Why choose Rust?
answer: Initially, he candidly says, enthusiasm around Rust influenced him more than a sophisticated tradeoff analysis. In retrospect the choice suited the tools very well. Cargo’s common build, run, and test workflow reduced the barrier to entering unfamiliar projects. As a new systems programmer he could focus on meaningful language and implementation challenges rather than assembling a toolchain. He now also values safety and efficient execution, and expects Rust to grow, while recognizing useful ideas in Zig and successful work in Go.

followups.question: Would you start a new project in C or C++?
answer: Personally he usually would not unless an existing system, a specific technical need, or deep team familiarity justified it. He expects others to disagree and frames this as his preference. Rust’s memory safety has become more valuable to him than he understood at the beginning. The answer is not a claim that every project can ignore ecosystem constraints.

blocks.question: Would AI make it worthwhile to rewrite your tools in another language?
answer: He sees the rate of change in agent workflows as extraordinary: his own work shifted from editor-based changes toward prompting through Codex in a short period. He is interested in other teams testing large automated rewrites but would not currently plan one for Astral’s major tools.

Understanding the transformed code is one concern. Another is exchanging known problems for unknown ones. Even a good test suite approximates behavior, and users may rely on implementation details that were never formalized as an API. Passing tests can therefore push undiscovered incompatibilities onto users. For him, safe rollout and the responsibility to those users are more troubling than the models’ ability to produce a plausible translation.

His acceptable level of review varies by project. He describes an internal custom linter generated without reading all its code, where users are only his team and incorrect output is easy to notice. A widely used package manager deserves a different standard. He sees experimentation as valuable while remaining uncertain how much code understanding future agent-based work will require.

followups.question: Is that simply the usual balance between change risk and verification?
answer: The spectrum is familiar, but agents create an additional extreme where no human needed to read the code even to produce it. He observes repositories where both contributions and conversations appear agent-written and is glad people are testing new models of work, while not feeling ready to copy every approach.

blocks.question: Do you block fully agent-generated contributions?
answer: The projects have an AI policy intended to keep useful human contributions while filtering interactions that create more work than value. The team itself uses LLMs heavily. What matters is that a submitter understands what is being contributed and supplies insight, an actual reproducer, or information the maintainers can use. Pasting a generated answer to each maintainer question provides little value when maintainers can query a model themselves.

followups.question: How can you enforce understanding?
answer: He admits detection is imperfect. Excessive detail, gratuitous formatting, unnecessary links, or invented jargon can be clues, but undetectable useful material would not be excluded solely because a model helped. More deeply, open source historically invested in people whose learning compounded through feedback. If comments merely pass from maintainer to contributor’s agent, that human development may not occur. Cheap plausible PRs can impose long review sessions on technically difficult projects such as ty. He does not yet have a complete solution.

blocks.question: Was the large rewrite discussed earlier reviewed by humans?
answer: He does not think humans read significant portions, but explicitly bases that on his impression. He expects a forthcoming explanation of a phased process with validation steps, rather than assume it was one prompt. Those unverified impressions are recorded as such; the section does not declare the other project’s actual review practices.

followups.question: Would you block a teammate’s rewrite even if the target language were agreed to be better?
answer: At present, yes. His team still values deeply understanding its code, toolchain, and ecosystem. He acknowledges that his judgment could change and that the project’s consequences matter.

blocks.question: How much of the speed improvement came from Rust?
answer: For early Ruff, changing implementation language was a large part. But multiple Rust designs can have very different performance, and subsequent improvements still matter. In uv, architecture contributes more because package management is dominated by network and filesystem work. An intentionally designed cache makes repeated installation cheap in time and storage. Native implementation supplies a useful baseline; algorithms, representations, I/O, and cache design determine much of the result. Python programs also benefit from better design.

blocks.question: Which technical work has been especially interesting?
answer: He highlights a version representation designed by a teammate known as BurntSushi. Resolving Python projects creates and parses many version values; representing most common cases in one 64-bit integer reduced allocation and memory costs. He admires the implementation and measured results.

For ty, the larger architectural challenge is lazy, incremental analysis. Opening a file should not require checking the whole project, and editing it should recompute only dependent results. The system is built around queries using Salsa, also used by rust-analyzer. This requires accurate dependency tracking rather than merely making an individual checker faster.

followups.question: What is hard about incrementality?
answer: Changes have to flow through exactly the affected parts of the dependency graph. Large-project language servers must also manage memory, not just latency. He has used Codex to search for small improvements under constrained goals, as well as broader fixes for pathological cases. He enjoys being able to keep running such optimization experiments without calling the process autonomously self-optimizing.

blocks.question: Could an agent invent the compact version representation?
answer: Possibly with collaboration, but he would not expect that from a generic request for a moderate improvement. In his experience, models first make local changes around existing representations. A human can steer from profiling to allocation cost to asking whether the representation itself should change.

He retells another engineer’s example where a model greatly improved a deliberately poor renderer but still fell far short of a better first-principles design. The numerical anecdote is not an independently demonstrated benchmark here. His lesson is to ask how fast the system ought to be, rather than accept a large percentage gain from a bad starting point.

followups.question: Why encourage your team to use agents despite those limits?
answer: They build tools for engineers increasingly working with agents, so firsthand understanding of that experience matters. He believes he ships more, but teammates now scrutinize his PRs more closely because confidence in his handwritten work does not automatically transfer to generated work. He agrees with that feedback and has sometimes reread yesterday’s PR with disappointment. Agent use can lower the standard without its author noticing.

blocks.question: What helps prevent plausible but substandard generated changes?
answer: He wants more of the meaningful verification to be automated, while acknowledging that green checks do not yet make review unnecessary. ty runs performance and memory measurements and before-and-after diagnostics across ecosystem projects. These tools were needed even before agents, and now help assess the larger flow of changes.

Authors are expected to run agent review, maintain instructions and shared skills based on recurring errors, understand each changed line, and reread their own PR in the review interface. One recurring question was what an if-condition still protects when every test passes without it; he added a pass to look for obsolete conditions left after refactoring. These are practices being refined, not a guarantee against all unnecessary branches.

His initial fear was becoming more productive while losing the pleasure of programming. He feels better as tools improve and he discovers cheap experiments. An agent could move uv’s many test snapshots out of source files while he worked elsewhere. It did not provide the hoped-for general compile-speed benefit, but made snapshot-only iteration avoid recompilation. The value was answering a costly question quickly; production adoption still required work. Design thinking and fixing users’ problems remain sources of satisfaction beyond typing code.

blocks.question: How important is engineering experience when using agents?
answer: He remains concerned about using the tools without substantial experience. The strongest engineers on his team are also effective at directing agents and correcting them. Some highly productive people use many tokens, but he explicitly does not infer causation or reward token consumption: such leaderboards can create bad incentives. Early-career learning is a difficult open question because a beginner may learn from an unreliable agent rather than supply the expertise that keeps it on track. His team is small and senior, so he acknowledges limited firsthand evidence about junior training.

blocks.question: Why turn Ruff into a company, and how did fundraising begin?
answer: He left his previous job after a friend suggested founding together, initially explored overlapping ideas, and found himself spending spare time on developer tools that did not fit the friend’s interests. He started investor relationships before intending to raise, expecting to return months later with a clearer plan. Ruff’s growth and those conversations convinced him a company could exist sooner.

Potential investors helped articulate a roadmap and offered a psychologically useful exit: if he hated founding, he could stop and return the money. He doubts he would have done so but found the reduced pressure helpful. Starting felt less stressful than success later, when a team depended on him. He describes the process as unusually collaborative and fortunate, not a standard fundraising formula.

followups.question: Why did you not announce later funding rounds?
answer: He kept finding reasons to wait and did not consider the announcement the most important work while products and the business progressed. The planned announcement was overtaken by the acquisition described in this interview. He says the seed, Series A, and Series B were initiated by investors rather than active campaigns.

followups.question: Did willingness to walk away give negotiating leverage?
answer: He agrees that he had a strong position while declining to portray himself as an expert negotiator. He emphasizes aligned, supportive investors and little pressure beyond suggestions to grow more aggressively. That positive experience was fortunate; he recognizes other founders can have different relationships.

blocks.question: How does a company make money while its tools are free?
answer: Astral launched a commercial private Python registry, described as a hosted counterpart to uv. Private artifacts and enterprise requirements created needs adjacent to the free tools. Integrating client and server helped address issues and improve speed. Existing open-source adoption supplied a funnel to a small set of high-quality customers. The plan was free tools plus paid complementary platform services, rather than charging for the tools themselves. In the acquisition context he hopes to release some platform work more widely, including prebuilt compatible packages for difficult GPU/PyTorch environments. These are his business history and intended next steps, not a verified present availability claim.

blocks.question: What surprised you as an engineer becoming a first-time founder?
answer: He distrusts universal startup advice because successful founders can give contradictory instructions and survivorship bias hides alternatives. Choose principles suited to the team and the life you want. Remote work let him hire a team he could not have assembled in one location, despite real benefits of meeting in person. Fundraising optimized for trustworthy partners, reasonable terms, and getting back to work. He did not force a cofounder relationship merely because it was recommended, though he later felt the absence of a peer sharing the burden.

followups.question: How did you compensate for founding alone?
answer: He leaned on his wife, consulted the early team, and built relationships with other founders. Each source of support has limits, including how much to place on family or employees. He also chose to work extensively himself without requiring everyone to do so: he wanted people to succeed during normal hours and be rewarded for useful performance. His advice is to make the actual culture honest and deliberate, rather than imitate a fashionable schedule.

blocks.question: What book or learning resource influenced you?
answer: He does not read much technical material and instead names a talk by Zig creator Andrew Kelley on data-oriented design. It changed how he looked at memory, allocation, and compiler design early in his systems-programming experience. He qualifies that his recollection is imperfect; the section preserves the influence without inventing the talk’s exact title or reproducing an unseen argument.

blocks.question: What advice would you give yourself after graduation?
answer: Trust decisions made for sound personal reasons, while remaining aware that hindsight can make a lucky path look inevitable. He worried that choosing Khan Academy cost him big-company experience and compensation; he now values the experience he actually wanted. He would not pretend to know how the alternative would have gone.

followups.question: Could the broader ecosystem exposure have been essential?
answer: He agrees and adds his earlier startup experience. That company did not achieve all its ambitious drug-discovery goals, which briefly made him question the years invested. Being an early employee taught him both how a company develops and technical lessons later used at Astral. In retrospect the experiences connected to building tools he loves. He recognizes that this reassuring account comes from a path that worked well, rather than proving every disappointment will produce the same payoff.

blocks.title: A contribution creates two kinds of cost

steps.title: Produce a plausible change
steps.text: Agents can reduce drafting time dramatically.

steps.title: Establish meaning and behavior
steps.text: The author supplies understanding, reproduction, and design judgment.

steps.title: Measure and review
steps.text: Benchmarks, ecosystem tests, and reviewers assess the actual consequences.

steps.title: Learn from the result
steps.text: Improve instructions and human judgment, rather than merely forward comments to an agent.

blocks.caption: Editorial synthesis of Marsh’s contributor-policy and team-practice discussions. Fast drafting does not establish cheap verification.

sections.title: Judea Pearl: Early AI, Causal Reasoning, and the Limits of LLMs
sections.deck: Judea Pearl traces the path from superconducting memory and early AI to causal reasoning, and argues that LLMs cannot reach causal understanding on their own.

blocks.text: In Pearl's view, causal reasoning needs explicit assumptions and a new algebra that probability alone cannot supply. Pearl traces the route from early computer-memory research and superconducting films to Bayesian networks, and then to a formal calculus of cause and effect. Pearl argues that LLMs draw on human-written summaries of causal knowledge rather than on raw data, so they cannot reach causal understanding on their own. Pearl says general intelligence would need causal AI that can intervene and reason counterfactually, and describes academia as dogmatic and slow to change.
blocks.heading: Pearl's view: causal reasoning needs assumptions that probability cannot supply

blocks.question: Electrical engineering and physics seem far from causal reasoning and AI. How did you get there?
answer: Pearl grew up in the years before 1948, when high school teachers included academics who had fled Germany in the 1930s. Pearl says they taught science as a human story: who discovered what, when, and what the inventor did not know.

Pearl says students came away believing each of them could find a new proof of the Pythagorean theorem. Pearl calls that a useful illusion. It made the class assertive, and students made noise until a teacher slowed down to explain.

followups.question: What is the advantage of learning science that way?
answer: Pearl says it makes the student an actor in science rather than a passive observer. The student is puzzled too, and can follow the route the original discoverer took.

As a child, Pearl insisted that a square kilometer holds 1,000 dunams, while the class said a dunam was a square kilometer. The teacher later apologized to the class. Pearl took from it that insisting on one's own understanding is worth it, and links that stubbornness to the path into AI.
followups.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.question: What interested you in physics, and what made you passionate about it?
answer: Pearl says physics lets a person predict results while sitting in a chair. Pearl admires Maxwell, who reasoned from a wave equation that the wave's speed matched light, and suggested light is an electromagnetic wave, without an experiment.
Pearl recalls waking one night convinced Maxwell was wrong, and being calmed by Pearl's wife. The next morning Pearl agreed Maxwell was right.

followups.question: Do you have a favorite scientist of all time, and why?
answer: Pearl says analytic geometry produced an almost physical excitement. Every geometric construction could be carried out in algebra, and Pearl found that transformation enormous.
Pearl found the same thrill in physics, where two languages describe one phenomenon from different perspectives, as with a field and a force.
followups.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.question: What was your early work on computer memory like?
answer: Pearl worked mornings at RCA's laboratory in Princeton, New Jersey, while studying at Brooklyn Poly. Core memories were slow and clumsy, so Pearl's group aimed for superconducting memories and built 16-by-16-bit plates.

While studying persistent currents in thin superconducting films, Pearl found a new effect, now called the Pearl vortex. A current in such a film circulates indefinitely and can be read by flipping it, which makes a memory. The group never made it competitive with semiconductors.

followups.question: Why did you not believe in the semiconductor direction at the time?
answer: Pearl says the team doubted that a memory could be trusted to a battery, and was not impressed by early semiconductor results. The semiconductor groups beat the team.
Pearl adds that even then, researchers widely believed computers would one day emulate all human functions. For Pearl, the question was how and when, not whether.
followups.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.question: What did researchers expect about the timeline for human-level machine intelligence back then?
answer: Pearl recalls early work on associative memory and pattern recognition, which excited researchers even on room-sized machines that ran on punch cards. Pearl says people were more optimistic than reality.
Pearl recalls a forecast in 1965 of about twenty years, which would have meant around 1985. Pearl says the field had not got anywhere close by then.

followups.question: Are people more optimistic than reality today, or is this history repeating?
answer: Pearl says it depends on who is asked. Some people are extremely optimistic. Pearl is not doubtful that AGI can be reached eventually, but doubts that LLM methods alone will get there.
Pearl calls LLMs a great surprise that also has clear limitations.
followups.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.question: What made the industry job frustrating, and why did you move to academia?
answer: Pearl says the three years at Electronic Memories were frustrating. Pearl had to handle administrative problems, such as hiring and firing, and technical problems in chemistry, which Pearl did not know well.

Pearl's wife suggested academia. Academia then looked with reverence on people from industry, since major advances came from companies such as Bell Labs. Academia hired Pearl without an application or recommendations, which Pearl says was a good time to be hired.

followups.question: Did Bell Labs disband its research group, and where did the frontier of research move?
answer: Pearl says disbanding was part of it. The frontier of research moved to academia, where inference, logic and expert systems were developed. Pearl was hired at UCLA around 1969 or 1970, first through an engineering systems department and then into computer science.
followups.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.question: How did your work move from computer memory toward AI at UCLA?
answer: At UCLA, Pearl taught computer memory, then moved into pattern recognition and image compression using transforms that send fewer bits. That revived Pearl's old goal of understanding how the brain works and how computers might emulate it.

Pearl began teaching AI, which then meant game playing such as chess, checkers and puzzles like the eight puzzle. Pearl was drawn to chess because it captures what people do heuristically, and the interplay between formal analysis and gut feel about a position. Pearl links this to the fast and slow thinking framing, in which each mode feeds the other.
blocks.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.question: How do fast intuition and slow search interact in a chess program?
answer: Pearl says a program can spend more time on the immediate static evaluation of a position, or search deeper. That is a trade-off. The program searches the game tree to a horizon, evaluates positions there, and backs the values up to choose the strongest move.
Pearl agrees that the intuition sits in the evaluation function.

followups.question: Can the evaluation function itself improve through learning?
answer: Pearl says yes. Samuel's checkers program used regression to set weights for features such as control of the center and material balance. Pearl calls this the first machine learning.
followups.speaker: Judea Pearl

followups.question: Were chess programs already superhuman at that time, and what did you prove about search?
answer: Pearl says no, since beating a champion such as Kasparov by machine was still a dream. Pearl proved that alpha-beta pruning is optimal, in the sense that no method can inspect fewer positions at the search horizon. Pearl then grew tired of search.
followups.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.question: Why did expert systems run into trouble?
answer: Early medical expert systems encoded rules from doctors, such as the questions a doctor asks after seeing a fever. The hurdle was uncertainty, since real evidence is noisy.
Pearl later proved that these systems could not combine uncertainties well, because rules do not combine the way logical assertions do.
blocks.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.question: Why was probability considered impractical, and how did you make it workable?
answer: Pearl says a probability model is a table with a number for every combination of events. Conditional probabilities need exponentially large tables and time, even for a small task such as judging malaria risk from travel and fever. Yet people reason fairly well, so Pearl asked what they rely on.

Pearl's answer is conditional independence: most facts are irrelevant to a given query, such as an uncle's eye color when diagnosing a disease. Bayesian networks encode those independencies in a graph, so relevance can be read from the graph instead of a full table.

Pearl calls the match between conditional independence and graph separation a philosophical revolution. Pearl developed a theory of graphoids with a Technion colleague in the 1970s to capture that shared logic.
blocks.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.question: Where does the graph come from, and is judgment an acceptable source?
answer: Pearl says the input can come from data or from judgment. Judgment is acceptable when it is meaningful, condensed, and something a person is willing to defend. A few such judgments can buy a great deal of computation.
Pearl's example is that the sun does not respond to a rooster's crowing. Pearl says that claim is defensible without an experiment.

followups.question: But what if your intuition is wrong?
answer: Pearl agrees that this is part of the problem. A large language model's output is an average of countless internet judgments, over which it has no control. Pearl says there is wisdom in the crowd, and danger too, so trusted judges should count for more.
Pearl admits being wrong earlier. Pearl was sure probability captured human reasoning and protected against paradoxes, and came to see that this was mistaken. That led to causality.
followups.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.question: What showed you that probability alone was not enough?
answer: Pearl says experts who encoded judgments as Bayesian networks always drew arrows from cause to effect, never the reverse, even when asked for the link between a symptom and a disease. The relation from disease to fever is stable in a way the reverse is not. Pearl calls this invariance.

In car troubleshooting, moving one component, such as a charger, to another spot changes one part of the model while the rest stays intact. That works only in the causal direction, and it led Pearl to think probability was insufficient.
blocks.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.question: Can causation be programmed into a computer?
answer: Pearl says humans handle causation well, but cannot separate their assumptions from their conclusions, since everyone shares the same assumptions. A robot needs them separated. Pearl argues that science has been bound to algebra since Galileo's time, and that the equality sign is symmetric.

That symmetry lets people ask questions both ways, such as how a beam breaks under a load or how to shape a beam for a load. It limits causal reasoning. Atmospheric pressure affects a barometer, not the reverse, yet a symmetric equation could suggest that adjusting the barometer changes the weather. Pearl argues algebra needs a notation for direction.
blocks.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.question: How does the new algebra handle cause and effect, and what is the causal ladder?
answer: Pearl says the assignment operation in computing is not reversible. Putting that logic on top of algebra gives a causal calculus. The ladder has three rungs: association, intervention, and counterfactual explanation. A question on one rung needs assumptions from that rung or a higher one.

Association is ordinary statistics, such as how observed smoking relates to lifespan. Intervention asks what happens when someone is forced to act, which needs experiments or assumptions. Explanation asks what would have happened had the input differed, given what was observed. Pearl adds that even the first rung is hard with finite samples.

followups.question: Where would you place LLMs in this causal hierarchy?
answer: Pearl says LLMs do not look at raw data, such as patient records. They work from text written by doctors and researchers and summarized online, which already holds higher-rung information, so they do not break the ladder. Their answers carry the assumptions of those authors, and how LLMs summarize that material is a mystery no one has decoded.
followups.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.question: Could this approach lead to superhuman intelligence or AGI?
answer: Pearl does not think so, not with this approach. A system would need an understanding of causality, so that it could learn without access to the internet. Pearl points to babies, who are born curious about controlling their environment. A baby plays with toys until it learns which ones make noise, and the restlessness settles once it understands cause and effect.

followups.question: What if we built a baby robot that plays with toys, gathers data and feeds it into LLMs?
answer: Pearl says that could produce some discovery, but it carries danger. A robot with that craving for control would treat people as part of its environment, and could turn them into pets or tools to satisfy its need.

Pearl compares human curiosity with that of monkeys, which are motivated by rewards such as bananas. Pearl says the wider need to feel in control shows in beliefs that sacrifices or better dinners can control outcomes.
followups.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.question: Do systems need human-like drives, such as a need for control, to reach AGI?
answer: Pearl thinks so. Without such drives, autonomy would not appear, and autonomy is part of general intelligence. A text-only system might pass a Turing-style test, but Pearl says a real test should expose the system to raw data, not to internet articles.

Pearl describes an automated scientist that examines patient and smoking data and proposes experiments. Pearl thinks today's LLMs cannot do that without internet articles. AGI would combine LLM-style estimation from finite samples with causal AI that adds intervention and counterfactual reasoning.

followups.question: What if a fleet of robots ran experiments, fed the data back into an LLM and repeated the cycle?
answer: Pearl says that could help, but Pearl first wants to know how humans achieved this. Monkeys never invented Maxwell's equations. Pearl's hypothesis is that innate curiosity to control the environment is necessary, though Pearl is not sure it is sufficient.
followups.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.question: Do the major AI companies really believe LLMs will lead to AGI?
answer: Pearl is not sure they do. Pearl says Hinton recently said the current approach is a dead end, and that there is no consensus on LLM capabilities. Pearl says people at some labs, perhaps Anthropic, expect results within three to five years.

Pearl criticizes anthropomorphic claims, such as that consciousness can now be programmed. Pearl says such claims need a definition of consciousness, a test, and proof that earlier limits have been overcome.
blocks.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.question: If an LLM fakes intelligence convincingly, should we treat it as intelligent?
answer: Pearl says it depends on the test and the definition. Playing good chess already meets one definition. Under a stricter standard, Pearl says the Turing test has not yet been passed.

Pearl says faking is having it, because correct answers to causal queries would need memory that grows super-exponentially with the number of variables. LLMs skip that cost by drawing on text that people have written.

followups.question: So the intelligence came from training data that intelligent people wrote?
answer: Pearl agrees that this training data is very useful. Pearl says the first rung, estimating properties of a distribution from finite samples, is a very useful tool among the many that AGI would need.
followups.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.question: Why study how people think rather than how machines might think differently?
answer: Pearl says self-understanding is the main motive, and Pearl admits to being egotistic and lazy. Pearl raises the possibility that organic material limits human thought in ways silicon does not, and sees little reason to study biology, since silicon can capture most functions.
Pearl calls it a legitimate scientific question that others can pursue, and says Pearl is more interested in other questions.
blocks.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.question: Why is rebelliousness valuable in a scientific career?
answer: Pearl says the academic community is among the most dogmatic, conservative and anti-progress institutions humans have invented. Cause-and-effect theory has struggled to reach statistics and economics, which Pearl sees as thinking like a century ago, and Pearl is disappointed by the forces of inertia there.

Pearl advises students to rebel against professors and not accept a professor's word as authority. Pearl recalls students who said Pearl knew nothing about AI, and Pearl later agreed that this pushed Pearl to study other aspects of the field.

Pearl says Pearl's own early work was dismissed as controversial because of dogmatism. Even very able statisticians, economists and philosophers, Pearl says, were held back by a few basic molds in their thinking.
blocks.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.question: If you could give your younger self advice at the start of your career, what would you say?
answer: Pearl says Pearl might have learned more chemistry, but hated its memory demands. Every researcher must decide where to spend computational resources, and Pearl chose physics, engineering and mathematics over chemistry. Pearl admires people who master several fields.

followups.question: Did you think physics and math were superior to chemistry because chemistry just requires memorization?
answer: Pearl says yes, and that Pearl could not stand the memory demands. Physics and mathematics rest on a few basic axioms from which everything can be derived when needed. That is why Pearl is a strong advocate of world models, which derive answers instead of storing every question and answer.
followups.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.speaker: Judea Pearl

sections.title: Leonardo de Moura: Lean, Formal Proofs, and the Future of Verified Software
sections.deck: De Moura explains how Lean checks proofs, why AI may make verification practical, and why hybrid human and AI work is expected rather than an end to handwritten math.

blocks.text: De Moura argues that Lean is both a programming language and a platform for machine-checked proofs. Tests can show that bugs are present but not that they are absent, while a proof can cover every case. AI now writes and maintains many proofs, so verification becomes practical and people focus on specifications. The view expects hybrid workflows, in which people still write some proofs and set the goals, rather than an end to human work.
blocks.heading: De Moura's view: AI makes machine-checked proofs practical, and people still write the specifications

blocks.question: What is Lean, and how can it show that a program has no bugs when testing cannot?
answer: De Moura describes Lean as a programming language and a platform. Users write code, state properties of that code, and prove them. The proofs are machine-checkable, and independent checkers can verify them. The host frames this with Dijkstra's remark that testing shows the presence of bugs, not their absence.

followups.question: How does Lean connect to software written in other languages?
answer: De Moura separates two cases. Lean programs can be reasoned about directly, much like mathematical definitions. For other languages there are two routes. Shallow embedding translates a program into Lean, and a tool that maps Rust into Lean already exists. Deep embedding writes the other language's semantics in Lean, so a C program becomes a Lean data structure that can be reasoned about.
followups.speaker: Leonardo de Moura

followups.question: What is a step-by-step example of proving a property of a C program?
answer: The example is an array access. The index must stay between zero and the array size, which can be written as a mathematical statement. Users would build automation, and triples state what must hold before and after a statement. The proof works like metadata on the C code, checked line by line. Proofs must stay modular to scale.
followups.speaker: Leonardo de Moura

blocks.speaker: Leonardo de Moura

blocks.question: Is the proof a second software layer on top of the code, and could the process run in reverse?
answer: De Moura agrees that the proof works as a second layer, which must stay clean and easy to edit. The reverse is also possible: a person writes what they want mathematically, and AI synthesizes code that is checked against that specification.

The guest cites a colleague, Kim Morrison, who asked AI to translate zlib, a C compression library, into Lean, pass its test suite, and prove that decompression restores the original data. The project succeeded in about a week, according to the guest, and the optimized version still kept its proofs. The guest calls it surreal, since six months earlier it would have seemed like science fiction.

followups.question: Is a specification even better than a comprehensive test suite?
answer: De Moura says yes. Tests show the presence of bugs, while a proof covers all possible cases, including corner cases a test suite may miss. Property-based testing is popular, and people who write properties can now prove them rather than only test them.
followups.speaker: Leonardo de Moura

blocks.speaker: Leonardo de Moura

blocks.question: How much more work is a good specification than a good test suite?
answer: De Moura says the effort varies. Developers often know the properties they care about, even when the full specification is unclear. A simple, inefficient program can serve as the specification. That is easier to write than a clever optimized version, and AI can produce the optimized version and prove that it matches the naive one. Specifications are not always easy to find.
blocks.speaker: Leonardo de Moura

blocks.question: Jane Street has invested heavily in formal verification. What is the main drawback: how much more time does verified software take to write?
answer: De Moura points to a verified microkernel that was done by hand before AI tools. AWS has used formal verification for about a decade, but only for the most safety-critical components, because it was expensive. Writing the specification is not the most painful part. The main cost is writing proofs by hand and maintaining them as code changes.

De Moura says AI is very good at writing and maintaining proofs. In one example, de Moura asked an AI to rewrite proofs without a feature that was about to change, even though the proofs had been written by someone else and de Moura did not know what they covered. The AI produced new proofs. This is crucial for making formal verification mainstream.
blocks.speaker: Leonardo de Moura

blocks.question: You describe Lean as a proof assistant. Is it typical for one to also be a programming language?
answer: De Moura says some proof assistants, especially those based on dependent type theory, are programming languages too. Definitions can be programs with types and structures. Lean is close to Haskell, a functional language, with support for proofs.

followups.question: Are there major uses of Lean as a programming language, without the proofs?
answer: Yes. Much of Lean's own tooling is written in Lean, including the Lake build system and a documentation authoring system. At AWS, a compiler for AI accelerators, about half a million lines of Lean, uses Lean mainly as a programming language. Proofs about its design are a bonus that can expose problems.
followups.speaker: Leonardo de Moura

followups.question: What tooling and proof layers does a proof assistant need?
answer: De Moura says the tooling is familiar. Lake plays the role of Cargo, and editors such as VS Code give completion. The main difference is the InfoView, a panel beside the file that gives constant feedback on code and proofs. Proofs are often written in tactic mode, a domain-specific language in which each step changes the goal shown in the InfoView until no goals remain. Some users treat this as a game.
followups.speaker: Leonardo de Moura

blocks.speaker: Leonardo de Moura

blocks.question: Is Lean itself verified in Lean?
answer: De Moura says Lean is too large and changing too fast to have a full specification, since users keep asking for new behavior. Only the kernel must be trusted. The kernel checks that each proof has the type claimed for it. The default kernel is not verified. Another kernel, written in Lean, has been verified against Lean's semantics. Several independent kernels, including some written in other languages, are the best way to confirm results.
blocks.speaker: Leonardo de Moura

blocks.question: Which Lean results have impressed you most recently?
answer: De Moura cites a gold medal at the International Mathematical Olympiad, which was once thought impossible. Such problems are now used as a benchmark, though de Moura says they are still very hard. De Moura also cites a unit-distance conjecture. An OpenAI proof of it was informal, so Kim Morrison posted a formalization challenge. A one-million-line formal proof followed, which de Moura estimates would take experts months by hand.

followups.question: How long did the formal version take after the challenge?
answer: De Moura recalls about a month from the informal result to a solved challenge, with the formal version completed about two weeks or less after the challenge was posted. These are recollections, not checked dates.
followups.speaker: Leonardo de Moura

blocks.speaker: Leonardo de Moura

blocks.question: How popular is Lean among mathematicians compared with software engineers?
answer: De Moura says Lean first grew with mathematicians, after the Mathlib library began in 2017. A large formalization project begun in early 2020 checked a result from a Fields medalist, which the mathematician had not published and was unsure of. The team used the InfoView to guide them, and they simplified a proof without fully understanding it. De Moura says this drew the math community, since people can trust a formal proof without trusting its author.
A prominent mathematician began using Lean after that project and became absorbed in it.

followups.question: When you say addicted, do you mean the game-like proving?
answer: De Moura says professors report that students split in their views of Lean. People who enjoy problem solving, including International Mathematical Olympiad medalists, tend to love it, because each proof gives a satisfying solve. De Moura describes being a Lean developer rather than a user, and says proving things can be addictive.
followups.speaker: Leonardo de Moura

blocks.speaker: Leonardo de Moura

blocks.question: How is Lean used in the IMO gold-medal work, such as AlphaProof?
answer: De Moura says DeepMind surprised people with a silver medal in 2024. Startups have since earned gold.

followups.question: So the specification is the hard part, and the AI fills in the proof?
answer: Each problem must first be written as a Lean statement, which Mathlib makes easier, since problems use concepts such as real numbers. The proof then has to be supplied. Sometimes the solver must also define an object that has the required properties.
followups.speaker: Leonardo de Moura

followups.question: Can Lean and LLMs generate novel mathematics, or only verify existing results?
answer: De Moura says there is evidence that AI can find novel proofs, but not yet that it can invent new mathematical concepts, which some current challenges require. De Moura expects people to keep investing in this and does not bet against AI, but has not seen evidence yet that AI can come up with new math.
followups.speaker: Leonardo de Moura

blocks.speaker: Leonardo de Moura

blocks.question: When should someone consider formalizing something in Lean?
answer: De Moura says the main cases are when a result is safety-critical or when the author does not understand it well. Formalizing deepens understanding, much as implementing an algorithm does. Proved properties also allow bolder optimizations, since developers no longer need to fear changing code they do not fully understand. AI can prove a property or find a counterexample.

followups.question: If formalization costs fall over three to five years, how does that change software and handwritten math?
answer: De Moura says both would change dramatically. Large labs only recently began training for formal verification, so current results should improve. Costs should fall, and languages such as Lean may become more mainstream. When AI writes most of the code, the level of specification matters more than how the code is written.
followups.speaker: Leonardo de Moura

blocks.speaker: Leonardo de Moura

blocks.question: Could handwritten math or handwritten proofs end within ten years?
answer: De Moura expects some handwritten work to remain. People will still write proofs as artifacts for communication, and others will polish them for human readers. Hybrid workflows are expected, and a workflow with no AI at all would be surprising. Some people find this future uncomfortable, but de Moura finds it exciting, because software development is painful and many steps are repetitive patching that AI removes.

followups.question: Does this future mean fewer mathematicians or computer scientists?
answer: A question raises the worry that fewer mathematicians and computer scientists would be needed. De Moura says AI can bring more people in. Humans stay in the loop, since someone must say what is needed and understand the abstractions. Many people like prototyping but not productization, and AI can take over that part.
followups.speaker: Leonardo de Moura

blocks.speaker: Leonardo de Moura

blocks.question: You worked on the Z3 SMT solver. What is it, and how does it differ from a SAT solver?
answer: De Moura describes Z3 as a solver with background theories such as arithmetic and arrays, built for test-case generation and software verification. Z3 is fully automatic and push-button, while Lean is interactive, with automation that the user can guide. Z3 is not a programming language. It works more like a constraint solver, and can prove only simple things.

followups.question: What is an example of inputs and outputs to Z3?
answer: A Sudoku can be encoded as constraints, which Z3 solves almost at once. For a suspected security bug, a code path can be turned into constraints. Z3 then reports that the path is unsatisfiable, so it cannot run, or gives an input that reaches it. Properties with many universal quantifiers become undecidable, and the hand-coded heuristics often failed. Lean was started to prove the absence of bugs, a gap that Z3 did not fill well.
followups.speaker: Leonardo de Moura

followups.question: Does it typically terminate in practice, despite being undecidable?
answer: Bounded hardware problems, such as searching for a bug in the first ten steps, usually work well, because programs and hardware are correct for simple reasons. Non-trivial properties often time out. A colleague at Amazon named this proof instability, since changing the order of terms can break a proof. In Lean, the user controls the steps, so the proof stays stable.
followups.speaker: Leonardo de Moura

blocks.speaker: Leonardo de Moura

blocks.question: What was the most technically challenging part of building Z3 or Lean?
answer: De Moura says Lean is much harder than Z3. Z3's interface is SMT-LIB, a simple, low-level language built for tools, where a program passes a file and gets back yes or no. Lean is a full programming language with libraries, a user interface, a language server and a build system. Z3's users were sophisticated software developers, while Lean's first users were mathematicians with different expectations. Others want Lean as a programming language, and de Moura's background is automated reasoning rather than programming languages.

followups.question: Was there a single component that was especially hard?
answer: The guest says the switch from C++ to Lean was painful. The guest was building Lean with co-founder Sebastian before the nonprofit existed. The guest recalls wanting to cry when Lean finally compiled, and calling Sebastian to say it was insane. Sebastian was excited too.
followups.speaker: Leonardo de Moura

followups.question: What made the switch from C++ to Lean hard?
answer: The team had to implement Lean with only the features needed to compile itself, about 100,000 lines of human-written code. The first file failed to compile. Each fix exposed a difference between the old and new versions that had to be reconciled. Dependent types made the work harder, and some proofs had to be written with no interactive help, which de Moura compares to assembly programming. Many people thought the team would fail.
followups.speaker: Leonardo de Moura

blocks.speaker: Leonardo de Moura

blocks.question: What are the pros and cons of the different proof assistants?
answer: De Moura admits to bias. Users value Lean's extensibility, since Lean is implemented in Lean. Users can add automation in the same file, and AI can write these extensions. Asked to isolate a problem in Lean, AI often writes a Lean meta-program to test its conjecture about the cause.

Others have built on Lean. A French mathematician built a teaching environment with point-and-click suggestions and a proof language that reads like a textbook, in English or French. Other teams built domain-specific languages, such as Veil for protocol verification, and talked to the Lean team only after they finished. Interactivity, a large library, an active community and quick responses to users are, in the guest's view, why people stay. An early mathematician user could request a feature and get it the same day.
blocks.speaker: Leonardo de Moura

blocks.question: What is the difference between dependent type theory and higher-order logic?
answer: De Moura first chose higher-order logic because it was easier to implement. Jeremy convinced de Moura that serious mathematicians would want dependent type theory, which is more powerful for abstract objects. In it, types depend on values. A structure field can be a proof that x is greater than y, so the structure cannot be built without that evidence. A function can require a proof that y is not zero. Such proofs were once annoying to write, but AI can now synthesize them.

followups.question: In higher-order logic, could you express the same things?
answer: De Moura says no. Higher-order logic loses the dependencies. In Lean, a function can take a group and return a new group, treating the structure as a first-class object, which the guest says is a mess in higher-order logic. Mathematicians the guest has talked with agree. Listening to what a community needs matters if it is to be served.
followups.speaker: Leonardo de Moura

blocks.speaker: Leonardo de Moura

blocks.question: Where is Lean going, and what are you excited about?
answer: De Moura says a nonprofit behind Lean began in 2023. The project became a product with a team of engineers only after the nonprofit existed. The main push now is Lean as a programming language, where people prove properties of their programs. AWS made the largest donation so far to these nonprofits, aimed at that path, which de Moura says lacks funding.

De Moura says they no longer write tests but properties, and AI proves most of them. Proofs also enable optimizations for free: an AI can optimize code and supply a proof that the result computes the same thing.

followups.question: Is this the decade of formal verification of software?
answer: De Moura says the team is very excited to make it happen. Scalability is key. Math statements are usually small with cheap proofs. Software statements are large and their proofs are shallow, but they must manipulate big objects.
followups.speaker: Leonardo de Moura

blocks.speaker: Leonardo de Moura

blocks.question: What top technical book would you recommend for learning Lean and formal verification?
answer: De Moura points to the Lean website, which hosts several books on functional programming, theorem proving and mathematics in Lean, plus one on the mechanics of proof that is good for teaching.

De Moura says learning Lean with an AI agent is now very efficient. A learner can talk in natural language, ask for examples, and split the screen between Lean code, the InfoView and an agent that explains what is happening. The agent can tailor the lesson to what the learner already knows.
blocks.speaker: Leonardo de Moura

blocks.question: If you could go back to the start of building Z3 and Lean, what advice would you give yourself?
answer: The guest first jokes that the answer will stay a secret, since ignorance is bliss. Then the advice is to build people skills. The guest describes being very introverted, and says that working with a community was hard and that these skills matter a lot.
blocks.speaker: Leonardo de Moura
