sections.title: Stay close to users, code, and the next useful capability
sections.deck: Boris Cherny traces growth through generalist product work, shared infrastructure, earned trust, corrective decisions, and building Claude Code for a changing model frontier.

blocks.question: What work led to your senior-engineer promotion at Meta?
answer: Cherny recalls a project connecting Messenger chats with Facebook groups, after several earlier attempts to bring the products closer. The product hypothesis was that interaction was moving from public social spaces toward more casual, real-time conversation. He picked up a PM’s idea, built an early version, then recruited a few engineers and design and data-science support as it showed promise.

The small team did work beyond coding. Without dedicated user research, they showed features to cafeteria workers and watched whether they could accomplish tasks without much prompting. He taught teammates the same method. The rough early experience still helped test whether the core idea worked.

He values that generalist approach at Anthropic too: engineers with product sense, design interest, and willingness to speak with users, plus other functions willing to code. His own background in small companies taught him to own the whole outcome. He says the initial half brought his promotion and the next half brought promotions for the rest of the early engineering team.
blocks.speaker: Boris Cherny

blocks.question: What is latent demand, and why does it matter?
answer: Cherny describes it as existing user intent expressed through a product not designed for that purpose. People were already buying and selling in Facebook groups; dedicated commerce groups and later Marketplace made that behavior easier. He cites observed proportions of group posts as an example of the signal, rather than as current measured usage.

He offers profile-view behavior as another hypothesized signal behind dating features. The broader principle is to notice what users are already trying to do, especially how they bend a flexible product, then reduce friction around that intent. His claim that a product cannot make people do something they do not already do is deliberately strong product philosophy, not a proven universal limit on innovation.
blocks.speaker: Boris Cherny

blocks.question: How do you work across organizations with very different cultures?
answer: His Facebook product team prioritized rapid releases and engagement, while Messenger prioritized reliability and performance. The clash was built into goals, incentives, and organizational design, not just personalities. Messenger engineers had reason to fear changes that would damage the metrics they were responsible for.

He believes a version of the project failed partly because the benefit was much clearer for Facebook than for Messenger. Find a goal, hypothesis, or interest that both groups can genuinely share; simply expecting collaboration despite divergent rewards is weak.
blocks.speaker: Boris Cherny

followups.question: What would you change if you could revisit that project?
answer: He would seek an organizational arrangement with a closer common manager and better-aligned incentives, potentially bringing Messenger into the Facebook organization for the effort. He is describing a hindsight proposal, not a reorganization he carried out then.

blocks.question: How did side projects such as Undux affect your career?
answer: He values curiosity outside one’s main assignment, even when the interest is not technical. Undux began because he found React state management unnecessarily difficult and wanted a simpler approach. A nonprofit used his early library; at Facebook he recognized that repeated support questions reflected the same problems he had encountered.

An initial announcement brought some users but did not by itself drive broad adoption. He grouped support complaints by team, contacted each team’s leadership, and gave many focused technical talks. Meeting users where their specific pain already existed worked better than expecting a general post to persuade everyone. He recalls it becoming widely used before newer tools replaced it.

Other side explorations included a TypeScript book and a meetup. The book consumed roughly a year and he does not lightly recommend that commitment, but it let him go deeply into the language. Meeting prominent JavaScript creators also made ambitious work feel more accessible: they were people building things, rather than an unreachable class of geniuses.
blocks.speaker: Boris Cherny

followups.question: Did the state-management project help in performance review?
answer: He thinks it appeared, but calls it a bonus rather than the work that alone earned the next level. Its larger value included learning, relationships, and useful experience with adoption.

blocks.question: Did that language knowledge prove useful in later work?
answer: He describes an unusual start to language exploration: a motorcycle accident injured both arms, making coding difficult. He experimented with languages requiring fewer keystrokes, including CoffeeScript and Haskell, then a colleague introduced him more deeply to Scala and functional programming.

Functional Programming in Scala is the technical book he says most changed his thinking. He recommends the way it teaches problem solving even to people who may never use Scala. The lasting idea is to think in types and pay attention to signatures as a guide to clean structure.
That habit transferred across Flow, Hack, Python, and TypeScript in his later jobs. He distinguishes the mental model from the particular syntax used at a given company.
blocks.speaker: Boris Cherny

blocks.question: Why do you think entering Meta underleveled was fortunate?
answer: Lower expectations gave him space to explore and build things without immediately satisfying a larger set of project and people requirements. The host suggests that exceeding an initially lower bar can also create momentum and a strong first impression; Cherny agrees. He sees a downside to seeking a higher title at every move if it raises pressure before the person understands the new organization. This is his personal benefit from one circumstance, not a universal recommendation to accept lower compensation or responsibility.
blocks.speaker: Boris Cherny

blocks.question: What work led to the staff-engineer promotion?
answer: He wanted a better JavaScript-based web experience for Facebook groups, which still relied heavily on PHP with fragmented interactive state. Leadership initially resisted because supporting infrastructure was not ready. When the broader Facebook desktop rewrite, Comet, began, he offered groups as an early customer and helped argue that participating would let the team get ahead of required migration work.

The effort grew from an initial group of roughly a dozen engineers into a substantially larger migration. By helping build the platform rather than merely consume it, his product team could shape abstractions other teams would later use.

One example involved optimistic button updates and server responses arriving out of order. He built queuing around mutations to preserve consistent state. He recalls choosing a consistency tradeoff suited to the problem, and the shared work built relationships with the infrastructure team. His broader lesson is that product engineers can go a layer deeper into infrastructure and infrastructure engineers can talk to users.
blocks.speaker: Boris Cherny

followups.question: What additional opportunities came from being early?
answer: Besides shared infrastructure, the team helped define what product quality should mean on the new platform. Cherny wrote notes and gave talks about lessons others could reuse. Getting ahead of the migration gave the team a chance to set standards rather than only comply with them.

blocks.question: How many people would that migration require with contemporary coding agents?
answer: Cherny revises the original scope to perhaps 20–30 engineers over about two years, then guesses that tools at the time of the interview might support roughly five engineers over six months. He imagines parallel agents building changes and using browser feedback to refine the interface. He explicitly warns that the estimate could change in three or six months, perhaps radically. These are speculative comparisons, not measured results from rerunning the same migration.
blocks.speaker: Boris Cherny

blocks.question: Why did you joke that VPs usually pick the middle of three options?
answer: It was deliberately tongue-in-cheek. He thinks a distant decision maker wants evidence that the team explored options and tradeoffs, while also wanting to contribute a decision. A middle option can provide that. He qualifies the observation: some leaders investigate for themselves, and leaders differ in how much they trust teams. The “80%” framing is a joke from his story rather than a reliable statistic or a reason to manipulate every review.
blocks.speaker: Boris Cherny

blocks.question: How did reporting to a very senior manager affect your opportunities?
answer: Cherny treats this as company-dependent. At Meta, access to leaders could help an engineer find scope and navigate an impact-focused review system. At Anthropic, he sees highly senior people reporting to line managers, so reporting level says less about authority or capability.

He also likes common titles because they make it easier to do useful work outside a narrow role. He describes Meta engineering titles and Anthropic’s broader member-of-technical-staff convention as supporting that culture.
blocks.speaker: Boris Cherny

followups.question: Do common titles make it harder for another team to know how seriously to take you?
answer: Yes, but he thinks the upside is stronger: people must earn trust rather than assume a prior title gives them authority in a new setting. Everyone deserves respect, yet authority over a particular decision still requires evidence and relationships. He recognizes the lost shorthand and considers it an acceptable tradeoff.

blocks.question: How did you scope work for hundreds of engineers?
answer: Cherny recalls a large investment in Facebook groups as a community platform, leaving leaders to determine what newly allocated engineers would do. He produced many rough scoping documents with options and staffing estimates. In hindsight, he would have added people more gradually as specific products found fit: solving users’ problems is not made easier simply by distributing a huge allocation all at once.

A difficult groups-and-pages data-model problem stalled despite senior involvement. He brought technical leads into a short architecture exercise, split them into two groups, and gave both the same requirements. After a few hours, the designs overlapped substantially. Agreement showed where execution could begin; differences exposed risks to investigate with small technical spikes.
This let the team stop treating the whole problem as unknowable. The exercise created a concrete comparison without requiring one person to understand every detail in advance.
blocks.speaker: Boris Cherny

followups.question: Did people accept the unusual design competition?
answer: He scheduled it and made it appealing as an engineering problem. He thinks a leader sometimes needs to act to create a process through which consensus can form, while at other times acting without consensus would be wrong. Here the uncertain path made convening people useful.

blocks.question: What helps a technical lead produce a quick scope?
answer: Start at a high level and time-box the initial pass rather than disappear into unlimited detail. Cherny suggests roughly half an hour for a very rough view, or a few hours when code investigation is needed. Identify experts and show them a strawman instead of only asking open-ended questions; a concrete proposal makes feedback easier. He now sees coding agents as another way to explore relevant systems, but that is a tool-assisted extension of the same need to expose a reviewable first plan.
blocks.speaker: Boris Cherny

blocks.question: What made the public-groups project a senior-staff-level challenge?
answer: The visible change sounded simple: allow people to read, and in some cases comment in, public groups without first becoming approved members. The downstream changes were much harder. Following without reciprocal approval raised questions about how to represent membership, what admins needed, and how to handle more spam.

A senior engineer argued for separate data-model representations, and the team undertook a lengthy migration. Cherny also used a simple simulation of comment quality and spam to make moderation risk concrete, helping bring an integrity team into comment ranking. The work involved many experienced engineers whom he initially felt awkward directing because they shared his nominal level.

After auditing many call sites, he concluded the migration had mostly added branching without changing substantive logic. The old member field could support the needed behaviors. He pushed to reverse the migration, asking the senior engineer with the most context to help undo it. That engineer accepted the evidence and later supported Cherny’s leadership. The reversal was costly but reduced confusion for future developers.

His eventual judgment is that level does not reliably determine who has the best result. The achievement was not simply leading a large migration; it included recognizing when its premise was wrong and earning the trust to correct it.
blocks.speaker: Boris Cherny

blocks.question: How can a strong technical disagreement improve rather than damage a relationship?
answer: Earn trust first. Cherny initially disagreed but committed to implementing the senior engineer’s decision, then developed evidence and showed technical judgment. A relationship in which both people know you will execute honestly makes later pushback easier to hear. His recommendation is to invest in that trust before assuming a correct argument alone will carry the disagreement.
blocks.speaker: Boris Cherny

blocks.question: How did you deal with imposter syndrome while leading strong peers?
answer: He says not to assume that others at any level have everything figured out. His confidence did not arrive in one dramatic moment; it grew with experience. He regards some discomfort as a possible sign of stretching into unfamiliar work. This is encouragement grounded in his trajectory, not a complete technique that instantly removes anxiety.
blocks.speaker: Boris Cherny

blocks.question: When should an engineer fill a product-management gap versus ask for more PM support?
answer: Understand the decision maker’s tradeoffs before arguing for a preferred answer. A project may be hard to hire for, PMs may be needed on something more important, or an organization may have spare PM capacity that could sensibly be reassigned.

The same request therefore means different things in different settings. Think about what leadership values, what work your request displaces, and whether the proposed allocation helps them succeed. He does not give a universal rule that engineers should always absorb another function’s work.
blocks.speaker: Boris Cherny

blocks.question: How do you find useful engineering opportunities and give them to others?
answer: He looks for repeated friction in his own coding and asks how to eliminate it. During review he kept a list of recurring comments with examples; once the same issue appeared repeatedly, he wrote a lint rule rather than continue to police it manually. Automation freed his own time and could improve work for many engineers.

He did basic validation on ideas, then connected engineers who wanted those opportunities. He thinks understanding their goals is better than simply ordering them to do a project. At Meta, better-engineering work helped an evaluation dimension many people struggled to demonstrate, so a useful project could meet both a system need and an engineer’s growth goal.

He also warns that prolonged distance from code weakens a technical leader’s intuition. Hands-on experience anchored the opportunities in actual constraints. His very large approximate count of people involved in side projects is a recollection, not a precise audit of his personal influence.
blocks.speaker: Boris Cherny

blocks.question: What is a concrete way to source repeated, high-value side projects?
answer: He gives large-data testing as an example. Ordinary tests did not cover a group with millions of members, a highly followed profile, or a very large event, so scale failures appeared only in production. Seeing the same pattern across products, he proposed infrastructure for creating and testing large objects; another engineer took it on and recruited help. The pattern is to notice recurring pain, check whether others share it, and build an abstraction that prevents a whole class of incidents.
blocks.speaker: Boris Cherny

blocks.question: Why did you move from Facebook groups to Instagram in Japan?
answer: The move began with his partner’s dream job in rural Japan rather than a calculated promotion strategy. He tried several internal arrangements, but sponsorship or organizational rules blocked the earlier options. An engineer building the Instagram Tokyo office offered a workable path.

He joined despite having scarcely used Instagram, then came to value its emphasis on craft, human experience, and simplifying products as well as measuring them. The new setting taught him different habits from the Facebook organization he knew.
blocks.speaker: Boris Cherny

blocks.question: What does “unshipping” mean?
answer: Features compete for limited screen space and attention. Adding something useful to a small group can clutter the experience for the majority who do not use it. Cherny describes requiring a usage bar and deleting a feature that fails it, accepting that some users will be disappointed. His argument is about the opportunity cost of accumulated features, not that every low-usage feature lacks strategic value in every product.
blocks.speaker: Boris Cherny

blocks.question: How did you rebuild credibility in a new organization from far away?
answer: Leaders and colleagues helped him connect with people working on code quality and technical debt, but he still had to earn trust. He spent early weeks meeting people, mapping goals and the organization, and writing code to understand the codebase.

The severe time-zone gap made meetings difficult, but unexpectedly restored time for coding after years of documents and conversations had left him unhappy. He says he still avoids standing one-on-ones. That made it possible to do work others wanted done but could not fit around their obligations.

He explored migrating parts of Instagram’s Python environment toward Hack and Meta’s infrastructure. He considered the original simple choice sensible at small scale but less suitable after years of product growth and a much larger engineering group. This is his contextual assessment; his praise of the alternative serving stack is not a universal language ranking.

He began with the people most likely to disagree, building personal trust before debating the migration. Supporters who had been reluctant to speak then joined the discussion. In a product-led organization, creating space for an engineering-led investment required those relationships as well as technical scope.
blocks.speaker: Boris Cherny

blocks.question: When did you delegate the large migration, and how did you decide to trust another lead?
answer: Cherny saw a colleague closer to the relevant organization as an excellent owner. He recommends delegating something you understand and care about so you can judge progress, rather than treating delegation as a way to dump disliked work. He cites High Output Management as an influence. Check more at first and less as evidence of reliability grows; with a proactive and technically strong lead, he needed little intervention. The handoff matched the project’s needs rather than preserving personal ownership for its own sake.
blocks.speaker: Boris Cherny

blocks.question: What happened around the principal-engineer promotion?
answer: His manager proposed putting him up for IC8, and he agreed. He had not been campaigning for it. He credits the manager’s willingness to notice readiness and advocate for people, with large modernization projects providing the context. He does not offer a detailed promotion packet or claim that a simple conversation alone caused the result.
blocks.speaker: Boris Cherny

blocks.question: Did levels guide how you sought more impact and leverage?
answer: Cherny sees levels as company tools for communicating expectations, comparing people in reviews, and planning costs. His own motivation was interesting problems, useful products, and making people’s experience better, rather than the next level itself.

He pitched ideas from his earliest weeks as IC4; several were rejected and one appeared in another form later. The point is a willingness to seek useful work without waiting for a higher title. His career happened to reward that approach, while he does not claim every company will do so automatically.
blocks.speaker: Boris Cherny

blocks.question: Why leave Meta for Anthropic?
answer: Using an early ChatGPT product while living in Japan made AI feel like a field he had to work on. He was fascinated by the technology and by speculative possibilities he had encountered through science fiction. Conversations at Anthropic gave him a strong sense of shared interests and people thinking deeply about the same questions.

He also wanted to help make the technology develop safely. He describes becoming more conscious of risk after seeing new models and Anthropic’s investment in safety and alignment, including delayed releases. His examples of possible misuse and existential risk are his assessment, not independently established capability claims in this book.

The decision combined fascination, a cultural fit, and a mission. His metaphor of models as an alien life form conveys his excitement; it should not be mistaken for a factual claim about consciousness or biology.
blocks.speaker: Boris Cherny

blocks.question: What felt different about Anthropic’s engineering culture?
answer: He values a startup’s shorter distance between decisions and consequences: useful changes can seem obvious enough that less effort goes into persuading multiple layers. Mission is also personally powerful. He had felt it in Facebook groups’ community work, felt less of it in Instagram, and felt it strongly again at Anthropic. He acknowledges that geography or his own experience could have influenced the difference. He is describing what motivates him, not a ranking of how meaningful every employee’s work is.
blocks.speaker: Boris Cherny

blocks.question: Why did Claude Code catch on when other model-connected tools already existed?
answer: Cherny contrasts the then-dominant coding autocomplete and Q&A model with a tool intended to act more broadly. His manager pushed him to build for capabilities expected about six months later rather than only what the current model could already do.

The product was initially weak and he used it for a small portion of his own coding. Later model improvements made the existing tool much more useful, matching the horizon the team had aimed for. He reports high fractions of agent-written code within his team and some others, plus a substantial increase in per-engineer productivity while Anthropic expanded.

Those usage and productivity numbers are internal claims made in the interview. The caption does not clearly establish the productivity metric, so the book does not convert them into an exact causal benchmark. His product lesson is to stay close enough to the model’s trajectory to serve near-future capabilities while avoiding a plan too far ahead to test.
blocks.speaker: Boris Cherny

blocks.question: How do you avoid accepting large amounts of poor or subtly flawed model-generated code?
answer: Use the same quality bar for human and model code. If a change is poor, the team should refuse it and ask for improvement rather than lower expectations because an agent wrote it. Cherny thinks users can also ask for changes that are too large before learning to direct the tool well.

He chooses the method according to the work. Throwaway prototypes can be generated loosely. For maintainable product work, he usually aligns on a plan, inspects the implementation, and iterates with the model. Some core-loop details still matter enough to him that he writes them by hand.

He is enthusiastic about progress without saying the models are already excellent at every task. He sees substantial room to improve and warns that judgments about capability move quickly. That combination of optimism and retained review standards is more useful than treating generated volume as evidence of correctness.
blocks.speaker: Boris Cherny

blocks.title: Three coding approaches in Cherny’s workflow
rows: Loose generation
Disposable prototypes and experiments
Decide whether the result is useful enough to keep exploring
Pair with the model
Maintainable product work
Agree on a plan, inspect changes, and request improvements
Handwritten implementation
Details where he has strong, specific preferences
Control the implementation directly

blocks.question: What do you think of Claude Code being used beyond software engineering?
answer: He discovered a neighboring data scientist using it for SQL and analysis, then saw multiple sessions supporting data work, pipelines, and coding. He also reports salespeople connecting it with Salesforce and other sources. Those uses were not the original product intent. The examples return to latent demand: observe what users do with an adaptable tool rather than define its limits solely from the name.
blocks.speaker: Boris Cherny

blocks.question: How do you view competition with Codex, and what makes users stay?
answer: He does not give a feature comparison because he says he does not personally use the competing tools and is unsure. The stickiness part of the host’s question therefore does not receive a definitive mechanism.

His management principle is to avoid letting competitors replace user problems as the product roadmap. Copying a visible feature is easier than discovering a better solution, but he wants the team focused on its own work, researchers’ needs, and users’ problems. He interprets more competitors partly as evidence of an important market, rather than only as a distraction to fear.
blocks.speaker: Boris Cherny

blocks.question: Has not having a computer-science degree held you back?
answer: He studied economics and left to build startups. He has not felt the missing CS degree blocked his own path and recommends learning programming through practical work, then adding theory as it becomes useful. His reasoning is that concepts are easier to connect to an actual product than to exercises without context. This is his experience and preference, not evidence that a degree never matters for a particular employer or technical field.
blocks.speaker: Boris Cherny

blocks.question: What productivity advice would you give now?
answer: His answer has changed with coding agents: learn to automate toil and coordinate several agents rather than depend only on faster manual typing. He describes a teammate using many parallel sessions and a task board to implement a feature over a weekend in a container. This is an anecdote about her workflow, not a verified effort comparison or a blanket recommendation to remove safeguards. Earlier his advice would have centered more on ordinary scheduling and focus habits.
blocks.speaker: Boris Cherny

blocks.question: Do agents change the need for long coding focus blocks?
answer: In his own work, somewhat. He still enjoys quiet coding time, including weekends, but can begin several tasks from a mobile or web interface in the morning and inspect them later at a computer. He sometimes merges after review, or brings a change locally to edit.

He sees this as making coding accessible in fragmented schedules, including for managers who have not recently written much code. He is describing a changing interaction pattern, not declaring concentration unnecessary for understanding or reviewing complex systems.
blocks.speaker: Boris Cherny

blocks.question: What would you tell yourself at the start of your career?
answer: Use and develop common sense. Organizational history and misaligned incentives can pull people away from what users and a business actually need. In startups as well as large companies, he would trust practical judgment, examine assumptions, and build toward the real market or user problem. The advice ties his generalist work, side projects, migrations, and product choices back to the same habit.
blocks.speaker: Boris Cherny

sections.title: Thariq Shihipar: How Anthropic Builds, Harnesses, and Where Engineering Is Heading
sections.deck: Thariq Shihipar of the Claude Code team describes how Anthropic works with its models, from harnesses, loops and verification to writing, maintenance and career advice, and argues that taste, context and technical depth remain human.

blocks.text: Thariq Shihipar, an engineer on the Claude Code team at Anthropic, argues that the most useful habit is to treat Claude as a thought partner and to work one level of abstraction above the code: build the system that builds the system. In Thariq's view, harnesses, verification, skills and context matter more as models improve, while taste, domain knowledge, clear intent and technical understanding stay with people. The host probes onboarding, autonomy, prompting, code maintenance, writing, career visibility and whether anyone should still learn to code. Product and model names follow the auto-generated captions and were not independently checked.
blocks.heading: Thariq's view: move up an abstraction level, but keep taste, context and technical depth

blocks.question: If an engineer joined from a less AI-focused company, what should they start doing to onboard onto the Claude Code team?
answer: Thariq's top tip, for people inside and outside Anthropic, is to treat Claude as a thought partner and give it the context it needs to work out next steps. Start from whether Claude can do the task, and if not, ask why not.
Thariq also recommends asking whether the work can move up an abstraction level: instead of building the product, build the system that builds it.

followups.question: Does Claude replace the onboarding buddy completely?
answer: Thariq says teams still assign onboarding buddies, but for social and cultural reasons more than technical ones. Someone good at working with Claude can get most technical onboarding from it. A buddy still helps with how the team works, how to win buy-in, and simply having a friend at work.
followups.speaker: Thariq

blocks.speaker: Thariq

blocks.question: Why is there such a big gap between how Anthropic staff talk about AI capability internally and how the outside world sees it?
answer: Thariq says Anthropic has a decent record of its claims proving true over a long enough time scale. Many engineers there are no longer in the IDE, and Thariq reports that some large enterprise customers say they have not typed a line of code in six months.

Anthropic treats it as part of its job to learn to work at a higher abstraction level, so a day spent failing to get Claude to do something autonomously is not wasted: it shows where Claude falls short.

Thariq says the calculation differs in an ordinary job where the task is to produce output. Automation is an investment that can fail, and a boss will not be happy with someone who spent the time on harness setup and shipped no code. The odds of payoff rise as models improve, but an individual still has to take the leap. Thariq calls the gap mostly cultural: Anthropic tries to live in the future and builds what it learns into the product and harness.
blocks.speaker: Thariq

blocks.question: What practices make a big difference at Anthropic that people rarely show on Twitter?
answer: Thariq points to using Claude Code for knowledge work. If you can describe a task as code-like steps, the model can carry them out. Thariq does personal accounting with Python scripts through Claude Code instead of Excel, and edits video with FFmpeg and rendering libraries.
In Thariq's view most knowledge work reduces to code and coding agents, and other people do this less than they could.
blocks.speaker: Thariq

blocks.question: How important is the harness compared with the model?
answer: Thariq calls the harness super important and rejects the idea that better models make it unnecessary. As models improve, the harness has to become more complicated so the model can do more.

Thariq's example is auto mode, a classifier tied to the actions that would otherwise trigger a permission prompt. With earlier models, which Thariq names as Opus 4 and perhaps Opus 4.5, turns lasted a few minutes and pressing enter was tolerable. Now Claude can run for hours, so it must work safely and follow instructions. Thariq calls auto mode and sandboxing complicated software.

Longer runs also raise the question of how Claude reports eight hours of work. Anthropic uses artifacts for this, which Thariq treats as a form of prompting. Thariq calls harness engineering an unintuitive mix of science and art, and says pieces such as auto mode and workflows have become load-bearing.
blocks.speaker: Thariq

blocks.question: What share of changes at Anthropic is fully autonomous, compared with pairing with a model as a year ago?
answer: Thariq says it depends on what counts as autonomous and on the function. A designer might hand over a Figma file that Claude Code reads through a Figma MCP, but the designer has still done real work. Anthropic's goal is for Claude to handle the glue work, such as rewriting that file in React.

Thariq frames the question as: what is the unique work I must do today? The more time spent on that, the better. If the work only translates what someone else did, Thariq asks whether Claude can do it. Even a fully generated PR usually reflects decisions and context the person supplied.

followups.question: How close are we to telling Claude "here is the ticket, don't tell me until you're done"?
answer: Thariq says it depends on the ticket. With a spec written precisely enough, Claude can probably do it. But a typical GitHub issue raises earlier questions: is it worth fixing, is it several requests combined, and does it fit a cohesive product vision.

In practice, Thariq says, people have not worked out what they want or the unknowns in the problem. Writing code used to surface those questions. Now people need new ways to find what they do not yet know, and chatting with Claude can help.
Thariq names a failure mode: tagging Claude with a one-sentence request and no context, disliking the result, and iterating forever instead of working out quickly what you actually want.
followups.speaker: Thariq

blocks.speaker: Thariq

blocks.question: At Meta, intern projects were almost line-by-line specified. If Claude can handle that, what does an intern do at Anthropic?
answer: Thariq says there is a great deal of new work nobody has done before, such as evaluating new coding behaviors or measuring Claude's performance across millions of users and tasks with trade-offs, especially on the research side. Specs are harder to write and less existing experience applies.

Experience still helps with getting work done and learning, though Thariq notes interns also gain those skills at college. Internships are now less about writing React code. Fresh eyes help, and interns need to be more proactive and opportunistic than in a pipeline-style program.
blocks.speaker: Thariq

blocks.question: How far away is computer and browser use from wide adoption?
answer: Thariq says the models have improved a lot and calls Opus 5 a really good computer use model. Edge cases remain: it cannot type a password for Thariq because the passwords are in a password manager, so it gets stuck.

Thariq expects APIs and MCPs to take over many uses of computers. Claude Tag, for example, rolls many things into APIs so Claude can work on a user's behalf without literally clicking through a virtual computer. Some tasks have no API and still need a browser.

followups.question: Why does computer use feel so slow?
answer: Thariq says it is hard to make a small model very good at the task, because it needs much knowledge about how things fit together, and smart models are slower. Many people expected this sooner, and it has been harder than expected.

Thariq passes on someone else's remark that a computer is a state machine whose whole state you do not control. Add the wrong item to a DoorDash cart and you need a new flow to undo it, where you can err again. In code you control the state and can undo with git; in computer use, actions are harder to review or reverse.
followups.speaker: Thariq

blocks.speaker: Thariq

blocks.question: If someone had infinite compute, what workflows would you tell them to run?
answer: Thariq says the difference is smaller than people think. Thariq uses a Max subscription on weekends and has almost never hit a five-hour limit. Much of Anthropic's heavy compute goes into probing model capabilities, such as testing math ability, rather than everyday work.

People can reproduce the practice by thinking at a higher level. Thariq's example is a funnel in which Claude drafts feedback for a user. Thariq monitors it and asks Claude for improvement ideas, annotates features with events Claude can access, and runs a morning loop to check which events fired and what changed. Thariq says this takes fairly modest compute.

More often Thariq sees people hit limits the opposite way: they start with a small task such as refactoring a function, then iterate through follow-on effects. Stating goals, letting Claude explore and write out a schema, and then letting it run would probably give the same output.

followups.question: What is loop engineering, and would it hit limits on a Max plan?
answer: Thariq defines loop engineering as setting up a system that prompts Claude rather than prompting Claude directly. With Claude Tag this comes naturally: ask it to do something every day and that is a loop.

Around ten loops, for example to triage feedback and implement fixes, take real work on skills, triage quality and verification so changes land. At that level Anthropic has something monitoring issues the team could never have kept up with, which raises velocity. Thariq says full autonomy is possible in some cases but is a lot of work, and like hiring someone it has to be worth it.
followups.speaker: Thariq

blocks.speaker: Thariq

blocks.question: What is the next big shift that will spread across the industry?
answer: Thariq names Claude Tag first. In Thariq's description, Claude Code is good at implementing code, and Claude Tag covers the rest of the software life cycle: feedback, code review, babysitting, CI/CD and incidents. Thariq expects each part of the life cycle to become a routine or loop.

Thariq also expects generative interfaces. Artifacts will become a larger way to read and interact with Claude, and Thariq uses them for almost everything. If Claude Tag finishes work and produces a report, an artifact can make it readable on a phone.

followups.question: What are artifacts, and how do people use them?
answer: Thariq describes an artifact as Claude uploading a web app for you to use. Artifacts can now call your MCP, for example to read, sort and tag your inbox, or show a coding plan with diagrams, file snippets and schemas.

As Claude does more jobs, Thariq says, text in and text out is not enough for everything, and Claude is getting better at building the right interface at the right time. Thariq encourages asking how you could interact differently, to learn, understand or stay in the loop. It is still early.
followups.speaker: Thariq

blocks.speaker: Thariq

blocks.question: Do engineers at Anthropic use different daily-driver models, or just the most intelligent one?
answer: Thariq says the aim is to get the most out of frontier models with well-shaped tasks and a good verification harness. For now there is not enough compute for everyone to run Fable at 100 percent of rate limits, but Thariq does not see choosing a model as a durable skill.

Today Thariq uses Fable for planning, brainstorming, finding unknowns, writing detailed specs and building verification aids such as schemas, and Opus 5 with workflows for implementation. Thariq expects people to think much less about model choice by next year.
blocks.speaker: Thariq

blocks.question: Is prompting a durable skill, given that each model has its own spiky intelligence?
answer: Thariq says prompting is more than the typed text. It includes skills, data and everything built up as context. When Anthropic staff write small prompts, they have spent a lot of time on the harness, verification and skills. Thariq thinks it stays valuable to improve at it.

Each model has quirks to learn and later unlearn. Citing a recent Anthropic post about removing 80 percent of Claude Code's system prompt, Thariq says one finding was to remove examples from tool descriptions. Examples used to be needed for good output, but now they mostly steer the model wrongly, because Claude is good at sticking to your intent.
So the skill being built is the skill to adapt. Thariq's first model was GPT-2, where getting JSON out was remarkable, and that experience still helps with prompting Fable 5.
blocks.speaker: Thariq

blocks.question: Is there any tribal knowledge or quirky tip for today's models?
answer: Thariq pushes back on advice like "just believe in yourself". Thariq reads Jared's post about the Riemann hypothesis as mostly giving the model permission to use compute, not encouragement. Thariq's habit is to say a problem is hard, that Claude may use sub agents and workflows, and that it should use its own judgment.

Thariq explains that models by default do what the average user wants: respond and start fast, and finish without spending a crazy amount of compute. To change that, nudge the model, for example "don't work yet, brainstorm with me", or invite it to use workflows. Overnight, Thariq may set the slash goal and let it run. The common thread is giving permission.

followups.question: How did you prove that removing so much of the system prompt made things better?
answer: Thariq says Anthropic used user metrics, internal and external evals, and internal reports. Some changes are hard to catch: there is no eval for Claude finishing its work and telling the user to go to sleep.

The team removed lines, ran evals, watched reports and adjusted. Thariq says this was a full-time job for several people over a long period, so Anthropic published what it learned rather than recommending everyone repeat it.
followups.speaker: Thariq

blocks.speaker: Thariq

blocks.question: Claude Code is excellent on objective work but hit or miss on taste. How do you instill a style, for example in front end work?
answer: Thariq's method is to stay in the loop and give references, ideally with data. An HTML file beats a screenshot and a Figma file beats a raster image, because Claude can read a value such as a border radius from the Figma component and copy it. References in code are best.

For a non-designer, Thariq starts by admitting how much is unknown, including what good looks like. Ask Claude for help: say you lack design vocabulary, find reference sites, mark what you like and dislike, then ask for several mock-ups. Thariq prefers self-contained HTML mock-ups, then starts a new session to implement one.

Thariq argues that knowing what good output looks like will become more valuable. Thariq says Jared prompted the Riemann hypothesis work but could not tell whether it was correct until Lev, whom Thariq calls one of the world's best mathematicians, worked with it and asked follow-ups the Anthropic people could not follow. Domain knowledge is how you get good outputs; otherwise Claude might solve something and you would not know. The hardest part, Thariq says, is knowing when something is good enough and when to push harder.
blocks.speaker: Thariq

blocks.question: How much glue writing, such as launch posts, updates and design docs, is now written by LLMs at Anthropic?
answer: Thariq's rule of thumb is that if you would be happy to show someone the prompt, you can send them the output. Often the prompt just collects context. Before each one-on-one, Thariq has Claude read Slack messages, GitHub messages and PRs and compile a report of what Thariq did. The manager lacks that context, and Thariq is comfortable with them knowing the prompt.

For data readouts, Thariq suggests showing you have read the result, for example with small edits or a sanity check of the numbers. For a pitch or new concept, people want to know you believe in it. Even if Claude's idea is excellent, Thariq would say that Claude generated it and that Thariq thinks it is great. What people dislike is feeling misled.

Some writing depends on individual words. Anthropic's internal essays arguing for a direction are generally human-written, and Thariq says having Claude write your essay is looked down on, because every word should be intentional.

followups.question: So routine writing is AI-written but human-reviewed, and novel thinking stays human?
answer: Thariq agrees and adds that writing is a way of thinking, so if you need to think more about a readout, summarize it yourself. Gathering context is different: no one will hold it against you, and acknowledging the shortcut is good.
followups.speaker: Thariq

blocks.speaker: Thariq

blocks.question: Is there a "prompt blame", like git blame, that shows which prompt produced a change?
answer: Thariq says this is tough, because a prompt includes context and skills, so a basic-looking prompt may not be basic. Thariq treats a PR as no different from an artifact now, since Claude writes nearly all the code.

When Thariq sends a PR, Thariq usually attaches an artifact of every prompt sent to Claude, including failed approaches, so reviewers see what was considered. For a one-shot, Thariq says so and shares the prompt. Thariq wants to avoid sending a 10,000-line PR and being asked how much was read, so for large PRs Thariq shows the work as much as possible.
blocks.speaker: Thariq

blocks.question: With AI generating so much code, what works for code ownership and maintenance?
answer: Thariq says to revisit what matters. Naming used to matter because it reflected how a team thought about an abstraction, but it matters less now, as do many stylistic things. A team should decide which opinions still matter.

On maintenance, Thariq stresses scaffolding: a verification harness and skills. Thariq's team uses the simplify skill a lot, but does not want the model to simplify by default before the work is correct, which wastes tokens.

Thariq wants a harness that gives real confidence Claude tests every part; a PR to Claude Code returns a recording of the feature in use. Thariq suggests about a hundred times more testing code than before: fixtures for everything, production data pulled to build mock databases on the fly, and Storybooks for front end.

The human part is deciding where the code base should go. Thariq's example is undo: in a single-player app it can stop working after four or five steps and few notice, while a multiplayer app needs composable operations. If you know your direction, put it in your skills. For Thariq, maintainability means having a vision of what the code base is good at.

Thariq expects every code base to face a moment of asking the model to rewrite all of it, for example in a faster language or as WebAssembly in the browser. Thariq says maintainability still matters but the mental model needs updating.

followups.question: A friend leaves tech debt because the next model will refactor it. Is that sensible?
answer: Thariq says it is not completely wrong and depends on the case. It is the classic startup trade-off between refactoring and delivering customer value.

Thariq suggests thinking on shorter time scales and delivering value over the next month or two. If a project is meant to deliver value over six or twelve months, it may make sense to wait a little for the next model, while making the short-term delivery really good.
followups.speaker: Thariq

blocks.speaker: Thariq

blocks.question: Friends at big tech companies see more incidents as AI use rises. What has worked at Anthropic to prevent breakages at higher velocity?
answer: Thariq calls this a byproduct of moving faster and says Anthropic's uptime is not where it wants it either. Thariq notes that Anthropic is only around six years old and that no company has grown so fast, partly because Claude let it build more products faster.

Thariq's approach is to use Claude to improve uptime. The team asks what the dream testing and deployment environment would be: replaying requests across mock databases and fixtures, and chaos-testing everything.
blocks.speaker: Thariq

blocks.question: Does everyone on your team have their own set of miscellaneous tools and scripts?
answer: Thariq says yes, and that it is partly the job. People sometimes build their own harnesses for a while to see if they are useful, and integrate them if they work.

Many have unique Claude Tag setups. Thariq has it manage calendar invites: anyone can tag Claude in a channel, and Thariq accepts what it puts on the calendar. Others use it for email, and Thariq has seen multi-Claude tmux setups showing around 50 Claude Code sessions.
blocks.speaker: Thariq

blocks.question: Should software engineers post on Twitter or X to build visibility?
answer: Thariq says to share your work externally as much as you can, though some employers do not allow it; side projects are an option. Before joining Anthropic, Thariq worked with different companies, built things, and wrote and talked about them. Thariq says this increased their "surface area of luck", and that the bar is much lower than people think.

Thariq says they give this advice to many people and almost none follow it, while everyone who did is in a job they are excited about or running their own company. The recipe: ignore your resume, choose an interesting project, work hard and lock in, then ship it and write about it. There will be reasons not to, but if the first attempt fails, do it again.

Twitter may not be the right place; Reddit or Hacker News might fit better. The goal is to find people who like what you do. People want high-quality content, which is a lot of work, and Thariq says there is no shortcut such as asking Claude to run your Twitter account. Engage authentically. Thariq compares it with going to the gym daily: simple, disciplined and easy to quit, and Thariq says they have not seen anyone who kept trying fail.

followups.question: Can you give an example of expanding your luck surface area?
answer: Thariq describes how they got the job at Anthropic. Thariq did a fellowship at Good Fire, an interpretability AI company, doing applied research on using interpretability to make better products, and agreed up front that the goal was to share what Thariq built.

Thariq built an interpretability visualization and posted it. It got about 500 likes, which was big at the time. Several people saw it, some sent direct messages, and Thariq got an intro into a role at Anthropic. The project took about a month, and Thariq was paid for it.
Thariq says there is no shortcut: do interesting, novel work, work hard and be proud of it.
followups.speaker: Thariq

blocks.speaker: Thariq

blocks.question: Boris said coding is largely solved. Should people still learn to code?
answer: Thariq says being technical is really important: knowing how computers and programs work, what a back-end service or a cache is, what memory allocation is.

Thariq argues that only a great mathematician can tell whether someone really made progress on a hard open problem, and likewise only a great engineer can tell whether great software was built. To stay in the loop, reflect on your process and use Claude as a thought partner. Thariq cites Karpathy that learning should feel like effort: if Claude explains something and you only nod along, you have not learned it.

On "coding is solved", Thariq reads Boris as meaning that we no longer get stuck the old ways. Coding used to be high variance, with a bug taking a day or two weeks, and software projects rarely went well. Hiring someone to build software for a car dealership would almost certainly end in being scammed, not from malice but because software was so hard. Now coding can be used for things never done before. That is still a lot of work, but no longer a rare, difficult thing that mostly fails.

followups.question: The host used to be shocked when software worked first try and now expects it. How should we read that shift?
answer: The host says the expectation has flipped: now the host is surprised when Claude's code does not work on the first attempt.

Thariq says humans get used to abundance quickly. Thariq cites an article about a modern apartment's wonders, such as music on demand suited to your mood, where once you would have hired a musician. Thariq believes more people are paid to make music now than ever and music reaches more people, and expects the same for software and math: given abundance, people want software in everything.
followups.speaker: Thariq

followups.question: Does the earlier FFmpeg example suggest technical people still have an edge?
answer: The host notes that a non-technical person might not think to call FFmpeg to automate video editing.

Thariq agrees and says knowing how computers work matters. In Thariq's view the best CEOs tend to be technical, citing Zuckerberg and Elon. Thariq says they probably have not written code in a long time, but they understand systems and constraints.
followups.speaker: Thariq

blocks.speaker: Thariq

blocks.question: If you could go back to when you entered the industry, what advice would you give yourself?
answer: Thariq describes it as two wolves. The first is to believe in yourself. When Thariq joined, it was rarer to believe in younger people, which Thariq links to the idea behind Y Combinator. Thariq suggests seeing yourself not as someone being trained but as someone who can do something incredible right away, and wishes they had done and shared bigger, bolder things.

The second is to learn from people. Young people tend to fail in one of two ways: not being bold enough, or being so bold that they never learn what others tried and why it failed. Everyone has a different failure mode. Thariq thinks they did not use mentors enough and had to relearn many things. Thariq adds that there is probably no universal advice, only things to think about when entering.
blocks.speaker: Thariq

parts.title: Growing as an individual contributor
parts.introduction: Career stories reveal how scope, technical ownership, visibility, and timing interact. These are particular experiences and organizational practices, rather than a universal promotion formula.

sections.title: Ambition, impact, and the limits of promotion checklists
sections.deck: A host and CTO debate how to make valuable work visible without reducing career growth to a transactional promotion checklist.

blocks.question: Should an engineer organize a career around promotion or around developing useful behaviors and impact?
answer: The guest strongly favors impact over title. In evaluating advancement, he wants to see important outcomes rather than an attempt to negotiate a checklist whose completion mechanically triggers promotion. A person can technically satisfy a stated activity while performing it in a way that adds little value; that leaves the underlying reason for advancement unmet.

He also acknowledges a personal reaction: repeated attempts to pin leadership down on rewards can feel transactional and annoying to him. That is his perspective as a leader, not a guarantee that all managers respond alike. His substantive argument is that genuine impact remains what should be recognized.
blocks.speaker: Guest

blocks.question: How should quieter engineers balance impact with making their work visible?
answer: The host challenges a pure impact-first account: good engineers can be weak at communicating their results and may lose out when promotion decisions depend on people noticing. He distinguishes useful visibility from cynical self-promotion.

The guest agrees that visibility matters. Engineers need contact with people who understand important challenges, coordination with collaborators, and recognition of their capabilities so others can entrust them with bigger work. His distinction is the purpose and framing of the communication: making work understandable and coordinating it can lead to different behavior than trying to brag about oneself.

Updates should also recognize collaborators and thank the team. That makes the contribution legible without implying only the sender mattered, helps others feel valued, and supports the trust required for leadership. The host observes that two motives can produce superficially similar updates; the guest emphasizes how much the message centers the individual versus the work and other people.
blocks.speaker: Guest

blocks.question: Does the loud high performer often get promoted sooner than an equally strong quiet colleague?
answer: The host argues that persistent lobbying can win extra attention even when both people have real impact. The guest says outcomes depend on organizational culture and that his own culture tries not to reward that behavior. He admits there are edge cases where lobbying earns consideration simply by keeping someone top of mind.

He does not advise abandoning ambition. He wants ambition expressed as a desire for greater impact: ask whether you are working on the most important problem, what you could learn, and where you could contribute more. A hardworking engineer can otherwise spend extraordinary effort on a low-priority task and still miss the outcome they sought.

Making those aspirations known and asking for opportunities are valuable conversations. What he opposes is reducing the relationship to contractual boxes followed by a demand for promotion. The debate therefore retains a real tension: the host worries about unequal recognition, while the guest prefers impact-centered visibility and managerial judgment to promotion bargaining. Neither establishes that recognition will always perfectly match contribution.
blocks.speaker: Guest

omissions: Closing full-episode pointer and feedback request at 00:09:12–00:09:28 are omitted.

sections.title: Ask what the title is supposed to give you
sections.deck: Bryan Cantrill argues that promotion and financial goals need an underlying source of meaning, including a plan for life after success.

blocks.question: Should an ambitious engineer focus on work or explicitly target promotions?
answer: Cantrill offers a third path: first understand why the desired title matters. A distinguished-engineer label is an external marker; attaining it leaves the person facing the same question about meaning. He would help a mentee identify work that is important to them and supports continuing development.

He points to unhappy senior engineers and wealthy people to challenge the assumption that achievement necessarily supplies fulfillment. His provocative counseling jokes are condensed into that underlying concern, rather than presented as psychological diagnoses. He thinks meaningful motivation provides the fuel from which work and promotion can follow.

followups.question: What if the actual goal is financial independence?
answer: He asks what independence enables. If it means never needing to work for money, what would the person then choose to do? He wants that motivating activity identified now rather than assuming money itself answers the question.

followups.question: What if the meaningful activity cannot support a living?
answer: Then the person must balance it with a sustainable career. He recognizes the need to provide for oneself and a family, but objects to postponing all meaningful activity until an uncertain future financial milestone.

He recalls dot-com wealth existing on paper and then disappearing. The bust forced many people to rediscover why they were in technology apart from money. Some people who sold successfully faced a different problem: they no longer needed to work but still had to find purpose. Buying more houses or consuming more did not automatically answer it.

blocks.question: Why do some people reach financial independence and then feel lost?
answer: A singular goal can organize life so completely that completion removes the structure. Cantrill says this can happen even after a meaningful engineering achievement: he anticipated a letdown after Oxide shipped its first rack because people had pulled toward that goal for so long. A financial milestone may create the same gap without having supplied meaningful work along the way. He does not endorse responding merely by escalating the amount one wants.

blocks.question: What about someone who would be happy simply relaxing?
answer: The host offers a real counterexample to the work-centered view. Cantrill responds with a story of an early Yahoo employee whose fortunate equity position made him wealthy despite limited interest in work. The employee’s responsibilities eventually narrowed considerably, and he still complained about the job.

The anecdote illustrates that unusual financial luck and dislike of work can coexist. Cantrill hopes the person found meaning elsewhere, but does not know that outcome. He does not actually establish that nobody can be content with leisure, so the host’s broader counterexample remains unresolved.

sections.title: Choose a career you will still want after the promotion
sections.deck: A compilation of experienced engineers’ advice connects ambition with values, relationships, confidence, distinctive strengths, and useful judgment.

blocks.question: Before optimizing a career, how do you know the destination is worth reaching?
answer: The first guest would spend more time clarifying values and what he actually wanted. A clear target made his early choices simple: he took roles that moved him toward development management. Once he reached that target and a high level comparatively young, however, he lacked a model for the decades of work still ahead and experienced a serious loss of purpose.

He warns against wanting only the attractive part of somebody else’s life. Wealth, title, age, circumstances, and daily work come together; admiring one feature does not mean you want the whole life. His lesson is to examine the destination before treating speed toward it as success.

He also remembers working until 11 p.m. while his fiancée was visiting, giving their relationship only a late dinner. They stayed together, but he regards that outcome as fortunate rather than proof that relationships tolerate unlimited strain. Some things recover from pressure; others break. Reaching the same senior level at 30 rather than 38 may matter less over a long life than maintaining a spouse relationship and family. Choose the tradeoff knowingly rather than assume everything else will wait.
blocks.speaker: Guest 1

blocks.question: Are you pursuing your own goals or seeking other people’s approval?
answer: Another guest reflects on a prescribed sequence of school, job, marriage, and achievement that encouraged comparison and validation from others. He would ask whether he wants the goal itself or is simply climbing a ladder placed in front of him. The person whose judgment he ultimately needs to satisfy is himself. He doubts his younger self would have absorbed that lesson immediately, which keeps the advice from sounding like an effortless mindset switch.
blocks.speaker: Guest 2

blocks.question: What did imposter syndrome delay?
answer: A third guest would trust his judgment sooner. Successful projects, good collaboration, and feedback eventually built confidence, but earlier anxiety kept him from trying some ideas because he feared rocking the boat. Several of those disruptive projects later worked well. He wishes he had tested them earlier and spent less time worrying, while grounding the eventual confidence in experience rather than claiming every first idea was right.
blocks.speaker: Guest 3

blocks.question: What deserves the same intentional planning as a career?
answer: Another guest would invest more in friendships, romantic relationships, and life outside work. The imbalance concerned attention and optimization as well as working hours: he planned career goals carefully but did not apply similar effort to the rest of life. Moving to Los Angeles and developing friendships outside the technology bubble changed that. His work continued to go well, while stronger mutual support, including friends willing to help him move, made life more fulfilling.
blocks.speaker: Guest 4

blocks.question: How can a combination of ordinary strengths become distinctive?
answer: A guest who admired specialists in design and engineering worried that being only moderately strong across several areas would not work. His actual advantage was negotiating across those areas. He would focus less on being the best at a single discipline and more on the unusual combination he could bring.

He would also be braver about sharing ideas. His fear of public speaking at school contrasted sharply with his comfort pitching a product he cared about. Explaining material as a test of knowledge made him anxious; advocating for a change he wanted to create gave him a different purpose. Passion did not magically remove every challenge, but it changed what speaking meant to him.
blocks.speaker: Guest 5

blocks.question: What would you keep and change about a career spent in fast-growing companies?
answer: This guest would keep choosing growth. He compares his career ladder with an escalator: personal effort mattered, but the companies’ expansion also carried opportunities upward. He would change how late he recognized that jobs involve other humans. Expertise and correctness should be paired with relationships, friendship, and a reputation. Introversion need not prevent this; writing and online tools can build connections in a comfortable format. He recalls Amazon approaching him for a job as an example of the value of being known.
blocks.speaker: Guest 6

blocks.question: What matters beyond being the person who writes requested code?
answer: Addressing his younger self as Dwayne, this guest would ask how anyone knows that a requested implementation is the right thing to build. He would seek participation in those decisions, instead of defining his value only by what he can type. That wider role would have helped counter his early imposter syndrome and clarify that ideas and judgment can matter more than raw output.
blocks.speaker: Dwayne

blocks.question: How would you become more courageous without pretending embarrassment disappears?
answer: Addressing himself as Brian, the next guest would be more courageous and less embarrassed by failure. He immediately qualifies the short advice as the beginning of a larger conversation about understanding feelings, not a command that makes them vanish. He thinks being more in touch with emotion, possibly through therapy, can help both the person and their relationships.
blocks.speaker: Brian

followups.question: Is that easier said than done when embarrassment is something you simply feel?
answer: Yes. He agrees and says the two-sentence advice would need deeper discussion of the feelings and how to understand them. He does not supply a complete technique for eliminating embarrassment.

blocks.question: How do you choose an environment that values your strengths?
answer: Another guest says a strong front-end engineer can struggle on a back-end team, or a person who loves improving frameworks can receive poor results on a team focused on product delivery. Activity alone is insufficient: even hundreds of changes may not serve the team’s priorities. Recognize a persistent mismatch and seek a team and management chain that need what you are good at. The principle is fit between strengths and valued work, rather than simply doing more of a strength in any environment.
blocks.speaker: Guest 9

blocks.question: What if a difficult technical area is intimidating?
answer: The next guest encourages trying instead of treating others’ current ability as a permanent barrier. They may be better now, but sustained interest and continued effort can build competence. His framing is encouraging and informal: computers are learnable, and liking the work is a useful starting point.
blocks.speaker: Guest 10

blocks.question: What should guide you when an organization’s inherited practices seem strange?
answer: The final guest recommends common sense. Large companies can have misaligned incentives and processes retained mainly because they have always existed. Startups also need judgment about what markets and users actually want. He would trust and develop that practical judgment rather than assume organizational convention has already answered the problem.
blocks.speaker: Guest 11

sections.title: Discover performance gaps while you can still act
sections.deck: An Amazon principal engineer describes the limits of stack ranking and recommends explicit, early conversations about role expectations.

blocks.question: How many people does Amazon expect to manage out?
answer: The guest declines to give an exact figure. Five or six percent appears as a hypothetical illustration, not a disclosed quota. In his account, guidance became more of a mandate in recent years, while a lack of backfills made repeated cuts more troubling.

He acknowledges the limits of his perspective as someone who considers himself a high performer: he has participated in decisions but cannot fully represent the experience of fearing dismissal. He stresses that performance conversations concern real people and emotionally consequential outcomes.

With ordinary backfilling, he could view some departures as an exit from a cultural mismatch. Without replacement, repeated cuts reach people who would previously have been considered strong enough. He was surprised by colleagues who lost their jobs and is particularly uneasy about applying percentages to very small management populations.

followups.question: Does repeated stack ranking begin to remove people who are doing good work?
answer: Yes, that is his concern. A repeated six-percent illustration applies to the remaining group each time; it is not simply three times six percent of the original population. As the group shrinks, people near the middle may be affected. The transcript does not supply enough data to infer a company-wide policy or actual cumulative rate.

blocks.question: What happens in performance discussions, and how does a senior IC participate?
answer: Senior engineers begin to be pulled in, and L7 or higher participants are regularly involved in his account. He describes lengthy meetings that can reduce people to metrics and feedback. He does not disclose the detailed process, but says it is not a simple linear algorithm. Time tends to concentrate on the edges of the distribution rather than allocate equal discussion to every person, partly because the population is too large.

blocks.question: What advice would you give engineers near the performance boundary?
answer: He dislikes treating a difficult fit as proof that the person is inherently a low performer. Passing a demanding interview already suggests considerable ability; the company’s expectations, culture, and the person’s assumptions may simply differ.

His advice is to identify the specific dimension on which expectations are not being met, then work toward solid performance before targeting exceptional ratings or promotion. Ask the manager directly what the expectations are and whether you meet them. If something is missing, agree early on a concrete improvement plan.

He views this as proactive growth rather than waiting for a formal performance-improvement process. The point is to discover actionable information while there is still time to respond. His estimate that few engineers explicitly ask about expectations is an impression, not a measured survey.

followups.question: Should someone literally ask for a proactive PIP?
answer: He would not use those words. The useful request is for clarity and a plan: what does the manager expect, is it happening, and what should change?

followups.question: Isn’t meeting expectations obvious advice?
answer: He thinks the missing step is often asking explicitly. Engineers may guess the standards rather than hear them from the manager. Even an uncomfortable answer that performance is falling short is better than remaining unaware.

followups.question: Why seek bad news early?
answer: A problem surfaced early in a career or review cycle gives someone a fighting chance to address it. Discovering the same issue shortly before a review leaves little room to act. He attributes the saying about early bad news being merely news to a colleague, without claiming certainty about its original source.

blocks.title: Turn uncertainty into an early improvement conversation

steps.title: Ask the standard
steps.text: What are your expectations for my role?

steps.title: Ask the assessment
steps.text: Am I meeting those expectations?

steps.title: Identify the gap
steps.text: Which specific dimension is holding me back?

steps.title: Agree the next steps
steps.text: Create a plan while there is time to improve.

blocks.caption: Editorial synthesis. Arrows show the sequence of the guest’s suggested conversation; they do not guarantee a particular review outcome.
