sections.title: Carey Nachenberg: From Symantec Fellow to Google X, Project Taste, and Imposter Syndrome
sections.deck: Nachenberg says that choosing impactful projects, focusing on other people's outcomes, communicating well and leaving jobs once learning stops mattered more to his career than raw intelligence, and that imposter syndrome held him back.

blocks.text: Nachenberg, a former Symantec fellow who later worked at Google X, Chronicle and Lyft and now teaches at UCLA, argues that career growth owes far more to project taste, focus on other people's outcomes, and communication than to raw intelligence. He traces his own rise at Symantec to choosing impactful projects nobody had assigned. He says imposter syndrome and a loss of confidence kept him in a comfortable job too long and later held him back at Google. The conversation ends with his views on how large language models (LLMs) change teaching, software engineering and product work, and with the advice he would give his younger self.
blocks.heading: Impact, outcomes and communication outweigh raw intelligence

blocks.question: Can you give the high-level story of your time at Symantec and how you grew to fellow?
answer: Nachenberg started in about 1992 as an intern at the Peter Norton Group, which Symantec later acquired. He thinks he was the first intern there and says the company had no desk for him, so he worked in the QA lab. By the time he left in 2016, he had gone from the most junior person to the most senior engineer at Symantec.

followups.question: Did you set out to work in cyber security, or did it happen by chance?
answer: By chance. Nachenberg first worked on a file-management utility, not security. In his third internship, Symantec bought an antivirus product and renamed it Norton Antivirus. The team that analyzed computer viruses needed an intern, and he was placed there with no experience.
followups.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.question: What did the career ladder look like at Symantec, and how did hiring work for someone as senior as you when you joined Google?
answer: Nachenberg says the levels tracked those at Google and Meta from junior engineer up to staff. They differed at the top, with distinguished engineer and fellow at Symantec. Google told him it could not hire a fellow without knowing how he would perform there. He was effectively downgraded to principal engineer, level 8, from what he says would have been about a level 10 and a vice president role at Symantec.

followups.question: Was your hiring process tailored to your seniority?
answer: Yes. Nachenberg did not apply. A former Symantec chief operating officer had moved into Google X, where a stealth project was starting, and invited him to talk to the team. He had a meet and greet with the founders in Venice, then about eight interviews in a day. He had an offer letter roughly six weeks later.
followups.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

followups.question: Did that loop include LeetCode-style coding, or was it mostly behavioral?
answer: Nachenberg does not recall any coding problems and thinks there was one design problem. Most questions were leadership-style: how he solved a hard problem, how he handles conflict, and where the field is going. Some sessions were effectively sales pitches about where Google X thought the world was heading. He believes the team already thought he was a good fit, so the day was mostly about going through the motions and selling him on the role.
followups.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.question: What do promotions at the highest levels look like?
answer: At Symantec, Nachenberg says, promotions up to senior technical director were handled within the organization, provided a vice president or senior vice president agreed. Distinguished engineer and fellow went to a core group of technologists led by the chief technology officer. The group met quarterly, reviewed applications, and had candidates present their work. The aim was a consistent bar across the whole company, not division by division.

followups.question: Was your promotion to fellow a big moment, or something you expected?
answer: Nachenberg skipped that process. After Symantec merged with Veritas, which already had a fellow role, the company needed to set the level. He was nominated without his knowledge, his portfolio was passed to the evaluators, and he was told he was a fellow.
followups.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.question: What set you apart from other engineers on the way to fellow?
answer: Nachenberg credits impactful projects, not always the most technically difficult ones. He looked for gaps: things the company needed that no one was stepping up to do. Symantec in his early years was, in his words, the wild west, with no agile process and no engineers testing their own code. He was never handed a boxed-in project. Because he already knew the technology as an intern, he was told to work out what to do and do it, and he says he chose projects that landed, shipped and transferred into the product.

followups.question: How did you train your project taste?
answer: Nachenberg says he looks for large business impact and for gaps. His example was polymorphic viruses, which mutated themselves into huge numbers of variants. Teams hand-wrote assembly to catch each variant, a process that took six months because the product shipped twice a year. New variants appeared the next day. He saw a need to respond faster, noted that such threats could not be found by searching for a string, and picked the problem. It became his master's thesis and then a product feature.
followups.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

followups.question: Was your career a series of self-chosen side projects?
answer: Partly. Nachenberg says that perhaps six or seven times he spotted a company need and spent from six weeks to five months on prototypes and talking to engineers. About 80 percent of his career was then incremental work on those systems, such as helping transfer the technology into products, fixing bugs and improving them.
followups.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.question: Can you tell the story of Stuxnet, which you used in talks?
answer: Nachenberg calls Stuxnet unfathomable for its time: probably the first multiplatform malware discovered, reaching Windows machines and the controllers that ran centrifuge frequency converters. He recalls it used about six vulnerabilities, many of them unpatched zero-days. It hid itself on a USB drive, auto-launched, and hid its own logic on the controller. If someone downloaded the controller logic, it removed itself from the copy. If they uploaded updated logic, it reinserted itself.

followups.question: Who do you think wrote it, and did you analyze the code?
answer: Nachenberg says it is fairly safe to say the Israeli and American governments, and he recalls coding styles that implicate both. He stresses he did not analyze Stuxnet himself. Early in his career he disassembled malware by hand, but later he built algorithms to detect it.
followups.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

followups.question: Did you write assembly at Symantec?
answer: As an intern, yes, though most code was in C. The first antivirus engines were in assembly for speed. Nachenberg ported one to C after joining full time. It had less code and ran about five times faster, he says, because the original developers did not know algorithms. In his example, hash tables or binary search replace a linear scan over about 60,000 signatures, with no help from an optimizing compiler.
followups.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.question: What kept you at Symantec for so long?
answer: Nachenberg says, honestly, imposter syndrome. At Symantec he felt secure because he was well known there. He worried that his success came from having grown up in that company, and that he might not be good enough for Google or Meta. He stayed because it was comfortable and he complained a lot. Near the end he was unhappy, since senior roles bring more meetings and less building, which he describes as a lot of BS.

followups.question: What helped you overcome it?
answer: An outside pull. Someone at Google X said they wanted to interview him. Nachenberg was sure he would fail but went ahead. He says he needed that push to take the chance, and it worked out.
followups.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

followups.question: How do you avoid the BS at senior levels?
answer: Nachenberg says some senior people stay hands-on, but as an individual-contributor vice president he found the strategy meetings inevitable. They bring many opinions, debate and power posturing. His best moments were picking his own projects and going two months with no one asking what he was doing. He gives one example: he wrote Symantec's technology strategy and the CEO agreed with it, but product teams then objected because of revenue targets. He calls those debates draining.
followups.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.question: What was Google X like, and were there cultural differences?
answer: Fewer than expected, Nachenberg says. The main difference was the quality of the people, who were very smart, whereas Symantec lacked an engineering culture, at least until it began to form around 2016. What was the same was that many people lacked project taste. They were smart, but he doubted they picked projects that would land or were feasible. He says this is true of engineers at any company.

followups.question: Why was one very bright colleague still at a low level?
answer: Nachenberg describes a colleague he judged astoundingly brilliant who was still at L4. He says the reasons were weak communication, work that interested the colleague but had little business impact, and apparently poor collaboration. He concludes that intelligence alone does not guarantee success.
followups.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

followups.question: If intelligence matters less, what matters more?
answer: Nachenberg says a baseline is needed and that most Google engineers had it. He does not consider himself especially intelligent and says he learns slowly. Beyond that baseline he names communication and collaboration, including getting what you need from people without telling them they are wrong. He admits he has not mastered this and has failed at it. The big one, he says, is focusing on outcomes: engineers naturally focus on their own, such as making something 10 percent faster, but the company or another team has different outcomes. Identify those, the metrics behind them, and the few requirements that matter most, and he says that will take you much further than intelligence.
followups.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

followups.question: Is career growth in industry meritocratic?
answer: By and large, yes, in Nachenberg's experience. He saw exceptions where a senior vice president pushed a promotion mainly to retain someone, which he says damages standards. The committees he sat on weighed the complexity and impact of work, communication and patents. He also found Google's discussions careful and fair. In his view senior levels required being well rounded, or at least very strong in some areas.
followups.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.question: How did Chronicle begin inside Google X, and what did its product do?
answer: Nachenberg says it started as the stealth Project Lantern, with no fixed product. The team spent about six months deciding what to build, then built prototypes and an MVP. Before the product existed, they sat in customer security teams and watched where they struggled, which he found very useful.

The product, Backstory, treated security as a big-data problem. Firewalls, web proxies, DHCP and email systems produce huge logs. Nachenberg says a competing product forced customers to ingest a small fraction of that data and wait about 30 minutes per query. Chronicle ingested petabytes and indexed them, so an analyst could enter a file hash, IP address or file name and see affected devices and first and last infiltration in about two seconds. Nachenberg worked on the indexing.

followups.question: Why did Chronicle spin out and then return to Google?
answer: Nachenberg says X aims to incubate viable businesses, give strong teams freedom and spin them out. He says he can only guess at why Chronicle came back, and that it fit Google Cloud as a storage- and compute-heavy cloud service. After the spin-out it stayed under Alphabet, like Waymo. One benefit was one-page performance reviews in a slide, instead of Google's long written packets.
followups.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.question: Why did you eventually leave Google?
answer: Nachenberg again cites imposter syndrome, plus a wish to work at a startup instead of a slower, more regulated environment. He says there were big problems he could have taken on, such as moving Chronicle's expensive storage design off heavyweight systems like Spanner. He lacked the confidence to try. Expectations at senior levels are high, and at Google he did not feel leadership would back him if a months-long attempt did not land. At Symantec his managers had known him for years and gave him rope. He was offered other roles, such as secure databases that compute on encrypted data. He wanted something new, and talks with Waymo people while at X had made him want to work on self-driving cars.

followups.question: Did you consider asking for a demotion to reduce the pressure?
answer: Not at Symantec, where he could do what he liked. He thought about it at Google but concluded it would not help. Even at lower levels, he says, there are expectations he might not meet if he went off for a couple of months to think, which is how he had been most successful. He calls himself a loosey-goosey prototyper who does not enjoy testing every edge case. Google expects that, so he would have had to do things he disliked to do the things he wanted.
followups.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.question: How did you get hired into autonomous vehicles at Lyft?
answer: A former UCLA student who worked at Lyft urged Nachenberg to apply. He doubted they would hire him. He had tried to move to Waymo from X and had not been taken, which he attributes to being senior, expensive and without domain expertise. The student arranged a meeting with Lyft's president, followed by seven or eight interviews that included some coding and design. He says there was no dynamic programming, which he says he would fail, and he was hired.
blocks.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.question: What project at Lyft were you most proud of?
answer: Nachenberg says Lyft used the classic robotics architecture of hand-written decision algorithms with hand-tuned parameters, with neural networks used only for perception. He thought that was a dead end, citing conflicts such as switching from a lane-change routine to an avoidance routine, and parameters that interact in unpredictable ways. He says Tesla used the approach until recently.

He designed, with the team's old-school roboticists, an architecture that could host an end-to-end neural-network driver inside a safety layer. In his account the layer takes precedence, preventing collisions, stopping safely and following legal rules the network might miss. He guesses Waymo now uses end-to-end networks too, but says he does not know. He says the work was mostly influence, since he had no robotics degree and the roboticists resisted. They defined the approach together so that they could own it.

followups.question: How do you make sure you get credit for shared work?
answer: Nachenberg says he lacks a good recipe and was not credited for this project; he says someone else took credit. He advises juniors to take notes when a project ends, recording accomplishments and metrics, which are hard to recall later. When writing a review, state what you did and its value without embellishing, and claim only your own parts, because committees notice overclaiming and it costs credibility. At senior levels it is harder, he says, because the work is soft power. He did not push his own credit so as not to alienate collaborators, and at review time he learned the team's manager was seen as having initiated the project. He says it still bothers him.
followups.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

followups.question: What was Lyft's plan to win in self-driving?
answer: Nachenberg says it was not clear that there was a strategy. Lyft's effort was young compared with the roughly decade-long work at Google X and Waymo. He joined to learn and work with smart people, not to beat Waymo. The division was eventually sold to a Toyota subsidiary, which received the intellectual property, and he then retired.
followups.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.question: How did you become a lecturer at UCLA, and how do you make your lectures engaging?
answer: Nachenberg taught programming at Learning Tree around 1990 to 1991, including to DeVry staff. He also ran evening whiteboard sessions at UCLA as an undergraduate. Years later, a colleague at Symantec who lectured part time at UCLA told him to apply. Nachenberg assumed his lack of a PhD ruled him out. After months of silence, UCLA called in a panic when a lecturer dropped out, and he had two weeks to plan an undergraduate course. That was about 25 years ago.

For lectures, he designs for roughly the 30th to 50th percentile of the class, and uses himself, a slow learner, as the model. He asks what he would want to know on first meeting a topic, and what students are likely to be fuzzy on. He says he spends days with ChatGPT o3 simplifying concepts, then checks with Gemini and compares differences, because he finds good online material scarce and textbooks poor. He also wants students to enjoy class, so he adds humor, color and surprise.

followups.question: What tips do you have for public speaking?
answer: Practice, says Nachenberg. He finds his own speaking declines within a year of not using it. He suggests giving a lunchroom talk about a project even when nothing requires it. People appreciate it, and you improve. He recalls giving his Stuxnet and malware talk privately inside X, after which colleagues said he was one of the smartest people they had met. He says people read good communication as intelligence, and it brings credit and opportunities.
followups.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.question: Are students cheating more with LLMs, and are they learning less?
answer: Nachenberg says last fall he allowed LLMs for autocomplete and simple, peripheral parts of projects. In retrospect he considers it a mistake, because students used them for much more than that. He saw large gaps between perfect project scores and poor exam results. He mentions a recent study on reduced brain connectivity when people use LLMs, but says he forgets the numbers. This fall he plans to allow LLMs for clarifying concepts, but not for projects.

He says plagiarism software compares every project with every other one, and LLM use shows up as shared word-for-word error messages, variable names and idioms. He adds that the latest models could probably earn about 95 percent on the projects, with poor code, because the course grades correctness, not code quality.
blocks.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.question: Should people still get a software engineering degree as LLMs automate the work?
answer: Nachenberg says it depends on how the models develop, and he describes two scenarios. In the first, models stay very good but short of what he calls AGI programming: they solve tightly specified sub-problems and write tests, but need supervision on choices such as the algorithm used or a deep versus shallow copy. In that world, he says, software engineering stays a great field. Someone must read the code, understand the company's mission and standards, and decide what to fix. He thinks the ability to read and write code is valuable. He acknowledges that jobs are down now, probably partly because of LLMs.
In the second scenario, an AI could take on an L5-level project that takes weeks and do it correctly and securely. He says all bets are off in that world and the required skills differ.

followups.question: What skills would matter in that second world?
answer: Nachenberg says engineers, or perhaps no longer engineers, would focus on what to build and why, not how. The best would deeply understand a customer's pains and how the customer measures success, then communicate those requirements clearly to an LLM. Clarification and outcome analysis would be the key skills. He expects big companies to remain, but thousands of smaller companies to serve niches such as pet sitters and doggy daycares, built by domain experts with these tools.
followups.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

followups.question: Is that essentially a product manager, with the LLM as the engineering team?
answer: Yes, Nachenberg says, a competent product manager, though he says he has met very few. In his view competence means understanding customer outcomes and the metrics customers use, using methods such as jobs to be done or outcome-driven innovation. His own example is that he drools when brushing his teeth, and the mess is a metric by which he would judge a toothbrush. He says many product managers think in features and copy competitors instead of finding what customers struggle with, how often, and whether it matters. He also holds that empathy can be a repeatable process built on interviews and observation. He allows that there may be exceptions.
followups.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.question: Looking back, is there anything you regret or would change?
answer: Nachenberg says he should have left Symantec earlier. His rule is to stay while you are learning, building skills and feel free to fail occasionally. He lost that at Symantec, but stayed because he lacked confidence, not because the work interested him. He still values staying five or even ten years as long as you learn. Switching teams can keep a good reputation and institutional knowledge. Staying too long makes you stale and comfortable.

He also notes the cost of leaving. At Symantec he was widely known and appeared on TV and in major newspapers about Stuxnet. At Google nobody cared what he had done before, so he had to rebuild trust and reputation, which is stressful.

followups.question: What about golden handcuffs, where you earn well but no longer learn?
answer: Nachenberg would never say to leave a good package. People need different amounts of money to feel safe, and people balance several things. Being comfortable and well paid for a while can be fine. But for someone who is solving for enjoyment and hard problems, he thinks too long in that state can become toxic.
followups.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.question: How can someone find what they enjoy in software engineering?
answer: Nachenberg advises students to try many internships, though he acknowledges jobs are tough now and the market is cyclical. He found cyber security by chance, through three different internships. He says jobs that sound boring can turn out to contain interesting problems, good colleagues and interesting customers. His advice is not to wait for the perfect job, but to find a good manager, hard problems and room to learn, which might lead to a 25-year career.

followups.question: Is the approach to search broadly first, then go deep?
answer: Yes, Nachenberg says. But if a first-year internship is interesting and going well, he would stay with it. He calls the approach a greedy breadth search.
followups.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.question: If you could advise yourself on graduating from UCLA, what would you say?
answer: Nachenberg says there is no single item. First, do not let fear of failure hold you back. You can probably do more than you think, and he says he might have had a richer career had he listened. Second, focus on outcomes: who will use the work, what they care about and how they measure success. Problems often need a small square piece, not a perfect round thing.

He says he once presented technology to senior leaders, who did not care how the algorithm worked. They wanted to know whether it was faster, by how much, and what it meant for revenue or headcount. Speak to their needs, not your own. Third, find a good manager who trusts you and gives you rope, since a manager can make or break your career and happiness. Fourth, learn to collaborate and not assume you are right and tell others they are wrong. He says he still struggles with this.
blocks.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

sections.title: Choose the staff role with its responsibilities in view
sections.deck: Ricky explains a fast Google promotion path built on ownership and measurable impact, while questioning whether faster advancement always improves daily life.

blocks.question: What was the overall promotion and compensation timeline?
answer: Ricky joined Google as a new graduate in 2017 after an internship. He reports approximately $180,000 annual compensation plus a signing bonus, then promotion to L4 after a year and a half at about $250,000, L5 after another year and a half at roughly $350,000, and L6 three years later at roughly $500,000–$520,000. The amounts are retrospective figures from his own situation, including equity effects, rather than current compensation guarantees.

He credits a fortunate team match and considers reaching senior in three years faster than the typical path he observed. Staff took longer and involved a different kind of responsibility. The career story combines his deliberate work with opportunities he did not control.
blocks.speaker: Ricky

blocks.question: What happened in the junior-to-midlevel promotion process?
answer: In the review system Ricky describes, ratings arrived every six months. He first met expectations, then exceeded them, and received a still stronger rating alongside promotion. He believed his impact and independence matched the next level but worried that short tenure might count against him. His manager supported the attempt.
blocks.speaker: Ricky

followups.question: Who should initiate promotion discussions?
answer: He recommends employee initiative supported by an ongoing conversation with the manager. He regularly asked whether his current projects demonstrated the next level and aligned expectations about timing and scope. Managing upward made an accelerated path more deliberate; it was not a promotion that arrived without discussion.
followups.speaker: Ricky

blocks.question: What behavior made the first promotion possible?
answer: Independence: finishing projects with less handholding and finding ways to unblock himself. This did not mean refusing to ask anyone for help. It meant learning enough to move the project without requiring the manager to solve every obstacle.
blocks.speaker: Ricky

followups.question: How did you become better at unblocking yourself?
answer: He deliberately asked questions despite fearing he would look incompetent. His alternative was worse: staying silent, learning nothing, and failing to deliver. Colleagues generally wanted him to succeed. Asking the knowledgeable engineer helped him learn to do the work himself.

They recommend a real attempt before asking, but not remaining motionless for half a day or longer. Repeatedly asking the same question or receiving the same code-review feedback without improvement is different from healthy learning. The desired pattern is increasing independence and fewer repeated mistakes over time.
followups.speaker: Ricky

blocks.question: What changed when working toward senior?
answer: He became the owner and go-to person for a defined area, learning its code and delivering several impactful projects there. Ownership meant being able to answer questions and advance the area, not merely shipping more isolated changes.
blocks.speaker: Ricky

followups.question: Did you choose the area through an explicit promotion plan?
answer: At first he simply found a part of the advertising experience visually unappealing and interesting to improve. The improvements could also produce measurable impact. Repeated projects and exploration gradually made him the owner, rather than a manager initially assigning a complete senior-level charter.
followups.speaker: Ricky

followups.question: Did you have to compete for that scope?
answer: His team allowed engineers to choose many of their own projects. He sought work with meaningful impact and enough challenge to extend his skills. He recognizes that managers may assign useful work too, but relying only on assignments would not necessarily supply the scope needed for his desired growth.
followups.speaker: Ricky

blocks.question: How did you recognize projects that were genuinely at the next level?
answer: He studied teammates’ successful senior promotions to understand the scope and complexity expected, generated comparable ideas, and asked his manager to calibrate them. Roughly a year before his promotion he proposed a roadmap and asked whether completing it would meet the bar.

This gave the manager something concrete to assess and made the growth plan explicit. The roadmap emerged after approximately six months of exploration following L4, rather than immediately on the day of that promotion.
blocks.speaker: Ricky

followups.question: When did you put that roadmap together?
answer: After the midlevel promotion he tried different projects and learned what interested him. He then wrote the one-year plan himself and sought managerial buy-in. Exploration preceded the more committed roadmap.
followups.speaker: Ricky

blocks.question: What did you do when requested work did not advance that roadmap?
answer: He learned to say no to unrelated projects that consumed time without helping him grow. He distinguishes that from accountability: a bug he caused, or a bug within his owned area, still needed attention. A new request could also be worth accepting if its impact and scope were stronger than the existing plan.
blocks.speaker: Ricky

followups.question: How can someone say no without damaging the relationship?
answer: For an outside request he would bring the tradeoff to his manager and understand why it was assigned. For the manager’s own request he would ask whether it was required and explain the competing projects’ impact and growth value. This is a discussion of priorities, not a license to ignore obligations.

He believes managers should try to match important work with reports’ growth and interests. His own early record of finding and delivering projects earned trust, although the manager continued to guide which ideas were useful.
followups.speaker: Ricky

blocks.question: How did you learn which ideas would have impact?
answer: First define what the organization values. In his advertising area, revenue was a central metric, alongside whether the work helped users, advertisers, and publishers. Other teams might care about active users or product interactions. Running experiments exposed gaps where improvements could move the relevant outcome.

He found measurable results persuasive in arguments about project value. His emphatic statement that numbers settle the matter belongs to his experience in a revenue-measured area; it should not be treated as a claim that every engineering contribution is captured by one number.
blocks.speaker: Ricky

blocks.question: How did the senior promotion itself feel?
answer: It felt more uncertain than the first promotion. Ricky believed he was ahead of the timing commonly observed around him and worried that the committee might want a longer record of next-level work. His manager supported submitting while setting realistic expectations that it could fail. It succeeded on the first attempt, which Ricky describes as fortunate.
blocks.speaker: Ricky

blocks.question: Were there growing pains in becoming a leader?
answer: Yes. Handing project ideas to junior engineers made him anxious about whether experiments would succeed; some did not. He had to become comfortable with a portfolio of ideas rather than expect every one to work. A comparatively good success rate, mentoring, and positive influence on other people’s projects supported the case, while confidence developed through practice.
blocks.speaker: Ricky

blocks.question: Did you feel stuck waiting for staff?
answer: Rather than wishing it had arrived sooner, he sometimes wishes the opportunity came later. Senior offered more flexibility for breaks and personal activities, whereas broader projects created meetings and a more rigid schedule. He advises looking at the actual calendars and work of nearby staff engineers before deciding the trade is desirable.
blocks.speaker: Ricky

followups.question: Is staff required by an up-or-out policy?
answer: In the Google context he describes, senior engineers could stay at senior without an expectation to advance to staff. He is less sure about whether the same applies at midlevel. He frames staff as a choice to take on more responsibility rather than an obligatory badge of success.
followups.speaker: Ricky

blocks.question: What was the biggest difference between your senior and staff work?
answer: At senior he knew and owned a space and delivered projects within it. Toward staff he challenged the boundaries of that space, questioned the established direction, and guided consequential decisions across teams and functions. Some changes required senior-leadership buy-in. Knowing an area became a platform for shaping where it should go, rather than only operating effectively inside it.
blocks.speaker: Ricky

blocks.question: How did you find the anchor project for staff?
answer: Deep familiarity made him question practices that no longer made sense. In one example, established user research supported a conclusion but product experiments contradicted it. He pushed the evidence that another direction could produce greater impact. He does not disclose the specific product decision, so the lesson remains about examining assumptions and reconciling conflicting evidence rather than a reproducible advertising tactic.
blocks.speaker: Ricky

blocks.question: How did you influence other teams and partners?
answer: He had developed a reputation for finding impactful projects. He shared ideas, collaborated without trying to displace others, and turned proposals into projects that launched successfully. Relationships and repeated results gave his judgment weight.
blocks.speaker: Ricky

followups.question: Did your previous results make that easier?
answer: Yes. Trust would have been harder to build if the projects repeatedly failed. Staying in the same organization let colleagues accumulate evidence of his work, whereas a new senior hire would need to establish that record. Ricky is cautious about the host’s description of him as a rising star but agrees that past successes made his proposals more credible.
followups.speaker: Ricky

blocks.question: Why did you want to try management?
answer: He already enjoyed helping colleagues grow, finding projects for them, and seeing them succeed. A formal management opportunity appeared after he had expressed that interest, and the team supported it. Fulfillment in developing others was the principal motivation.
blocks.speaker: Ricky

followups.question: Did the manager closely vet your motivation first?
answer: He does not remember a formal process of that kind. He had raised the aspiration earlier, and the right opportunity eventually appeared. Becoming a manager young felt awkward at times.
followups.speaker: Ricky

followups.question: What did feeling insufficiently mature mean?
answer: He felt younger than the more experienced managers around him and encountered an unfamiliar social-boundary issue when seeing reports at a music festival while drunk. He thinks it was probably fine, but it illustrated situations he had not anticipated before taking the role.
followups.speaker: Ricky

followups.question: Was there prior management experience or a structured preparation path?
answer: He does not describe prior formal management experience and was surprised by how much learning happened after entering the role. Google had many resources, but he had expected a more structured guide to becoming effective. The earlier discussion of informal mentoring should not be mistaken for having already held the full manager job.
followups.speaker: Ricky

blocks.question: What changed most between IC leadership and management?
answer: Technical leadership supplied enjoyable elements of helping people succeed. Formal management added difficult performance feedback, review writing, and calibration overhead. At the same time, seeing an actual report get promoted felt especially rewarding because he had direct responsibility for supporting that growth.
blocks.speaker: Ricky

blocks.question: Do you regret becoming a manager?
answer: He mainly wishes it had happened later. In an unusual period with around twenty new hires, he was informally helping many of them; becoming the formal manager of four narrowed that responsibility and gave some time back. Nevertheless, he would have liked a few more years of senior-level flexibility and lower stress.

He now better understands what higher-level work entails: much of the influence is through other people, so meetings increase whether one is an IC or manager. A nine-to-five calendar can still be an intensely committed day with little discretion about naps or gym trips. Ryan adds that fragmented daytime meetings pushed his own technical work into evenings after reaching staff. The title’s appeal should be assessed against its daily experience.
blocks.speaker: Ricky

blocks.question: Was the staff promotion different from the previous applications?
answer: He again felt uncertain despite sustained top ratings. Moving from senior to staff could feel like a job change: being an exceptional senior with high impact did not automatically prove readiness for the broader role. A supportive manager and a successful first submission made the outcome fortunate.
blocks.speaker: Ricky

followups.question: Did every promotion succeed on the first attempt?
answer: Yes. He did not experience a rejection-and-resubmission cycle at any of these stages and repeatedly acknowledges the luck in that record.
followups.speaker: Ricky

blocks.question: Could you repeat that career path, or did luck explain much of it?
answer: He benefited from enjoying the team he was matched into, organizational stability, and managers able to support him. Reorganizations, poor fit, or a manager’s absence could have delayed otherwise good work. He separates the chance that an opportunity appears from being prepared to use it. Effort helped with the second; it did not fully control the first.
blocks.speaker: Ricky

followups.question: How much was ability and how much luck?
answer: He offers a rough fifty-fifty impression rather than a measured estimate. He feels confident he would eventually have reached senior with continued growth and effort, but another team might have required a move and a new ramp-up. His speed depended on the unusually good fit. Ryan notes that even a stronger engineer can struggle in an organization with repeated disruption.
followups.speaker: Ricky

blocks.question: Why stay at Google for seven years?
answer: He regularly reassessed whether he enjoyed the work and whether the team still offered what he wanted: growth, travel, and work that was sufficiently interesting. Staying was an active decision, not proof that he never considered alternatives. He also acknowledges survivorship bias: people without comparable growth or fit might have had good reasons to leave.

Ryan describes the accumulated advantage of staying in a healthy setting: relationships, code knowledge, and organizational context can expand from expertise in one area to many. That momentum can enable unusually fast growth, while changing employers can offer other benefits. They do not reduce the choice to a universal rule about job hopping.
blocks.speaker: Ricky

blocks.question: What advice would you give your new-graduate self?
answer: Trust his judgment more and try boundary-pushing ideas earlier. Anxiety made him postpone ideas he later pursued successfully. He believes earlier confidence could have reduced stress and enabled more experimentation, though he developed it gradually through results and good feedback.
blocks.speaker: Ricky

followups.question: Was the impostor feeling about technical ability?
answer: He worried that he had been hired for personality rather than ability because his interview and internship had not felt spectacular. At low levels he also lacked a way to judge his own performance. Repeated reassurance that he was doing fine did not answer his internal question of whether that meant barely passing or excelling. Successful projects and collaboration eventually supplied more convincing evidence.
followups.speaker: Ricky

sections.title: David Fowler: Microsoft Promotions, Permissionless Projects, and the Distinguished Engineer Path
sections.deck: Microsoft distinguished engineer David Fowler explains how building prototypes without permission, learning to delegate, and focusing on impact over cleverness carried him from intern to distinguished engineer.

blocks.text: David Fowler, a Microsoft distinguished engineer, tells the host that his climb from intern to distinguished engineer came from building working prototypes without waiting for permission, then learning to scale through other people instead of through his own typing. In Fowler's account, impact matters more than cleverness at every level, mentors who are blunt about how promotion decisions get made are worth seeking out, and several habits that carry an engineer to senior can block the move beyond it. The talk also covers debugging, the culture change after Satya Nadella became CEO, and why Fowler stayed at one company. Everything below is Fowler's account of his own experience unless marked as an editorial note.
blocks.heading: Fowler's view: build things, scale through others, and let impact drive promotion

blocks.question: How does Microsoft's leveling system work, given that levels run upward from 59 with about two levels per title?
answer: Fowler says he cannot explain why numbering starts at 59, and guesses the lower levels cover non-engineering roles. A college graduate typically starts at 59 or 60, depending on how many times they interned and how well they did. Fowler equates entry level with an SDE I at other companies.

A title maps to a band of about two levels, so a title does not reveal which level someone holds. Principal is the exception at three levels, and Fowler says that band is so broad that a new arrival from senior and a long-serving principal share a title. Above principal come the partner levels, which Fowler says have three bands, and then technical fellow.
blocks.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.question: How did you end up at Microsoft?
answer: Fowler grew up in Barbados and left at 18 for Florida Tech, chosen partly because it held career fairs and was one flight from home. He started in computer engineering, decided after the first class that it was not for him because he wanted to code, and switched to computer science. He had been coding since about age ten, and was surprised that no one in the first Java class knew how to code.

Fowler and a close friend built games on nights and weekends. To stand out at their first career fair, they brought a laptop with a game demo. That produced about four internship offers. Fowler chose Microsoft over GE and smaller Florida firms, and the friend went to EA. After campus interviews and an in-person whiteboard round, he interned in 2006 and 2007, which he found eye-opening.

followups.question: What was it like going to Bill Gates's house as an intern?
answer: Fowler says every intern group traditionally ended the summer there, and he was in the last set to go. Interns had phones taken and were bused in from a church parking area. He was chatting when a rush of interns ran toward him, and Gates was standing behind him. Fowler shook Gates's hand and says they spoke once.
followups.speaker: David Fowler

followups.question: What did the Microsoft interview process look like in 2006?
answer: Fowler says Microsoft was known for puzzle questions, citing the book How Would You Move Mount Fuji? and the manhole-cover question. His interview began with an easy coding question on paper, then a puzzle about making exactly four gallons from a three-gallon and a five-gallon jug. He had seen the film scene but could not recall the steps, and worked them out. The last question was how to count the gas stations in Florida. He asked whether it was a trick question, was told no, and saw no point. He thought it had gone badly but got a call back.

The host adds that LeetCode-style questions at least relate to the job, and recalls being asked to add two numbers in base negative two. Both agree interviewing has changed a lot, in some ways for the better and in some for the worse.
followups.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.question: What is the story behind NuGet, the .NET package manager?
answer: Fowler says NuGet is now more than ten years old, and its impact today feels jarring compared with its start. The team was building a new web stack to compete with the LAMP stack, and Fowler did not question whether that made sense, because the leaders above him said to do it. Ruby on Rails and its gems had just arrived, and another group was looking at WordPress and Drupal, which also had packages. The consensus was that the platform needed a package manager so people could extend it.

The first version was an in-browser package manager in the style of WordPress. In a meeting with Scott Guthrie, whom Fowler describes as an EVP now, a product manager showed a PowerPoint mockup. Fowler and an architect had already built something and asked whether the team could start from there. That meeting formed the NuGet team: Fowler as first engineer, the architect David Ebbo, and Phil Haack. They also talked with people behind other open-source .NET package managers.
blocks.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.question: What did your performance review look like after NuGet, for someone who was not yet a senior engineer?
answer: Fowler's first promotion came about eight months after joining, before NuGet. Because he had interned twice, he arrived with a lot of Microsoft experience. Beyond assigned work, he read forums for feedback on Microsoft's products, built features to answer it, and showed the results to product managers, architects and the team. Looking back, he says those people became sponsors and positioned him to build NuGet.

Fowler calls himself a code-first, ask-questions-later person and says code is currency: a working sample beats a PowerPoint or a document. A director once told him he would send people to talk to David because David has energy.

followups.question: Did the lasting impact of something like NuGet carry over into later reviews?
answer: Fowler says the bigger promotions felt like accumulated history plus current success. Impact is officially meant to be for the year, and crossing a band boundary, such as to senior or to principal, takes more than moving within a band. He is unsure whether Microsoft has an official deferred-impact rule, but says it clearly mattered at the higher principal levels, where the question was whether he had shown repeated impact over ten years.
followups.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.question: How did SignalR start?
answer: Fowler says the name came from the era when web products dropped letters from their names. The project began on nights and weekends. Google Docs had just appeared, and Fowler was enthralled by smooth co-editing. He set out to build Google Docs for code, did not finish it, but learned about WebSockets, which he says had not shipped yet, and how to build that kind of app.

Damian Edwards, a product manager, was building a talk on long-running streaming apps in .NET. Fowler proposed building a library together. Microsoft allows moonlighting on projects outside official work, so the two worked until midnight and open-sourced it, and people started using it. Later a product manager said it should be made official.

Fowler calls it the first thing built from his own idea, after years of working on other people's ideas. He became a pseudo tech lead without ever being a manager, hired college graduates, and at one point led a team of about eight.

followups.question: What pushed you to give up weekends and late nights for it?
answer: Fowler had not seen anything like it. Google Docs was the first product of its kind to work that well, and Node.js with Socket.IO showed a new way to push data from server to client. The project hit limits deep in the core platform and taught him a lot about the networking stack. He says the volume of problems was like catnip.
followups.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.question: How can others start projects like this within a large company, when the motivation comes entirely from them?
answer: Fowler's one-sentence answer is that you can just do things, which people now call agency. He does not recommend spending every night and weekend on projects, but early on his goal was to get better at software engineering, and the way was to build everything possible: games, websites, many kinds of software.

The second habit was to find someone on the team whose career he wanted. Fowler attached himself to the architect David Ebbo, whose role spanned several areas and looked ahead, copied his behaviors, and for a while coded Ebbo's ideas, which turned into doing it independently. He then built prototypes and showed them to an advocate, the architect or the product manager, to ask whether they were useful. He says he would build a thousand things and maybe one would hit.

followups.question: So agency at a big company came from energy, moonlighting and doing more than the assigned work?
answer: Fowler agrees in part. Once an engineer builds a reputation for building things, more opportunities arrive and people ask for a take on new work. He cautions that this is not guaranteed, but in his case it was clearly true and continued after SignalR.
followups.speaker: David Fowler

followups.question: Is permissionless agency a way to bypass the credibility that permissioned opportunities require?
answer: The host puts it that way, and the exchange adds that a stronger track record earns more room to be permissionless, because each success buys more latitude to fail. The host describes fast-growing engineers as trusted people management lets loose on risky projects, while an engineer struggling to meet expectations gets directed work and monitoring. Fowler agrees.
followups.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.question: What led to the promotion to principal?
answer: Fowler recalls a boss who, when he reached senior, said promotions would slow. The jump to principal turned out to be large. Alongside SignalR, he built Kudu, an early Azure tool that let people push code and deploy an app instantly, as Heroku and AppHarbor did. A director then pulled him onto a new project that became the cross-platform .NET Core.

Fowler was senior, and he and another principal engineer were chosen as architects over about 30 engineers with free rein, which he calls amazing and terrifying. At first he tried to code review every change and was burnt out within a year, and had to learn to trust people and separate urgent from not urgent. He had his first child and was promoted to principal that same year.

followups.question: How did you scale yourself out of necessity so you did not burn out as architect for so many engineers?
answer: Fowler learned the first lessons on SignalR, a team of seven or eight including two new hires. Before that he never delegated to grow someone and assumed he could do the work faster himself. It flipped when he saw that investing in smart new hires would amplify impact even if early tasks took longer. He calls the senior-to-principal leap doing more through others than yourself, and the point where many engineers plateau because they prefer coding alone.

On .NET Core, where he says the team rebuilt the package manager, runtime and libraries from scratch, he stopped treating everything as equally urgent and let people fail. He says traits that get an engineer to senior, such as being a control freak or insisting on one way, hurt when scaling to a thousand engineers. The fix was to inspire others through one-on-ones and example, and to become outcome-focused.
followups.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.question: What does the architect role mean at Microsoft?
answer: Fowler says it is a semi-official role open to the middle principal bands. When he joined, he saw a principal software architect and decided that was the role he wanted. He describes it as breadth over depth: overseeing the design of the whole system. Other archetypes at the top include a super coder who builds enormous amounts, deep specialists such as one of the leading garbage-collection experts working on the .NET collector, and people overseeing a hugely impactful product area.

As architect for ASP.NET Core, he oversaw the web framework, the web server and how packages shipped, vetting decisions that could last 20 years. He had not done this before and learned by shadowing mentors who had.
blocks.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.question: As a distinguished engineer, how has the share of your time spent writing code changed?
answer: Fowler says the job may no longer reward daily coding, but selfishly he codes every day and currently sends many pull requests on a project involving Aspire. He does not want to be an architect who gives instructions without knowing the code and then disappears. He wants to be a peer on the team, facing the builds and the tests.

followups.question: If you stopped coding and only led, would your performance review still look fine?
answer: Fowler thinks so. A distinguished engineer is measured on organization-wide or company-wide impact, so part of the job is keeping the architecture sound, looking ahead, talking publicly, inspiring and mentoring. He gave four internal talks on using AI for software engineering, which began when someone asked after seeing him use it. He argues such talks matter because credible engineers explaining how they work persuade more than a boss giving orders.
followups.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.question: What is the story behind the promotion to distinguished engineer?
answer: Fowler calls it the craziest promotion he has experienced. Distinguished engineer is the last level within partner, and it comes through an official process, not an annual review: a set of technical leaders peer-reviews the candidate. Guido van Rossum, who created Python, is at the same level, and Fowler describes maximum imposter syndrome. He also thought he was young for the role, though that did not count against him.

Fowler says earlier work carried it, because the role requires a body of work and a track record, not one good year. The email promoting him from principal to partner cited .NET Core, by then about seven years old, and he had acted as architect helping many teams adopt the new .NET internally. NuGet and SignalR counted as signals of how what he helped build affected the industry and the company. He says the fellows decide.

followups.question: Were you involved in that process, or was it a surprise?
answer: Fowler helped his leadership with content, supplying papers he had written and code contributions, and did nothing else. What affected him most was hearing other fellows say the promotion was well deserved and about time.
followups.speaker: David Fowler

followups.question: Do you worry about the lofty expectations of the level now that you have held it for a while?
answer: At first Fowler called himself a baby DE. After roughly two and a half to three years he feels confident he can perform at the level. In his first review cycle he felt pressure to document all impact and tell his boss, because the level sits just below executive. He found a pattern of talking to bosses and staying visible, and feels less pressure now, though he adds that things could change.
followups.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.question: What does the final level, technical fellow, look like?
answer: Fowler says people at that level are unicorns with different paths, so the useful move is to look for proxies for impact, not copy anyone. A fellow needs industry-wide impact. His examples: Anders Hejlsberg, whom people in his division idolize, made Turbo Pascal, Delphi, C# and TypeScript. Dave Cutler, who Fowler says built Windows NT, the Azure operating system and the Xbox hypervisor, is the only senior technical fellow, a title Fowler says is simply his own.

Fowler adds that Microsoft recently hired a fellow who invented RSS, and that a teammate was once an intern for Tim Berners-Lee and is on the HTTP specification. These are Fowler's own statements and were not checked against other sources.
blocks.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.question: Were there unexpected perks of becoming a distinguished engineer?
answer: Fowler says the best perk is an email alias called engineer that reaches every distinguished engineer at Microsoft. There is also an internal forum where they meet every couple of months. Access typically works through a sponsor, and when he became a partner he asked management for a mentor who was a fellow, reasoning that anyone wanting to become one should have fellows as mentors.

One was Jeffrey Snover, who invented PowerShell and, Fowler says, recently left Microsoft for Google. Fowler calls him one of his best mentors and a main sponsor, and he attended one of the technical leaders' forums as a result.
blocks.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.question: What did that mentor say that made a difference?
answer: Fowler says much career advice is vague, such as telling someone to do a super impactful project, whereas Snover was direct. He suggested going to the people who decide, including the CTOs, and asking what the role requires. Fowler found it jarring, since no one had told him to ask the source, but very helpful, because it showed him what he should and should not be doing.

A second mentor helped after Fowler received a feedback package from his manager and peers listing strengths, weaknesses and behavior under stress. His first reaction was to fix every weakness. The mentor said to amplify his strengths instead, because no one is promoted to these roles for being average. About five years ago this changed how Fowler works. He now builds teams around his gaps: he does not schedule meetings or run every shipping checklist, and makes sure someone who is good at that does. The host likens this to a power law, and Fowler agrees.
blocks.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.question: Which engineers do you look up to, and what makes them impressive?
answer: Fowler's team includes about five other partner-level engineers with more than 20 years at the company, each excellent for a different reason: a garbage-collector expert, a super coder who he says is a true 10x engineer, someone who seems to know obscure details across C, compilers and the operating system, and others with a strong eye for what to build.

On the C# language design review team, Fowler sits with Hejlsberg, whose feedback he says never talks down and stays pragmatic, even though the code Hejlsberg commits looks like it is inventing theory no one has seen. Fowler also names Mark Russinovich, CTO of Azure, who still codes and recently emailed about a performance improvement he wrote. Fowler is inspired when senior engineers still code.

He warns about the meeting trap. After becoming partner, he sat in meetings all day and was sad. A mentor told him an individual contributor needs time to think and build, and to block at least eight hours a week. It took him a while to learn to decline meetings.
blocks.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.question: If you designed a university course on refactoring, what would its key concepts be?
answer: Fowler says computer science is not software engineering. A first job involves a lot of time understanding what exists so the first change can be surgical and not break the build. He would put students in an artificially large codebase, changed every year so they cannot copy earlier work, and ask them to fix a bug and write a test. Working out where to put code, he argues, builds skills a LeetCode question or textbook exercise does not.

Each assignment could be a single fix. Fowler notes that many jobs are about tweaking existing software, and even someone working on Windows is unlikely to change the kernel unless building a new operating system.
blocks.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.question: Why do you say the high-leverage skill is debugging rather than writing new code, even though interviews focus on writing?
answer: Early on, Fowler worked with platform engineers on the .NET team and watched them diagnose crashes, race conditions and threading issues. He concluded that shipping an app and handling crash reports and production problems calls for a second skill set, distinct from authoring code. He would like an interview that hands a candidate a crash dump, to see what they start doing, such as adding logs, rerunning, reasoning about race conditions or printing thread ids, not whether they solve it.

He tells of an early-Azure night at 1 a.m. when his CVP messaged asking if he was free, and he was added to a call of about a hundred engineers trying to work out why a very popular site was crashing. It turned out to be a concurrency problem in a dictionary. Fowler concludes that writing code is a small piece of an engineer's skill set.

followups.question: What about the fixer archetype, who makes a one-line change after heavy investigation?
answer: The host describes the fixer as someone who drops in and makes a one-line change that makes something two or three times better. Fowler says someone on his team does this: when a thread starts about a performance issue in a gRPC call, he adds that engineer, who returns a trace and solves it.
followups.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.question: What prompted your lukewarm take that the lower you sit on the technology stack, the fewer mistakes you are allowed to make?
answer: Fowler works on the platform, and says changes there break services in ways that people higher up would find unheard of. Changing the order in which a method returns results, for example, can take down a company's website. He suspects the tweet followed a bug found during first-party adoption of .NET, where upgrading teams hit issues that shocked him, such as a method with about 400 arguments reaching a limit.
blocks.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.question: You tweeted that when promoted to senior you felt others were smarter and should have gone first. What did you take from that?
answer: Fowler worried about being promoted early on a fast path. His team had four people from MIT and two from Carnegie Mellon, and he had gone to Florida Tech, so he worked through imposter syndrome by working very hard.

The promotion taught him that impact is not about being the smartest, but about whether the work is at the top of the business, as NuGet and SignalR were. He had always felt he needed to go deeper on some technology, and now asks whether that is for you or for your career. He says an engineer does not need to know how TCP/IP works to be promoted to senior. It helped him separate being smart from making impact.
Co-workers were happy for him, at least outwardly. When he asked about others who had risen fast, he was told everyone knew it would happen, and he adds that you never know which category you are in.
blocks.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.question: One of your big-company tips is to ask when the last reorg was before changing roles. What is the thinking behind that?
answer: Fowler calls big companies machines and recalls hearing, perhaps tongue in cheek, that executives show motion through reorgs. A reorg is always coming or has just happened, so learn about the last one: who the leaders are, what triggered it and where the org is heading. Because Microsoft is so big, he says, every new org is effectively a new company. The tweet likely followed a mentee who had been reorged several times in a row, or something that happened to him.

followups.question: Is this about reading what a reorg means for your future?
answer: Yes. Fowler also relays advice he heard recently: when changing jobs, think about what you hate, not what you love, because the things you love will be easy. Someone who hates open offices should not join a company with open-plan seating.
followups.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.question: What has kept you at Microsoft for so long, since your internships?
answer: Fowler describes himself as part of a millennial generation that broke from the boomer-parent habit of staying in one place forever, and says many job-hopping friends were paid well for it. His closest call came when he was senior and a boss who had left for pre-IPO Twitter asked him to interview there. He interviewed at Twitter and GitHub, got both offers, and stayed after much deliberation. The morning Twitter went public, he adds, brought instant depression that lasted about a week.

Microsoft's counteroffer was fine but not the main reason. An executive vice president told him he would be a distinguished engineer in five years, which Fowler says oversold it. What mattered more was that he had built something impactful and permissionless and had gained autonomy, and leaving meant starting over. People overlook the network and track record they have built, and the people matter as much as pay: not just good engineers but good people to work with.
He also stayed because he got to work on something new about every two years, by design, which kept him from feeling the need to go elsewhere.

followups.question: If a mentee at Microsoft had a pre-IPO offer from a company like OpenAI, would you say stay or go?
answer: Fowler would tell them to go. He recalls a mentee with an offer from another company who was not in a place to do their best work, and told that mentee to leave despite any counteroffer. He says that, in the same situation himself, he might have gone.
followups.speaker: David Fowler

followups.question: You tweeted that once in a career you should stay on a project long enough to see the long-term impact of your decisions. What prompted that?
answer: Fowler's career had been to work on something and move on, still helping those who took over. .NET Core, at about ten years, is the longest he has worked on anything. Seeing the effects of decisions made in the first two years, good or bad, gave him a new perspective. He jokes that on a ten-year project every small issue you postponed becomes a big one, because somebody will hit all of it.

He is unsure twenty years on one project is good for career growth, but says it teaches you the implications of your choices and what you would fix in the next version. The host wonders what a chain of ever-higher jumps does for judgment if each project declines after the person leaves. Fowler does not fault either path and has done both. He cannot name the ingredients of a successful project, but can tell when he is on one, like a fine-tuned internal model built over experience.
followups.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.question: Did you notice the culture shifting internally when Satya Nadella became CEO?
answer: Fowler says the shift was huge, but it is hard to see the jump from Steve Ballmer's era because he lived through it and it happened gradually. A big one was that, historically, two teams could work toward the same end state and one would win. Under Nadella the focus moved to collaboration over being first. He saw teams building solutions before knowing the problem, though not on his own team.

He describes changes in meetings, email and remote friendliness. He remembers being surprised by someone raising a hand in a Teams meeting, having grown up in a culture where you wait for a pause and talk. Earlier meetings were often a highest-paid-person's-opinion affair, where a loud senior person could stop others from feeling safe to speak. Early in his career he saw people shouting and wondered whether he would have to shout too. Now leaders model behavior such as inviting quiet people to share their views.

Collaboration also became part of reviews: engineers who avoided other teams' work, or cloned it, were marked down. The host summarizes this as a change driven by performance incentives and top-down messaging, and Fowler adds the behaviors leaders modeled. The host recalls the XKCD comic that draws Microsoft as people pointing guns at each other. Fowler says the real shift went from guns to ambivalence, with teams staying out of each other's way, and then to rewarded collaboration.
blocks.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.question: Looking back, do you have major regrets people can learn from?
answer: Fowler says no major ones, but early in his career he was very arrogant and lacked empathy, and the tone of old GitHub comments would show it. Building teams and influencing through others taught him patience and empathy. Being right is only one of many things, he says, and software engineering has many shades of gray. He has more self-awareness now, though it still creeps out occasionally.

He names as a possible regret that he did not take early opportunities at Twitter or Facebook, which would have paid a lot for a senior engineer. A smaller regret outside the career: a friend messaged him in 2008 about starting a Bitcoin company, and he dismissed the idea. The host jokes that the friend must now hold a lot of Bitcoin.
blocks.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.question: What was your work-life balance like throughout your career?
answer: Fowler used to say there was no balance, just working hard and playing hard. A comment he found useful recently is that balance is not about stopping at five o'clock but about what gives you energy and what drains it. He works a lot because programming is a passion as well as a job, and dials back now and then. Once he came back from vacation and began making games for fun, then took what he learned into work.

What drains him is meetings that feel purposeless. If he were in meetings all day and then went home to do the work he wanted to do, that would feel like burnout. He sees being paid to code as a privilege and plans to keep doing it until he can no longer.

followups.question: Is intrinsic motivation the unfair advantage behind careers like yours?
answer: The host says almost every very successful engineer seems to have it. Fowler agrees and recalls a talk by Andrej Karpathy about how much practice it takes to get good at anything (the captions garble the figure Fowler cited, so it is not reproduced here). Asked which book made him good, Fowler says he wrote and read a lot of code, and is not sure that is good advice but did not get good from a blog post.

His advice is to build everything: databases, distributed systems, games. He calls his GitHub a graveyard of projects, each of which taught a skill that only showed later. At 16 he tried to build a Street Fighter clone with art found online, purely to learn how a fighting game and key combos work. That need to understand how things work has lasted to this day.
followups.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.question: If you could advise yourself when graduating college and entering the industry, what would you say?
answer: Fowler's answer is to negotiate the salary. He did not know it was possible when he took his first job. A new graduate should get multiple offers and push the number up. Coming from Barbados and grateful for the most money he had seen, he was shocked to watch friends decline offers and say they would check Google or Facebook first. Having since sat on hiring committees for interns, he finds it impressive to watch a candidate bump up an offer well.
blocks.speaker: David Fowler
