sections.title: From producing code to choosing the right problem
sections.deck: Dwayne Reeves’s growth on Hack shows how migration strategy, trusted types, delegation, and approachable leadership can create value beyond personal code output.

blocks.question: Why did you join Facebook as a new graduate?
answer: Facebook was not his original goal. Google appealed partly because of its East Coast offices, and Twitter because he liked Scala. A friend at Facebook persuaded him to interview as practice. Meeting engineers changed his view: behind the website were interesting problems in caching, scale, and a custom PHP runtime.

He also felt wanted. The offer was his strongest, the recruiter increased it without a request, and a senior company leader met accepted MIT graduates personally. He contrasts that experience with another recruiter’s response in his own process. These examples describe his recruiting experience at the much smaller company of that period.
blocks.speaker: Dwayne Reeves

blocks.question: How much does college prestige affect later success?
answer: He values the education he received at MIT, but sees access to opportunity as the clearest differentiator. Recruiters were willing to speak to him from his first year; an early internship also helped open the next opportunity.

He worked with equally capable engineers from other educational paths, including people who had not attended college, whose entry into the company depended much more on chance. His point is that recognizable credentials can open doors without defining the person’s eventual engineering ability.

That access was striking to someone raised in Bridgeport, Connecticut, in public schools and a family of immigrants. Companies he had regarded as distant dreams became normal places for classmates to intern.
blocks.speaker: Dwayne Reeves

blocks.question: How did you end up working on programming languages?
answer: His first team was building a service and a custom language to move some computation out of the main PHP codebase and closer to data. He initially translated PHP into the new DSL, then developed language features. The project was eventually canceled.

He moved into privacy infrastructure, representing policies more clearly than chains of conditionals. That framework adopted Hack and types early. Later, he tried to add Hack types to a core API originally designed without them. What looked like one or two weeks of work took a quarter and involved considerable scripting and collaboration with the Hack team.

He reports that migration exposed errors in roughly 20% of the moved call sites, often involving null handling. The result made types’ value concrete at scale and strengthened the case for broader Hack adoption. It was an outcome from that migration, rather than a prediction that every codebase would show the same error rate.
blocks.speaker: Dwayne Reeves

blocks.question: Are statically typed languages objectively better for industry work?
answer: He calls the judgment subjective, while making a strong case for types in a large, shared codebase. As code and contributors multiply, keeping every assumption in one person’s head becomes impractical. Types communicate intent and help tools track that intent.

Autocomplete, search, and static analysis add value beyond error messages. He allows that a person working alone might move quickly in a dynamic language; his argument concerns the communication burden at organizational scale.

Peterman summarizes the mechanism as making more state and intent explicit in code so tools can inspect it. Reeves agrees, emphasizing the power of ruling out particular classes of errors by construction. That is a guarantee about what the type system establishes, rather than proof that the entire program has no bugs.
blocks.speaker: Dwayne Reeves

blocks.question: What is the uncanny valley of type systems?
answer: A partially typed language can look familiar enough to invite expectations from a fully static language, while behaving differently in subtle places. Developers may become more uncomfortable as the system approaches the expected behavior without actually supplying its guarantees.
He used the graphics analogy to explain the transition problem on Hack. It gave the team a shared way to describe why almost-reliable types could still be frustrating.

There was also a specific technical source of the gap: some inherited PHP behaviors conflicted with making the checker sound. He argued for removing those behaviors so that annotations could become dependable. The goal was not simply to maximize the number of written types while preserving exceptions that undermined their meaning.
blocks.speaker: Dwayne Reeves

blocks.question: Which experiences changed your idea of how an individual contributor creates value?
answer: The first was a broader PHP-to-Hack migration. He spent much of a half talking to engineers, identifying useful work, and helping people contribute, while writing less code himself. At first he thought this was his worst period. His manager initially suggested he find more time to code, then revised that advice to focus on the outcome.

Adoption grew from roughly 20–30% to 60–70% of the codebase in his recollection, and Hack became a default choice. He received his highest review so far and a promotion to IC5. The result challenged his assumption that personal code volume defined his contribution: the job was to identify and solve problems, sometimes through clarity and coordination.

The second came after he joined the Hack team as technical lead. With much of the previous team gone, he was learning what that role meant. He designed changes to the collection system, secured runtime-team agreement, and saw implementation begin. He wanted to finish the project himself as a route to IC6.

His manager asked him to hand it off. The analogy was a staged rocket: Reeves had done the work of getting the effort moving; another person could carry the next stage. He reluctantly delegated and moved to another problem, then learned he had already been promoted. In both cases, his mental model of the next level lagged the work the organization actually valued.

A good manager relationship is a through-line he sees in his career. Connection and clarity helped him do his best work; disconnects were associated with frustration. The lesson combines choosing the right direction with being willing to release direct control of every implementation step.
blocks.speaker: Dwayne Reeves

blocks.title: How his contribution changed

steps.title: Find the problem
steps.text: Recognize a migration or language issue worth solving.

steps.title: Create a direction
steps.text: Explain the need, design an approach, and secure alignment.

steps.title: Enable execution
steps.text: Give others the context and ownership to carry it forward.

steps.title: Move to the next need
steps.text: Apply judgment where the organization next needs it.

blocks.caption: An editorial outline of the two promotion stories; it does not make their timing a universal ladder rule.

blocks.question: Why did you try management?
answer: It was not his original plan. As the team grew, his manager suggested he become a manager; he initially declined. A technical-lead-manager role sounded like a way to retain technical involvement while experimenting with management.

His manager first warned that it could mean two jobs, then supported trying it. Reeves had noticed that several useful career changes came from doing something outside his comfort zone, so he accepted the chance to learn.

followups.question: Did combining technical leadership and management work?
answer: Initially it did. His reporting group grew from a few people to roughly a dozen, and he began supporting other managers while still giving technical direction.

As the organization expanded, the best use of his technical leadership for a group of around 35–40 people could differ from what his six or seven direct reports needed from a manager. He was doing strong technical leadership and adequate management, but was not optimizing those individuals’ development as a focused manager might.

The conflict was therefore about responsibilities and organizational health as much as workload. He could replace himself as technical lead and focus on management, or return to the IC path and focus on broad technical needs. Finding a manager for the smaller reporting group seemed easier than replacing the broader technical role, so he returned to being an IC.

blocks.speaker: Dwayne Reeves

blocks.question: What differs between supporting an IC and supporting an engineering manager?
answer: The center of attention shifts from technical problems toward people and organizational problems. Both coaching relationships have a longer feedback loop than coding: advice might not visibly help for six or nine months. The manager-of-managers loop can be even less immediate.

He admits that he remained focused on whether the organization was operating adequately so he could continue technical work. A more intentional organizational leader would also examine the structure, how managers coach their teams, what opportunities they should create, and whether the role is still right for each person.

He enjoyed one-on-one coaching, particularly helping people with their technical challenges. But switching from a day dominated by technical direction to a smaller portion focused on organizational design did not come naturally. His reflection is about where his attention and strengths were, rather than a claim that managing managers is merely more delegation.
blocks.speaker: Dwayne Reeves

blocks.title: The two responsibilities that pulled in different directions
rows: Broad technical leadership
The larger language organization.
Strategy, technical challenges, and coordinated execution.
Direct people management
The engineers he directly supported.
Individual development and the conditions for doing their best work.
Supporting other managers
Teams led by those managers.
Coaching, organizational structure, opportunities, and leadership effectiveness.

blocks.question: What led to the senior staff-equivalent promotion?
answer: The uncanny-valley argument became a shared technical vision. As the organization executed it and results accumulated, the effect became attributable to his direction. This time he discussed the path more actively with his manager; they needed to see enough progress against that vision.
He was still a manager when promoted and returned to the IC path afterward. He believes the promotion reflected technical contribution more than organizational leadership.

The scale was substantial. When he joined in 2015, there was a mixture of PHP and Hack, and only a small fraction of Hack files used strict mode. By the later period he describes, the relevant codebase was more or less strict Hack, alongside runtime and language improvements. The adoption and strict-mode percentages refer to the codebase and times he discusses, not all programming at Meta.
blocks.speaker: Dwayne Reeves

blocks.question: Which colleagues helped you develop?
answer: He credits a colleague who brought the product developer’s perspective to changes Reeves saw from the language side. That perspective helped the team plan migrations around what engineers actually needed to build.

Another colleague was a patient sounding board for language and compiler questions. Reeves had little prior compiler experience when he joined Hack and remembers not knowing what a lexer was. The ability to ask basic questions safely was crucial.

He also describes learning from Andrew Kennedy, whose foundational type-theory work initially made Reeves feel junior by comparison. Kennedy’s humility and willingness to consider a practical viewpoint helped Reeves recognize that different strengths can each contribute. He could offer useful insight without possessing the same background.

followups.question: Did that experience make accomplished engineers feel more approachable?
answer: Yes, and he wants to pass that experience on. He does not want newer engineers to see his years on Hack as a reason to withhold their ideas. Past accomplishments do not make him always right, and he wants to keep learning. Senior colleagues who explained concepts patiently set the example he thinks others should follow.

blocks.speaker: Dwayne Reeves

blocks.question: Why have you stayed at Meta for so long?
answer: He has considered leaving and interviewed elsewhere. Before accepting a move, he asks whether it would solve the fundamental issue or merely react to a temporary period of discomfort.

He values the influence he has earned, opportunities to help bring in diverse talent, an unusual chance to work on a programming language, and a strong team. In several cases, the temporary issue improved without leaving.

He does not treat staying as an unconditional rule. Feeling fundamentally unvalued, no longer believing in the mission, or being in a toxic management environment would be different. Those were not his circumstances. He emphasizes the good fortune of his experience and the difference between solvable frustration and a persistent mismatch.
blocks.speaker: Dwayne Reeves

blocks.question: What would you tell yourself at graduation?
answer: When asked to write some code, first ask how the requester knows that it is the right code to write. Aim to participate in deciding what should be done. He wanted his earlier self to see the value of his ideas and judgment beyond keyboard output, especially when impostor feelings made that value harder to recognize.
blocks.speaker: Dwayne Reeves

sections.title: From Strong Output to Scalable Ownership on Instagram Web
sections.deck: An Instagram senior staff engineer traces three promotion projects, explains why collaboration can block a promotion, and shows how tooling and ownership multiply a specialist’s impact.

blocks.question: Why specialize in front-end engineering?
answer: Marius describes a longstanding enthusiasm for the web, dating to school lessons in HTML and a CSS book he requested as a Christmas gift. He deliberately sought jobs where he could build web applications, including agency work while studying computer science.

The specialty was a positive choice about work he wanted to do, rather than merely the first technology assigned to him. That preference later helped him decide which opportunities and teams fit his career.
blocks.speaker: Marius, Instagram senior staff engineer

blocks.question: Why did strong performance ratings not immediately lead to promotion from IC4 to IC5?
answer: In his account, one behavioral gap held back the promotion: cross-functional collaboration. Strong conviction about his ideas sometimes came across as too insistent or intense. Advocating for a proposal was appropriate, but he needed to recognize when continued pressure became counterproductive.

He distinguishes a rating for delivered impact from promotion readiness. A person can deliver a great deal while still missing one behavior expected at the next level. His promotion also encountered a later company-wide pause during the early pandemic, after he had worked on the feedback. He describes these as separate causes, and his eventual promotion came at the end of 2020.
blocks.speaker: Marius, Instagram senior staff engineer

followups.question: So a high rating and a specific performance concern can coexist?
answer: Yes. A retrospective impact rating does not establish that every next-level behavior is present. Marius believes calibration wanted to see the collaboration issue addressed over another period before promoting him.

blocks.question: How did you handle the frustration of a delayed promotion?
answer: He acknowledges frustration, especially after peers reported a visible improvement and an external company decision still blocked the result. He reminded himself that careers are long and a half-year delay has limited meaning across that span.

He continued growing and taking work beyond his current title. With a lagging promotion system, refusing to demonstrate next-level behavior until the title arrives defeats the process itself. The work and learning could continue even while the paperwork lagged, and were eventually recognized.
blocks.speaker: Marius, Instagram senior staff engineer

blocks.question: What work led to the redefined-expectations rating and IC5 promotion?
answer: As an IC4, he took a leading role in a large web project considered IC6 scope. More than ten engineers and several partner functions contributed. Delivering it on an ambitious pandemic-era timeline required much more than coding: interpreting product ambiguity, dividing workstreams, coordinating people, running meetings and communicating progress.

Operational excellence mattered too. A large launch that breaks systems does not become successful simply because many changes were submitted. The project landed without major issues, with attention to release hygiene.

Marius does not claim to know every detail of the calibration conversation. His interpretation is that work two levels beyond his assigned scope made the unusually strong rating easier to explain. Ratings need an articulated progression from expected work to additional contribution, rather than an unexplained assertion of excellence.
blocks.speaker: Marius, Instagram senior staff engineer

blocks.question: How did an IC4 get trusted with an IC6-sized project?
answer: The opportunity arose through a staffing domino effect. A senior engineer was on parental leave while a major priority changed the team’s work. Another engineer covered that gap, and Marius took a project that might otherwise have gone to someone more senior.

There was luck in the timing, but preparation shaped who was considered. He had established himself as a web specialist who wanted responsibility for that platform and had a record of strong delivery. A relevant opportunity was therefore a plausible match. He calls this increasing the surface area for luck, while recognizing that wanting the project did not guarantee receiving it.
blocks.speaker: Marius, Instagram senior staff engineer

blocks.question: Have you always been ambitious about this work?
answer: Yes. Understanding conditions and loops in JavaScript gave him an early sense of agency: he could make the machine do something of his own choosing. The web also appeals to him philosophically as connected documents making knowledge widely available.

His later ambition grows from that intrinsic interest, not solely from the promotion ladder. That distinction helps explain both his sustained effort and his preference for particular kinds of engineering.
blocks.speaker: Marius, Instagram senior staff engineer

blocks.question: What led to the next redefined-expectations rating and IC6 promotion?
answer: He led another time-sensitive web project that enabled other pieces of a larger investment. Missing its hard deadline would block their impact. More time was unavailable, and other people were already assigned to important work, so he had to manage scope and quality with the team he had.

His preference was to reduce scope rather than casually sacrifice performance, reliability and design craft. A smaller well-built outcome was preferable to a broad but poor implementation. Some concessions can be necessary, but he wanted them made deliberately.

Product-management support was limited and important questions remained unresolved. He received credit for operating as a product-engineering hybrid: clarifying what needed to be built, aligning the decision with product and engineering leadership, defining success, sequencing work and then contributing heavily to implementation. He likens the early ambiguity to exploring a fog-covered map before the work becomes operational.
blocks.speaker: Marius, Instagram senior staff engineer

blocks.title: The delivery constraints in Marius’s IC6 project
rows: Extend the deadline
The project unlocked other work and had a hard date
Plan around the fixed deadline.
Add engineers
Available people were already allocated
Coordinate the small group already assigned.
Cut scope
Possible, but an empty minimum product would not meet the need
Choose reductions carefully while preserving the useful outcome.
Lower quality
Some concessions were possible, but quality mattered strongly
Favor a smaller implementation with performance, reliability and craft.
Wait for product answers
Product support was stretched
Clarify ambiguity and obtain alignment before executing.

blocks.question: Why switch to Instagram web after things were going well?
answer: His previous organization’s priorities moved away from the work he wanted to pursue. He had learned that web engineering and product quality—performance, reliability and design craft—were especially satisfying. Staying successful on a less aligned direction was not necessarily the right long-term choice.

The Instagram web team had recently migrated its technology stack and needed quality work. The opening matched his experience and interests. He began with the notifications surface, which needed modernization and alignment with the native applications, then spent much of his time in product infrastructure.

That layer sits between visible product features and deeper infrastructure: code structure, safeguards, testing and architecture that help other engineers iterate confidently. It offered increasing leverage as the expectations for his own impact grew.
blocks.speaker: Marius, Instagram senior staff engineer

blocks.question: What do you mean by engineering leverage?
answer: Leverage means shaping defaults and tools so other well-intentioned engineers can succeed without personally consulting the specialist for every decision. The framework guides them toward a good outcome. Marius illustrates this with front-end reliability and React error boundaries, which contain a rendering failure to part of an interface.

Adding one missing boundary fixes one location. Auditing the whole site systematically solves a broader problem. Writing guidance that explains how to trigger failures and how to distinguish primary, secondary and tertiary content lets other teams apply the approach themselves. Adding lint rules can make the editor warn about a known unsafe pattern before a change is submitted.

He uses that sequence to illustrate increasing levels of impact, while treating the level labels as his practical interpretation rather than an official formula. The more comprehensive solution continues helping after he moves on to performance or another problem. He cannot personally inspect every web product in the company, so direction and tooling extend his contribution.
blocks.speaker: Marius, Instagram senior staff engineer

followups.question: Is the leverage that other people can prevent or fix these problems themselves?
answer: Yes. Guidance and automated checks scale beyond the places he can directly work. The aim is to solve a class of problems sufficiently well that recurring intervention by the same expert is no longer necessary.

blocks.title: From one reliability fix to a repeatable improvement
blocks.caption: An editor-assembled progression from Marius’s error-boundary example; arrows show broader ways to address the same class of failure.

steps.title: Contain one failure
steps.text: Add an error boundary around one vulnerable region.

steps.title: Audit the surface
steps.text: Trigger failures systematically and harden the site.

steps.title: Teach the decision
steps.text: Explain testing and how fallback behavior depends on the importance of missing content.

steps.title: Encode the default
steps.text: Use lint or framework safeguards to guide future changes.

steps.title: Move to the next constraint
steps.text: Let the improvement keep working while attention shifts to another problem.

blocks.question: How did you begin working on Threads web?
answer: His manager offered an introduction to a small, initially secretive project. Marius discussed the needed web work with its hiring manager and became the only web engineer for roughly the first six to eight weeks. Scope was initially limited and later expanded.

He values that rare opportunity to help launch a new application from its beginning inside a large company. Other engineers subsequently joined, so being first is not the same as having built the entire eventual product alone.
blocks.speaker: Marius, Instagram senior staff engineer

followups.question: Did you start a separate web application from scratch?
answer: He first experimented inside Instagram web, hiding the existing interface to render something for the new product. He then decided a distinct surface needed separate components and organization to avoid unintended coupling. That separation was a reasoned architectural choice; it was not obvious at the first experiment.

blocks.question: What made the Threads work a convincing IC7 promotion case?
answer: The work was intense, but its impact story was clear. Threads needed a web presence. Marius established its foundations, helped grow and organize the team, led delivery and wrote a substantial amount of code. The scope grew from logged-out viewing and sharing to a logged-in client with feeds, notifications, settings, search and posting.

The launch and reception made the outcome visible. He says this was an unusually easy self-review to write because the connection between business need, his responsibilities and delivered work was straightforward. That clarity does not mean the project was easy or that his teammates’ contributions were unimportant.

Attribution also required senior reviewers to understand that his involvement materially changed the result. Clear ownership and responsibility for the outcome supplied that connection more convincingly than a count of isolated tasks.
blocks.speaker: Marius, Instagram senior staff engineer

blocks.question: What does owning a launch actually require?
answer: Marius thinks through failure modes before launch and works backward to prevent them. A new domain raises DNS and infrastructure questions; the right experts should verify the setup rather than the team simply assume it works. Other predictable risks deserve the same treatment.

Not every problem can be anticipated. Operational readiness includes error reporting, QA, release hygiene and responsive feedback channels so an unexpected browser-specific problem can be diagnosed quickly. Ownership covers the outcome of that system of preparation, not only writing the feature.
blocks.speaker: Marius, Instagram senior staff engineer

blocks.question: Does being the directly responsible individual mean doing everything yourself?
answer: No. He divides the product into meaningful areas owned by other senior engineers. Those engineers are accountable for their areas, while he remains accountable for the overall launch. Delegating a portion does not allow the overall owner to blame that portion if the product fails.

The difficult skill is adjusting the amount of oversight. A lead should give people room to grow without disappearing from the work. His driving-instructor analogy places a hand near the emergency controls while someone is learning, then gradually increases freedom as trust and capability become established. The relationship should prevent avoidable failure without turning every decision into micromanagement.
blocks.speaker: Marius, Instagram senior staff engineer

blocks.question: How should a senior engineer distribute scope while preserving their own impact?
answer: Marius favors reasonable ownership boundaries matched to people’s capabilities. A stretch assignment can develop someone; work far beyond their ability can set both the person and the project up to fail. Work far below their capability may also be a poor match.

He does not expect every change written by a senior staff engineer to contain extraordinary technical complexity. Sometimes the important contribution is quickly implementing many straightforward pieces that unblock a critical workstream. At other times the right role is coordinating work across teams or organizations.

The value is the necessary result and the role in achieving it. Hoarding work or judging every diff in isolation misses the context that makes the overall contribution important. He treats fast coding and broad coordination as different tools for different situations.
blocks.speaker: Marius, Instagram senior staff engineer

blocks.question: What are you considering for the next part of your career?
answer: He has no fixed answer about IC8. At the time of the interview, he had moved from Threads web to an important Instagram server-side project, deliberately extending beyond his front-end comfort zone toward fuller-stack work. He finds that both exciting and a little intimidating.

Management is not his preferred direction because he enjoys deeply technical individual-contributor work. He wants his work to matter and offer learning, without assuming that the next title must be the immediate goal. He also offers the Tron: Legacy soundtrack as a personal recommendation for concentrated coding.
blocks.speaker: Marius, Instagram senior staff engineer

blocks.question: When you reached IC6, did you immediately start aiming for IC7?
answer: Not in the way he had immediately looked ahead after reaching IC5. A more senior promotion needs a business need that matches the level as well as successful execution. Threads web supplied a timely opportunity of that shape.

The opportunity was necessary but not sufficient: the work still had to land. Conversely, an engineer without such an opportunity may struggle to make a case despite ability. His story therefore combines delivery, fit and timing rather than treating ambition alone as the explanation.
blocks.speaker: Marius, Instagram senior staff engineer

blocks.question: Have higher-level expectations ever frightened you?
answer: Yes. As an IC4, he saw IC5 as the eventual expected destination under the policy he understood then, was apprehensive about IC6 and believed he never wanted IC7. His preferences changed as he grew. Even later, he was not actively pursuing IC8 because the role would need to fit and he would not want to lose too much work he enjoys.
The account is a reminder that a person’s view of the next level can change with experience. It does not prescribe indefinite promotion seeking, nor establish a current company policy for every role.
blocks.speaker: Marius, Instagram senior staff engineer

blocks.question: What was your most unusually high coding output?
answer: He recalls just under two thousand diffs during the year Threads launched. The number suggests an intense implementation period, but he immediately cautions that diff counts are gameable and at best directionally interesting.

He sees no meaningful automatic distinction between, for example, three hundred and four hundred changes in a period: one person may simply split work into smaller commits. Output volume should be interpreted alongside the outcome and the context, not converted into a universal target.
blocks.speaker: Marius, Instagram senior staff engineer

blocks.question: What advice would you give yourself when entering the industry?
answer: Things are going to be fine; do not add unnecessary pressure. Early ambition led him to publish a blog post every week while balancing degrees, near-full-time agency work, friends and a demanding hobby. He sometimes wrote late at night merely to keep the commitment.

He enjoyed that work, learned a great deal and thinks his public writing helped a recruiter find him. He does not regret it. But he no longer considers that intensity a healthy default and would tell his younger self that the existing effort was already enough.

His practical web work also complemented university fundamentals. Theory gave him useful concepts, while years of building applications supplied expertise in the technologies he used daily. The lesson is a sustainable combination, rather than dismissing either kind of learning.
blocks.speaker: Marius, Instagram senior staff engineer

followups.question: Would you have reached the same position without that early intensity?
answer: He cannot know. The counterfactual is uncertain, and he does not rewrite his past as a regimen he hated. He valued it at the time while recognizing that he would choose a healthier balance now.

sections.title: Getting to Staff Engineer at Big Tech: A Five-Person Panel on Scope, Relationships, and Promotion
sections.deck: Five engineers who reached staff level at Meta, Google, Activision, Netflix and Airbnb discuss the projects behind their promotions, how to find scope, and why relationships and communication matter as much as technical depth.

blocks.text: Rahul hosts four engineers (Lee, Ryan Peterman, Carly and Zach) and also answers as a panelist. Between them they have worked at staff level, or the equivalent, at Meta, Google, Activision, Netflix and Airbnb. Their shared view is that staff level changes the kind of work, not only its size. A staff engineer is expected to influence other people, to find problems that are worth the company's time, and to be known well enough that others can vouch for the result. They disagree on details, such as how much a staff engineer should still code, but they return again and again to three points: relationships, clear communication, and a direct read of the company's own promotion process. Everything below is the speakers' own experience and opinion, not company policy.
blocks.heading: The panel's view: staff scope is found through problems and people, not through code alone

blocks.title: Levels discussed, as summarized by the host from a levels.fyi diagram
rows: Google
L5
L6
Facebook / Meta
E5
E6
Amazon
SDE III
No staff title; the level after senior is principal

blocks.title: Panelists and the background each one stated
headers: Background as stated in the panel
rows: Lee

In software engineering since 2004. At Amazon from 2012, first as an SDE II and later in people management. Then a staff-level IC role at Meta, which Lee says did not go well. About a year and a half before the panel, moved to Google as a staff engineer (chat, then Gmail notifications).
Ryan Peterman
Staff engineer at Meta, working on Instagram. Graduated in 2017, spent about eight months at an Amazon satellite office, then joined Meta as a new graduate. Three promotions in about five years.
Carly

At Activision. A senior manager who also holds an IC title equivalent to staff (lead engineer). Finished graduate school in 2017, started as a junior data scientist, joined Activision at senior level and took about two years to reach lead. Works in security.
Zach

Began in data engineering at Facebook in 2016. Then Netflix, where every engineer held the senior title. Then Airbnb, where Zach received the official staff title and stayed two years. Left about six months before the panel to create content full time.
Rahul (host)

Runs Taro. About four and a half years at Meta, going from senior to staff. About two and a half years at Pinterest, where Rahul was rejected for promotion twice. Before that, a startup that Pinterest acquired.

blocks.label: Pace: promotion is not a race (Lee and Rahul)
blocks.text: Rahul says being rejected for promotion twice at Pinterest gave Rahul both the manager's and the candidate's view of the process. Lee says Lee failed three attempts at the senior SDE III level at Amazon, and also failed the first try to reach L6 as a manager. Lee reached the staff-equivalent level roughly 16 or 17 years into a career. Lee's point is that several panelists rose very quickly, by changing companies or succeeding fast inside one, but that is not the only path and a missed first senior promotion is not unusual.

blocks.question: What project or projects got each panelist to staff level?
answer: Zach moved up by changing companies. At Netflix every engineer held the senior title, but Zach felt the responsibilities were already staff-level, and Airbnb later hired Zach at staff. The project Zach credits is an asset inventory at Netflix. Netflix used microservices, which give each team ownership but also leave thousands of separate applications that could each hold their own vulnerabilities. Zach built a graph database describing applications, code bases, data sets and employees and how they connect to one another. The work took about two years.

Lee was also hired at staff level rather than promoted into it. Lee had managed people for about three years at Amazon before joining Meta. Lee says technical work alone was not enough. Some people point to a large, complex project they delivered alone, but staff-level readiness also depends on whether they planned the work, split it into parallel work streams, and reduced risk so the hardest part was not left until last. Lee's hardest technical project was a custom class loader that let an Android app use multiple executable files before Google supported that, so that Amazon's video app (now Prime Video) and its combined apps did not hit the method limit. Lee did not want engineers forced to write poor code to fit a technical limit.

Ryan Peterman describes a large efficiency project that made video processing at Instagram much cheaper, 94 percent cheaper for some basic encodings. Ryan says the project reached staff level because Ryan created the scope: Ryan found the problem, convinced people it was worth doing, got buy-in, and led execution. Ryan stepped in personally only on the riskiest components. Several engineers did most of the work while Ryan led and reviewed code. Ryan stresses that staff is one of the first levels where influencing others is a baseline expectation, because software is collaborative.

Carly says the step up is not just technical brilliance. It comes down to trust and to being a collaborator that others rely on. Carly points to a presentation of security findings to an executive leader and the CTO. Carly could explain technical work to people who did not want to sit in an engineering meeting, and received a job offer from a leader in that meeting. That became an internal move to staff. Carly says this is not a normal route. The wider lesson is to know your numbers, be ready to state your impact to technical and non-technical audiences, and work on large, cross-business problems that address a real pain point. The people who decide on promotion are often both kinds of audience.

Rahul names two projects at Meta. One was an internal tool that improved debugging of the product. Rahul measured that it saved thousands of engineering hours in a year, and other engineers could plug in their own debugging tools, which multiplied the impact. The other was re-architecting the product's calling architecture, moving it onto another team's set of APIs. Rahul's lesson is to think in terms of a portfolio of bets. A big-tech company has many things outside your control, so pair one main project with a smaller one you control, and switch when one is blocked. Two or three projects is realistic, not ten. Rahul adds that a company must also have enough business need for staff-level scope, so some people get promoted simply by moving to a company that needs their skills.

followups.question: Is a staff promotion usually a sudden result of one project?
answer: One panelist says no. A promotion packet is normally a track record covering several half-year review periods. By the time it reaches the promotion committee, people should already know the candidate's name and the candidate should have been doing near-staff or staff-level work for some time.

followups.question: What kind of impact makes people notice a staff engineer?
answer: Zach describes two directions of impact. Vertical impact is the direct effect on the business. Horizontal impact is helping a team move faster by improving how work gets done, not only what is built. Zach's Netflix example was a Groovy script that removed unused dependencies from the deployable file for pipelines. Zach estimates each deploy saved one to seven minutes, which at five or six deploys a day is about 30 minutes to an hour a day per engineer. Zach says the rest is adoption rather than technical excellence.

Another panelist adds a rough calculation: a 16 percent speedup across 66 people is the equivalent of a 10x engineer. The same panelist says that the very senior engineers they studied, three levels above staff, often make compounding improvements to tooling used by thousands of engineers.

blocks.question: How should a senior or staff engineer balance delegating work and doing it personally? (An attendee, Brian, asked, and Rahul rephrased the question.)
answer: Zach recalls weekly conversations with an Airbnb manager about whether Zach was managing, delegating and coding enough. Zach loves to code Scala all day, and says that doing so has sometimes been to the team's detriment. Frank talks with a manager about how time is spent helped Zach see when more leadership was needed.

Lee says each person should know their own bias. An engineer who came from management may spend too much time on people and too little on reducing technical risk, while others lean the other way. The split does not need to be 50/50 each week. Lee also asks whether the engineer is leading from the front, finding the path and sending others down it, or from behind, pointing people in a direction. The answer varies by team: a team of peers differs from a team of new graduates. Lee says a manager's input helps here. A manager can point out that a 4 percent performance gain is good, but that no one knows which tools were used and nothing would be committed if the person were unavailable. In Lee's view how you do the work matters as much as what you do, and pairing with junior engineers helps them follow the threads.

Carly gives a manager's view, using Zach as an example. Carly would rather Zach had input into research, design and the roadmap of the big projects, so that someone with Zach's depth can quickly say what will break, and others do the deep implementation. Zach would step in when something is very complicated. Carly says the balance is hard to get right and is something to settle in talks with the manager.

Lee builds on this: one of the most powerful tools is asking the right question at the right time. A senior person who hears a team plan to re-architect something can say it is not the right focus and that it can sit behind a shim for now. Twenty minutes of that person's time can save two or three developer-years. Lee says that people's time should go where a design matters, because a missed hallway conversation can be costly.

followups.question: How should a staff engineer decide what not to work on?
answer: Zach tells of starting at Airbnb, when stakeholders were loud about certifying profitability numbers. As a newcomer Zach leaned on their requests. After about six months, Zach asked what difference certification would actually make, and the answer was essentially none, with roughly a one-day delay at most. Zach told the manager it was a case of diminishing returns, because the pipeline was too complicated to finish and the effort should move to higher-impact work. Another panelist notes that four people working on it for about four months likely cost the company a million dollars or more in salary alone, before counting what else they could have done.

A panelist adds that staff engineers must persuade, not just execute. Managers lean on staff engineers to identify what should and should not be worked on, which takes courage to tell stakeholders their project is being deprioritized. Explaining the reasoning is what keeps cross-functional partners' respect. Without it, the panelist says, mistrust builds first and resentment follows, and team dynamics can fall apart.

followups.question: Is a staff engineer always less hands-on?
answer: A panelist says no. It depends on the project and on the person's strengths. On a project with many senior people, staff may lead. Some very productive specialists, or people whose execution is worth four or five engineers, can have staff-level impact by doing most of the execution themselves. They are still expected to scale by sharing their knowledge. The panelist says not every staff engineer fits the tech-lead type: some are heads-down coders and some are domain specialists. Another panelist recalls that Meta had a "code machine" archetype for this kind of person.

blocks.question: Where does a staff engineer find, or make up, the scope?
answer: Lee says that as you become better than your managers at your job, they can no longer see the landmines or the technical constraints on a project. Lee rejects the idea of making up scope to justify a promotion as a bad choice. The job is to identify what is hurting the team and holding it back, raise it, and convince others to fix it. Lee compares this to the question of whether calculus was invented or discovered. Lee says most scope is discovered: work that others fear, do not see, or do not think is valuable, and that you must persuade them will speed up the next three projects or enable something the product could not do before. It may be found by looking through code, or in product requirements where there is a gap.

Lee's own habit is to put a hand up when no one else will. Lee gives the example of an old, fragile system that no one wants to touch. Lee says that when someone suggests turning it off, it may turn out to generate hundreds of millions of dollars in revenue, so it is worth a gradual replacement such as the strangler fig pattern. Lee admits that this sometimes leaves a person stuck with something awful.

Rahul sums up that asking how to find scope to justify a promotion is already the wrong question. The right one is what the most burning problems are, and what is on the mind of the manager, director and other engineers, and whether you can build something that helps them. Rahul compares it to a startup: you start with the problem, not a solution. Knowing those problems takes relationship building and being embedded in the organization.

blocks.question: How deliberate were you about building relationships with mentees, tech leads, managers and directors who might speak for you at review time? (Rahul)
answer: Carly calls it extremely intentional. Carly looks for people with a common problem or approach and teams up with them. Carly now has friends across business units, including people Carly seldom works with. Carly says that being remote full time makes this much harder than working in an office. Carly describes being an introverted extrovert and says people have to push against the urge not to message others, because no one will argue for you if no one knows you. Carly adds that someone working late and shown as online will not be noticed for that. People vouch for those they have seen deliver on time, on scope and on budget, and waiting to be rescued is the wrong approach.

Another panelist says that they were poor at happy hours, but their work was highly visible and they were promoted even during the pandemic. The key for them was to communicate the work: share the plan, get buy-in, and report the results. Writing and communication are strong tools, because in practice work does not market itself. A manager can be a cheerleader for only so long.

Lee says that being known was the difference between being stuck at L5 and being the person who pulled together Android engineers across Amazon, with data on when apps would run out of methods. People then send others to that person, and the person can point to the next step even when they lack the answer. Lee says human relationships are all there is. Lee worked remotely at Meta, never visited, and did not succeed. Lee had decent relationships but not the visibility, and so lacked help once things went wrong. Lee began asking one off-topic question a day on an Amazon team during the pandemic. Lee now does so in the chat rooms of two organizations at Google, and says people recognize Lee as the question person, which makes it easy to ask a product manager for help. Lee also suggests asking a manager whether anyone on the team needs a mentor, since even a no changes how they think of you, and sitting in on a product managers' event to understand their process and offer a developer's view. Lee says it may sound like politics, and sometimes it is, but it is part of the job. Lee, who describes being autistic with many social challenges, says Lee still has to do this to succeed.
Rahul offers a litmus test. If you asked a teammate what a person is known for, would they answer cohesively, such as saying that person is the expert on a system? If not, that is a bad sign.

followups.question: Is telling people about your work just self-promotion? (Sean, an attendee, asked what happened to modesty.)
answer: Rahul says do not frame it as bragging. Frame it as telling teammates how the work benefits them. Rahul's debugging tool at Meta made it faster to debug issues, and Rahul pitched it as a way to ease the work, help the product, and even help their performance reviews. Rahul's reframing is to give a call to action: here is how you can get plugged in.

Other panelists agree that sharing knowledge is mutual. Explaining what you tried, what failed and what worked, or building a lower-level framework others can reuse, makes the work more useful and spares others from learning the hard way. A panelist notes that big-tech engineers are often curious and open, and so they want to hear it. Lunch-and-learns and demos, such as a short screen share of a browser extension, can change how others work. The panelists draw the line between bragging and teaching there.

blocks.question: What heuristics improve the chance of promotion to staff, for example the choice of team, its size, or infrastructure versus product work? (Rahul)
answer: One panelist advises talking to someone above staff, such as a senior staff or principal engineer, asking what they would fix if they had the time, and doing that. A principal who supports your document goes a long way. The same panelist says to write the promotion document now, not when it feels ready. Show it to the people who review promotions and ask why they would reject it, then work on those gaps. Otherwise a promotion project might turn out not to be the right one, and that is the candidate's own fault. If the feedback is that you have never led anyone, the next project needs to show leadership rather than more code. Not understanding the process, the panelist says, leaves the outcome to luck.
Another panelist says they favor work on churn and finance-related problems at each company, because that is where the pain in the business is.

Zach puts the relationship with your manager first: without it, even a star will struggle. For data engineers, Zach says the data sets must be ones many other pipelines read from, such as master data. A data set made only for a visualization is not staff-level. A staff analytics engineer may instead own the whole chain from logging to data set to visualization and perhaps a model.

Another panelist describes three common rubric dimensions. One is the size of the work stream, such as the number of engineers and the duration. A second is complexity: could someone a level below solve it, or does it need domain knowledge such as distributed systems or AI? The third is impact: does it span several teams or reach significant business goals? This panelist says leverage comes from building things that other engineers build on, which biases toward infrastructure and tooling teams. Leading a very large product initiative is limited to a few places, and someone must grant permission, so those chances are fewer and harder to compete for.

followups.question: Is the preference for infrastructure a fair measure of staff-level work?
answer: Lee calls the focus on infrastructure and backend a legacy bias. Companies understood what top-level work on backend systems for billions of users looks like, but not what a principal front-end engineer does. Lee says people were advised to switch to a backend team to get promoted, which Lee considers wrong, though it has been real.
Zach adds that data engineering was new in 2016, and Facebook had only one staff data engineer at the time and now has dozens.

Rahul says the bias is not strictly front end versus back end. Engineers who build client-side infrastructure, such as an Android build system or a framework for client and server requests, also count. The key is that other engineers use what you build, and that is usually one layer below the people building the user-facing product.

blocks.question: Audience question: once you are at staff level, how do you keep exceeding expectations?
answer: One panelist says behaviors at staff and above are similar: influencing through others, growing people around you, and taking on the largest problems. What changes is that the initiatives are a step bigger. To exceed, find something larger in scope, such as influencing two larger organizations instead of one group of about 50, or building infrastructure for hundreds of engineers instead of dozens.

Zach, who says they received an exceeds rating at staff level at Airbnb for 2020, describes two parts. One was delivering the main "big rock" project, which for Zach was refining pricing and availability metrics. The other was design work on longer-term questions, such as a document on best practices for moving data from the data lake back into the Airbnb app, with feedback from principal engineers on edge cases. Zach says that missing the first means not meeting expectations at all, and doing both is what moves a person toward the senior staff level.

blocks.question: Audience question (Alan): what resources help with technical communication and finding mentorship?
answer: Rahul says the core skill is knowing your audience. At Meta, Rahul checked who belonged to an internal Workplace group before posting an update: engineers, leadership, or a cross-functional mix. Rahul then adjusted the depth, avoiding both too much detail and too little. Before a stand-up or meeting, find out who will be there and how much they know and care. Rahul has no book or video to suggest, and says the way to build empathy for different audiences is relationship building, which gives a sense of the personas you address.
Zach adds that posting on LinkedIn almost every day while at Airbnb taught Zach to say dense information concisely, because the platform rewards short posts. Zach recommends that skill for growth.

blocks.question: Audience question (sesh): should a senior engineer become a tech lead first on the way to staff?
answer: Ryan Peterman sees tech lead as a set of behaviors that can occur at any level, not as a level between senior and staff. Senior engineers on some teams lead smaller projects. Ryan suggests checking the company's own leveling system.

Another panelist cautions that if the missing pieces are leadership and visibility, being a tech lead may give more chances to practice them. But it is not necessarily a stepping stone, and doing the behaviors well does not guarantee a path to staff. A further panelist says the expected behaviors at each level should be written down at the company. Use that with your manager to see where you exceed and where you fall short, and ask for the documentation if you do not have it, because otherwise you can only guess.

blocks.question: Audience question (Sam): how can a data engineer show backend work to a manager who is not their day-to-day lead?
answer: Zach says that if there is no shiny front-end piece, part of the answer is to work with the data scientist or analyst who builds the visualization on top of your data. The other part is to show downstream impact. Zach says a data set can be sold as improving one of three kinds of decision: an executive's strategic decision, a data scientist's or analyst's product decision, or a machine-learning algorithm's automated decision. Zach's pricing and availability data sets at Airbnb fed Smart Pricing, an algorithm that sets prices for listings, which had a large effect on the business.

Zach adds that data engineers can also cite optimization numbers, such as a pipeline running 30 or 40 percent faster. At Airbnb, Zach cut the size of the pricing and availability data sets by 90 percent, so the company could use data 10 times smaller. Zach admits that data engineering can fall into the shadows because it lacks the show-it-off quality of a front end or a SQL query. Where the gain is only visibility, Zach suggests building a story around it.

blocks.label: Rahul's closing takeaway
blocks.text: Rahul's view is that the vast majority of engineers aiming for staff or senior roles, which Rahul puts at 99 percent, lack the skills of relationship building and talking to people. In Rahul's opinion, the task is less about the code than about working out what the problems are, who is hitting them, and how to solve them. The figure is Rahul's own estimate.

sections.title: Getting to Staff: Scope, Promotion Timing, and Visibility at Big Tech
sections.deck: Five panelists on reaching staff argue that high-scope work, early and explicit promotion conversations, willingness to take feedback, and visibility matter more than title alone.

blocks.text: Editorial summary of the panel's shared view: the opening framing treats staff as the first level where an individual contributor must lead without managing people. Progression runs from tasks to features to projects, and then to several projects or a whole product. The panelists argue that reaching that level depends on choosing work with real scope and visible impact, asking for promotion early and explicitly, and then acting on feedback. They also say title opens doors without settling scope, that managers differ in how much they control promotion, and that infrastructure and product teams offer different routes. Several points are offered as personal experience rather than general rules.
blocks.heading: The panel's view: scope, early asking, and visibility shape the path to staff

blocks.question: How do you tell which problems are worth solving, when a staff promotion needs enough scope?
answer: Zach describes a move at Netflix from an automated threat-detection project, which looked too ambitious, to a shared graph database that other teams could use in many cases. The shift brought more pay, more respect, and a larger leadership role.

Zach adds that scope is not the only test. Risky projects that may never pan out also waste time. Senior engineers can judge how much impact a project will have before investing in it, so a small request to them may sit in a backlog.

followups.question: How do you build the judgment to see which work will matter?
answer: Ryan says the main method is to read the incentives of the organization. Most teams publish plans with metric targets, so a person can compare an idea with a team goal and judge whether it is large enough.
Ryan also worked on an ads project outside Ryan's own team, which no one assigned, because the revenue opportunity looked large. The work had clear impact and was linked to a senior promotion.

blocks.question: For Carly and Lee: how explicit should someone be about wanting to reach staff, and how much should they tell a manager?
answer: Carly manages staff engineers and says people raise promotion in different ways. In Carly's experience, about half of the requests to move to staff came from people who were not yet ready. The other half came from people who were ready long before they asked. Carly sees two groups: people who ask readily, sometimes before they are ready, and people who wait until readiness is proved, often a year past it.
Carly suggests reflecting honestly on readiness without setting the bar so high that a reserved person holds back.

Lee says promotions often trail performance at large tech companies, so a person who never raises the question may not know what is missing. Lee suggests stating the goal directly: a wish to grow on the technical track rather than into management. Ask what is missing, build a plan, and write down the evidence, so the manager has the material when the person is ready. Lee notes that not everyone wants a promotion, and some people prefer their current level.

followups.question: Should a manager wait to be asked, or raise a promotion first?
answer: Carly says both happen. Carly has raised promotions with people who did not ask, when Carly judged them ready. With a large team, year-end reviews are the main time to reflect, but Carly prefers that people speak up between reviews when they feel ready or are clearly above the bar. Carly calls waiting a passive approach and sees little downside to asking too early.

followups.question: What should someone do if their manager says they are not ready?
answer: Carly says to listen. Feedback usually points to a blind spot the person cannot see, and a well-meaning manager is not trying to block a ready person. Carly also treats the response to feedback as part of readiness. A staff engineer must take feedback from leaders and teams, act on it, and reflect on it without turning combative.

Another panelist describes a first attempt to promote them into a manager role at Amazon that did not go through. The panelist asked which objections were raised and what evidence would answer each one, then tracked those gaps. The promotion came later, and the panelist says the change was the response to feedback, not one more project.

followups.question: What if you disagree with the feedback?
answer: A panelist says that if you disagree and think the feedback is wrong, you can test it by interviewing elsewhere, because the market gives its own view of readiness. The panelist has been promoted internally only once, from junior to mid-level, and got later promotions by changing companies. Some feedback is unreasonable, the panelist says, but learning to take feedback still matters, and leaving is one valid option rather than a required one.

followups.question: How should someone phrase a request for promotion?
answer: A panelist says framing matters. A new hire who asks for a promotion right away is unlikely to get support. A better frame is to name a first goal, such as ramping up and having impact, and ask for a check-in in about three months to plan the path. A manager is likely to agree, because the request then shows both interest in promotion and sound priorities.

Another panelist says asking early and explicitly is worth doing, even when it feels uncomfortable. At each level, that panelist asked what it would take to reach the next one, and the manager was glad to help because the team gained impact. Once a promotion looked likely, the panelist also asked about the level after that.

blocks.question: Does a high performer have leverage with a manager?
answer: A panelist says strong performers have leverage inside a company, because a manager wants to keep someone who solves the team's problems. Asking for growth from that position is more likely to get a receptive response than asking from a less central role.

The same panelist names the limits. A manager cannot promote someone on request, because processes and other decision-makers are involved. A manager can still steer projects toward the gaps named in a promotion plan. If the current team cannot offer that work, the honest options are to move to another team or look outside.

blocks.question: How much control does a manager have over promotion at each level?
answer: Zach says that at Airbnb, managers decided promotions up to senior, while promotion from senior to staff and above went through a committee. Zach describes Amazon before it used committees for promotion, where decisions moved up the management chain through skip-level managers and directors above the senior level, not only the direct manager.

followups.question: How does the process change at the highest levels?
answer: A panelist says that from junior to mid-level, the direct manager's view is usually decisive, so alignment with the manager matters most there. At the highest levels, sign-off from VPs and other senior leaders is needed, and the manager becomes more of a messenger for the committee. That is why it helps to ask early, so the manager can collect the committee's feedback sooner.

blocks.question: How should someone judge which team is the best place to earn a staff promotion?
answer: A panelist offers a rough test. At a company with many products, a team that works on the core product usually has more visibility than a team on a side product. The panelist jokes that working on a smaller app such as Garage Band is unlikely to lead to a promotion, while the flagship product gives visibility almost for free.

Another panelist says a team with less visibility can still make progress. Find the team that owns a weak spot, show them the problem in their code, and offer to help or pair with them. Fixing a real problem with that team makes a person a strong partner, which is different from a small cosmetic change.

A third panelist says caring about the work matters as much as its impact. During a Google interview, that panelist was offered an ads role and said it did not interest them. Work a person cares about gets their best effort, and that makes it easier to advocate for the product to others.

blocks.question: Do product or infrastructure teams offer a clearer route to staff?
answer: Ryan says staff-level opportunities are more common on infrastructure teams. Ryan's view is that product engineers usually reach high impact past senior by leading large projects, and there are few such seats. Infrastructure work has leverage built in, because foundational technology helps many teams move faster, which creates more roles. Ryan says Ryan's own infrastructure team is quite senior compared with others.

followups.question: Does the same leverage show up in data and engineering roles?
answer: Zach follows up with experience in both kinds of role. At Netflix, Zach was a staff-level tech lead on an infrastructure team building a graph database. At Airbnb, Zach was a tech lead on pricing and availability, which was closer to product. Zach says data engineering shows the difference most clearly. The more a person changes how other engineers do their work, rather than building one pipeline, the more leverage they have.

followups.question: Does infrastructure work lead to promotion on its own?
answer: A panelist agrees with Ryan's point and adds that changing how other engineers work, such as saving each engineer a few minutes a day, scales across hundreds of engineers. Then the panelist frames it differently. Infrastructure work often spans several teams and can have built-in impact, but the question is what impact is actually available, whether managers in that area know how to promote people, and who sees the work. If only the most senior person on a team sees it, the work may not support a promotion. Infrastructure teams offer more chances, but the team setup still matters, and product work is not ruled out.

blocks.question: How do remote or hybrid engineers compete with colleagues who sit close to the manager?
answer: A panelist says the main answer is documentation, communication, and proof. Written evidence of impact lets the manager and others see the work without relying on physical proximity. The panelist has worked only in fully remote settings, so the hybrid case is an extrapolation.

blocks.question: Did staff promotion require unusually long hours?
answer: Panelists give mixed accounts. One says the project that led to promotion took more than 40 hours a week. Zach recalls about 50 to 55 hours, including the Netflix graph-database build. Another panelist says 50 to 60 hours was common but still left time for sleep. A further panelist notes that some people are promoted while working 40 hours.

Panelists who moved into management say hours mattered less. One says that as a manager, the panelist did not exceed 40 hours a week, and that multiplying other people's output shows impact in fewer hours than personal delivery. Another plans by goal rather than hours, working around 60 hours one week and around 30 the next.

blocks.question: Do inflated startup titles lead to down-leveling at big tech?
answer: A panelist says down-leveling happens when a candidate does not meet the level the company expects. The panelist does not think it can be avoided, except by being stronger or interviewing better. Startup titles are often inflated, so the panelist advises comparing the scope of the work with what each company expects at each level, rather than targeting a title.

Another panelist says title matters less than pay and meaningful work. That panelist moved from a mid-level role at a startup to a junior role at Facebook, for about an 80 percent pay increase, and calls that a good trade.

blocks.question: Seniority opens doors, but bigger projects tend to come after promotion. How do you break that cycle?
answer: A panelist says seniority helps but matters less than internal brand. The person a manager or director thinks of first for a hard problem usually gets the work, and level often tracks that trust. Being known as someone who gets things done brings opportunities even without a senior title.

Another panelist says title is one way through the door, not the only way. A person can be trusted with larger scope than their title suggests if a manager or senior sponsor vouches for them, and their own actions build that trust. A director-level sponsor can push for the scope, but the person still has to go find it.

blocks.question: How do you get visibility without feeling that you are self-promoting?
answer: A panelist says visibility is necessary to move up, even when it feels awkward or the person is reserved. Visibility does not mean posting about every win. It can come from giving tech talks after a major launch, running a talk series that brings others in, or answering questions on an internal forum. The key is that the people who speak for you know what you do.

Another panelist adds that an internal brand comes from being approachable and helping teammates get unblocked. A promotion case usually needs peer feedback from three or four co-workers who can vouch for the person. Reaching across disciplines, such as product managers and data scientists, strengthens that case, because a person who wins over only one group is still not moving up.

blocks.question: What was the main reason to seek promotion: money, title, or work-life balance?
answer: One panelist says the main reason was the kind of work. Senior and principal engineers at Amazon were doing influence-heavy work, such as mentoring people, helping engineers grow, and shaping decisions above their own team. The panelist wanted that work. Pay was welcome, but it was not the main draw.

followups.question: Does moving up change pay in a meaningful way?
answer: A panelist says pay at big tech does not rise evenly with level. The jump from senior to staff is usually much larger than the jumps before it, and more of total pay shifts into stock. Money gives optionality, but stock adds risk. Another panelist recalls a grant worth about $1.5 million on paper that was worth roughly $600,000 six months later, after the share price fell. That panelist also says stock outcomes vary across companies and years.

followups.question: Does a well-known employer still help after you leave?
answer: A panelist says pedigree matters because people pattern-match. A name-brand company, such as a staff role at a large tech employer, can set a floor on a later job or a startup. The panelist acknowledges that pattern-matching can also work against people, including on race and gender, and calls that obviously bad. The benefit still mattered to the panelist's own job hopping.

blocks.question: How many people does a staff engineer typically affect?
answer: A panelist thinks about the number of people affected rather than team size. A senior engineer should affect at least their own team and the scope of the senior manager above them. The panel's rough estimates are about 20 to 30 engineers at senior, up to 50 to 60 at staff, and into the hundreds at principal, which can mean a VP's organization.
Another panelist recalls an Airbnb marketplace organization of about 75 engineers, with around five staff engineers within it.

blocks.question: How does office politics affect advancement, and what should people do about it?
answer: A panelist says politics is mostly about people. Some colleagues are difficult, and some use relationships to get ahead in harmful ways. The panelist does not expect a person to change or remove those colleagues, so the better move is to raise your own standing. If the environment is truly toxic, the right answer may be a different place.
The same panelist adds that when people talk about politics, they often mean difficulty communicating with executives or with another team. That gap can be fixed, and fixing it is part of the job.

followups.question: How can someone who is right but blunt get their ideas heard?
answer: A panelist says a manager once told them they were right on most points, but that the way they said things was too blunt for people to hear. The panelist learned to ask questions instead of declaring an idea wrong, to ask whether a design would hold at a larger scale, and to point to an earlier system that had failed in a similar way. The panelist says being heard matters more than being right, and that the questions a person asks can be a sign of intelligence.
