sections.title: John White: Promotion Culture, Meta Teams, and Career Regrets
sections.deck: John White describes how promotion incentives shaped Meta's AI infrastructure and monetization teams, why he treats team culture as a choice, and what he regrets most.

blocks.text: In John White's view, big-tech promotion systems reward a visible career story more than the work itself. He says that in Meta's AI infrastructure and monetization groups, promotion goals pushed teams to ship projects many people expected to fail, and to build systems tightly coupled to other systems, because a rollout that touched many systems helped with promotion. He argues that engineers still have real agency to choose a healthier team, even though that choice can mean slower promotion and lower pay. Editorially, the rest of the conversation covers his early years on experimentation tools, the cost of treating industry as a fallback, statistics and A/B testing rigor, and his regrets.
blocks.heading: John White's view: promotion incentives, not only pay, steer what engineers build and how teams work

blocks.question: Is John still bullish on Meta and MSL after working there from the inside?
answer: John says he is very bullish on Meta as a company, now as a stockholder rather than an employee. He is much less bullish about being an employee who holds little equity, which he says describes most people, since most staff are paid mostly in cash.

He says working at Meta is less enjoyable than before, even though the business is run very well for the bottom line. He keeps investing in the company and expects to continue. He describes being an employee there as a more stressful time than before.

followups.question: What makes being an employee harder now?
answer: John says the labor market for engineers has shifted across Silicon Valley. Employers once made large sacrifices to keep scarce engineers. Outside a small set of AI researchers at frontier labs, he says, most employers now see engineers as oversupplied, and some worry that AI makes the surplus worse.
So employers spend less on pay, perks, and staff voice. John says this is a general pattern, not unique to Meta, and it makes being an employee rougher overall.
followups.speaker: John White

followups.question: Could weaker employee leverage also shape reorganization decisions?
answer: John agrees. Earlier Meta did many things that were bad for the business but made sense for keeping talent, and the company is doing less of that now. He says the fear of layoffs is the biggest emotional stressor for most people, more than perks such as food. After layoffs, people who had complained about losing perks became more tolerant of losing them.

He says MSL feels more stressful than some other frontier labs because layoffs seem possible there. The captions make his comparison with OpenAI and Anthropic hard to follow, so it is not restated here.
followups.speaker: John White

blocks.speaker: John White

blocks.question: Did the promise of career growth change as a retention tool at Meta?
answer: John says many Meta divisions stopped talking about pay, purpose, and enjoying the work as reasons to stay. People instead said the only reason to do anything was a clear story about a promotion. When he moved from data infrastructure into AI infrastructure, he found almost no one whose first goal was not promotion.

Monetization was the strongest case. It hired people out of AI infrastructure with detailed plans for getting promoted. John says that worked for promotions but wrecked many teams, including several he later managed and had to repair. People on those teams agreed the work was bad and unlikely to succeed, yet shipped it to meet their promotion bar.

He says this made good software decisions almost impossible, and that the skills that would help careers most became separate from promotions. When the market turned against employees, managers told people to fear layoffs more than they hoped for promotions. He does not think that was a good cultural fix, though he sees it as an attempt to undo earlier damage.

followups.question: Did you see people keep playing the promotion game even when they saw unusual behavior?
answer: John says unless a VP is ready to fix the culture and shut it down, people have to play along. He calls not playing the game irrational, because one person cannot unilaterally disarm. He says the culture was dominant in AI infrastructure and monetization, was bad for nearly everyone, and left people in a demoralizing rat race.
followups.speaker: John White

followups.question: What could someone do about a culture like this?
answer: John says people have a lot of agency in choosing their team's culture. Meta had many teams without the promotion-first culture, PyTorch among them, where people worked for the love of the craft. Inside the system you still have to follow its rules, but you are not forced to stay in that machine. Not everyone would meet the bar for those teams, but many could.

He chose stable teams that would improve over time and keep a healthy culture, even though that meant slower promotion. He says he is torn. If the goal were lifetime earnings, fast-promoting and fast-firing teams might be economically rational. For him, enjoying the craft mattered more, and he was willing to accept about 20 percent less compensation to work somewhere he was prouder of.
followups.speaker: John White

followups.question: Did outsiders see PyTorch engineers as under-leveled?
answer: John says outsiders often believed PyTorch held a higher bar for promotion, which made it easier to convince others that PyTorch engineers were ready for higher levels. In hiring conversations, candidates sometimes asked whether PyTorch was under-leveled. John would say they might be, or that PyTorch held the right levels and the candidate had to decide whether to take a chance on them. He says PyTorch also trained people who became remarkably good.
followups.speaker: John White

blocks.speaker: John White

blocks.question: How was your early time at Facebook on the experimentation tools, before the promotion pressure?
answer: John says his first two years at Meta were some of his happiest, though also among the most frightening. He had asked for six months of leave to work on Julia, a language he was a core contributor to. While he was away, the manager who hired him left, and the team he had joined split into core data science and data science infrastructure.

He wanted to join core data science but worked closely with data science infrastructure, which owned the experimentation tools. He says that work was the most valuable thing he did as an individual contributor, and that people who know him from Meta remember him for it. Core data science was turbulent, with reorganizations, new managers, and churn.

A few months in, a paper from a research-leaning group that John was affiliated with became a major PR problem for Meta. John remembers it as something like 'Emotional Contagion in Social Networks'. He tried to prevent the problem but lacked the authority. The author later apologized to the company in a Q&A. John found himself in meetings with the head of legal, and his team faced the possibility of being disbanded. He calls it a formative experience, though the fallout faded.

Over the following years he became one of the main developers of Deltoid, its third iteration. When most senior engineers left within about six months, he became the only person who remembered how the system worked. At about IC5, he became a de facto tech lead and drove the vision for the A/B testing tools for years. He calls it some of the most fulfilling work he did at Meta.

followups.question: What was Deltoid, in short?
answer: John confirms that Deltoid is an A/B testing framework, where users are assigned to one code path or another and the team measures downstream effects. He says the Statsig product he knows looks almost identical to Deltoid in interface and features. He says he should have built a Deltoid-style startup years earlier, but lacked the wisdom to. He is not sure of Statsig's current state.
followups.speaker: John White

blocks.speaker: John White

blocks.question: What is Julia, and what was the data science language war about?
answer: John says he may have made Julia part of that war more than it needed to be. He argues that programming languages are products in zero-sum competition, and that saying otherwise misleads people. Julia's pitch was high-level code that reads like Python or MATLAB and still runs fast. MIT mathematicians designed it to replace MATLAB, so it targeted that market more than data science, though John helped push it toward data science.

His example is a distance-matrix function. The underlying C code is a set of plain loops, and a naive translation into R keeps the same loops, yet R runs far slower. John estimates 1,000 to 10,000 times slower than C. He was frustrated that many Python and R users treated speed as both impossible and unimportant. Julia rejected that view. John was a heavy R user and was disappointed by how often R fought him.

John says Julia has become less fashionable but is still doing well, and he believes it is among the top 25 languages by users. He thinks it is probably the only community still fighting that fight, even though he does not think it has won.

followups.question: What is the intuition behind R being about 10,000 times slower when the code looks similar to C?
answer: John says slow code usually does work it does not need to do. R pays a heavy overhead because it allows dynamic behavior that may never be used. In R, the brace used to mark a block can be redefined, so you must check whether it has changed. John says he may be misremembering whether it is braces or parentheses. Each such check can cost hundreds to thousands of machine cycles, while adding two 64-bit integers takes one.

R is also lazily evaluated, so function arguments become promise objects. John recalls a paper by two students and a senior professor, Jan Vitek, on the design of R. It found that most promises could have been evaluated eagerly, perhaps 70 to 90 percent, though he is not sure of the figure. Python's inspect module can also change the symbol table, so names cannot be trusted without checking. Fast languages have many guarantees, and R has very few.
followups.speaker: John White

blocks.speaker: John White

blocks.question: Why did John find it frustrating that grad students and postdocs see industry as a safe fallback?
answer: John says what frustrated him most was that many PhD students wanted to be professors or postdocs, and treated industry as the fallback if they failed out. In interviews, some candidates clearly did not want to be there and saw the interview as a failure, which is not a good sign for an employer.

He also says many academics assumed industry jobs would be easy, as if smart people stayed in academia and weaker people went to industry. One candidate, effectively a computer science professor, could not pass values between functions in code. They printed values in a REPL, read them, and retyped them by hand. John says that method would not work for production code, and that the belief hurts students across the academic system.
blocks.speaker: John White

blocks.question: Why does John hold such strong views on statistics, and which books does he recommend?
answer: John says he loves statistics but calls it one of the craziest fields. It sells the idea that statistical methods work in real life, yet much of the work is pure mathematics about idealized settings. In pure math, a proof only has to be internally consistent. In applied fields such as software, it is enough that the code runs. He says statistics reasons mathematically and then makes practical claims, and that is where opinions come in.

He says some statisticians hold themselves to a very high bar, while others call a claim true because they said so. His top recommendation is Larry Wasserman, whose books he calls the embodiment of intense honesty. Wasserman states what is assumed and what is implied, and avoids claims that are not true. John says no book has been better for learning statistics. He also recommends a book he recalls as something like Introduction to Agnostic Statistics, by an author the captions render as 'Peter Eranell'. He calls that author hyper-rigorous, and says the book is a little less math-heavy than Wasserman's, which suits social scientists and practitioners.

followups.question: Do people in industry approve launches on a green bar without checking the statistics underneath?
answer: John agrees and gives an example from the Deltoid 3 launch. Deltoid 1 was still the default. A reviewer blocked the launch because a holdout that had been a statistically significant win was no longer significant under Deltoid 3, and the reviewer read that as a regression. John replied that it might be a regression, or it might be the truth, and that nobody knew which. The reviewer wanted to wait until the half ended and goals were met. John argued that a result that close to the line is not a real win, since mild code changes could flip it.

John calls it a dangerous culture to treat results that barely cross or miss the significance line as clear wins or failures. He describes a team he managed that shipped code to hit a goal, although it planned to delete the code a day into the next half. He asked why they were shipping it, and they said they could not miss their goals. He argued that goals should not reward shipping code that will be deleted right away. He convinced them not to ship, since as the manager he decided ratings.
John says weak statistical understanding feeds other odd evaluation habits, and the two together become especially dangerous.
followups.speaker: John White

blocks.speaker: John White

blocks.question: Do you have a regret that others could learn from?
answer: John says he has a stock answer, because he is asked often. For his first several years, his skip-level manager, Javi, ran office hours. John's manager, Danny, kept suggesting that someone should go. John did not go, because he felt he had nothing valuable to say to Javi.

Later, as John ran office hours for a larger organization, he wished people would come, and he realized Javi had felt the same way. John says he missed a valuable opportunity and made things worse for Javi as well. He calls it a decision made out of fear that harmed both parties.

His advice for junior engineers is to go when a leader says they want to hear from people. Directors and above are far removed from the work, and John says he sometimes had managers managing managers. Bring a concrete idea rather than asking how to get promoted, he says. Leaders welcome that, and many people are afraid to do it, which makes everyone worse off.
blocks.speaker: John White

blocks.question: If you could go back to the start of your career and give yourself advice, what would you say?
answer: John says he holds strong opinions but can be more self-conscious than he should. His advice is to believe that bigger work is possible, and that with high discipline it is. From high school through college, he says, he too often cast doubt on what he could do. He calls that the biggest set of mistakes he has made: not being ambitious enough, or not believing a problem was tractable.

He also says people over-convince themselves of others' greatness and under-convince themselves of what they can achieve. That combination makes them take fewer risks than they could. Until he worked with many people who succeeded, he says, he did not see how often those people were not much better. They just tried, and others did not. For a 20-year-old version of himself, that is the main lesson he would give.
blocks.speaker: John White

sections.title: Let the problem choose the role
sections.deck: Ilya Grigorik traces a founder, manager, and principal-engineer career built around curiosity, self-sufficient teams, and a versatile combination of skills.

blocks.question: Why are Waterloo’s co-op students so effective?
answer: Grigorik credits alternating academic terms with work terms, rather than treating industry experience as an optional interruption after years of study. Roughly six placements offer repeated experiments with industry, company size, role, and working environment.

A short placement can disprove a preconceived preference without the resume stigma of repeatedly leaving permanent jobs. Someone who imagined Wall Street may discover the city, people, or work do not suit them. Repeated choices build a better model of personal fit.

The applied work also puts theoretical tools in context. An engineer must solve a real problem under constraints and recognize when a theoretically sophisticated optimization does not matter—for example, when the array has only ten items. He would like more universities to adopt that repeated learning loop.

blocks.question: Why found PostRank after graduation?
answer: He initially planned graduate school partly because he did not know what to do. During the summer, he explored a product idea: links could signal useful content, but comments, likes, and other social interactions could add signals in the newer web. PostRank aggregated those interactions to rank posts.

His launch brought both demand and implementation problems. He recalls several sleepless days because the servers struggled, admitting that poor code contributed. Publicity led to investor conversations.

Facing the graduate-school start, he noticed that the courses most appealing to him concerned entrepreneurship. He could study those ideas academically or learn while already speaking with investors. He postponed the program, closed funding, and never returned to complete the degree. The choice was an experiment connected to a real opportunity, rather than a predetermined founder identity.

blocks.question: How did Google’s acquisition conversation begin?
answer: After a conference presentation, a Google Analytics product leader approached the team and invited a conversation. The discussion was friendly and exploratory, beginning with understanding the product and asking whether they could work together. Grigorik later understood that Google’s response to Facebook and its social initiatives created demand for relevant talent and infrastructure. Analytics could use their experience to understand social engagement, making a mutually useful connection.

followups.question: How did Google decide levels and compensation for an acquired team?
answer: The team, including Grigorik, underwent full interview panels in an accelerated group process. Google evaluated engineering quality and level rather than assume acquisition alone established those. Deal negotiations also had distinct layers: people, customers, product, and intellectual property.

followups.question: Was an acquisition payment simply a large signing bonus?
answer: Not necessarily. Different deals acquire different combinations of assets and people. PostRank supplied useful intellectual property, but its product largely had to be rebuilt within Google Analytics. Moving from tens of thousands of accounts to internet-scale pipelines changed the engineering economics: even a small field addition could imply enormous storage. He remembers learning from reliability engineers to scrutinize such changes.

blocks.question: What was your role in Google Analytics, and why leave a director trajectory?
answer: He joined as an engineering manager because he had been founder and CTO. He remained committed to the original aim of helping publishers understand engagement and spent about a year rebuilding the stack. With the team on a sound trajectory, he considered another direction.

A VP offered a clear path toward director, but Google’s technical environment drew his curiosity. Internal documents showed work far ahead of published papers, and engineers sometimes lacked time rather than permission to share the advances. He became interested in contributing to a broader web ecosystem.

The Make the Web Fast group worked across cellular systems, protocols, proxies, and the fundamental question of measuring speed. Grigorik chose a lateral move into IC work even though he might be downleveled and reset the conventional management path. He valued more self-direction, fascinating problems, and collaborators he admired.

followups.question: Were curiosity and control of your time the actual tradeoff?
answer: Yes. He says a manager’s calendar largely serves other people’s needs. He wanted another mode in which he could direct more of his own work toward research or projects where his skills were especially useful. He acknowledges substantial uncertainty in making the choice.

blocks.question: Why later return to management in developer relations?
answer: He regards movement between IC and manager as an underappreciated pattern among senior engineers. A person may first discover a path alone, then realize that building the full solution requires a team. His analogy distinguishes cutting a trail from constructing a highway.

His performance work moved into browser standards and metrics. Once those metrics existed, the bottleneck became adoption across analytics vendors and open-source projects. One person could not do all that outreach. A developer-relations team could accelerate adoption that otherwise might take several years.

He therefore returned to recruiting and organizing people in service of the problem. The management move was a means of carrying work through a new stage, not a permanent declaration that people management was the only kind of growth.

followups.question: Is a tour of duty about whichever role best serves the mission?
answer: Yes, while not every problem must become his personal mission. Often success means helping a team reach the point where it can execute without him. Continuing dependence suggests he has not sufficiently strengthened it. If he commits to lead for a period, he still needs a succession plan: finish the problem or establish a self-sufficient trajectory, then step back and find the next problem as an IC.

blocks.question: What does principal-to-distinguished growth at Shopify require?
answer: He does not supply a checklist or name one promotion project. A principal engineer must identify useful work amid ambiguity. He expects someone entering an unfamiliar area to learn the landscape, build partnerships, understand leaders’ problems, and determine where their skills apply.

For distinguished work, he emphasizes a demonstrated range across technical layers and business requirements. Someone must understand low-level constraints, reconstruct the actual problem, and connect it to what product and business partners need.

The execution mode also changes with the situation. A frontier problem requires rapid experiments that reveal unknowns; a long-lived platform API requires slow consideration of consequences for the ecosystem. In either case, exploration must lead to a recommendation and useful execution. He compares the role’s ambiguity with a VP receiving difficult problems that lower layers could not solve.

followups.question: Why aim to be the only person rather than the best?
answer: He respects deep specialists but considers a portfolio more resilient if demand changes. Modest design, sales, support, hosting, security, and engineering skills can combine into a useful capability that otherwise requires a team. When a specialist arrives, he can hand over one part and focus elsewhere.

Cross-functional learning also lets him translate among marketing, PR, engineering, and business partners. He recalls intensive marketing reading to learn their vocabulary. His rapid-learning percentages are personal heuristics; they are not demonstrated learning rates for every domain.

The senior person need not know the most. His responsibility can be finding experts and helping them navigate the difficult space between platform possibilities and business requirements. Knowing how to find answers and facilitate decisions is different from memorizing every API.

blocks.question: Does a broad skill intersection make a generalist distinctive?
answer: He agrees. A person with sufficient knowledge of several relevant areas can combine them for an unusual problem and change their contribution as circumstances change. Management experience is another available tool: even as an IC, he can coach, give feedback, and partner effectively with managers. His probability-language analogy expresses uniqueness; the interview does not establish an independence-based mathematical model for career success.

followups.question: Should an IC try management, and is returning a demotion?
answer: He suggests team leadership as a way to explore and management itself if it suits the person. He wants organizations to permit movement in both directions without penalty. Senior managers can value what they learned while still remembering an earlier technical role as their happiest period. Returning to that kind of work can be a new challenge rather than a failure.

blocks.question: What regrets should others learn from?
answer: Do not let success raise the threshold for trying so high that it stops learning. His early writing and code now seem embarrassing, but publishing them generated feedback and encouragement that made improvement possible.

A larger audience creates an expectation of exceptional output. That can suppress ordinary observations and experiments that would once have been shared freely. He continues to struggle with that filter and encourages the courage to be mistaken or disliked without claiming to know everything.

followups.question: How do you enter an unfamiliar domain when people expect a distinguished engineer to know the answers?
answer: Set expectations explicitly. He arrives to help and learn, asks foundational questions, and explains that he needs to build a model quickly. Curiosity can otherwise sound like an attack. Acknowledging both what others know and what he can contribute makes the exchange collaborative: they supply domain expertise while he can remove obstacles or connect ideas.

blocks.question: What author or book influenced your career?
answer: He recommends Sir Ken Robinson’s books and talks about education, creativity, and finding one’s element. The philosophy resonates with the co-op discussion: allow people to discover their strengths and combine skills rather than fit a rigid age-based factory model. He recognizes that implementing such an education system is difficult; his endorsement concerns its direction rather than a ready-made policy.

blocks.question: What would you tell yourself at the beginning?
answer: Value the ability to combine skills rather than feel inferior because friends excel more deeply in individual areas. Early uncertainty about his own broad but uneven competence eventually gave way to recognizing its usefulness.

He would also be braver and filter himself less. Public speaking once terrified him; pitching a product he cared about felt entirely different from performing knowledge for a class. Passion changed how he engaged. He could not have predicted that communication would later become a large part of his job.

blocks.title: A tour of duty changes with the problem

steps.title: Find the path
steps.text: Investigate and define an uncertain problem as an IC.

steps.title: Build the team
steps.text: Recruit and organize when execution exceeds one person.

steps.title: Make progress durable
steps.text: Solve the problem or establish a self-sufficient direction.

steps.title: Plan succession
steps.text: Remove dependence on the original pathfinder.

steps.title: Return to exploration
steps.text: Choose the next contribution and the role it requires.

blocks.caption: Editorial synthesis. Arrows show a possible project lifecycle in Grigorik’s account, not a required promotion ladder.

sections.title: Life after the next promotion stops being the goal
sections.deck: Philip Su examines career limits, the emotional cost of stepping down, and the need for meaning beyond status and financial security.

blocks.question: What did you think when you reached distinguished engineer—did you want another promotion?
answer: Early in his career, Su assumed that promotions would continue every few years and did not consider an eventual end. By level seven, he recognized that higher roles require more scope and that the business must actually need that scope. An organization might limit partner-level positions for budgetary and organizational reasons, irrespective of an individual’s ambition.

When Facebook first introduced level nine, the initial promotees seemed extraordinarily accomplished and universally recognized. He did not consider going further realistic. His recollection challenges the idea that every promotion simply starts another predictable step upward: roles narrow, opportunity matters, and people encounter limits.

blocks.question: What kept you growing through staff and beyond?
answer: For much of his Microsoft career, levels provided a substitute for the grades and tests he had enjoyed at school. Professional work offered few clear numerical indicators, so promotion felt like an achievement score. He actively pursued that score into his early thirties.

Beyond level seven, he became unsure whether he would enjoy the changing work or meet its expectations. His later promotions to eight and nine were consequences of work he found interesting, rather than explicit targets. Facebook was then small and mission-focused; he says he did not even know levels existed there until his manager told him he had been promoted.

blocks.question: What changed your view of promotion?
answer: The reward became less uncomplicated. A promotion brought expectations he was no longer certain he could fulfill. Staying at a level where he already enjoyed the work began to feel comfortable, and he recognized that it might be his final level.

He recalls immediately asking how to reach eight after a mentor promoted him to seven. The mentor asked whether they could spend one meeting celebrating. Years later, Su realized that this respected, more experienced mentor was himself at the same level. He now sees his earlier response as insufficiently humble: doing excellent work at an existing level is already a substantial accomplishment.

followups.question: What calmed the intense desire for more?
answer: He thinks age may contribute, while explicitly valuing young people’s ambition. A more concrete factor was the changing job. Up to about IC6, the work often felt like a larger version of coding, refactoring, and longer-term engineering projects.

For a generalist beyond that point, advancement increasingly means setting team direction, judging whether a product is worth building, and resolving conflicts between organizations. More meetings come with the work on either the IC or management path. He became less enthusiastic about those future changes. He acknowledges rare engineers whose exceptional coding ability supports another path.

blocks.question: Before seeking a demotion, did you ever ask not to be promoted beyond IC7?
answer: Not when moving from seven to eight: that promotion surprised him, and the smaller Facebook of that period still involved relatively little organizational overhead. Later, the Seattle office alone had grown from a handful of desks to more than two thousand people. Senior roles in a much larger organization contained more coordination and less direct technical work.

He distinguishes enjoyable people work—welcoming colleagues and creating collaborations—from politics, unhappy colleagues, and constructive feedback. He felt effective leading Facebook London but much less effective at some of the latter responsibilities. Even a senior IC without direct reports is expected to improve people around them, so opting out of management does not remove interpersonal demands.

followups.question: How did moving from IC9 to IC7 feel?
answer: It was difficult despite choosing it. Rising had felt like progress; being at the top mixed remarkable opportunities with exhausting expectations. He felt a continuing spotlight on whether the company was receiving value from a highly paid senior employee.

Watching people formerly below his level rise above him brought wistfulness rather than a wish to limit their success. He remembered being capable of that work and wondered whether he could do it again. His Beowulf analogy expresses the desire to deliver one last great performance, while accepting that this may no longer be right for him.

blocks.question: What changed that made the higher level harder to sustain?
answer: His environment changed. In a small company, his generalist range was useful: for Facebook video calling, he wrote code, negotiated partner contracts, dealt with testing arrangements, and spoke to the press. A large company assigns those tasks to specialized functions. He thinks senior domain experts fit that setting better, while his own strengths became less relevant.

One later team spent an entire half fixing bugs in an internal tool. He was willing to help, but it was not work in which he felt especially distinguished. Meanwhile, he tired of the pressure to meet senior expectations. Earlier, being the weakest person on a team could feel exciting because he was catching up; later it felt like a recurring risk rather than a desirable challenge.

followups.question: Was that pressure mostly impostor syndrome, given your promotions?
answer: He allows that some may have been, but considers much of it an honest assessment of fit. At IC4 he could imagine doing many IC5 jobs with time. At IC7 he could see peers doing work he did not believe he could do. Higher-level business roles also become more specific: the organization needs a particular combination of technical and other strengths, and his own shape did not match many of them.

blocks.question: Why did you work extreme hours after you stopped pursuing promotions?
answer: Shipping the first Facebook video-calling version brought a strong sense of mission. During six weeks in Menlo Park, he describes moving almost directly between work and sleep and losing about ten pounds. He was not seeking a level; he enjoyed seeing users benefit from fixes and believed easier video calling would matter.

The tiny team created a sense of responsibility to colleagues who were working equally hard. Direct contact with user problems and a meaningful product supplied motivation that the promotion score had previously supplied. His recollection explains his choice; it is not presented as a prescription for everyone’s hours.

blocks.question: Looking back, was working so hard worth it?
answer: Su understands why successful, wealthy people telling younger people to slow down can sound unpersuasive. Some tradeoffs become clearer only after living them. For his personality, very senior roles with broad people-oriented pressure became a poor long-term fit.

He also recognizes what the career bought him: enough savings to spend two years building his own software. He does not reject the earlier work outright. His regret is that he pushed without understanding the exchange he was making. Greater awareness could have connected present effort to future freedom and made competing priorities explicit.

blocks.question: Is advice useless if people only understand it after experience?
answer: He distinguishes ignoring advice from never having heard it. Advice provides a reference point: when the consequence arrives, someone can recognize it and act sooner. It can also cause a person to pause at a later decision even if they do not follow it immediately.

His small example is buying an expensive, highly recommended pen once he felt financially secure. It was slippery and rolled away; he preferred a cheap familiar pen. The disappointment made advice about consumption and happiness concrete. He uses the story to show delayed understanding, not to claim every expensive purchase disappoints.

blocks.question: After financial security, what provides meaning outside the earnings treadmill?
answer: He distinguishes personalities that remain content with prolonged leisure from his own need for goals. A week on a beach feels wonderful; an extended stay starts to feel purposeless. His analogy of an animal endlessly triggering pleasure expresses why pleasure alone does not constitute fulfillment for him.

He imagines that the saving phase of financial independence could be more satisfying than retirement for someone like him: it gives a measurable goal and repeated evidence of progress. He says he never adopted the movement himself. Periods without work exposed his difficulty answering what he should do next. This is self-description, not a judgment that others’ retirement preferences are wrong.

blocks.question: Would you have been happier with slower promotions spread across your whole career?
answer: He initially thinks spreading the rewards out might have helped, then acknowledges the dilemma. Six promotions over a forty-two-year career would imply seven years per step, which he would have found painfully slow at the beginning. Faster early growth leaves very long intervals later, or decades with no promotion.

The arithmetic is illustrative rather than a proposed career plan. It reveals that promotion cannot remain the sole source of motivation for an entire career. He also wonders whether a late reward has the same appeal as an earlier one, using a sports-car purchase as an analogy. He remains torn rather than endorsing deliberate slow advancement.

blocks.question: Have you found meaning without an immediate career goal?
answer: For him, regular social contact is essential. Work supplies a recurring shared place and schedule. After quitting Facebook for six months, he expected coffee with former colleagues to fill that gap, but they were busy working.

His best period between jobs came when two former colleagues were also available. They skied on weekdays and spent time together regularly. He uses an imaginative comparison with leisure-class social life to express the difference: free time is more satisfying when others can share it. Whether employed or not, he now considers a reliable social setting central to happiness.

blocks.question: Which book helped you think about life and career choices?
answer: He recommends Four Thousand Weeks because viewing a life as a finite number of weeks made time more precious and clarified his need to examine values. The recommendation is his account of what helped him, with no claim that it answers every reader’s situation.

followups.question: What practical question did it help you ask?
answer: Visualize your largest current goal, then imagine you have achieved it and ask what happens the next day. A satisfying answer suggests something durable beyond the goal itself. Su did not have that answer and compares the resulting difficulty to athletes who reach the peak without building another identity or set of skills. He encourages planning for the day after success.

blocks.question: If you could begin again, what would you change?
answer: He would change periods when he made himself maximally available to the employer and minimally available to friends and family. Some work he justified as helping the family also meant he was rarely present with them.

Interestingly, he does not single out the intense video-calling launch as the main regret. His family moved to California with him, and he remembers that arrangement as making the period more acceptable even with very little daily time together. Other periods involved routine absence without that shared context.

followups.question: Would prioritizing family have reduced your career success?
answer: Possibly, and he considers the exchange worthwhile. He does not know the counterfactual: breaks can improve performance when fatigue creates errors, so shorter hours might sometimes have helped him professionally.

He also rejects an unconditional promise that forty hours produces the same results as longer work. All else equal, he expects sustained additional effort to affect results and rewards. His conclusion is therefore candid about costs: he suspects greater family availability could have affected his career, and would still accept that tradeoff.

blocks.title: What changed as Su’s career and company grew
rows: Promotion supplied a clear achievement score.
Interesting work, fit, and acceptable expectations mattered more.
A small company rewarded broad generalist contributions.
A large company separated those tasks into specialist roles.
More scope could resemble larger coding projects.
Greater scope involved product judgment and organizational influence.
Progress supplied the next goal.
Financial security and a senior level required a new answer to what comes next.

sections.title: Michael Novati: Early Facebook, the Coding Machine, and Reaching Senior Staff
sections.deck: Michael Novati, an early Facebook engineer who rose to senior staff, argues that output was constant over a career and that taste, trust, and feedback loops are what moved him up.

blocks.text: Michael Novati joined Facebook as an intern in 2009, when the company had roughly 200 engineers, and later reached senior staff (IC7). In this interview Novati argues that raw coding output was already high in the first week and barely changed over the career. What moved Novati up the ladder was accumulated taste and judgment, built through repeated feedback, plus the credibility to make wide-reaching changes safely. The host, who is not named in the captions, also asks about early Facebook culture, stories about Mark Zuckerberg, whether LLMs threaten the coding-machine archetype, and why Novati left Meta. Everything below is Novati's account and opinion unless marked as an editorial note.
blocks.heading: Novati's view: output gets an engineer started, but judgment, trust, and feedback loops carry the career

blocks.question: What was the story behind joining Facebook as an intern, and why that company when it was small?
answer: Novati started as an intern in May 2009, between undergrad and grad school. A PhD in human-computer interaction at the University of Washington was already planned, with housing and a research assistantship lined up. Novati wanted work experience at a top company doing interesting product work, and applied online only to Facebook and Google. Getting interviews was not hard then, Novati says, and seems harder now.

The Facebook fit was close to accidental. Novati happened to interview with an engineer building internal collaboration tools: diff review, tasks, and discussion. That was the kind of "social network for work" Novati most wanted to build. After doing well on the LeetCode-style questions, Novati joined that engineer's team, with that engineer as manager. Novati calls it the stars aligning.

followups.question: How big was the company then in terms of engineers?
answer: About 220, Novati says, with a caveat. Production engineers were not classified as software engineers at the time, so the exact count depends on how the line is drawn. Roughly 200 is the safe figure.
followups.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.question: What drew Novati so strongly to Meta's culture?
answer: Novati names a technical pull and a social one. On day one, following the setup instructions, the dev environment ran Apache and PHP locally against a MySQL database, much like a side project, only with a larger federated database behind it. Novati says it felt like home and in tune with how the company built things.

Socially, Facebook was a product everyone had heard of and had opinions on. Novati could get plenty of feedback about what people liked and disliked, and found it motivating to build something people cared about. Novati adds that the company went through ups and downs, even during the tenure.
blocks.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.question: Many engineers who joined then were put off by PHP. Did Novati feel the same?
answer: Novati gives a split answer: yes and no. Meta now mainly uses Hack, a derivative of PHP, and the path there took stages. The first was a compiler that turned PHP into faster code. There was also a debate about rewriting the whole codebase in Java or Python, and the company chose to optimize and customize the language instead. Novati recalls type-related changes, described as "loose typing", among the early additions.

Off-the-shelf PHP carried a stigma at the time. Novati's reading of Facebook's approach was to make the language better than any other could be for this company, by customizing it at the language level so it was easier for engineers and faster. The host adds a view of their own, that PHP gets more criticism than it deserves and that Hack is a much better experience.
blocks.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.question: What does Novati think of "move fast and break things," now that the culture has changed?
answer: Novati describes having been "the move fast and break things person" at the time and still likes the framing. In Novati's reading, the "break things" half was partly an outside perception, and Facebook did not want to tell the public that people were recklessly breaking everything. The original spirit was breaking norms: first-principles thinking, trying things from scratch, not following trends for their own sake. It was not meant as causing havoc.

Novati still thinks it would be a fine motto today. At a larger, more mature company, though, even the smallest bug can cost millions or tens of millions of dollars, so Novati can see why the company dropped it.
blocks.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.question: Did the culture change over the years, given that Novati started when there were about 200 engineers?
answer: Novati describes an extremely engineer-driven culture. Designers and product managers had to win engineers over, because work an engineer would not build did not get built. Nearly all internal tools were written in-house and used by employees, which set an engineering-first tone that Novati loved.

Novati sees the 2012 IPO as a turning point. The stock fell afterward because people asked how Facebook would make money, a question that had barely come up in the first three years. As the company grew, Novati developed a more mature view: ad optimization, cost savings, and efficient infrastructure became more important. Early on, senior engineers argued out designs head-to-head, largely independent of management. By the end, VPs of two teams more often negotiated and the result percolated down.
blocks.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.question: What was the mood at the IPO? Ecstatic, or scared by the stock drop?
answer: Not scared, Novati says. It was celebratory but grounded. Zuckerberg was good, early on, at keeping things humble and not chasing press or perception. Novati describes the IPO as a rational way to raise funding rather than a party, yet still something that pulled employees together. Nasdaq brought the bell button to campus and a stage was set up. Novati says there was a story about how it was wired up and suggests asking internally.

Zuckerberg's parents stood right beside Novati in the crowd, with tears in their eyes, and Novati later told Zuckerberg about it. Novati found the moment impactful. Financially, nothing changed at first, because the stock vested about six months after the IPO.

followups.question: What was it like when the stock vested after it had fallen?
answer: Novati remembers the day clearly. About 20 colleagues were at a movie theater when phones went off all at once with notices that vested stock had been deposited. The IPO changed little in behavior over the short term. Over a longer horizon, Novati says, people could afford houses and children in the expensive Bay Area.
followups.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.question: Did Novati hold the stock, or diversify as soon as it vested?
answer: Novati held the IPO-era shares and still has all of them. At some later point, Novati says, vested shares were sold as they vested in order to diversify; the timing is not remembered. Novati was grateful for classes, taught by veterans of the Google and Yahoo IPOs, on managing finances and stock-based compensation. Having grown up in Canada, Novati had not deeply understood stock pay and found the lessons on risk "infinitely helpful".

followups.question: Was Novati sweating when Meta stock fell to around 90?
answer: A little, Novati says. Holdings were diversified enough that retirement was not at stake. The host notes the price had been around 150 to 180 when the host joined in 2018.

Novati draws a lesson for people comparing offers, from watching stock swings. Novati knows people who joined during the dip and saw their stock rise nearly sixfold in about three years (Novati's own estimate). Candidates often compare offers in today's dollars and agonize over single-digit percentage gaps. Novati calls it reasonable to care, but stresses that the numbers are estimates and that stock prices, acquisitions, and scandals are outside anyone's control. Novati advises prioritizing the company where the candidate will fit and perform well, because performance is more within one's control and is rewarded over time. The host adds that early in a career, a single promotion can mean about 40 percent more pay.
followups.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.question: What was the internal newsletter that made Novati well known, and why start it?
answer: It was called "the weekly Novati", a weekly post on the Notes product, Facebook's blogging feature. Notes had no owner when Novati joined in 2009, so Novati improved it at hackathons, adding rich text to what had been plain text. The change was an 11,000-line diff, so large that Novati had to organize an in-person meeting to review it. Novati also used the product constantly, as part of Facebook's dogfooding habit.

A few slightly controversial posts about product building drew traction, so Novati posted more regularly, often off the cuff. Facebook was adamant about staying on the Menlo Park campus, while startups such as Stripe and Uber in San Francisco were drawing employees away. Novati wrote repeatedly about it, including a post proposing a South San Francisco office, and that office later opened.

followups.question: Would Novati recommend an internal newsletter like that today?
answer: Overall, Novati says, no. There was no strategic reason to write it. It came from Facebook's value of being open and transparent: Novati wanted to strip away pleasantries and look at products honestly, for example admitting when a product grew through luck and not substance. Novati contrasts this with startups and boot camps that treat a little traction as proof they built something great. The posts had nothing to do with performance reviews or influence.

The cost was friction. Novati once openly called out that engineers with titles such as network engineer or data engineer could not move between teams as easily as software engineers. Novati did not realize it was a sore point behind the scenes, and executives said the post did not help and that they now had damage control to do. Novati's lesson is that an off-the-cuff style has consequences, though Novati still tries to be direct and open on Reddit and LinkedIn.
followups.speaker: Michael Novati

followups.question: Did HR ever ask Novati to take posts down?
answer: Nothing took the form of a takedown order, Novati says, but HR did give feedback. One post covered which companies were poaching Facebook engineers, and Uber was then offering very large stock grants. HR pointed out it might unintentionally encourage people to explore other jobs. Novati had not thought of that and says such off-the-cuff posts may not have been worth the friction.
Concerned, Novati messaged Zuckerberg directly. Zuckerberg was fine with it and encouraged Novati to keep posting.
followups.speaker: Michael Novati

followups.question: Could Novati really message Zuckerberg directly and get a reply?
answer: Yes. Facebook was small when Novati joined, and Novati dealt regularly with the executives. When leaving, Novati messaged each executive one-on-one, including Chris Cox, and says they replied with thanks. Novati felt a relationship with all of them, formed from interacting genuinely while the company was small, and got to know Zuckerberg best, partly outside work. Novati has not spoken with many of them in the past couple of years as Facebook has grown.
followups.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.question: Did Zuckerberg still write code when Novati joined, and did Novati ever see a diff from him?
answer: Novati worked with Zuckerberg on a 2009 hackathon project built on Zuckerberg's idea that anyone should be able to react to any post with any emoji. Novati was skeptical but thought it feasible. Novati and another engineer got a version working, but the code was so bad it never shipped. Zuckerberg did not give up, and when reactions launched later under a product manager, Novati thought it was done properly and so much better than Zuckerberg's code.

Novati also tells a story from a 2010 lockdown, when Facebook worried a rival product (the captions say only "plus") might dent its user base and pushed to ship features fast. At a company-wide Q&A, Novati bet Zuckerberg would not commit code by the end of lockdown, and offered to stop riding a Ripstik around the office if he did. Zuckerberg committed it, and Novati was banned from riding. Roughly 2012, Novati adds, the head of HR emailed the five most prominent riders for feedback on a draft email banning Ripstiks, a classic way to win over opponents.

followups.question: When Novati first arrived, could you see the founders' names in the codebase history?
answer: Occasionally, yes. In company lore, the earliest engineers were not known for the best-quality code, but they wrote fast and did the job. Later a wave of more experienced engineers arrived, including some poached from Microsoft, and began laying down structure and framework. Others wrote the core abstractions that became the foundation for the product infrastructure team, which Novati says existed for a very long time. Their names were all over the codebase, including Evan Priestley's, and they were Novati's role models when Novati wanted to become the coding machine who writes a lot of code.
followups.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.question: Which engineers impressed Novati most, and why?
answer: The product infrastructure team, which built PHP abstractions that evolved into today's React framework. Novati watched the framework go up brick by brick and saw those engineers as a different type, a specialty that was not Novati's. The person most like Novati was Evan Priestley, who Novati says was the top committer before Novati. Priestley wrote the internal code-review suite essentially alone, and it was later forked and open sourced (the captions render its name unclearly).

followups.question: Would Novati choose Priestley or four regular senior engineers for a new product team?
answer: Priestley. Novati then qualifies it as context-dependent. Being called a coding machine is not magic: it comes from hard work, from holding a lot of code in memory, and from attention to the littlest details. Novati says that on Oculus firmware, productivity would be slow at first. In a comfortable codebase where everyone has ramped up, Novati would pick the coding machine. For something truly new, a more diverse group may bring more flexibility and creativity. A coding machine, Novati says, makes things happen that people thought impossible.
followups.speaker: Michael Novati

followups.question: Can Novati give an example a team of seven senior engineers would not have finished?
answer: Novati's canonical example is a framework called Preparables. A component had a data-fetching function and a rendering function, so all data could be fetched in parallel before rendering. It was later replaced by async/await and more modern approaches. Thousands of classes used it, and Novati manually and relentlessly refactored every one away, roughly three to six thousand by Novati's estimate, until the parent class was gone. It took several months and was a solo effort.

A second project removed every direct PHP endpoint hit on the server in favor of the routing framework. Neither was the company's top priority, Novati says, and without personal drive they would have consumed resources better spent on new products. One person doing them made all engineers' lives easier by removing legacy frameworks.
followups.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.question: Will LLMs kill the coding machine archetype, given that a large refactor like that sounds doable by an LLM?
answer: Novati did the Facebook work in Vim, with an in-house indexed code search tool and a class-name tab-completion plugin, and was very productive. Modern editors would have made Novati more so. Novati sees LLM tools as the next step, like going from Vim to VS Code: they make refactors and changes faster. Agentic flows are emerging with some success cases but are not mainstream.

In Novati's view, most engineers still use AI tools much less than those at the leading edge. If everyone used them the way leaders do, the industry would already have changed massively, coding machines included. How agentic flows will affect coding machines and everyone else, Novati says, is undecided.

followups.question: What is the biggest difference between the old Vim workflow and working with LLMs?
answer: Novati works in a roughly 500,000-line codebase and still knows most of its structure, so multi-file agentic flows are used only occasionally. The main use is speeding up code Novati already knows how to write. For something like a 100-line page component, Novati makes a real-time call about whether typing it or prompting it is faster, and builds up prompting intuition prompt by prompt.

Novati says the product workflow is similar to six months earlier but code output is about five times higher (Novati's own estimate). There is no fixed endgame, Novati adds, since each new model or command-line tool brings new intuitions.
followups.speaker: Michael Novati

followups.question: How would Novati feel if coding became a hobby and programming was no longer driven by humans?
answer: Novati thinks it is a cool future. Clocked honestly, much engineering time is copy-paste, searching, and staring at the screen. Without that, engineers could focus on the fun parts: creative product work, and for Novati the joy of cleaning up code and merging unrelated things into one concept. Novati offers Sergey Brin dropping into whatever he wants to work on as a model.

Novati also finds it scary for the profession, because it raises the question of what being a software engineer means: writing code, designing data models, systems work, or gluing things together. For the near term, Novati is more confident that experienced engineers with strong taste become more productive and that building that experience gets harder for newcomers.

Beyond that, if AI writes and maintains its own code, Novati expects it will not look like today's code. It might manage services behind contractual APIs, in code no one reads. Novati expects the change to come step by step, not as an overnight dystopia, and says people should try to make that world as good as possible and not push back.
followups.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.question: What impressed Novati about the React-framework engineers, whose archetype differed from Novati's?
answer: Novati files them under the specialist archetype: people very good at one stack. Another example is an engineer who was one of perhaps ten people in the world who deeply understood email protocols, including the practical side of spam and routing. Novati likes a sports-team analogy: on a baseball team every player can play most positions reasonably, yet you want distinct roles and mutual respect for each player's place. Novati respects those engineers and sees the team as exceptional when it has different kinds of players.

followups.question: Was it that they solved problems others could not?
answer: Yes, Novati says, and their abstractions were especially impactful because every engineer used them daily. Novati's own cleanup work also eased everyone's life, so there was some similarity. Their frameworks cut the mental overhead of tasks such as fetching data. Novati notes that an elegant, fast, easy-to-use API is very hard to design, and that making things simpler can be more work than writing a lot of code.
followups.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.question: Novati has said about 30 percent of time went to the team and 70 percent to self-directed projects. How does that work?
answer: Novati frames it as being a senior engineer on a team of about ten while spending more than half the time on codebase-wide initiatives: cleanups, refactors, a new framework, one-off help, and emergencies. The 30 percent was a share of mental focus, not a slice of the eight-hour day. Novati was on the team all day, reviewing code, bouncing ideas off junior engineers, mentoring them toward promotion, and writing features the team had queued. Novati also joined product meetings and assessed feasibility of what product managers proposed. The volume of code from team work was that of a senior engineer.

followups.question: How did Novati manage the relationship with the manager, given that most bandwidth went elsewhere?
answer: Novati often, though not always, reported to more junior managers and acted almost as a peer who helped them manage the team. The skip-level manager usually did the performance reviews, and Novati effectively reported to that skip unofficially. Novati met a VP monthly for the whole org and the skip every two weeks. On the org chart Novati reported to a frontline manager, but in practice Novati was a dotted-line resource for senior people, "a weapon of the org" that went wherever needed.
followups.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.question: How did Novati transition into IC7, solving the hardest problems for the whole org?
answer: Novati says output was already at coding-machine level from day one. What improved was taste and judgment. As an example, there were two forks of the task tool on the same data source, one fast and streamlined, one bloated with features and slow. In a week or less, Novati merged them into one with the speed of the first and the features of the second. Novati told no one, posted to the whole company that the tools were merged, and says this could not be done now.

Everyone congratulated Novati, but the lesson was that surprising hundreds of users with changed URLs was not the best way. Novati had not understood the consequences for teams. Over many large changes, some too fast and some buggy, Novati kept the same speed while improving judgment: how much to change at once, what other people will feel, and which spots are sensitive. That accumulation of judgment and taste is what crosses the line into IC7, Novati says. Advice on building it depends on context: talk to a manager, then a skip-level manager, then a very senior engineer in a similar org.

followups.question: So high productivity and initiative let Novati take on extra work and become known for it?
answer: Yes, Novati says, but judgment and taste matter more than the code. They extend to the push process. Facebook had no continuous integration then. If something broke in production, the pushing team had to ship a fix, and an engineer who broke too much lost its trust, which would hurt a coding machine. Novati built that relationship, and more than once said a change needed to land and that if it broke the site Novati would resign. Novati had burned credibility before, so had to be very sure of the fix. An engineer who simply writes a lot of code, without years of built-up trust, could not get away with it.
followups.speaker: Michael Novati

followups.question: Would Novati have resigned if it had broken again?
answer: Novati thinks so. The statement puts so much pressure on Novati, perhaps a personality trait, that Novati triple-checks every line and thinks through every odd case.
followups.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.question: What do taste and judgment mean for a software engineer?
answer: Novati likens taste to the patina on a cast-iron pan, built up in layers of history. Some people have stronger instincts early, perhaps from upbringing or from experience outside code such as dancing or sports. In general it takes experience. Novati's second image is a speed skater: you cannot read a book, put on skates, and be fastest. It takes years of feeling the ice at different temperatures and the difference between a skate used once and twice.

Novati sees too many people early in their careers trying to jump ahead, like entering the Olympics before building that feel. That is okay, Novati says, and nothing is wrong with them. The advice is to put in practice and reps, get feedback, iterate, and have the grit to keep going; without feedback, practice does not improve skill.

followups.question: Is taste about how to design software, or about which problems are worth solving?
answer: Both, for different people, Novati says. A product manager's taste is mostly about what to build, built by shipping many things and watching some fail. Novati says the exceptional ones have shipped mostly things that failed or were mediocre, and learned at each step (a loose, unmeasured claim). For an engineer, Novati says, taste applies to the code itself and to strategies for moving fast.
followups.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.question: Novati was touching everyone's code. Did other teams give feedback, and how was it handled?
answer: Yes. In one case Novati refactored an old framework in the live version of a team's tool while that team was building a newer tool and carefully maintaining backward compatibility. They had many diffs in flight, and the refactor caused merge conflicts. They wanted it reverted. Novati had not paid attention to that, and the lesson is to be careful where teams are mid-migration on complex, longer-term work.

followups.question: Did anyone object that Novati added something without owning its maintenance?
answer: That never came up, Novati says. The philosophy then, which Novati reports Kent Beck also described recently, was that every line you write you are responsible for. If you are willing to be woken at 3 a.m. to fix your code, you can skip tests. If you want to work nine to five, write more tests so the code is stable while you are away.

Novati did not refactor and forget. Sometimes two years later an automatic bug would be assigned because Novati had touched the code last, and Novati fixed it as now Novati's. Novati had no territorial conflicts and did not step on people's product judgment. Novati compares it to surgery, learned the hard way through early over-aggressiveness: finding the line between disrupting people's day-to-day work and still getting the cleanup done.
followups.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.question: As engineers get more senior they are pulled into more meetings. How did Novati protect focus time?
answer: Novati minimized meetings. When calendar invites arrived without context, Novati asked what they were for and pushed back on many. Novati skipped standups unless relevant, for example during a crunch to ship within a month, and did not attend ones that were social chitchat. Novati was strict about time and chose teams deliberately, valuing managers who understood that their job is to help reports perform exceptionally. Novati's managers protected Novati from unnecessary meetings so impact could be highest.
Novati admits being too arrogant at times. Novati recalls walking out of a meeting or two after deciding it was no longer useful, and now regrets it, feeling bad for whoever ran the meeting.

followups.question: Did HR ever ask Novati to be nicer?
answer: No, Novati says, because it was not a table-flipping situation. Novati had good relationships with the product managers, who liked that Novati built and fixed things fast, including bugs that were not Novati's. Meta's product managers want things moving fast and watch every pixel. They would often give Novati permission to leave when a meeting no longer needed Novati. Novati describes the attitude as cutthroat about not spending time in meetings when Novati could be coding.
followups.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.question: How did Novati develop the skill of picking problems that mattered, so the code was more impactful?
answer: Novati says first that Novati is not great at it and is still poor at prioritizing. Novati tended to pick things where Novati could already see the answer, so the only question was how fast the code could be typed. That is also why LLMs help Novati so much: the idea is in Novati's head and the tool gets it out faster.

Novati calls this one of the things that probably held back the career. When a manager asked for task A, and Novati could not see the answer, Novati did B through H instead. That earns a passing grade and is appreciated, but if A really mattered, the company's overall impact would likely have been higher had Novati done it. Novati frames it as a weakness, limited by what Novati can figure out how to do.

followups.question: So the priority list was whatever Novati could crank out instantly, not full business value?
answer: Novati agrees and adds that if you crank out enough, it adds up and can have huge impact, but it is a different way of thinking about work.
followups.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.question: What did the IC7-plus engineers have in common?
answer: Novati says there was a common bar regardless of archetype, whether coding machine, specialist, or fixer. Everyone showed extremely strong diligence and conscientiousness, and was sharp. Novati cites a straight-A school record and a sense of being fairly smart, yet acknowledges that many in the group are probably smarter. In a room, a newly proposed protocol would not get an hour-long presentation; people would ask sharp follow-up questions at once. Attention to detail was very high.

For Novati these are personality traits, such as using obsessive tendencies productively on every detail of the product. Others reached them through 25 years of experience. In conversations with junior colleagues, Novati says, context is often missing, follow-ups are less sharp and take longer, and projects are usually smaller in scope.
blocks.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.question: What are the top tips for landing code fast, for someone who wants to absorb the coding-machine skill?
answer: Novati's step one is to do something, anything. Many people who ask for advice think too much and do too little. Step two, which Novati calls critical, is to get feedback from respected people with experience, taste, and judgment, act on it, and repeat. Novati once thought a manager hated Novati because the manager spent all day reviewing a flood of fast, problem-filled code and kept asking for style conventions to be followed. Novati says that annoyance is the loop working: get the gears turning, take the feedback, iterate. It compounds quickly.

Novati names three mistakes. The first is not turning the gears at all. The second is getting feedback from the wrong people, such as a boot-camp graduate taking feedback from a peer only slightly ahead, which lacks the experience and taste one wants to learn. The third, which Novati made often, is treating feedback as judgment or approval and not as information. The host summarizes it as shortening the cycle time, getting good feedback, and internalizing it.

followups.question: For someone already productive, what advice takes things to the next level?
answer: Be more ambitious. Take on something that pushes beyond the normal scope. Novati says this is specific to Meta, where impact is judged by breadth and scope, so a coding machine in a department needs to push beyond it. The advice Novati gives, despite saying Novati is poor at accepting leaders' prioritization, is to reach out to senior people in other areas. Novati had many one-on-ones with the senior leadership, such as a 15-minute chat with Chris Cox, and says a credible but stuck coding machine can use such talks to find wider-scoped projects.
followups.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.question: Why did Novati leave Meta, and what was the career thinking?
answer: Novati says Meta got big fast. Around three-quarters of the way through the tenure, the feeling faded that the company had Novati's back completely and Novati had the company's, a feeling Novati admits was a bit culty. It started to feel like a business relationship, and that was the first sign Novati was open to leaving.

Vesting logistics sharpened it. Some years had longer grants and overlapping vesting cycles, and Novati expected take-home pay to drop about 80 percent over a period (Novati's own figure; details withheld). After the previous performance cycle, Novati told the manager that Novati would leave in three months, did a farewell tour on a Messenger-for-kids project, and slowly ramped down, taking things home from the desk. Novati describes being either all-in or not, says that all-in feeling broke as Meta grew, and wanted to put the dedication elsewhere.
blocks.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.question: At the highest levels of performance, how much is talent and how much is hard work and growth?
answer: Talent exists, Novati says, shaped by biology, upbringing, and opportunity, and some of it is undiscovered. Someone who feels untalented may simply not have found it yet, or may be talented at something that is not their day job. Novati says this is the mission behind the current work of helping people find the most impactful work they can do, since not everyone had the chance to explore. Novati believes everyone is better than most at something, and finding it is a big piece of high performance.

Hard work, in contrast, is within your control. A friend of Novati's makes the point that talent and luck are outside your control and effort is not. If you are good at your job and like it, Novati says, you can outwork similar people and will probably be recognized for it.
blocks.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.question: What percent of Novati's career growth is luck?
answer: Novati says 50/50. Coming from Canada, Novati's first day at Facebook was a surprise: Novati took a laptop and left onboarding, and was called back because Novati had not collected a phone. Facebook handed over a phone and accessories as if rolling out a red carpet, and Novati wondered what it all was. Staying in Canada would probably have gone well, Novati says, but without the same acceleration.

The luck was landing at Facebook when Novati did: a perfect fit for Novati's personality then, aligned values, and code that matched what Novati could handle. Novati has seen people without the same drive who got the luck and are doing well, and says either factor can work out. Novati says both applied here.
blocks.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.question: What advice would Novati give to a just-graduated self?
answer: Novati sees many people, including those preparing for interviews, seeking approval: a green check mark, a perfect grade. Novati was that person, wanting an A+ without really knowing what was being learned. Because of that, Novati treated feedback as a grade to judge by and not as input for improving, and pressured toward 100 percent next time instead of toward improvement.
The advice to ambitious people who want perfect scores is to reflect on feedback and push past the comfort zone, instead of treating feedback as judgment.
blocks.speaker: Michael Novati
