sections.title: Rapid growth, broader learning, and the costs of chasing the next rung
sections.deck: Evan King and Ryan Peterman compare fast staff-engineer paths, showing how initiative and support create growth and why a successful ladder can still leave gaps.

blocks.question: Did fast career growth require starting programming as a child?
blocks.speaker: Evan King and Ryan Peterman
answer: Evan encountered computer science in a high-school AP course near Seattle. Classmates with Microsoft-employed parents seemed far ahead of him, and the subject initially threatened his identity as a straight-A student. He worked hard enough to succeed but did not enter college determined to study computer science. In an introductory engineering course, his small head start suddenly made him feel capable relative to beginners. Enjoyment followed that experience of competence.

Ryan had no AP computer-science course and did not know what the field was until UCLA. He entered engineering undeclared, chose electrical engineering because he liked computers and games, and switched to computer science and engineering in his junior year when he understood its employment path better. Overlap in the degree requirements allowed him to reuse earlier coursework. Neither presents his later progression as evidence of childhood programming genius.

blocks.question: Why start a college hacking club, and what did it teach?
blocks.speaker: Evan King and Ryan Peterman
answer: Evan played Division I soccer at Cornell until his junior year. The training, early workouts, and weekend travel consumed time, yet he knew he intended to become a software engineer rather than a professional player. Quitting created room for building things. After participating in capture-the-flag competitions with teams found online, he recruited locally with flyers, assembled founding officers, and grew a core competition team of roughly 25 people; some weekly teaching sessions attracted as many as 200.

The club combined technical practice, friendships, and teaching. Evan remembers peers who were stronger technically than he was, and he learned by building sophisticated projects with them. Ryan connects organizing, recruiting, communicating, and aligning people with the work of senior engineers. A leadership role can have lasting value beyond improving an application, especially when the activity itself is enjoyable.

followups.question: What made your own side projects useful?
answer: Ryan built a Raspberry Pi service to indicate whether his engineering club’s lab was open. Because an officer had to be present, the service watched the lab Wi-Fi for known officer-device MAC addresses and let students query a Slack bot for current presence. It solved a real problem and gave him a concrete interview story.

They recommend noticing problems nearby and writing software that people actually use. A project chosen from a generic list may still provide practice, but without users it resembles another class assignment and misses the learning involved in taking a useful solution all the way through delivery.
followups.speaker: Evan King and Ryan Peterman

blocks.question: Did competitive hacking make the hiring interviews easy?
blocks.speaker: Evan King and Ryan Peterman
answer: Evan found algorithm interviewing difficult at first and spent many hours practising with classmates. His successful Meta campus interview included a hard problem whose trick he had skimmed the previous evening. He believes that lucky encounter mattered materially: without it, the rest of this career path might never have happened.

Ryan also struggled despite spending most of his Bloomberg internship’s spare time practising. His assigned project took only a small part of the summer, but intensive preparation did not prevent him from failing his later onsite algorithm interviews. He finished with a Bloomberg return offer and an Amazon offer obtained through an unusual campus logic-test format. He chose Amazon partly to remain on the West Coast.

Evan recalls badly misreading a Palantir interview: being released early was described as compatible with either exceptional success or failure, so he waited confidently for an offer and was devastated by rejection. Their comparison of then-prestigious employers—Palantir, Quora, Jane Street, and other finance firms—is a recollection of their college hiring environment, not a current ranking. The larger point is that preparation, expectations, and luck all influence entry opportunities.

blocks.question: How did you choose your first Meta team?
blocks.speaker: Evan King and Ryan Peterman
answer: Meta’s boot camp let Evan try tasks for several hiring teams before making a mutual choice. He had expected to join cybersecurity after years of hacking, but the particular teams he met felt less welcoming than he wanted. Content integrity offered machine-learning problems, a mission he found meaningful, and colleagues he related to. He joined a terrorism-content team being established in Seattle, initially with a manager shared across teams and a part-time technical lead.

Ryan selected Instagram infrastructure with much less understanding of the long-term tradeoffs than he has now. He then associated product work with front-end work and infrastructure with technical depth, assumptions he now calls mistaken. Instagram felt exciting, and when the preferred manager lacked headcount, Ryan made an earnest case for joining until the manager found flexibility. Both see agency as a way to convert available opportunities into a better fit; good opportunities may require actively seeking them.

followups.question: Where did boot camp happen, and did you deliberately choose a technical stack?
answer: Evan split boot camp between two two-week stays in Menlo Park and time in Seattle. He gravitated toward backend work without an elaborate stack-selection strategy. Ryan thought more explicitly about product versus infrastructure and which product organization to join, although he stresses how incomplete his knowledge was as a new graduate.
followups.speaker: Evan King and Ryan Peterman

blocks.question: What was surprising about onboarding into content integrity?
blocks.speaker: Evan King
answer: Evan’s early encounter with a colleague’s monitor displaying explicit content was jarring because it was plainly part of an ordinary working day. The team’s task required examining material that would be extraordinary in most offices; over time, colleagues became accustomed to that exposure. He remembers the team sitting out of the way in the Seattle office, and colleagues said that arrangement reduced accidental exposure to disturbing content. His story is about the unusual context of moderation engineering, including material more troubling than the initial anecdote.

blocks.question: What did the terrorism-content system actually do?
blocks.speaker: Evan King
answer: Evan describes Estuary, a backend system largely written in Hack, as a staged content-processing funnel. Cheap initial checks determined whether content warranted expensive model evaluation. Photo matching, model scores, thresholds, and combinations of human reviews fed an eventual action. The infrastructure made it easier for the team to swap models, adjust thresholds, and run experiments rather than hard-code a single moderation path.

blocks.question: Was the first promotion something you negotiated with your manager?
blocks.speaker: Evan King
answer: Evan’s first promotion arrived after roughly his first half year and was a surprise. He thought he was doing good work but had not discussed promotion or calibrated himself against colleagues. The manager’s praise, promotion announcement, and compensation change became a major confidence-building moment. He does not recommend relying on that kind of surprise.

An earlier Zillow internship had supplied another important boost. He completed the assigned work quickly, pursued interesting additional work, and received a return offer and unusually strong praise from a manager with substantial experience. That external confidence helped him enter Meta, although it did not instantly eliminate all insecurity.

followups.question: Had you interned at Facebook first?
answer: No. Evan had interned at Zillow. His memories of that internship and the first Meta promotion illustrate how specific encouragement from experienced managers helped him believe he was capable.
followups.speaker: Evan King and Ryan Peterman

blocks.question: What did those managers see in you so early?
blocks.speaker: Evan King
answer: Evan identifies curiosity and an unwillingness to treat the assigned task as the boundary of his job. At Zillow, after finishing his rental-team work, he turned posters about locking unattended computers into a playful internal security game. Colleagues could record an unattended machine, and leaderboards and graphs encouraged participation. Spending time with security colleagues eventually led to attending Defcon with them, despite security being outside his team’s charter.

He describes a similar pattern at Meta: completing the requested implementation created time to improve it and explore adjacent ideas. He frames this as pursuing useful, interesting work rather than merely doing extra work for its own sake.

blocks.question: How did you finish assigned engineering work fast enough to explore more?
blocks.speaker: Evan King and Ryan Peterman
answer: Evan initially resists claiming a simple secret, because the reputation for speed feels more grand than his conscious process. Ryan describes deep familiarity with a code area, a practiced editing-and-review workflow, and enough repetitions to know exactly where a requested change belongs. At one coding-heavy period he remembers submitting about ten diffs a day. He also worked very long days and acknowledges that adding working time is one way to create an extra budget for growth.

Evan kept searchable notes whenever he solved a problem so he would not have to solve it from scratch twice. He also became comfortable investigating a blockage for roughly an hour, finding the person who knew the area, asking a focused question, writing down the answer, and continuing. Ryan emphasizes that a well-timed question can save days of blind searching, dwarfing small editor optimizations.

Both highlight code search as a lasting skill. In a large monorepo, someone has usually solved a similar problem already. Guessing likely function or variable names, finding the analogous implementation, and understanding the surrounding context accelerates junior execution and later work on ambiguous cross-system problems.

followups.question: Does working extra only make sense if you enjoy it?
answer: They distinguish the experience of being absorbed in enjoyable work from forcing long hours on work one hates. Ryan enjoyed the novelty and growing fluency; Evan stresses that advice about extra hours becomes dangerous when detached from that motivation. The time-budget explanation describes their experience, not a claim that everyone should work those hours.
followups.speaker: Evan King and Ryan Peterman

blocks.question: What changed between the midlevel and senior promotions?
blocks.speaker: Evan King and Ryan Peterman
answer: As content integrity expanded, the initially tiny terrorism team acquired senior engineers and eventually split across terrorism, child-exploitation imagery, and graphic violence. Because Evan had arrived first, he held useful context and helped newer colleagues ramp up regardless of their formal level. His manager offered him responsibility for an underinvested graphic-violence area with a junior engineer and a research scientist.

He began setting weekly meetings, shaping the roadmap with management, and holding one-to-ones with teammates. The team improved its detection precision and recall, although he does not remember figures well enough to quote them. Guiding other people and improving a neglected area supplied the senior-level story; the informal tech-lead label mattered less than the responsibilities.

Ryan’s corresponding experience emerged when a cross-client/backend workstream grew around an area he understood deeply. He sometimes felt stretched while leading meetings but did the work anyway. An unusually capable intern showed him that entrusting execution to another person could free him for more scope. Evan similarly needed repeated managerial feedback before delegation clicked: doing everything quickly himself would eventually cap what the team could accomplish.

followups.question: Why did the manager trust someone so early in their career?
answer: Evan credits a strong manager who noticed potential, provided a larger challenge, and coached him through it. The preceding evidence was not just tenure: Evan was helpful in onboarding and willingly answered colleagues’ questions. His knowledge became useful to other people, which made expanded responsibility more plausible.
followups.speaker: Evan King and Ryan Peterman

followups.question: Did being the original owner create territorial feelings when senior engineers arrived?
answer: Yes. Evan initially felt protective of his work when a technically strong senior engineer joined. He recognized that response, discussed it with his manager, and opened himself to the engineer’s feedback. Reviews and design discussions then became a major source of technical growth, and the colleague became a lasting friend.

Ryan recalls senior collaborators similarly improving his documents and projects. He did not know exactly how each person’s performance review divided the credit, but the collaboration produced better work and learning. They advise treating shared scope as an opportunity for growth rather than assuming someone else’s contribution diminishes one’s own.
followups.speaker: Evan King and Ryan Peterman

blocks.question: By the senior promotion, were you openly discussing promotion goals?
blocks.speaker: Evan King and Ryan Peterman
answer: By then Evan and his supportive manager discussed target timing, requirements, and what still had to happen. Friends from his boot-camp cohort often lacked equally active advocacy. His advice is to state the desired next level and timing, ask whether the manager agrees with the plan, and surface gaps early—even if that feels vulnerable. Hearing bad news before review season is more useful than an unpleasant surprise afterward.

Ryan’s manager was supportive but did not proactively drive promotion dates, so Ryan repeatedly asked what the next level required and advocated for his growth. He sees strong performance and explicit discussion as mutually helpful: the manager has reason to invest in an engineer whose broader contribution helps the team. Evan later adopted more self-advocacy himself. They recognize luck in getting a capable, aligned manager and the engineer’s responsibility to make goals visible.

blocks.question: Why stay on the same team while many peers changed companies?
blocks.speaker: Evan King and Ryan Peterman
answer: Evan enjoyed both the mission and the people. The organization grew so quickly that staying did not mean doing an unchanged job: terrorism work, child-safety work, graphic violence, managers, and colleagues all changed around him. He was not solely optimizing promotions, although the growth was rewarding. Ryan more deliberately evaluated how to grow fastest and repeatedly decided that another clear promotion opportunity, good colleagues, and enjoyable work made staying attractive.

Both acknowledge a possible trap in always pursuing a next milestone that feels close. It can postpone broader technical experience elsewhere. Nevertheless, they have little regret about staying through a fast staff promotion: that level improved compensation and made direction-setting and working through others possible, activities they found satisfying.

followups.question: Do you wish you had changed environments sooner?
answer: At this point in the conversation Ryan defers the fuller discussion of his recent transition. They agree that a clear, enjoyable staff trajectory made staying reasonable, while recognizing that another environment might have produced broader technical learning. They present that as a tradeoff rather than a universal stay-or-leave rule.
followups.speaker: Evan King and Ryan Peterman

blocks.question: What was the anchor story behind the staff promotion?
blocks.speaker: Evan King
answer: Evan’s progression took one half year for the first promotion, two halves for senior, and three for staff. During the last stage he led graphic-violence engineering when the Christchurch mosque attack was livestreamed and copies circulated. He describes an emergency response involving integrity leadership and policy colleagues, repeated overnight work, model training, and changes to detection and content-matching systems. He emphasizes the victims and families rather than treating the atrocity as a career opportunity.

The response exposed underinvestment in detecting catastrophic events on live video, which differed from screening existing photos and recordings. The company formed realtime integrity around Evan and a product manager and asked them to determine staffing, scope, and a roadmap. Early progress was slow because the events were rare: training on the handful of known cases risked overfitting, and waiting for another tragedy was an unacceptable way to assess the system.

His golden-set-recall project curated past examples and built an evaluation environment that replayed videos and comments through real production infrastructure while isolating them from users. It tested the complete path rather than only a model. Evan reports that the initial measured recall for the better-represented suicide examples was roughly nine percent.

Looking closely at misses revealed a neglected signal: viewers’ comments often showed they understood the danger before image and audio models did. Adding temporal comment signals raised recall to roughly fifty to fifty-five percent in his recollection, created more detected training examples, and enabled further improvements. He says recall eventually reached the mid-nineties by the time he left, but the staff promotion came earlier, when evaluation and substantial initial improvement had been established. These are his retrospective figures, with some uncertainty in the precise intermediate numbers.

followups.question: How large did the new team become?
answer: At promotion time Evan remembers approximately four or five engineers. Realtime integrity later reached roughly twelve to fourteen before splitting into two teams of eight near his departure. Increased investment followed demonstrated progress and sustained attention from senior leadership; the original project was not assumed successful from day one.
followups.speaker: Evan King and Ryan Peterman

followups.question: Who decided to give you that scope?
answer: He does not know the exact decision maker. At the time he felt he had advocated strongly for the new team after the incident. Later he learned that his manager had done much more advocacy behind the scenes than he appreciated. His own initiative and leadership mattered, but he deliberately corrects a purely self-created-opportunity version of the story.
followups.speaker: Evan King and Ryan Peterman

blocks.title: Making a rare-event detection problem measurable

steps.title: Recognize the gap
steps.text: A crisis exposes weak real-time detection.

steps.title: Create safe replay
steps.text: Curate examples and replay the full path in isolation.

steps.title: Inspect the misses
steps.text: Measure recall and look beyond the model’s existing signals.

steps.title: Add a useful signal
steps.text: Use temporal comments alongside image and audio information.

steps.title: Improve with feedback
steps.text: More detections create data for further iteration.

blocks.caption: Editorial synthesis of Evan’s account. Arrows mean the sequence of learning and improvement he describes, not a guaranteed causal recipe.

blocks.question: Which behavior mattered most in the staff story?
blocks.speaker: Evan King and Ryan Peterman
answer: Evan points to trying the simple, obvious solution and keeping the whole problem in view. His multidisciplinary team crossed infrastructure and modeling boundaries, but technically sophisticated researchers could become absorbed in improving the model itself. With less investment in that particular expertise, he focused on what would move the actual detection number. Comments seemed obvious only after the team had been concentrating on pixels, audio, and complex temporal modeling.

Ryan describes a similar Instagram compute-efficiency project. He explored video-processing efficiency before pandemic usage made capacity critical. After brainstorming with strong engineers, the best improvement was a comparatively trivial removal of redundant work. He values the ratio of useful impact to time, complexity, and maintenance burden: a simple change with a large effect can beat an elaborate year-long project.

They praise the Meta culture they experienced for rewarding realized impact rather than merely implementation difficulty. The practical skill is to identify the important constraint, find what actually improves it, and drive the work even when the solution lacks technical glamour. Their descriptions of reward systems are personal observations of that context.

blocks.question: Were you acting partly as a manager while still an individual contributor?
blocks.speaker: Evan King and Ryan Peterman
answer: Yes. Evan’s role went beyond the usual technical-direction interpretation of tech lead. Engineers still had formal managers who owned promotion decisions, but he helped those managers understand performance, supported teammates’ growth, and participated in relevant discussions. An attempted invitation to calibration was ultimately rejected by a director; he does not know why.

He took people leadership seriously, observed his manager, and read a management book when given the graphic-violence team. He believes the arrangement worked because colleagues trusted that he was on their side. He qualifies that judgment rather than claiming to speak for them. Someone who feels competitive, aggressive, or inserted between an engineer and their manager could easily undermine the same arrangement.

Because levels were not public on his team, Evan could not rely on a displayed title as authority. He needed to earn credibility through useful technical judgment and supportive behavior. Ryan agrees that influence at staff comes from convincing people who do not report to you that the direction is sound and that they can trust you.

blocks.question: Did you consider switching from the IC path into management?
blocks.speaker: Evan King and Ryan Peterman
answer: Evan expected to reach staff and then become a manager, but a plausible IC7 path appeared while he had broad organizational context, senior-leadership visibility, and interesting cross-organization projects. Conversations with friends who had become managers also revealed the weight of directly owning people’s issues. He considered reaching IC7 first and perhaps later moving into a more senior management role.

Ryan faced a similar choice. His manager saw a clear continuation to IC7 but warned that management advancement depended more on organizational opportunity. Ryan nevertheless chose management to learn a different set of behaviors and preserve options for the longer term. He worried that a very senior IC career could become specialized to a handful of huge companies, with influence and compensation tied to internal credibility and equity.

Both describe these portability and compensation concerns as their reasoning, not a claim that senior IC skills have no value elsewhere. A fast internal progression may not transfer to an equivalent external title, and rebuilding trust takes time.

followups.question: What is a tech-lead manager?
answer: Ryan first moved into a role he describes approximately as seventy percent IC and thirty percent manager, with a small team focused on a narrow technical area. Contributions were still assessed primarily as IC work. He later moved toward conventional organizational leadership after deciding he wanted to grow further as a manager.
followups.speaker: Evan King and Ryan Peterman

followups.question: What has been the biggest learning from management?
answer: Ryan’s manager had been right about the career dependence: advancement became more closely coupled to team and organizational growth. Moving during an efficiency-focused period reduced that opportunity. He also found the work shifted toward people problems and a solid block of daytime meetings. As an IC he could arrange fragmented meetings and complete technical work later; as a manager, much of the job requires other people being available. Review season adds substantial writing after those meetings.
followups.speaker: Evan King and Ryan Peterman

blocks.question: What led you to leave Meta after reaching staff?
blocks.speaker: Evan King
answer: Evan remained for more than a year and a half after staff and was working toward IC7 with a new manager who treated him as a partner in growing the team. A former manager whom he deeply respected began discussing crypto and Web3 ideas with him outside work. Evan had related interests from college, and together they built a product that attracted roughly ten thousand users quickly.

His collaborator was ready to pursue startups; Evan had expected to stay on the corporate path and initially wanted funding before leaving. Eventually the side project became more compelling than his day job. He found himself waiting for work to end so he could return to those problems, and the chance to build with a trusted partner outweighed the attractive promotion and equity path. He left before funding, acknowledges periods of regret afterward, and says that in hindsight he does not regret the decision.

followups.question: What tipped the decision despite a very lucrative potential path?
answer: The cofounder did not pressure him. Evan describes a change in intrinsic motivation: the after-hours work had become what he most wanted to spend time doing. Some early traction and a trusted partnership mattered, but there was no fully secured financial result at the moment of departure.
followups.speaker: Evan King and Ryan Peterman

blocks.question: What happened across the startup experiments?
blocks.speaker: Evan King
answer: The first venture combined social activity around crypto with on-chain activity to create rankings and predictions. Evan reports roughly one hundred thousand users, fundraising, and acquisition interest. They sold around a market downturn, then faced a new question: what should this partnership build next?

Over six to eight months they tried many unrelated ideas. One product copied a website into editable Figma frames; technically valuable reverse engineering, mostly credited to his cofounder, led another company to buy the technology. Evan describes these as two acquisitions with some looseness about the term, not two identical company outcomes.

They eventually returned to an area they knew and cared about: interviewing and hiring. Initial AI mock interviews did not work particularly well. Human mock interviews offered to gather training data produced repeated requests to pay for more of the human sessions. After initially resisting that direction because they wanted to build technology, they followed what users valued. Hello Interview grew from that demand, later adding better AI-guided learning and educational resources.

blocks.question: Had the startup path financially outperformed staying in big tech?
blocks.speaker: Evan King
answer: Not at the time of the conversation. Evan explicitly distinguishes realized monetary compensation from the value of experience. He believes the technical breadth, learning habits, and company-building skills will improve his lifetime opportunities, but that future payoff is his optimistic forecast rather than an accomplished result.

blocks.question: What did startups teach that your Meta role had not?
blocks.speaker: Evan King and Ryan Peterman
answer: Leaving humbled Evan. His rapid promotions and broad team leadership had given him confidence, but he discovered large practical gaps. At Meta, he could change a narrow component and rely on an enormous surrounding organization to deploy it to billions of users. That did not mean he had independently learned to configure a database, create a cache, stand up a product, or build a front end.

In the startup he had to learn these pieces while delivering. He now feels more able to enter an unfamiliar situation and work out what is needed. Ryan mentions a counterview from another engineer: startup setup work can feel technically routine compared with deep specialist problems inside a large company. They therefore distinguish breadth from depth rather than asserting that all startups teach more in every way.

Evan thinks learning broad foundations first could make later specialized optimization more meaningful, while hesitating to recommend that order as the best career strategy. He also wishes he had used his time at Meta to investigate abstractions he consumed every day and read the engineering explanations that were available around him. Curiosity could have made more of the large-company environment without requiring a job change.

blocks.question: How should a big-tech engineer judge when to try a startup?
blocks.speaker: Evan King
answer: Evan recalls posting enthusiastic startup advice and being criticized for ignoring his own advantages. He was financially secure and did not have a family to support, which made unpaid risk possible. He now insists that personal circumstances determine what is feasible. His enthusiasm for faster learning cannot substitute for that judgment.

For a new engineer already in big tech, he would generally learn enough organizational and interpersonal foundations to reach senior before leaving. Someone who can afford the risk and prioritizes breadth might consider a move sooner; a later-stage startup can be an intermediate step before founding. These are his recommendations from his experience, with explicit financial and family qualifications.

They also note that contemporary AI coding tools helped their two-person company ship substantial work quickly. Evan acknowledges that such tools can help or slow particular tasks but does not develop a general tool prescription in this interview.

blocks.question: Which periods produced the greatest skill growth?
blocks.speaker: Evan King
answer: Evan identifies the startup period, even relative to the steep learning at the start of his career. It was stressful, uncomfortable, and sometimes emotional, and he credits his partner’s patience. His positive assessment rests on having come through that period, not on pretending it felt easy while it was happening.

blocks.question: How many hours were you working at Meta and in startups?
blocks.speaker: Evan King
answer: Evan realizes that saying he did not work much at Meta understates informal work. He usually arrived around eight or eight-thirty and left around five-thirty or six, then sometimes checked experiments, made tweaks at home, or woke to see whether a model-training run had completed. It exceeded an ordinary forty-hour week, although he also left early for weekly snowboarding and usually did not treat weekends as compulsory work.

The first startup was much more demanding. He was both learning foundations and supporting a fast-paced realtime analytics product where failures mattered financially to users. Days could run from morning until midnight or two, and he carried a laptop even to a friend’s birthday because an incident might fall to him alone. Hello Interview later became steadier; he still worked more than at Meta but could attend social events without carrying the laptop. The business’s incident profile changed the experience as much as the startup label did.

followups.question: How does that fit with your advice about work-life balance?
answer: Near the end of Meta, Evan had considered two broad ways to live: make work a central source of passion and fulfillment, or do a strong bounded workday that financially supports interests and relationships elsewhere. He thought he might adopt the latter after another promotion. Founding instead returned him to a passionate work-centered period. He admits the apparent contradiction and sees the quieter option as a possibility later rather than claiming he had already achieved it.
followups.speaker: Evan King and Ryan Peterman

blocks.question: What is your biggest career regret?
blocks.speaker: Evan King
answer: He wishes he had slowed down to understand why things worked. Iterating until a metric improved or a system functioned could produce immediate impact without building a durable explanation. The same shortcut appeared during early startup pressure: once something worked, he moved on.

As the company stabilized, he could finish required work with time left over and use that margin for reading engineering explanations and investigating underlying libraries and platforms. He sees a tension in an impact-oriented culture: it can reward shipping and moving on even when understanding the abstraction underneath would improve the engineer’s long-term foundation. He would keep the useful drive for impact while adding that inquiry.

blocks.question: What would you tell yourself when graduating?
blocks.speaker: Evan King
answer: Invest in friendships, romantic relationships, and life outside work with some of the deliberateness given to career goals. Evan had roadmaps and frequent checks for professional growth but applied much less effort to broader life. Moving to Los Angeles and making more friends outside the technology bubble helped him value mutual investment and everyday support.

He now finds those relationships a major source of fulfillment alongside continuing work. This is not only an hours-allocation lesson: even when there was time, he had not recognized what deserved deliberate attention.

followups.question: Would you accept slower promotion in exchange for stronger relationships?
answer: Given a strict choice, yes: he would prioritize relationships. But he rejects the premise that he actually had to choose. He believes he had enough time to build both and simply did not invest enough in relationships or understand their importance yet.
followups.speaker: Evan King and Ryan Peterman

blocks.heading: A final nuance about interview preparation
blocks.text: During the closing promotion, Ryan mentions a roommate who was initially overconfident in system-design interviewing because he already designed systems at work. The useful lesson is that an interview is a particular format that may require targeted practice; professional seniority alone does not ensure performance. The service endorsement itself is omitted.

sections.title: Retired Engineering Director: Netflix Culture, Hiring, Meta Leadership, and Work-Life Balance
sections.deck: A retired engineering director who worked at Netflix and Facebook recounts how Netflix culture scaled, how he hired engineers, what he learned leading at Meta, and why a 2004 illness changed his view of work.

blocks.text: The host introduces David as a retired engineering director who worked at both Netflix and Facebook, and the conversation follows his 36-year career. In David's view, strong engineering organizations depend on three things: colleagues who are good to work with, a fair and objective way to record who did what, and a pace that leaves people a life outside work. He argues that engineering judgment matters more than LeetCode speed, that a new leader must earn trust before changing a team that already works, and that a serious illness in 2004 turned him against 24/7 work culture. Everything below is David's opinion or recollection from an auto-generated transcript, and several names and figures are unverified.
blocks.heading: David's view: judgment, trust, and balance matter more than heroics and long hours

blocks.question: How did Netflix differ from the other companies David had worked at?
answer: David says every earlier employer, from IBM through several smaller companies, tolerated prima donnas: very smart people who were hard to work with, who yelled at colleagues and customers, and who could not admit mistakes. He describes one 1990s engineer treated as indispensable, with a cubicle packed with junk, who avoided other people and fixed problems overnight while managers did not understand his work. When he quit, the company survived, and the rest of the team came to understand the area he had guarded.

At Netflix, David says, nobody was like that. The culture deck said the company did not hire brilliant jerks and would let go anyone difficult or unapproachable, however smart. David calls this revolutionary in the early 2000s and notes that the large tech companies he knows now work the same way.

His interview with Patty McCord, then chief people officer, who approved every hire at that small company, surprised him. David says she told him Netflix did not value 24/7 work and that he should impress the company with what he could do in an eight-hour day. David later watched a manager say he could not keep working around the clock. McCord thanked the manager, then told him not to do it again and to set up his team so that he did not have to. David calls that unthinkable in 2008 or 2009 and says he learned more about leading and collaborating from McCord than, he thinks, even from Reed Hastings.

David gives his own example. During early, unstable attempts at continuous deployment, a strong engineer remarked that David must enjoy having weekends off, because the systems would fail if the team stopped working. David told him in a one-on-one to take a vacation and said he did not care if things broke. The engineer took a week off, others rested too, and David says the team then stabilised the system quickly with its own approach.

David ends with Hastings. According to David, Hastings saw DVDs by mail as a stepping stone to streaming, which is why the company is not called DVDsbymail.com. Hastings was not a video expert but built a team of strong leaders and engineers to solve the problem.
blocks.speaker: David

blocks.question: How did the Netflix culture change as the company grew?
answer: David first says the culture memo is aspirational. When people asked whether Netflix really worked that way, he answered that it described what the company aspired to be.

He then describes what failed to scale. Netflix credited the team, not individuals. When the company shipped on the PlayStation 3, David says, Sony's DVD division asked Netflix to stop because it had not designed the console for this, and Netflix carried on. Afterwards nobody named the foundational engineers; the credit went to Netflix. That worked when the company was small. As it took on many products, individual contributions got lost, and if engineers are not credited, he says, leaders collect the credit.

Netflix also had no engineering levels. Everyone was an engineer or a senior software engineer, and a business card could carry any title except manager, director, VP or chief. That suited an all-senior team. As it hired more juniors, David argues, teams contain strong, good and weak engineers, and without an objective way to tell them apart and reward wins, the best people leave. By the late 2010s he was arguing for levels. He assumes they have since been added, but he has been away for six years.

David adds that McCord interviewed almost every early hire and Hastings met a few new hires at a time, which could not continue as the company grew. When he left, he felt the memo suited a very small, aggressive, engineering-focused company.

followups.question: What is the culture memo?
answer: David describes a deck of roughly 15 slides, released around 2007 or 2008 by his recollection. Its ideas included no brilliant jerks, very smart people, inspiring people to sail the seas rather than telling them how to build a ship, top-of-market pay, and a "keeper test" under which the company fires aggressively. David calls it revolutionary at the time. In his reading it was about freedom and responsibility: hire excellent people, explain why the work matters, give context, and trust them to execute without micromanagement.
He adds that the talent was not limited to engineers. His HR partners challenged his hire and no-hire decisions, and he says he learned how to build a team from them.
followups.speaker: David

followups.question: If everyone was at the same level, how did Netflix pay people differently?
answer: David says Netflix generally did not hire new graduates, though he found ways around that. Pay followed a concept of personal top of market, and the memo encouraged people to interview elsewhere. His own starting salary in 2007 was $175,000, which he calls solid for then. If Google had offered him $200,000 a year later, he says, his manager would have had to match it or let him go. Leaders therefore had to track offers and market rates.

David says this became unsustainable. An engineer matched to a double-pay offer could, three years later, earn three times as much as a peer doing similar work, with no performance review or context to explain the gap. In another case, five candidates Netflix had made offers to each received Facebook offers about 1.2 times higher, the memo said to match, and without leveling nobody could justify it. He argued with his leadership using year-over-year spreadsheets and believes Netflix fixed this after he left, since a large company needs pay ranges.
followups.speaker: David

blocks.speaker: David

blocks.question: How does David identify really strong software engineers in hiring?
answer: David says his hiring succeeded all the way up to Meta. Large companies such as Meta, Google, Amazon and Microsoft need structure and consistent standards, so they use a formal interview system. At smaller companies, when he made the hire or no-hire decision himself, he, three team members and HR interviewed each candidate.

He tells of a late-1990s candidate who had built driverless-train software. David was the last interviewer, and his 45-minute slot ran to 90 minutes, with two whiteboards covered in state transitions. He says her grasp of a complex system of interacting parts was among the best he had seen. Others gave her coding questions and she did fine, but the panel was lukewarm and his boss pushed back. David argued that the team was struggling to integrate disparate systems and needed her. They hired her, and he says she excelled. He claims his hiring record at small companies was close to perfect.

David knows his next view is controversial: he does not love LeetCode. He says it shows how fast someone can write code for a problem practiced many times. He accepts that at the volume Meta and Google hire, they have little alternative.

His alternative is an engineering foundation: understanding complex systems, strong technical intuition, and sound decisions without enough data. He has seen engineers from other fields do very well in software. He has also seen people who aced LeetCode and rehearsed system-design questions such as Google type-ahead get hired and then produce poor engineering, which he saw in their review packets. He believes this foundation is largely innate, like musical talent, and says he can help someone improve their software but cannot teach them to make good decisions.

His second story is about a project partner in graduate classes at San Jose State, taken in his 50s just before he joined Meta. She was finishing a master's in civil engineering, worked in wastewater treatment, and wanted to move into software. David was impressed by her analytical mind and command of statistics and wanted Netflix to hire her. Her take-home video-software task took three weeks and had rookie mistakes, so to help close the deal David suggested she teach the team something. She spent two hours at a whiteboard on wastewater treatment, and halfway through David realized he was watching a very complex state machine. A manager asked what sewage had to do with software but hired her, and later told David at a Meta event that she was doing very well. David says that when you see a brilliant engineering mind, LeetCode speed or building a scalable type-ahead does not matter, because those can be learned quickly.

David accepts that this approach does not scale at Meta or Google, where legal and policy problems would break it, so they set a bar and a level. His level advice is to take a lower offer: someone who was a 6 elsewhere and is offered a 5 at Meta should accept it and execute at the higher level, because bonuses, multipliers and refresh stock follow. An over-leveled hire who struggles has no clean fix. His rule is that when in doubt, go low and earn the quick promotion.

followups.question: How do you spot that fundamental engineering skill? Is there a question you ask?
answer: David says to interview the person, not the process. The wastewater candidate showed mastery of a hard engineering problem and explained it to engineers who knew nothing about it, until those who understood saw a finite state machine. He argues that many engineering systems, such as engines and other mechanical systems, reduce to states and transitions, though structural engineering differs.

Netflix would have hired her at a junior level, such as data analyst. As a full software engineer against the usual expectations she would have failed. A smaller company, he says, is flexible enough to hire and build up such a person.
followups.speaker: David

blocks.speaker: David

blocks.question: Who was the strongest engineer David worked with, and what made that person strong?
answer: David names Giannis, though he usually avoids names. The captions garble the surname, so it is omitted here. They met in 2000 at InterVideo. Giannis had left the industry to teach signal processing in Greece, and in summer 2010 David brought him in during a break to help with ideas about parallel encoding. David says that work led to content-based encoding, which the whole industry now uses, and to an early patent.

Giannis later joined Netflix and, David says, took the idea further, in what the captions render as "convex all encoding", probably convex hull. David says it delivers the highest quality for a given bandwidth and is now the model at both Netflix and Meta. Giannis also built a cost-benefit model for codec evaluation. David sees his strength as forcing academic rigor into practice: decisions rest on tests across 10,000, a million or a billion videos, not on what two compressed videos suggest in theory.
blocks.speaker: David

blocks.question: How did David come to be recruited to Meta?
answer: David says the early Netflix culture deck advised interviewing often to learn your market value. When Facebook contacted him in late 2017, as he recalls, he had not interviewed in about ten years. He went in, in his own words, a bit full of himself, citing how Netflix had built the highest-scale encoding platform. One interviewer told him Facebook could not solve its video scale problem with CPUs. David was floored, later thanked him, and realized he had understood video too narrowly. He got an offer and turned it down because he was not ready.

Soon after, Giannis told David about a Facebook offer and the custom chip (ASIC) work he would do. David saw a passion in him that he had not seen for a while. He thinks Netflix's culture, not built around individual contributions, may not have rewarded Giannis, and that the problems may not have seemed big enough to him. David says he did not try to talk Giannis out of it: as his boss he did not want to lose him, but as his friend he could not argue against it. David had been interviewing mainly to exercise his interview skills, but in the end he came to see Facebook's video work as a very hard problem. His team was solid and a successor was ready, so in 2019 he left Netflix, and Facebook offered him a job quickly.

At Netflix his encoding team had grown from one person to about 55, and trust grew with it. At Meta he took over a video processing team of 55 to 60 who did not know him. In an early meeting he talked about what needed work. A team member told him in a one-on-one that he had been there two weeks and was already telling the team what to do. David concluded he needed to stop talking and build trust, a skill he had never had to develop.

His lesson is that leadership is about relationships. If a team is broken, the leader's job is to fix it. If it is already executing well, the job is first not to break it and second to help it move forward, and he had jumped to the second step. David calls the saddest thing about Meta that it was his last job. He believes he would now be a much better organizational and engineering leader but no longer wants that responsibility, and he says he learned the most about engineering leadership there.

followups.question: Concretely, what does building trust look like for a senior leader joining an existing team?
answer: David says it meant slowing down and spending a lot of time in one-on-ones, asking questions, taking notes, and learning the system, the roles and the people. In a technical role, he says, a leader must understand why the team does what it does.

His first decision came when the team needed a manager. Many told him to promote an existing manager, but he did not know them and refused to decide just because it looked politically right. After taking time with them, he concluded an existing manager was the right choice. That manager had felt the role was his, so the relationship was difficult at first. David told him he was sorry for the delay but had needed to understand first, and that he was now confident in him. By the time the manager left Meta, David says, he no longer assumed the worst.
Looking back, David thinks his investment was still too small. He would tell his boss that for the first six months he was in school and that critical decisions would be made together.
followups.speaker: David

blocks.speaker: David

blocks.question: What was David's favorite work or project at Meta?
answer: David first names bringing Netflix-level quality to Meta's scale, which he says succeeded. He then turns to COVID. He joined in late July 2019, and by March 2020 everyone was working from home. Meta planned for New Year's Eve from the summer because video traffic spiked for 24 hours. By April 2020, David says, every day looked like New Year's Eve in uploads, streams and live video. Systems that had never run at that sustained load were slowly bleeding out, with race conditions among the problems. He says the prime minister of India was addressing the country on Facebook Live, and he was terrified by the weight of it. The team worked from home, found the problems and resolved the race conditions. After about a month the systems and metrics held, and David says he was proud of that.

He also describes how his view of the company's value changed. He had first seen Facebook through a US-centric lens as a social app. He came to see what 3.5 billion customers means. By David's rough comparison, Netflix's roughly 300 million subscribers are the wealthiest 5 percent of the world by income, while Meta reaches the wealthiest 50 percent. He calls wealthy a loaded term, since at the bottom people live on about $68 a day. He says Instagram, WhatsApp and Facebook are a lifeblood for small shops across India, and an Uber driver from Somalia in Seattle told him WhatsApp kept his scattered family in touch.

David says US debate about social media focuses on harms such as fake news and overlooks how much the products improve lives elsewhere. He believes the company changed lives by giving people a business, a platform to share and earn from video, and a way to stay close to family, and that it feels good to be part of that in a small way.
blocks.speaker: David

blocks.question: How did work-life balance change across David's career?
answer: David says that in the late 1990s he worked hard for a visionary executive because the team was trying to catch up, not because anyone demanded it. At InterVideo, a startup, the expectation was 24/7. He arrived around 10:30 in the morning and left around 10 at night, sometimes at 2 or 3 in the morning, often seven days a week, chasing deals to lift the stock price after the IPO.

In January 2004 he fell ill on a Sunday and kept getting worse. On the Friday his wife took him to the emergency room, where, he says, a doctor said it was colon cancer, with a blockage that could kill quickly. He was in hospital for about three weeks with two surgeries and chemotherapy. It was stage three with lymph node spread, and he puts his five-year survival prognosis at about 25 percent. His children were two, four and seven, and he says the youngest barely knew him.

In hospital he decided that his way of working was wrong. He told his boss he still wanted the job but could not work that way, and he says that if a company threatens to fire you for not being there late, the best thing you can do is leave. He believes InterVideo used hours to cover for poor leadership. He calls work-life balance something thrust upon him, and he was determined never to be a leader who expects people to kill themselves for a job. Hearing at Netflix that the company did not value 24/7 work was a shock.

His advice is not to wait for cancer or a heart attack. Bake balance in early, take vacation, and leave the company alone for a week. If it cannot survive seven days without you, David says, that is its problem.

David says high-performance companies such as Meta and Netflix are often misunderstood. He recalls a Meta poster of a rocking horse that read, in effect, do not mistake motion for progress. He suggests agreeing with your boss on the most important work and telling the boss which tasks you will not do; if one matters, someone else must do it or priorities must change. Crunch time will come at big tech companies, but it should be the exception, planned in advance, such as a push in May and June followed by a vacation. He says balance is achievable even at Netflix or Meta, if the manager gives clear context.
blocks.speaker: David

blocks.question: Which job taught David the most, and why?
answer: David says his last four jobs each contributed. The first turned him into a high-performance software engineer, performing by problems solved, not hours worked. The second gave him a video foundation. Netflix, he says, was zero to one, and there he learned leadership, hiring and firing, context setting and cross-functional work, which he brought to Meta.

What he lacked on arrival at Meta was an objective process for planning, reviews and performance. He calls the PSC performance cycle both his most dreaded and his favorite time of year. In his account, everyone writes a self-review, the manager builds a packet with feedback tied to goals, and managers then defend their engineers in calibration meetings. Each manager thinks their team is the best, David says, so the aim is to persuade with data about who deserves what level and who did what on a project. He valued getting each engineer's impact on paper. He says departing employees keep every performance package they were ever given.

David had heard horror stories about the performance cycle but found it mattered once inside. His greatest joy, he says, was giving a direct report a top rating, and he also valued helping people who were below expectations recover. He adds that he used to think he understood scale from books on sharding and microservices, but in his view those authors do not know scale at Meta's level. The most valuable thing he would bring to a new job is a system for objective planning, review and performance.
blocks.speaker: David

blocks.question: Is there a top book that influenced David's career?
answer: David chooses a late-1990s book he names as 12 Secrets to Microsoft Success; the title comes from auto-generated captions and was not checked. He says it described radical thinking at Microsoft. One idea was betting the company, which he says he saw at Netflix, Amazon and Meta when a big opportunity is worth risking the company on without going all-in. Another was good failure: in a healthy company, projects and people will fail, and what counts is how you fail, what you learn and whether the bet was reasonable and managed early.

As he recalls the book, Microsoft was the first company to say publicly that it aimed to hire the top 5 percent of software engineers, and it coined the term dogfooding. When the NT server was failing badly in the mid-1990s, he says, Bill Gates made the whole company move to it, which put the bugs in front of everyone and got them fixed. After rapid growth Gates also imposed a company-wide hiring freeze because people were working on things that did not matter, such as Microsoft Bob. Executives were forced to kill projects, and David says the bottom 20 percent were cut, which he thinks should have happened anyway.

David says Microsoft set early models for modern engineering leadership, and others borrowed from it. Before the 2022 crash he thought the hiring rate did not add up. During COVID everyone accelerated hiring and nobody slowed. He believes that had big-tech leaders read the book, they would have seen in late 2021 that hiring was out of control.
blocks.speaker: David

blocks.question: Is there anything David regrets that others could learn from?
answer: David says his first six years out of school were wasted at very large failing companies. He names Hughes, spun off from General Motors, and an IBM division sold to Siemens, both of which failed. He had a good salary and an easy job, thought only about the moment, and did not think about growth. He does not mean being ambitious about a vice-president title in ten years, just thinking about growth.

For software engineers in particular, he says, everything learned will be obsolete in about five years. When he joined Meta, the bootcamp and the whole development environment had been replaced; he had been proficient as a director, but when he later went to an individual-contributor role he found everything had changed. His way of staying successful, David says, is to keep pushing toward the edge and keep learning new engineering skills.
blocks.speaker: David

blocks.question: What advice would David give himself at the start of his career?
answer: First, work on hard problems. David says that if the job is not difficult, you are not growing. Once a role flatlines, he says, an engineer at a company like Meta, where moving internally is easy, should find another hard problem. Hard problems are what move engineers forward.

Second, company size does not matter, but everyone should work at a small company or startup at some point, ideally while young. He cautions against being too taken with the technology and says to work for visionary leaders who can also execute, since vision without execution goes nowhere. He cites Zuckerberg and Hastings as visionary, and says Hastings was one in 1999, when Netflix had four people. Leaders should make you dream of sailing the seas, not just cut lumber for a ship.
Third, plan for work-life balance deliberately from the first job. Work and life are in tension, he says, but the best engineering comes from people who love the work and also enjoy time off.

Fourth, start financial planning on day one, because as technical people succeed they earn more and, without a plan, will not know where it goes. David recommends a deliberate plan for spending and for short- and long-term savings, small regular contributions in your 20s, and no extended credit or debt. He says that by the early 40s this will not usually allow retirement unless you were lucky, as with an early job at Facebook or Netflix, but it can give financial independence, so you could take a lower-paying job. In his view a 401(k) alone and Social Security will not be enough for those who start late. He knows many engineers in their 50s who earned well but have no plan, and says a good engineer employed for 30 to 35 years has no reason not to retire comfortably. He says elsewhere that he is not a financial planner, so this is one person's opinion.
blocks.speaker: David

sections.title: Ryan and Ricky: Internships, Promotions, and Big Tech vs Startups
sections.deck: Ryan and Ricky argue that visible work, frequent questions, and clear writing shape early careers as much as coding skill, and they compare big tech with startups.

blocks.text: Ryan and Ricky, who both studied at UCLA, share what they wish they had known before graduating. Ryan manages interns at Meta, and Ricky works on ads at Google. Their central view is that early career progress depends on visible impact, frequent questions, and clear writing, more than on coding skill or luck alone. They also explain engineering levels, how interns are judged, how to earn a promotion, and how to weigh big tech against startups. The talk then covers money, job changes, and AI's effect on entry-level work. These are the speakers' own views and experience, not general rules.
blocks.heading: The speakers' view: visible work, questions, and writing shape early careers

blocks.question: What do the engineering levels mean, from junior to staff?
answer: Ricky explains that junior engineers write and ship code with a fair amount of help. Mid-level engineers work more independently but still need help at times. Senior is often a stopping point, with few people expected to go further. Staff engineers set a team's direction and lead engineers at other levels. Ricky estimates that moving from junior to mid-level takes about two to four years, and mid-level to senior a similar time.

Ricky says some companies use an up-or-out policy, where people who do not reach the next level leave, and that Google is less aggressive about this. Ricky estimates, without exact data, that 90 percent or more of people reach these levels. The speakers say the levels site is fairly accurate, except that equity pay moves with the stock price.
blocks.speaker: Ricky

blocks.question: How do interns succeed, and how are they judged?
answer: The speakers say interns are judged on three things. The first is productivity: how much of the assigned project they finish, ideally in half the internship. The second is quality, shown by fewer rounds of code review by the end. The third is communication, including proposing improvements or a new project after finishing the first one. A strong intern does all three.

followups.question: What was Ricky's own internship like?
answer: Ricky's junior-year internship at Google produced only about 800 lines of code, which felt low. Halfway through, Ricky had about 300 lines, while a UCLA friend on the same program had about 11,000. Ricky spent much of the time learning the codebase and wrote a detailed design doc comparing several approaches. That work showed productivity, and Ricky received a return offer.
followups.speaker: Ricky

blocks.question: How did you get promoted so quickly to staff engineer in your 20s?
answer: Ricky says each level expects a different kind of work. Many projects at the current level do not earn the next promotion. One project at the next level, which clearly shows readiness, counts for more. Managers often describe these expectations as behaviors. Ricky and Ryan focused on projects that would move them up, not on busy work that would not.

Ricky also says that, after each promotion, Ricky asked the manager what the next level required and then took on that kind of work. The manager explained which skills to build, and Ricky credits this for the fast promotions.
blocks.speaker: Ricky

blocks.question: Is career success mostly luck?
answer: Ryan says luck is a big part of it, but people can raise their own luck through initiative. After about eight months at Amazon, Ryan felt stuck and could not see the path to the next level. Ryan applied to many companies and received offers from every company interviewed with except one. That led to Meta.

followups.question: Is luck mostly opportunity, or can preparation change the outcome?
answer: Ryan adds that grinding LeetCode problems and applying widely raised the odds, and that personal agency matters. Ricky frames luck as two parts: the opportunity itself, and being prepared when it comes. Without preparation, a good chance can pass by. Ricky adds that Ryan's move away from Amazon created more opportunities.

blocks.speaker: Ryan

blocks.question: What one piece of advice would the speakers give?
answer: Ricky says the main advice is to ask a lot of questions, at work and during an internship. Ricky once told a mentee to keep asking, and at the end of the internship the mentee said Ricky had not really meant it. Ricky says the biggest difference between people who succeed quickly and those who do not is how fast they start asking questions, learning, and unblocking themselves. Fear of looking foolish holds many people back.

followups.question: What separates strong interns from weak ones?
answer: Ryan has had five interns at Meta. The strong ones had the nerve to propose improvements and ask questions, even though Ryan was the senior person. Some suggestions were wrong, but many were right. The weaker interns were quieter, and Ryan could not tell how they were progressing. Time passed with little progress, and such interns often did not get return offers.
followups.speaker: Ryan

blocks.speaker: Ricky

blocks.question: Are the best engineers the smartest students in the class?
answer: The speakers say no. Strong engineers need solid technical skill and soft skills, such as persuading and influencing others. Work is a large group project, and disagreements are common. Telling a colleague that their idea is bad does not win them over. Naming the other person's frustration, acknowledging their view, and proposing a middle ground makes it more likely that the work ships. The speakers say these skills matter about as much as coding.

blocks.question: How much of the job is actually code?
answer: One speaker says code is a smaller part of the job than new graduates expect. Writing is a large part of it. A design doc comes before the code, a change needs a written description, and a finished project needs a write-up of its results. The speaker says this writing is how a person influences others, so people skills often decide how far an engineer goes.

blocks.question: Do experienced engineers still get imposter syndrome?
answer: Ricky says imposter syndrome is very common, and that most people feel it. Ricky felt it on joining Google, after passing the interviews and the internship, and found the other engineers very strong. Even after promotions, Ricky wondered whether the company had made a mistake. Ricky copes by learning as much as possible and doing the best job possible, on the view that even being fired would leave something learned. Ricky says the feeling still returns in waves.

followups.question: Did praise at work reduce the stress?
answer: Ricky describes being an anxious person who was always stressed about work. A manager once told Ricky to calm down. Ricky was not sure whether the praise meant a passing grade or a strong one. Talking through expectations with the manager helped, and the stress eased somewhat.
followups.speaker: Ricky

blocks.speaker: Ricky

blocks.question: How do you advocate for yourself at work?
answer: Ryan says good work is required but not enough, because people decide promotions and they must know about the work. The last few percent of effort is to tell people about it. That can mean writing about a result, presenting it in a meeting, or telling a manager that a milestone is done early and the next task is ready. Ryan says a clear post about strong results makes a return offer hard to refuse. Ryan says this step is often skipped, especially by introverted people.

followups.question: Is visibility a separate skill from doing the work?
answer: Ricky says visibility can come from a manager, a product manager, or teammates, as well as from the person's own writing. Ricky compares unseen work to a tree falling in a forest that nobody sees, and says people cannot promote work they do not know about.
followups.speaker: Ricky

blocks.speaker: Ryan

blocks.question: Should new graduates choose big tech or a startup?
answer: The room was polled first. Most audience members chose big tech. Those who chose startups cited first-mover upside and a larger share of impact at a smaller company. Ryan says big tech brings brand value, so a resume from a known company is an easier hire. Ryan describes Amazon as the lowest tier of the big companies at the time, yet recruiter messages arrived in large numbers after joining it.

Ryan frames the choice as a trade-off between high expected value and high variance. Big tech usually gives a better average outcome on a steady path, but rarely produces very large wealth. A startup can boom or fail. Someone who joins early and the company grows can rise quickly, which big tech rarely allows.

followups.question: Why did Ricky choose big tech over startup offers?
answer: Ricky had offers from both startups and big tech, and chose big tech for work-life balance. Ricky's startup friends work very hard, and the results have varied. Ricky says big tech teaches established practices with less variance, while a startup's role can change a lot. Ricky recommends big tech, at least for the first few years, to build prestige and a base.
followups.speaker: Ricky

blocks.speaker: Ryan

blocks.question: How do managers measure impact?
answer: The speakers define impact as the concrete, measurable results of the work, such as revenue, cost, speed, or user growth. The measure depends on the team. On an ads team it may be money. On infrastructure it may be the cost or latency of a database. On a growth team it may be daily active users or sign-ups at key steps. Engineers should learn the measure from their team and manager, because that is how their work is rewarded.

The speakers also say one small change that improves a key number can matter more than ten thousand lines of typo fixes. Their example is a one-line change that gives a 20 percent gain on something that matters.

blocks.question: Do you need an MBA for engineering management?
answer: Ryan says no, and Ryan is a manager without one. Ryan describes a graph from a company that gathers LinkedIn data, covering a few thousand directors and above. Pay with and without an MBA looked comparable, and pay without one was slightly lower. Ryan describes this as research done with a company, not a published study.

followups.question: Did family expectations about an MBA affect Ricky?
answer: Ricky's mother believed Ricky would not succeed without an MBA, and pushed for a top school. She has become more relaxed since Ricky reached staff engineer, and now reads about careers and thinks the path is good.
followups.speaker: Ricky

blocks.question: What was college recruiting like?
answer: Ricky says it was hard. Ricky describes a 15-minute coding challenge from Yelp, written in C++ on the merge step of a merge sort. The code looked right, but it kept crashing with a segmentation fault that Ricky could not explain, and Ricky was rejected. Ricky emailed the recruiter, insisted the code was correct, and asked for an engineer to check it. The engineer said the code looked correct. Ricky got another challenge, passed it, and reached the interview round. Ricky's lesson is that it is worth pushing back and advocating for yourself during recruiting.
blocks.speaker: Ricky

blocks.question: Is the first job the hardest to land?
answer: Ryan says yes. The first role is the hardest, new grads have to be scrappy, and later offers get easier. Taking less desirable companies can build experience. Ricky says Ricky's first role was at a little-known company that Ricky no longer lists on the resume, but it made the next application look stronger and opened the door to better companies.

blocks.question: How do you make as much money as possible?
answer: Ryan says it depends on the goal. For very large wealth, the usual path is a few years in big tech, then a company of one's own, or an early join at a company that grows fast. Ryan says that for a good life, with money for the things you want and for vacations, big tech and good work are enough.

Ricky says reaching that level of wealth would take the two speakers decades of promotions, plus a rising market. Ricky says that, for a good life, big tech and a solid job are enough. Ricky had no real idea about money in college.

blocks.question: Is work the most important part of life?
answer: Ricky says work is not everything. Looking back at their 20s, Ricky's happiest memories were time with friends and trips, not working or getting promoted. Ricky says people should work hard and also build a life beyond work. Someone whose whole identity is their job can struggle after a layoff, while a person with other interests can handle it more easily.

followups.question: Can work-life balance be framed as diminishing returns?
answer: One speaker describes diminishing returns: each extra effort in one area gives smaller gains, so a person who wants the most out of life should look for areas where returns are still growing. The speaker says this favors spreading effort across several parts of life.

blocks.speaker: Ricky

blocks.question: What are your goals now, and did you push for promotion?
answer: Ricky says Ricky was not very career-driven at first. Ricky and Ryan were roommates and still are. Ryan would ask whether they could aim for promotion faster than the usual timeline. Ricky had seen data on how long each level took, and Ryan's push made Ricky test whether a faster path was possible.
Ricky says Ricky put in the effort, was promoted faster than average, and did not give up other interests to do it.
blocks.speaker: Ricky

blocks.question: Should people change jobs every two or three years for pay or promotion?
answer: Ricky says the answer depends on the case. Ricky has stayed on the same team under the same manager at Google, while still looking at other teams. Ricky notes survivorship bias, because people who left may have had a worse time. Ricky suggests asking every six months whether you still want to be there, whether the opportunities still fit, and whether the team and manager support you.

Ryan says the common advice to job hop for promotion is more nuanced. Early in a career, job hopping can be the fastest route, because momentum matters less than reaching the next level. At senior levels it can backfire. Ryan says companies usually do not hire outside candidates straight into E7 or L7, and promotion there depends on credibility and a track record that frequent moves do not build. Ryan's advice is to job hop aggressively early and to be more deliberate later.

followups.question: Can leaving a company help someone come back at a higher level?
answer: Ryan says this is rare. Ryan has seen a person leave a company, join a startup, and come back to Meta at a higher level. Ryan says a person who leaves a clear ladder is harder to place, so a return can leave room for a higher offer, but few cases work this way.
followups.speaker: Ryan

blocks.question: Will AI reduce entry-level software engineering jobs?
answer: The speakers say it is hard to predict five to ten years ahead. In the short term, they expect AI to change things less than many fear. They note that engineers already use many non-AI tools that write code, and that this did not scare anyone. They see AI as a tool that empowers engineers. Their advice is not to change majors only because of job fears.

followups.question: What might entry-level work look like in five to ten years?
answer: One speaker says entry-level engineers may write less code, because AI will do more of it. They will still need to tell the AI what to build and check that the result is correct. The speaker expects AI to remain a tool, and people will still be needed to build it.
