sections.title: Vlad Feinberg: Kernels, Research Taste, and Landing a Frontier Lab Job
sections.deck: Vlad Feinberg, a Google DeepMind pre-training area lead, describes the skills, research habits, and hiring signals that matter for frontier AI labs.

blocks.text: In Feinberg's view, frontier labs hire for kernel and low-level engineering that makes LLM training and serving faster, plus research judgment: knowing the literature and estimating which ideas will work before trying them. Feinberg says the best evidence of fitness is work that others can use. Feinberg argues AI will not replace all roles, because people stay accountable for resource decisions, so people should build these skills now.
blocks.heading: Feinberg's view: frontier-lab jobs reward systems depth, research habits, and proof of work

blocks.question: What skills are in demand at frontier labs, and what does the work look like?
answer: Feinberg says the post offered a few tangible directions, not a complete list. The directions covered are kernel development and low-level engineering that speed up LLM runtime. Feinberg says demand for this skill is very strong across labs and projects. LLMs also tie research and product together more tightly than earlier machine learning did.

When a research project changes a network's architecture or reworks serving, such as KV caching, the team must implement the change efficiently. Feinberg says the core task is software that runs at large scale with high throughput and low latency. Feinberg calls this fundamental work, tied to classic back-end engineering.
blocks.speaker: Vlad Feinberg

blocks.question: Does DeepMind split applied work from research, as some other labs do?
answer: Feinberg hesitates to draw a sharp line. Teams have different focus areas. One team uses Gemini models to improve search results, which is an applied use. Feinberg says product work still needs hard research, such as making answers factual, citing sources, and judging whether a source is sarcastic or a joke.

Feinberg says classic LLM research teams still exist, including pre-training and post-training teams that build the models. Those teams also act as site reliability engineers for training runs. Feinberg says the two roles cannot be separated, and that research matters only to the extent it can be delivered. Feinberg sees a spectrum from research to applied work, and says everyone now needs to move across it.

followups.question: Where do software engineering and pure AI research roles sit on that spectrum?
answer: Feinberg says much of the team's new work rests on infrastructure. The team works on distillation, where a teacher model passes statistics about its training data to a student model. Those statistics come from a large model run over trillions of tokens, which costs millions of dollars in compute. So every operation and every byte counts, and much of the work is standard software engineering.

Feinberg says the distillation infrastructure has been rebuilt over three or four generations. Each rebuild revisited the research methods in use and widened what the system could do. One rewrite, which Feinberg puts at roughly four months, made distillation research much faster. Feinberg says recent Flash model results depended on these infrastructure investments. The design work covered abstractions, storage, and reads and writes across data centers.
followups.speaker: Vlad Feinberg

followups.question: Is there a crossover point where a back-end engineer placed on a model-architecture problem makes a bigger jump than infrastructure work?
answer: Feinberg says research differs from software engineering in its risk and reward. Research taste is an intuition about which path to take through a graph of milestones. A software project is mostly a fixed sequence of steps. A research project is a stochastic graph, where some ideas fail, so people must explore it.

Feinberg cites a post by Professor Jacob Steinhardt that frames research as a Markov decision process with unreliable transitions and some hidden nodes. Feinberg says the key skill is estimating, before trying an approach, how likely it is to work and how much time it will take. Feinberg says that estimate is what people often call research taste.
followups.speaker: Vlad Feinberg

blocks.speaker: Vlad Feinberg

blocks.question: What concrete examples show a back-end engineer falling short on a research team?
answer: Feinberg says the first gap is context on the research landscape. Research calls for a humble view that much related work already exists. A researcher must know the field's current frontier before extending it. Feinberg says the first skill is a literature review that follows a topic's citation tree.

Nobody has time to read every paper, so researchers must judge which papers are high value without reading them fully. Reading research papers also needs machine learning and computer science background, and often math and coursework. Feinberg says a researcher needs that understanding of existing methods, since improving a method requires knowing what is already there.

Feinberg says LLM research is organized around scaling laws. The practical question is whether a team can predict the final test loss of a scaling recipe as compute grows. Feinberg contrasts this with ImageNet work, where validation runs estimate final error. Each LLM pre-training run uses more compute than any before it, so a team gets one large attempt, and methods that work on small data often break at scale.

Feinberg describes a recipe as a function from a compute budget to a training routine. Paired with an accurate prediction rule, it lets a team decide how to improve the recipe. Feinberg credits earlier scaling studies, including the Kaplan and Chinchilla papers, with making that view feasible.
blocks.speaker: Vlad Feinberg

blocks.question: How do you judge whether a candidate can help push the frontier, such as their grasp of the literature and mathematical maturity?
answer: Feinberg agrees that mathematical maturity makes frontier papers easier to read. Feinberg calls the recent key papers table stakes and expects candidates to know them. The broader skill is reading a paper at that level and understanding it well enough to implement its idea.

Feinberg says ideas from papers may not apply to the lab's domain directly. A candidate who understands an idea deeply can iterate on it and improve it there. Feinberg says the key evidence is the ability to pick up an arbitrary paper and see how far its ideas carry over to Google's setting.
blocks.speaker: Vlad Feinberg

blocks.question: Beyond distillation and kernels, what other areas matter in frontier AI research?
answer: Feinberg names programming-language research first. Abstractions at the language level can speed up kernel development. Feinberg cites ThunderKittens, which lets a developer write kernels through a few functions instead of large amounts of C++. Feinberg says the skill is less about PL research itself than a passion for these abstractions and for low-level hardware. Hardware-specific domain-specific languages belong to this area too.

Feinberg names reinforcement learning. Deep RL methods such as PPO now run in production systems, a point that was once in doubt. Feinberg says the field has a rich literature, which a learner should enter through the basics before moving to value-based and policy-gradient methods.

For back-end engineers, Feinberg points to distributed systems and optimization. Training a network across many GPUs raises questions of asynchrony, gradient staleness, and pipelining. Feinberg says these system choices affect convergence and final model quality, and can be studied apart from LLMs. That makes them a good starting point for infra-minded engineers.
blocks.speaker: Vlad Feinberg

blocks.question: Do the demands differ between labs, such as DeepMind and Anthropic?
answer: Feinberg says the skill set is probably similar across frontier labs. Differences lie in business strategy, product offerings, and customers, which follow each lab's specialties. Feinberg sees a lot of overlap in what labs look for. After the post came out, people from OpenAI and Anthropic said they agreed with its advice, which Feinberg reads as some evidence of that overlap.
blocks.speaker: Vlad Feinberg

blocks.question: If people expect software engineering to shrink, will LLMs also take over research work, so there is no reason to favor research?
answer: Feinberg says the research skill set will matter more. Handling stochastic parts of planning will be a larger share of most jobs. Feinberg says people should start building the habit of leveraging AI in their own work, even outside software. Building systems around LLMs to do one's job better is what will set people apart.

Feinberg says some fear about AI is intentionally used in marketing, and does not think AI will replace all roles. Organizations allocate resources toward goals, and those decisions must trace to a human. Feinberg says people cannot hand off blame to AI. LLMs understand law and can review a contract, but they cannot represent a client in court or be disbarred. A professional must check the output.

followups.question: Was fear about AI the original motivation for the post?
answer: Feinberg says the post was meant to be constructive. Feinberg mentions a viral long-form post about an AI permanent underclass, and says it is easy to get stuck in that loop. Feinberg argues that people have agency over the future and should invest in skills that matter for tomorrow now.
Feinberg says the post also answers the question people ask most after a talk, such as a Princeton lecture: how to work at DeepMind.
followups.speaker: Vlad Feinberg

blocks.speaker: Vlad Feinberg

blocks.question: What signals matter most when marketing yourself to a frontier lab?
answer: Feinberg says the strongest signal is evidence of building something that others use, such as kernel work. A candidate can take an open-source LLM and optimize it. The improvement does not need to help in every setting, and it does not need to speed up GPU execution.

Feinberg says the serving stack around LLMs is a distributed system that manages KV cache memory, load balancing, and request queuing. Projects such as vLLM and SGLang welcome help. Feinberg also names TensorRT demos and Dynamo, a system for disaggregated serving. A project that uses or improves those components would be a very positive signal.
blocks.speaker: Vlad Feinberg

blocks.question: Does the advice change for an internal transfer, such as an infrastructure engineer moving into a frontier team?
answer: Feinberg says the advice so far assumed an external hire. Many large organizations do not build frontier models, but still use them. Feinberg gives the example of a colleague from the search side who moved onto Feinberg's team. That colleague's approach was to help the product area adopt the technology as well as possible. Feinberg says there is a large gap in applying and serving LLMs effectively inside such an organization.

Feinberg says becoming the person who closes that gap creates business value and raises the standing of the organization. It also makes that person the natural partner for the research side, so models work well inside that org. Feinberg says transferring is then optional. The work is already cutting edge, because it puts new technology into a product people use.
blocks.speaker: Vlad Feinberg

blocks.question: What was the concrete invitation in the post, given that Feinberg was hiring?
answer: Feinberg says the post tests for intent, mathematical maturity, and grit. The listed exercises cover basic knowledge of scaling laws, willingness to implement a real transformer, and the routine math used to size LLMs. Feinberg asks for handwritten work on the scaling-book exercises, with a video of doing them, plus the transformer exercise in the post. Candidates who can work in the New York office are offered an interview.

Feinberg says quite a few people have replied, and a couple of submissions are moving through the interview loop. The post drew a response within about a week. Headcount is limited, but the exercises build self-development and prepare people for interviews elsewhere. Feinberg offers referrals to other hiring teams.
blocks.speaker: Vlad Feinberg

blocks.question: Can you give a high-level overview of pre-training and its main challenges?
answer: Feinberg says the pre-training area delivers product models. These include the Flash model and a related model that power AI overviews and AI mode in Search. Other first-party models serve ads and YouTube. The team is also a technical point of contact for the Google-Apple partnership. Beyond these deliverables, the team does research to keep them state of the art and to support the Pro series model.

Feinberg says that research falls into three areas. The first is distillation. The second is inference co-design, which means designing neural architectures that run efficiently on the target hardware, including network topology, matrix shapes, and attention head counts. The third is new quantization methods, which change what is feasible for the other two.

Feinberg explains quantization as cutting the space that a network's weights take. Weights trained in 32-bit floats can often be stored at 4 bits with simple methods and keep quality. Quantizing runtime activations as well cuts the electricity needed for the math. Feinberg puts about 99 percent of AI hardware operating cost on power, a figure not verified here. The research goal is to push past the four-bit range.
blocks.speaker: Vlad Feinberg

blocks.question: Why is a low model flops utilization (MFU) not actually low?
answer: Feinberg defines MFU as the flops a network performs divided by the flops the accelerator could have performed in the same time. Full MFU would need the matmul unit busy the entire time, with no memory reads or other operations. Feinberg says that would not be a useful computation.

Real networks apply activation functions, run attention, and write outputs to memory. Those steps use the memory bus or vector units, or run more slowly than matmuls on the hardware. So a network does not run at the chip's rated speed, and a low-looking MFU is expected.

Feinberg says inference co-design uses all of the chip's rates: communication between chips, memory bandwidth, parameter reads, matmul flops, and vector flops. A network's shapes should use those units well. Feinberg says the shapes also affect training quality, so the work is a joint optimization. Because hardware rates change, the best shapes change too.
blocks.speaker: Vlad Feinberg

blocks.question: Why did Jeff Dean give a spot bonus, and what was the story behind it?
answer: Feinberg says the bonus came at the start of the Gemini program, for people who launched the first version of Bard. Feinberg's contribution was small. Feinberg helped with supervised fine-tuning for an early Bard version. At the time, Feinberg was doing pure research in Google Brain and focused on first-author papers at top venues.

Feinberg says a manager encouraged the team to join the effort. That push led Feinberg to hyperparameter tuning and engineering work to run the model on older TPUs. Jeff Dean recognized that small start, which Feinberg says grew into more LLM investment and eventually the current role.

Feinberg's lesson is that the value lies less in the fine-tuning itself than in joining a project that matters to the business. Some of that work is not glamorous, such as hyperparameter tuning or optimizing the XLA compiler to fit a program into a memory limit. Feinberg says such work matters for getting into very high-value projects.
blocks.speaker: Vlad Feinberg

blocks.question: What is your favorite war story from working on Gemini?
answer: Feinberg's favorite story is Flash 2.0, a very fast, low-latency model that is still good, which Search uses to answer quickly in AI mode. Earlier Flash models were dense, even though Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models add capacity. An MoE model holds more parameters, which must be spread across many chips. Routing a token to an expert on a distant chip adds communication to each forward pass, and latency grows with the number of chips.

Pipelining offered a way around that cost. A team member proposed applying pipeline prefill to MoE models. Instead of splitting experts across machines, this approach splits layers across machines, so experts can stay on one machine or a few. Communication can then run behind computation, since one layer works on early tokens while the previous layer works on later ones. Feinberg says this serving change helped make MoE latency attractive, and that the Gemini 2.0 report describes an MoE series.

Feinberg says the model was bigger than any the flash-scale team had trained, and training took about 40 days. A small team of about five people rotated shifts, handing off SRE-style work to keep the job alive. Tuned data iterators had to keep up, and any gap or indexing issue needed a fast fix, since it wasted GPU time.

followups.question: What were nights and weekends like during that stretch?
answer: Feinberg says the 40 days involved little sleep, with dual shifts across the Paris and Mountain View offices. The payoff came when the model launched around the time DeepSeek V3 came out.

Feinberg describes a Wall Street Journal article that framed the moment as a red scare about Chinese open-source models. A friend sent a leaderboard screenshot that seemed to show Gemini far behind, but Feinberg says the article's rows were badly written. The article now shows a Flash 2.0 thinking model well ahead of DeepSeek V3, which Feinberg says may have undercut its open-source narrative.
followups.speaker: Vlad Feinberg

blocks.speaker: Vlad Feinberg

blocks.question: If you could advise yourself just after college, what would you say?
answer: Feinberg's first advice is to chase the problems people face today. Feinberg says a person should not avoid a smaller or less glamorous part of a big problem, even if it is not fancy research math. Working on what matters shows what moves the frontier. Feinberg calls for humility in how to approach problems.

Feinberg's second piece of advice is professional: be the co-worker others want to see succeed. Feinberg contrasts this with workplace leaders who squeeze people for short-term results. Feinberg says the most effective people are kind, and cites a mentor who first introduced Feinberg to computer science as one example.

Feinberg says a generous approach can look naive when viewed as workplace game theory, but it builds collaboration and a willingness to help. That trust matters for large projects that need several people and skill sets to finish. Feinberg's summary is to be the kind of person other people want to see succeed.
blocks.speaker: Vlad Feinberg

parts.title: Choices, reinvention, and tradeoffs
parts.introduction: A career can change direction, and a desired title can fail to deliver the life imagined behind it. These reflections make room for curiosity, setbacks, personal values, and the cost of a chosen pace.

sections.title: Evaluate a path by what you learn, not only where its title ends
sections.deck: Brendan Burns reflects on doctoral study, curiosity, and the willingness to replace your own software.

blocks.question: Was getting a PhD worthwhile?
answer: Burns offers two different views rather than a simple endorsement. An undergraduate classmate went into startups while he completed a robotics PhD; they later found themselves at the same company and level. On that narrow career-level comparison, the degree was not clearly decisive.

But he enjoyed the work and learned skills he continued to use. His doctoral adviser helped him communicate ideas in writing and presentations, which later mattered when arguing for the ability to open-source Kubernetes. Teaching introductory computer science as a professor also helped him explain unfamiliar concepts such as containers and orchestration to new users. The benefit was not merely the credential: it was communication, teaching, and the enjoyment of learning. He does not claim these skills are only obtainable through a PhD.
blocks.speaker: Brendan Burns

blocks.question: What other question do people ask you most often?
answer: A common question is what to learn—especially whether to chase a fashionable area such as AI or study a field such as systems that already feels interesting. Burns says he cares more that a person is learning than that they pick the fashionable subject. Interest creates the energy to practice; a reluctant attempt at a supposedly hot topic may not produce much learning.

He says he never had a master career plan and instead followed things he found useful, enjoyable, or interesting. He acknowledges that this can go badly and that planning helps some people. Looking backward, apparent mistakes and dead ends can also turn out to have taught essential skills. His response to fear of choosing the wrong thing is therefore to notice whether learning is actually happening, not to guarantee that every choice has equal career value.
blocks.speaker: Brendan Burns

blocks.question: How could Kubernetes eventually disappear, and how do you feel about that possibility?
answer: Burns explains the larger point behind his remark that software eventually dies: do not remain attached to a system merely because you wrote it. Even his own Kubernetes code has been rewritten over the project’s history. Something better may offer similar usefulness with less complexity, and an engineer should be willing to replace the old work.

A system can also become invisible instead of vanishing. Just as users may think about Kubernetes without thinking about Linux beneath it, attention can shift toward AI while the infrastructure becomes a background layer. He imagines a reliable higher-level or natural-language interface as one possible simplification, while making reliable behavior a condition for that example.

He takes a very long view and doubts that Kubernetes will look the same a century later, but qualifies the prediction by observing how difficult technological timelines are. He cites changes in processor choices and the repeated delays in self-driving expectations as examples of futures arriving earlier or later than people anticipated. These remarks are speculative illustrations of adaptability, not the book’s current market or hardware forecast.
blocks.speaker: Brendan Burns

sections.title: Make sure you want the life that comes with the goal
sections.deck: Philip Su reflects on career ambition, early attainment, and the relationships that can be damaged along the way.

blocks.question: What advice would you give yourself at the beginning of your career?
answer: Su would first spend more time clarifying values and deciding what he actually wanted before committing to a direction. A clear target made earlier decisions easy—he could ask whether a job brought him closer to management—but he had not built an equally clear picture of what came after reaching that target.

He describes becoming a development manager and reaching a high level relatively young, then feeling that his purpose had disappeared. The “dog that caught the car” analogy captures a goal that gives direction until attainment exposes the missing plan for the rest of one’s life. He reports a difficult period of depression in that context. His advice is to consider the whole destination, not just its attractive feature, such as money or status.

He then recalls sleeping at the office and seeing his visiting fiancée only after work ended around 11 p.m. He says they remained together, but recognizes how easily the relationship could have broken under that treatment. Some things withstand strain and others do not recover. In hindsight, reaching his terminal level at 30 rather than 38 mattered less than he had assumed when compared with decades of work ahead and the health of his family relationships.

The question he would put to a highly ambitious younger person is therefore twofold: do you truly want the destination, and are you comfortable with what may break while pursuing it? This is his reflection on a particular period of his life, not a universal price that every ambitious career must pay.

followups.question: Would your younger self actually have accepted that advice?
answer: Su says no. He thinks advice about money and happiness often fails to land when the listener assumes they will be the exception. He was not mature enough then to receive the lesson. The value of a useful message therefore depends partly on readiness, not simply on whether the adviser can state it clearly.
followups.speaker: Philip Su

blocks.speaker: Philip Su

sections.title: Passion needs an operating model that survives your absence
sections.deck: Peterman recounts the transition from a six-month personal experiment to a self-sustaining podcast.

blocks.text: Peterman began the podcast while employed at Meta, partly to practice speaking and share career stories he found inspiring. The work kept drawing his attention after hours, but he says it had only lost money. A reorganization provided an opportunity to leave and test the idea using six months of savings. He describes a personal decision driven by the work he wanted to do, rather than a financially obvious career move.
blocks.heading: A bounded experiment outside the obvious career path

blocks.text: The early freedom came with an operational weakness: he personally researched guests, reviewed all the footage, and handled the production. Despite working more than before, he struggled to maintain one episode per week. If he stopped, the production stopped. Four months into the intended runway, he still had no revenue and had postponed finding sponsors because that effort competed with the parts of creating he enjoyed.
blocks.heading: The founder was the bottleneck

blocks.text: Illness made the fragility concrete. A nearly finished episode allowed him to publish during a week when he could not work, but the experience pushed him to take sponsors seriously and build a backlog. He made recording more efficient so he could produce two episodes a week when needed. He also reduced spending by filming episodes himself, including an interview in a guest’s study with two phones. Sponsorships then brought in revenue.
blocks.heading: Create room for interruptions

blocks.text: By the update, the six-month experiment had lasted nine months and he said the podcast was sustaining itself. His keyboard project had also raised its required Kickstarter funds quickly. He did not treat these facts as proof that leaving Meta maximized income: he expected the keyboard project could lose money in aggregate and emphasized that money was not its main goal.
blocks.heading: Sustainability and income maximization are different goals

blocks.text: His condition for continuing was practical: the podcast needed to cover itself and his living costs. He wanted to improve guest access and produce the keyboard at a high quality bar. He had been using an early manufacturing sample and described shipping as a future target. The captions do not provide the publication date needed to convert “early next year” into a reliable calendar deadline, and this account does not establish current shipping status.
blocks.heading: Define the condition that lets the experiment continue

blocks.title: Make the experiment less fragile

steps.title: Set a runway
steps.text: Bound the initial commitment of savings and time.

steps.title: Notice the bottleneck
steps.text: Identify what stops when the founder is unavailable.

steps.title: Build a buffer
steps.text: Improve production and keep episodes ready.

steps.title: Cover the costs
steps.text: Find revenue and reduce spending so the work can continue.

blocks.caption: Arrows show the sequence in this personal account, reconstructed by the editor. The diagram organizes the experience described in this update.

omissions: Promotional requests for podcast ratings, subscriptions, and project links are condensed; the operational changes and product status are retained.

sections.title: Turn a personal constraint into a product brief
sections.deck: Ryan Peterman describes how discomfort and dissatisfaction with existing keyboards shaped a hardware prototype.

blocks.text: Peterman traces the project to wrist pain that began while playing tennis and worsened during his work as a software engineer. He says ergonomic keyboards helped him, but many designs required a layout change he did not want to make while still using a laptop in meetings. Price also mattered. These are his own experiences, rather than general medical conclusions about a particular keyboard.
blocks.heading: Start with the actual constraint

blocks.text: The keyboard he settled on offered two features he valued: separate halves reduced an uncomfortable wrist angle, and tenting helped him keep his wrists in a more neutral position. But the product also left him with a specific list of frustrations: unused space, a wire connecting otherwise wireless halves, a plastic construction, and bulky tenting accessories. He cites a $100 keyboard and an additional $40 for plastic tenting legs as prices in his experience at the time.
blocks.heading: Convert complaints into requirements

blocks.text: The proposed alternative combined a minimal shape, fully wireless halves, an aluminum body, and familiar key positions. A compact tenting mechanism also served as a portable case. Peterman says manufacturing partners had produced a working prototype demonstrating feasibility. Fundraising and manufacturing were the next steps he described; the clip does not establish that the product had already shipped.
blocks.heading: Separate a prototype from a finished product

blocks.title: From discomfort to a testable product idea

steps.title: Experience a constraint
steps.text: Identify the problem in actual use.

steps.title: Compare existing options
steps.text: Record what helps and what still gets in the way.

steps.title: Specify the changes
steps.text: Turn those shortcomings into design requirements.

steps.title: Build a prototype
steps.text: Test feasibility before scaling manufacturing.

blocks.caption: Arrows show an editorial reconstruction of the sequence in Peterman’s story, not a guaranteed route to a successful hardware business.

sections.title: After a layoff: craft, identity, and an unwritten next chapter
sections.deck: The guest known as Asian Dad Energy discusses a 25-year career, consulting’s incentives, a return to hands-on work, and life after losing a job.

blocks.question: What happened during your layoff?
answer: His employer had already conducted several rounds of layoffs. Rumors indicated another was coming, but the affected businesses and numbers were unclear. Through relationships and his position in the organization, he learned both that the round was approaching and that he was on the list.

He was already questioning why he remained in big tech. When he learned that more junior engineers were also due to be cut, he says he arranged to move himself to the top of the list. His hope was to buy those colleagues some time. He explicitly does not know their ultimate outcome and speculates that later rounds might limit that benefit.

followups.question: Why do you think the layoff happened?
answer: He offers a hypothesis, rather than inside evidence: companies under pressure to show returns from AI investments might cut headcount to reduce costs while keeping revenue temporarily stable, then present the change as improved efficiency. He is careful to identify this as conjecture about his former employer and the industry.

blocks.speaker: Asian Dad Energy

blocks.question: How did you feel when you learned you were on the list?
answer: The prospect brought anxiety, panic, fear, hope, and excitement together. After years of a familiar routine, a major change was arriving without a clear answer about whether it would improve his life. For several days, that mixture felt emotionally unstable.
blocks.speaker: Asian Dad Energy

blocks.question: What did the exit process look like?
answer: He describes his former employer’s process as structured and transparent. The broad terms were communicated ahead of time: a period of garden leave, severance, payment for unused time off, and other support such as a stipend. Taken together, he considered the package generous.

The components and timing mattered because they made the transition more understandable. This describes the package available to him, rather than a promise about what another employer or employee would receive.

followups.question: Did you negotiate it?
answer: He did not. Although he thinks negotiation can be possible, his immediate priorities were emotional processing and reflection on his life. Pursuing a larger package was far down that list.

blocks.speaker: Asian Dad Energy

blocks.question: Why do you expect further layoffs?
answer: He worries that large AI investments are being added to many products without clear returns. In his account, headcount cuts could come from cost pressure, weak business lines, or attempts to demonstrate efficiency.

He repeatedly qualifies this as a feeling about the industry at the time and allows that he could be completely wrong. It is a prediction in the conversation, not a confirmed explanation of any later event.

followups.question: Could AI instead make employees more productive and valuable?
answer: Yes. Peterman raises the possibility that higher output per person could create demand for more work and more people. The guest agrees that the future is unwritten and says he would welcome that outcome. He simply considers the more negative scenario likelier in his own judgment at that moment.

blocks.speaker: Asian Dad Energy

blocks.question: What was the overall path of your career?
answer: He began programming in high school, studied computer science, and did small projects and consulting work during college. He then joined a digital consulting agency and spent years progressing through junior and senior development, technical leadership, application and enterprise architecture, and technical director roles.

After reflecting on the direction of that work, he moved into big tech as a senior or chief architect overseeing an ecosystem of applications and platforms. That was the role he held in the years before the layoff.
blocks.speaker: Asian Dad Energy

blocks.question: What does software engineering consulting actually involve?
answer: A consulting firm supplies skills such as content-management systems, ecommerce, backend integration, or digital transformation. Teams enter a client’s environment to build systems, working alongside the client’s technical staff and often other vendors.

The environment can be dynamic and chaotic. A consultant has to find a place among several actors, learn quickly, build as well as possible, and then move to another project. He enjoyed the pace and the need to adapt.

followups.question: Who maintains the software after the initial build?
answer: There are different arrangements. A retainer can support a relationship lasting years, with continued maintenance, enhancement, and accumulated knowledge of the system. He preferred that continuity, especially when the firm had built the platform from the beginning.

A short build-and-exit engagement can have different incentives: the agency needs a pipeline to keep consultants employed. Across multiple vendors, the client can accumulate redundant and incompatible systems. A later integration project then has to stitch together the resulting patchwork. He has encountered both models, with their different technical challenges and anxieties.

blocks.speaker: Asian Dad Energy

blocks.question: What is it like to be dropped into another company’s culture?
answer: It depends on the client. He has seen rigid hierarchies, cooperative environments, and internal startups. Technical skill alone is insufficient: a consultant must understand how client teams relate to one another and to outside vendors.

As seniority grows, navigating that environment and opening space for the firm’s next engagement can become part of the job. His own work gradually shifted from hands-on system design toward selling a vision to executives. The earlier learning and adaptation were enjoyable; the later shift eventually burned him out.

followups.question: What caused the burnout?
answer: The gap between the smooth vision sold to executives and the implementation reality. Diagrams promised a clean path from customer insight to decisions and revenue, while the underlying work involved incompatible systems, unmaintained code, broken integrations, and teams struggling to communicate. As the technical director responsible for making those worlds meet, he found the gap exhausting.

blocks.speaker: Asian Dad Energy

blocks.question: Does a consultancy still get paid when the implementation is poor?
answer: He frames the answer around the early digital-transformation period he experienced. Executives could see visible improvements, such as replacing an analog workflow with a mobile experience and delivery notifications, while having little visibility into the workarounds beneath the surface.

Moving from no digital workflow to a working one could produce substantial value even with an imperfect implementation. That did not mean the architecture or operational quality was good; it meant a visible business result could be enough to make the engagement look successful initially.
blocks.speaker: Asian Dad Energy

blocks.question: What prevents a consultant from overstating the quality of the work?
answer: The guest emphasizes engineering integrity: tell the client the truth about quality, even when a large investment has produced a poor result. Personal boundaries and pride in the work matter when the client cannot fully judge the implementation.

Peterman raises reputation and incentives. A firm that repeatedly delivers bad work can lose future customers. He also contrasts the client’s limited technical visibility with an engineering organization where technically informed leaders assess operational quality and reward it.

The guest agrees that poor work can be hidden temporarily, but describes a strong culture of care among the mentors, colleagues, and leaders he knew. His answer relies on both a human commitment to craft and the longer-term consequences for the firm, rather than claiming that the incentive problem disappears.
blocks.speaker: Asian Dad Energy

blocks.title: The tension inside a consulting engagement
rows: Visible client outcome
A new workflow, site, or customer experience.
Whether the system will remain reliable and maintainable.
Agency utilization
Keeping a pipeline of paid engagements.
Whether selling the next project serves the client’s actual need.
Engineering integrity
Truthful evaluation and pride in craft.
Communicating weaknesses even when the investment is substantial.
Long-term reputation
Trust and repeat business.
The delayed cost of poor work that initially appears successful.

blocks.question: Why do some employees react negatively to consultants?
answer: He thinks some of that reaction comes from management consulting associated with organizational cuts, rather than technical consulting itself. A study of people and processes can lead to redundancy decisions and layoffs, making a consulting team’s arrival feel threatening.

In his own technical engagements, most relationships became positive once people knew one another. He distinguishes the fear created by the situation from a belief that the individuals involved are necessarily unhelpful.
blocks.speaker: Asian Dad Energy

blocks.question: What changed when you moved into big tech?
answer: By then, his consulting role had become largely boardroom selling, and he felt detached from the implementation work he enjoyed. A former colleague introduced him to a chief architect role that turned out to be substantially hands-on.

He could dive into an important system, lead its construction, code a difficult component, debug with a team, adjust configuration, and participate in production launches. The appeal was the return to direct technical contribution, rather than only drawing architecture diagrams.

followups.question: How different was the compensation?
answer: In his experience, it more than doubled and approached three times his previous compensation. A higher base, bonuses, restricted stock units, and an employee stock-purchase program contributed. Appreciation of the shares he held further widened the difference. These are his historical results, not a general pay comparison or an expected investment return.

blocks.speaker: Asian Dad Energy

blocks.question: How did the employee stock-purchase program work for you?
answer: He could buy company shares using after-tax salary at a discount he describes as about 15%. His example is a $100 market price and an $85 purchase price. He then held the shares and benefited from their later appreciation.
The explanation concerns his employer’s program and his own experience. Program rules and eventual returns are separate questions; his successful outcome does not make future appreciation certain.

followups.question: Could you sell the shares immediately instead of holding them?
answer: He says immediate sale was available in his case. He preferred holding because he believed the pandemic-driven shift toward digital tools would favor the business, while acknowledging that markets are unpredictable and the future could differ.

Peterman points out that a discount and a decision to keep company shares are separable: a person might sell and use the proceeds differently. The guest’s account is a description of his choice, not a recommendation that readers hold their employer’s stock.

followups.question: If you had received cash instead, would you have bought the same company stock?
answer: He says he would probably have chosen index funds because he considered himself risk-averse. That reveals a tension between keeping stock already received and choosing where to invest fresh cash. The participants mention possible tax implications but do not resolve them, and the guest says he did not research the subject deeply.

blocks.speaker: Asian Dad Energy

blocks.question: Which period of your career produced the most growth?
answer: The progression from senior software engineer to senior enterprise architect was the period he valued most. It expanded his work from coding into design, integration, and understanding multiple applications. Strong mentors guided that growth. After director-level work became more about helping leads and selling to executives, he found less enjoyment and less personal growth.
blocks.speaker: Asian Dad Energy

blocks.question: What lesson from a mentor stayed with you?
answer: Stay flexible. Adapt to the technology stack, delivery pipeline, client teams, and changing conditions in front of you. In consulting, that ability was a survival skill as well as a way to keep learning.

followups.question: When did keeping up start to feel harder?
answer: For him, learning new frameworks became slower after about forty. He explicitly recognizes that others have different experiences, including people learning quickly in their fifties. This is his personal account of frustration and adaptation, rather than a general claim about the abilities of older engineers.

blocks.speaker: Asian Dad Energy

blocks.question: Why start recording YouTube videos after the layoff?
answer: He was confused and anxious, and his therapist suggested recording his thoughts. Turning on a camera felt easier than writing in a notebook. The first vlog was a way to process what he was experiencing; he did not anticipate it going viral.

followups.question: What did the response mean to you?
answer: The reach surprised him, and many supportive comments suggested other people felt similar things. Seeing that he was not alone was helpful to him.

followups.question: Did former colleagues recognize you?
answer: Several people from his former big-tech employer and earlier companies contacted him positively. He had not yet encountered a disapproving response, although he recognized that public visibility could eventually bring awkward encounters.

blocks.speaker: Asian Dad Energy

blocks.question: What do you want your next chapter to look like?
answer: He did apply to a few big-tech companies, without much result, but was also reconsidering whether he wanted to return to their schedules, goals, and priorities. He wanted to see how a period of partial or involuntary early retirement felt and spend more time with people he cared about.

After more than a month, he reported feeling better physically and emotionally. He was keeping his mind active through the channel and small coding projects. He remained open to a compelling future project, while declining to invent a settled plan before he had found one.
blocks.speaker: Asian Dad Energy

blocks.question: How can an engineer explain their work more clearly?
answer: Relax the connection between your identity and the topic. He remembers a technically brilliant engineer whose intense attachment to a cache-optimization project made it difficult to explain to a less technical audience.

Take a step back and choose the level of explanation the listener can use. Speaking in the same detail as your own technical thinking can obscure the point. A simpler explanation should help the audience understand what matters and the decision or support you need.
blocks.speaker: Asian Dad Energy

blocks.question: What would you tell yourself at the beginning?
answer: Work hard, keep learning, and stay flexible. Those habits connect the earlier consulting career with an uncertain next chapter.
blocks.speaker: Asian Dad Energy

sections.title: Build early, show the result, and define your own conditions
sections.deck: Jia Chen describes how hackathons led to a startup, while distinguishing a finished demo, a useful product, and the conditions behind her choice to leave school.

blocks.question: How did you become so involved in hackathons?
answer: She entered college as a finance major, having taken a Python class and encountered computer science in high school without much interest. At the first hackathon, she expected other builders might implement her idea. Instead, she spent the event building herself. The team lost, but the experience made her excited about creating things.

She went to another event in Ohio and won a hardware prize. During that period she combined classes with long hours learning tools, APIs, libraries, and microcontrollers. Her example is an unusually intense personal schedule, rather than a necessary formula for becoming a builder.

followups.question: What did you build for that early win?
answer: A Raspberry Pi Pico with modules that measured the distance to an object in front of it. She describes it as an exploratory aid for people with visual disabilities, extending the distance information a cane might supply. The discussion is about a hackathon prototype, not a validated assistive device.

followups.question: Did you have a team?
answer: She found someone through Discord and traveled with that person, but built the entry solo. For larger prizes, she considers a team an advantage because people can divide work and specialize.

blocks.speaker: Jia Chen

blocks.question: How do you choose good teammates?
answer: Look at demonstrated skills and projects rather than titles alone. She checks GitHub work, activity, and experience relevant to the proposed project. She also values enthusiasm, effort, resourcefulness, and a willingness to attempt the unfamiliar. The best credential is useful evidence that the person can contribute to this particular build.
blocks.speaker: Jia Chen

blocks.question: Do you arrive with an idea already prepared?
answer: Yes. A hackathon has a time limit, sponsor tools, prize categories, and a social environment. She researches those constraints and uses a document to map how the tools could support her ideas before writing code. The important question is whether the proposed product can be finished within the event.

She often prefers a simple, complete result to an elaborate unfinished one. More ambitious entries can work when the implementation steps have been thought through. Her example is a project tracing altered digital artwork back toward an original artist; the interview briefly discusses its provenance interface without supplying a complete technical description of the algorithm.
blocks.speaker: Jia Chen

blocks.question: What is the social part of a hackathon?
answer: It includes both the team and the judges. Inside the team, motivation matters over the whole event: one person giving up can affect a small group disproportionately. An enthusiastic teammate can lift the group, and she has seen the strongest results when everyone is fully engaged.
blocks.speaker: Jia Chen

blocks.question: How do you present a project to judges?
answer: Keep the pitch short: state the idea, explain what it does, and spend most of the time demonstrating it. Watch whether the judges understand and let them interact with the result. In her experience, many judges were not deeply technical, so a list of frameworks was less persuasive than a product whose value they could see.

This does not rule out technical ambition. A complex project can feel clear and simple when it works well and the presentation makes its purpose obvious. The mistake is assuming that complexity alone is the reason it should win.
blocks.speaker: Jia Chen

blocks.question: Does the idea matter more than execution?
answer: Both matter to her: a distinctive idea and a working connection between the frontend and backend. A strong presentation rests on something that actually functions.

followups.question: Can you win with a polished frontend and a mocked backend?
answer: It can sometimes look convincing, but she prefers a genuinely connected project because that enables further development. She describes a common failure: split into frontend and backend groups, add features independently, and leave integration until the end. The pieces can then remain disconnected.

Her approach is to connect the smallest useful path in the first few hours, test the communication, and iterate on that. Integration is an early milestone, rather than the final task after every component is polished.

blocks.speaker: Jia Chen

blocks.title: A workable short-event build

steps.title: Check feasibility
steps.text: Match the idea, tools, and available time.

steps.title: Connect the smallest version
steps.text: Make the frontend and backend communicate early.

steps.title: Iterate together
steps.text: Add features around the working path rather than in isolated pieces.

steps.title: Demonstrate the value
steps.text: Let the audience try the result and understand what it does.

blocks.caption: An editorial outline of her planning, integration, and presentation advice.

blocks.question: Which project was your favorite?
answer: She describes a homemade glasses prototype built from cardboard, glass, and an Arduino-connected OLED display. Whisper transcription appeared through a prism-like display, with a web application also collecting and summarizing the material. Bluetooth connected parts of the setup.

The team completed the build in about nine hours, according to her account. She assembled it from people who were already making things: one built rockets, and others spent time building in an entrepreneurship center. They remained in contact afterward. The account illustrates the value she places on practical builders; it is a prototype story rather than a claim of production readiness.
blocks.speaker: Jia Chen

blocks.question: Would you recommend doing many hackathons?
answer: She sees them as useful for learning to act in an unfamiliar environment, finishing a project, meeting recruiters, and gaining confidence. But she also sees diminishing returns. Her own suggested range is roughly three to five before considering other uses of the time.

For deeper learning and standing out, she would increasingly favor building a product people keep using. The finished project and real users can matter more than attendance at the event itself. Repeated short, improvised builds do not provide every lesson of sustaining a product.
blocks.speaker: Jia Chen

blocks.question: Did hackathons strengthen your initiative?
answer: She already had some willingness to try unusual things, but thinks the events helped. School sometimes felt repetitive, and building offered a more stimulating outlet. Coming from an environment where few people were seriously pursuing startups made that experimentation feel different from the usual path.
blocks.speaker: Jia Chen

blocks.question: How did you balance classes, hackathons, and content?
answer: During one demanding semester, she reports maintaining an engineering GPA above 3.5, attending fifteen hackathons, and growing an audience to around fifty thousand. She also describes the pressure of trying to satisfy several different expectations at once.

Time blocking helped: choose a time and place for homework, finish it before the weekend event, and focus on the environment she was in. Content was often short and casual rather than a heavily produced video.

She also deliberately placed herself where useful information and people were available. Office hours could teach her through other students’ questions even when she had no specific question. Later, being in the startup environment in California served a similar purpose. The account combines scheduling with choosing a setting that makes learning and connection easier.
blocks.speaker: Jia Chen

blocks.question: What can a student at a less recognizable school do to stand out?
answer: Develop initiative and responsibility: lead a club, help decide the direction of a substantial project, or make useful work visible. Her point is to become someone who makes decisions and carries them through, rather than relying exclusively on the school’s name.
blocks.speaker: Jia Chen

blocks.question: What did college give you, and where did it fall short?
answer: She thinks its value depends on the person. Structure, discipline, a learning path, and access to peers can be useful, particularly before someone knows what to learn independently. Completing the path can also be a good route into a desired career.

For her, aspects of school reduced enthusiasm and creativity. Even so, she does not regard the experience as irrelevant: college introduced her to hackathons and contributed to the person she became. She also describes earlier creative experimentation through releasing music in high school.

followups.question: What do you wish you had understood before college?
answer: How much relationships and information can shape opportunity. Advice about applications, access to experiences, and introductions can affect a path even when people have similar skills. Peterman connects that idea with the podcast’s effort to make experienced people’s knowledge more broadly available.

blocks.speaker: Jia Chen

blocks.question: How did you begin making hackathon content?
answer: A friend suggested vlogging an event. She delayed trying it until she had already won many hackathons, then found that the story attracted attention. Showing a student building and winning a substantial prize gave viewers something concrete and unusual to watch.
blocks.speaker: Jia Chen

blocks.question: What does a personal brand do for a student?
answer: It makes subsequent work easier to discover. A project shown to a small group reaches only that group; a visible body of work can reach many more recruiters or potential collaborators at once. She sees it as increasing the chances that useful opportunities find her.

followups.question: How did you overcome fear of putting yourself out there?
answer: She discussed ideas with a few close friends. Knowing that a small group would support her helped make negative reactions from strangers less important. She acted while still feeling nervous, with a grounding support network.

followups.question: What is one concrete step for someone who does not want to become a frequent creator?
answer: Move the project beyond localhost. Publish a working version, make the repository available where appropriate, and give people a usable link. Visibility can begin with sharing the work itself rather than posting constantly.

blocks.speaker: Jia Chen

blocks.question: How did a gap semester and a startup happen?
answer: She began an MVP one evening after deciding to try a company. The initial idea responded to questions from her audience about entering hackathons. She posted it the next morning, and the application crashed under the traffic.

Months later, a cofounder helped restore it. A trip with hackathon friends became a longer stay in San Francisco. She describes meeting investors at events, including an informal hot-pot gathering, while the product already had users and some business revenue.

An investor’s interest in the story and the match between her experience and the product brought an initial check. Posting about that moment attracted further interest. Her account combines prior building experience, a network, traction, and distribution; it was not a company emerging from a social post alone.

followups.question: Did you plan to return to the same school?
answer: At the time of the conversation, she thought returning to Michigan State was unlikely, while leaving open a possible transfer to a California school. The plan remained unsettled.

blocks.speaker: Jia Chen

blocks.question: What startup advice proved useful?
answer: Keep shipping, and also avoid exhausting yourself. She sees the tension between those instructions and now thinks consistent progress needs room for breaks and other parts of life.

The pressure was real: she describes a robbery in which laptops and personal belongings were stolen, followed by continued customer outreach. She reports winning business from several companies and reaching five-figure monthly recurring revenue in that period.

She does not label the experience as having fully burned out, but says it weighed on mental health and relationships. Continuing to work through a crisis is part of her story, rather than evidence that rest or security are dispensable.
blocks.speaker: Jia Chen

blocks.question: Would you recommend leaving college to start a company?
answer: She would not recommend dropping out immediately. Set personal conditions first. Her own conditions included a credible network for funding and customers, the ability to support herself, technical capacity with the right collaborators, and a way to distribute the product.

Those conditions made her position different from someone with only a fresh idea. The useful takeaway is to make the prerequisites explicit for your own circumstances, rather than treating her decision as a default recommendation.
blocks.speaker: Jia Chen

blocks.title: The conditions she checked before committing
rows: Technical execution
Do we have the skills and collaborators to build the product?
Distribution
Can we reach the people who would use it?
Customer and funding network
Can we connect with customers and potential supporters?
Ability to sustain the move
Can we support ourselves in the environment we are choosing?

blocks.question: Would you advise someone to pursue computer science now?
answer: She says it depends on the person, but recommends trying to build something people want to use. That experiment can reveal whether the person enjoys product building, create useful work in its own right, and supply concrete evidence to show a recruiter.
blocks.speaker: Jia Chen

blocks.question: What would you tell your earlier self?
answer: Be more open to experiences and people that can teach you something. She used to stay within a small social circle and decline invitations more readily. Her reflection connects learning with participation and relationships, as well as technical practice.
blocks.speaker: Jia Chen

blocks.text: The company discussed at the end, Sprint.dev, was intended to make hackathons more approachable through tools, support, and opportunities to build together. Her description of the builders she wanted emphasized creativity, execution, collaboration, and shipping useful work, rather than credentials alone.
blocks.heading: The product behind the story

sections.title: Choosing the work over the level
sections.deck: Igor explains why he sought a lower level, what made senior onboarding difficult, and the infrastructure work that had earned his earlier promotion.

blocks.question: Why did you ask for a demotion at Meta?
answer: Igor joined at senior staff and felt he had to acquire deep technical context, relationships, and trust quickly enough to perform alongside experienced peers. He describes a much longer ramp than the title alone suggests: an external hire can initially know less about the environment than an intern who has already spent a few weeks there. The higher the expected scope, the more layers of competence and context there are to rebuild.

After about a year and two months, his own assessment was that he had reached something closer to staff-level effectiveness. Performance pressure made that gap feel risky. His description of the company’s performance environment is his experience at the time, rather than a statement of current policy.

He also discovered a preference for the work in the E5–E6 range: coding, debugging, designing, and mentoring. The senior staff role involved more leadership, meetings, and design documents, with less direct coding. He asked whether he could drop a level, understanding that existing stock and compensation made this awkward. He was told that staying in the same job category while reducing the level was not supported by the process available to him.

followups.question: What made you think you were below the expected level?
answer: Much of it was his own comparison with other senior staff engineers, although he later confirms that he also received feedback. He stresses that capability is continuous and multidimensional, rather than a set of perfectly discrete levels. His desire for a change was also about enjoying the work, not simply judging himself incapable.

followups.question: Did you try to escalate the request?
answer: He asked and received a negative answer; he acknowledges that more escalation might have produced an exception. He instead chose to explore returning to Google, where he had spent fourteen and a half years before joining Cruise and then Meta. That was a familiar environment and an available alternative.

blocks.speaker: Igor

blocks.question: Why had the senior role worked at Google and Cruise?
answer: At Google he joined as a junior engineer and grew through repeated promotions, including attempts that initially failed. The senior staff promotion followed a substantial project on a team where he had already spent years. Expertise, familiarity, and credibility had accumulated together.

Cruise also required a difficult first-year ramp. Over time he found a role that combined coding, mentoring, and broader technical guidance. He was happy there before the accident and subsequent company disruption he describes led him to leave.

followups.question: What made the Cruise and Meta ramps different?
answer: Cruise was smaller, with less infrastructure to learn and more unclaimed work that needed an owner. In his Meta organization, the space for senior people felt crowded, so finding suitable scope was harder. He explicitly limits that observation to the organization he experienced.

blocks.speaker: Igor

blocks.question: What would you change about your onboarding?
answer: He spent too much time trying to build foundational knowledge by reading documents before doing enough actual work. In retrospect, he would learn and build in parallel: take a task, get his hands dirty, and acquire the relevant context while making progress.

He had not changed companies often, so this form of onboarding was new to him. He also felt the management team had limited experience ramping senior external hires because many senior employees had grown inside the company and already understood its basic machinery.

followups.question: What could the manager have done to help?
answer: A concrete example of how another senior external hire had recently ramped would have helped. He does not present the problem as management neglect: they tried to support him, but neither side had an established recipe.

blocks.speaker: Igor

blocks.title: A more practical senior ramp

steps.title: Take a real task
steps.text: Find work that exposes a useful part of the environment.

steps.title: Build and learn together
steps.text: Acquire context while attempting the work.

steps.title: Use experienced guidance
steps.text: Ask for concrete examples and help from people who know the system.

steps.title: Expand the scope
steps.text: Grow technical understanding and relationships together.

blocks.caption: An editorial synthesis of his onboarding reflection, rather than a guaranteed promotion process.

blocks.question: Does moving companies become harder for senior individual contributors?
answer: He has seen Google colleagues leave and return after a move did not work out. Such stories are harder to hear because people tend to share successes more readily than failures. He also suspects repeated moves could build the skill of ramping in a new environment; his own limited experience should not be treated as proof that every senior move will fail.
blocks.speaker: Igor

blocks.question: Did anyone give you feedback about the level gap?
answer: Yes, although he does not share the private details. He gives a project example: work he expected to take two weeks became much more complicated. Even if he completed it successfully, he did not think its scope would justify E7. Underestimating complexity and selecting insufficiently broad work were different problems that combined in the same project.
blocks.speaker: Igor

blocks.question: Would returning to Google also restore your old team context?
answer: No. The people and infrastructure would be new. The advantage was familiarity with the company’s operating patterns and culture, rather than retaining all of the specific knowledge and relationships from his previous role.

followups.question: What cultural difference affected you?
answer: In the Meta organization he observed, aggressive deadlines could be imposed repeatedly, missed, and then extended. He thought the resulting pressure could lose credibility: people learn to discount urgency when the deadline repeatedly appears artificial.

He contrasts this with the Google environment he remembered from much earlier, where exceptional pressure more often accompanied a concrete reason. He explicitly does not know whether that comparison still describes Google, and says he did not personally feel much pressure at Meta. The concern is about the pattern he observed around him, not a universal company ranking.

blocks.speaker: Igor

blocks.question: Was returning at L6 instead of your former L7 straightforward?
answer: It required work from the recruiter because the usual return process supported the same level or a higher one. A request for a lower level could raise questions about why the person wanted it and whether they would accept the lower compensation.

He explicitly reassured the recruiter that he understood and would accept a significant compensation reduction. They made the arrangement possible in his case. He does not claim to know how his hiring manager interpreted the request.

followups.question: What concerns might a hiring manager have?
answer: He speculates that a manager could wonder whether there were undisclosed problems behind the move. These are possible questions he imagines, rather than accusations or information about what actually happened in the hiring discussion.

blocks.speaker: Igor

blocks.question: How did the return hiring process work?
answer: The recruiter sent openings, he spoke with several hiring managers, and he pursued the team that seemed to fit best. He then spoke with engineers and the manager’s manager.

Despite having been away for about three and a half years, he did not have to repeat the normal interview process. There was a discussion of whether returning at L6 would require a coding interview because a more senior role might have involved less coding, but he received an exception.
He does not know whether that was a general return policy or a special arrangement for him. The process described is one person’s experience.
blocks.speaker: Igor

blocks.question: Why are you willing to discuss this publicly?
answer: He is generally open about positive and negative experiences, but also emphasizes the security that makes his openness possible. He does not depend on an employer for a work visa, has access to health insurance through his spouse, has grown children and no mortgage, and can afford time without work.

Those conditions reduce the consequences of losing a job after speaking publicly. He would not automatically advise someone with different constraints to disclose their workplace challenges. His willingness to share comes with a clear acknowledgment of privilege.
blocks.speaker: Igor

blocks.question: What changed between pursuing promotions and pursuing a lower level?
answer: Earlier in a career, it can be difficult to imagine what a role several levels above actually feels like. Experiencing the progression clarified his preference: his happiest work involved a relatively small team, substantial coding and debugging, design, and mentoring. A higher title was less valuable to him once its daily work became concrete.
blocks.speaker: Igor

blocks.question: If compensation were irrelevant, which level would you choose for quality of life?
answer: His personal answer is senior engineer, E5 or L5: meaningful technical work with more protection from organizational demands by a technical lead and managers. He enjoys programming itself and entered the profession for that reason. This is a preference about the work and conditions he values, rather than a universal quality-of-life ranking.

followups.question: Would two levels down be ideal?
answer: He considers that too extreme for his actual choice and feels comfortable with E6. He also allows that more time at E7 might have helped him become comfortable there. Capability and enjoyment are multidimensional, and his conclusion remains a personal choice under uncertainty.

blocks.speaker: Igor

blocks.question: What did strong senior peers do that you felt you lacked?
answer: He warns against combining everyone else’s strengths into one imaginary competitor. One colleague may be strong at presentations, another at communication, and another at leadership. Comparing yourself with the whole group can create an impossible standard.

He thinks that with enough time he could have become fully productive at E7. He simply was not enjoying the process and did not have to continue it. Friends and family questioned leaving before being forced out, or declining to seek the same level elsewhere. His response separates an ability to do something from a desire to spend his life doing it.
blocks.speaker: Igor

blocks.question: What project earned your earlier senior staff promotion at Google?
answer: He helped move ads machine-learning training infrastructure from CPUs to TPUs. The existing CPU infrastructure had accumulated years of monitoring, tests, reliability, and operational polish. The new system had to meet that standard while supporting a different form of hardware and online training.

Scale and utilization mattered as much as getting a model to run. The project required building something reliable around the accelerator, rather than merely replacing a processor in an otherwise unchanged workflow.

followups.question: How was the project executed?
answer: It began with him as technical lead and one other person building a prototype, supported by multiple teams including TPU, compiler, and TensorFlow specialists. Existing credibility and relationships helped make that collaboration possible.

Hardware decisions required risk-taking: the company had to order expensive chips roughly eighteen months before delivery, before it could simply test the final setup. The effort grew as the system began working, and later TPU generations required continuing infrastructure changes.

blocks.speaker: Igor

blocks.question: How could you test the infrastructure before the chips were available?
answer: Much of the work concerned reading, processing, and moving data. The old CPU setup could perform input work alongside comparatively slower model computation. Much faster accelerators changed the balance: the host could no longer be assumed to feed them adequately.

One useful test removed the model’s computation and measured how quickly data could flow through the rest of the system. That approximated an infinitely fast accelerator and exposed bottlenecks in scheduling, input pipelines, and output handling before new hardware arrived.

Storage introduced another bottleneck. Larger disks could store the same dataset with fewer devices, while their per-device read throughput did not grow proportionally. The team could need more disks for throughput rather than capacity. Adding them was constrained by racks, power, and deployment logistics, even when the disks themselves were comparatively cheap.
blocks.speaker: Igor

blocks.title: Testing the system around a faster accelerator

steps.title: Remove model computation
steps.text: Use an experiment that makes compute time negligible.

steps.title: Measure the data path
steps.text: Check feeding, scheduling, processing, and output speed.

steps.title: Find the new bottleneck
steps.text: Identify limits previously hidden behind slow computation.

steps.title: Address physical constraints
steps.text: Account for storage throughput, racks, power, and deployment.

blocks.caption: An editorial outline of the test and infrastructure constraints he describes.

blocks.question: Did the long-range TPU orders usually overestimate or underestimate demand?
answer: They generally ordered conservatively and ended up short. In a mature ads business, wasted capacity had a direct effect on the economics, so overprovisioning was undesirable.

The future model was also uncertain. New modeling techniques could require operations the specialized hardware handled poorly. He gives sparse embedding lookups as an example: hardware strong at matrix multiplication and large memory transfers could struggle with random access. His comparison with contemporary AI spending expresses his view in the interview; the engineering lesson here is the uncertainty created by long hardware lead times and changing workloads.
blocks.speaker: Igor

blocks.question: Is there a mentorship story you particularly remember?
answer: An intern he hosted when he was around L4 later joined full time and eventually became the manager of that team. Igor had moved to another project by then, so he did not report to his former intern. His lesson is straightforward: do not underestimate an intern’s potential.
blocks.speaker: Igor

blocks.question: What do you regret or wish others understood?
answer: Difficult experiences helped shape him, so he does not simply wish them away. He does describe losing an earlier idealized view of Google as an organization he wanted to join for its values alone. Over time, he came to see the positive and negative features of a corporation whose financial priorities could dominate individual interests.

One event he remembers was an office closure. In the explanation he heard, a senior sponsor withdrew support and no other leader took over the headcount. Employees could relocate or take an exit package. To him, the contrast between the human effect and the allocation decision was disillusioning. This is his recollection and interpretation, not an independently verified account of the decision.
blocks.speaker: Igor

blocks.question: What advice would you give your earlier self?
answer: Ask whether the work matters to the company and who needs it. He remembers working on projects whose purpose was unclear to him and that leadership later shut down. Choosing useful work is a more concrete guide than remaining on a project only because it has been assigned.

followups.question: What can a junior engineer do if the project seems unhelpful?
answer: Talk to other managers and look for a better project where internal movement is practical. He found movement easier at Google than at an earlier employer, and cautions that the advice depends on the company. He explicitly distinguishes his own experience from reputations he has only heard about.

blocks.speaker: Igor
