sections.title: Jay Jo: Robinhood Promotions, GameStop, and Leaving Big Tech for Crypto
sections.deck: Jay Jo describes a non-linear path from a Robinhood engineering role to a crypto startup, with views on risk, promotions and fundraising.

blocks.text: In Jay Jo's view, careers rarely move in a straight line; growth tends to arrive in step changes. Jay says the choice of job should follow what a person is optimizing for, such as pay or learning, and that the people around you are the biggest factor you can control. The conversation follows Jay from college internships to a fast-scaling Robinhood engineering role, a stretch of disengagement, and a move into crypto infrastructure. Jay argues that people are far too scared of leaving a job, because a competent engineer usually finds work again, and that a failed startup still builds skills employers value. Editorial note: the GameStop and company accounts are one insider's first-hand view and were not checked against outside sources.
blocks.heading: Jay Jo's view: careers move in steps, and people overrate the risk of leaving

blocks.question: How did Jay first get into big tech, and how much of it was luck?
answer: In college Jay wanted a brand-name internship at Facebook or Google, partly because that was what everyone else wanted. Jay was not strong at LeetCode-style problems, so Jay joined a friend's Friday-night problem-solving session. One problem from that session, counting islands in a grid, turned out to be the exact question in the second on-site interview for the Facebook internship. Jay calls the link a lucky coincidence, and says the offer shaped everything after it.
blocks.speaker: Jay Jo

blocks.question: Were Google and Facebook the only prestigious places to intern?
answer: Jay says what people value depends on their circle. At UCLA, Google and Facebook were the reference points, but later other companies, including Palantir and some pre-IPO startups, came to be seen as just as prestigious.

followups.question: How did the Facebook internship compare with the Pinterest one?
answer: Jay found the Facebook internship impersonal. The Pinterest internship, a Kleiner Perkins fellowship in San Francisco, felt more personal, partly because its intern class was smaller. Jay is still close to four or five people from it, and few from the Facebook class.
followups.speaker: Jay Jo

blocks.speaker: Jay Jo

blocks.question: Why choose Robinhood over going back to Pinterest or doing a master's degree?
answer: Jay was about to graduate and weighed three options: returning to Pinterest, which Jay was less keen on since friends were not going back; a master's that UCLA offers with automatic admission from its fifth year; and small companies full of people doing significant work. Jay visited the Robinhood booth at the Greylock Tech Fair in 2017, where it had the longest line, and found a strong team.

In hindsight Jay says the master's would not have mattered, and the Robinhood role offered more. The new-grad class was unusually strong, and about a third of it later raised money. Rapid scaling exposed Jay to many problems, which Jay says sped up career growth.

followups.question: What stage was Robinhood at when Jay joined?
answer: Jay signed the offer at Series C and joined at Series D. At the offer stage the company had about 100 people across two nearby buildings, one of them a house where engineers worked at standing desks.
followups.speaker: Jay Jo

blocks.speaker: Jay Jo

blocks.question: Why choose a smaller company when big tech is the common advice?
answer: Jay says a person has to pick what they are optimizing for. Pay upside is rarely found at big tech, Jay argues, because the largest gains usually come from very early-stage companies. Learning is different: a smaller company that is growing quickly offers far more of it, though the path is high-variance, since a company can stop growing and the learning can dry up.
Jay says career growth at Robinhood ended up looking like a normal company's, though the learning was much better than expected.

followups.question: Does big tech carry the same reorganization risk?
answer: Jay says it depends on luck in any role. The biggest factor Jay can control is the people to work with, because a startup's prospects can shift fast even when it looks promising. Surrounding yourself with very smart people is a good heuristic for choosing where to go.
followups.speaker: Jay Jo

blocks.speaker: Jay Jo

blocks.question: Did growth at Robinhood match what Jay expected?
answer: Jay says Jay joined a bit too late for the fast growth earlier hires got, and by then the company was already moving toward a more conventional big-company path. Jay missed the first review because of a late start, and went through the process at nine months, after long hours that sometimes ran until 2 a.m.
Jay also describes a painful on-call rotation, centered on an overnight batch process that ran after market close and sometimes went until 4 or 5 a.m., close to a business problem.

followups.question: What did the overnight batch work involve?
answer: Jay says the batch included trade settlement, which required coordinating with outside counterparties so every system matched. The jobs ran one after another, so a failure meant finding its cause, often a bad deployment, paging the engineer who wrote it, waiting for a fix, and rerunning the process.
Jay says the codebase was not architected in the most stable way and carried a lot of tech debt. Jay received a five-out-of-five performance rating, but no promotion or pay change followed.
followups.speaker: Jay Jo

followups.question: Did that leave Jay jaded about big tech?
answer: Jay says the time put in did not match the reward. Jay considered becoming more checked out and going through the motions, a pattern Jay saw in many colleagues. That made Jay jaded about the big-tech environment and convinced Jay there was something bigger to work toward.
followups.speaker: Jay Jo

blocks.speaker: Jay Jo

blocks.question: Why stay about three and a half years if the frustration began after nine months?
answer: Jay says a family death made leaving harder, and stock options would have cost about $400,000 to exercise. Jay's plan was to stay until the options no longer had to be exercised before leaving, or until the IPO. The IPO came in July 2021, which Jay describes as removing the handcuffs, and Jay then went much deeper into crypto.

followups.question: Did staying pay off financially?
answer: Jay says the pay was an order of magnitude higher than three and a half years at a Google or Facebook type of company would have produced, and that the decision looks fantastic in hindsight. At the time, though, Jay felt locked in, which reduced happiness.
followups.speaker: Jay Jo

followups.question: Was timing a factor?
answer: Jay says the group was lucky. Jay graduated in 2018, ahead of the 2021 wave of tech IPOs. Many friends at pre-IPO companies have still not listed, so their options may be worth little. Jay doubts a 2020 graduate would have had the same liquidity.
followups.speaker: Jay Jo

blocks.speaker: Jay Jo

blocks.question: Was Jay promoted while doing only the minimum?
answer: Jay says Jay was promoted in the second performance cycle and was technically up for another promotion before leaving. By then Jay was putting in the bare minimum to stay close to average and spending time elsewhere.

Jay says that at a company that grew about tenfold, being a competent engineer made Jay the only person who knew many systems. That turned Jay into a domain expert and an engineering lead for several systems.

followups.question: In a fast-growing company, does competence alone make someone load-bearing?
answer: Jay agrees that when both the team and the workload grow, competence is rewarded almost automatically. Jay also mentored three people, the first about a year and a half into the job, which Jay says is much less common at larger companies.
followups.speaker: Jay Jo

blocks.speaker: Jay Jo

blocks.question: What was the GameStop episode like from inside Robinhood?
answer: Jay describes a stock frenzy in which about a dozen stocks, including GameStop and AMC, surged during the pandemic. Short sellers had to buy back shares, which pushed prices higher in a short squeeze. Robinhood was where many people traded, and on January 28, 2021 it turned off buying on those meme stocks. Jay learned about it on waking, and many contacts, some of them invested too, reached out that day.

followups.question: How did the episode affect Jay and the people around Jay?
answer: Jay says many contacts were upset as GameStop's price fell, and Jay felt powerless as an insider. The episode showed Jay how archaic the financial system is. Trades then took two days to settle, so Robinhood needed billions of dollars of collateral for open positions. Jay says that realization was one of the things that inspired the later startup.
followups.speaker: Jay Jo

followups.question: Was the trading halt a deliberate move on the price?
answer: Jay says no. Robinhood turned off buys to raise collateral, not to influence the price, and Jay thinks the company miscommunicated the reason, possibly on purpose, while it was fundraising billions at the same time. Jay says the leaders were fighting for the company's existence with regulators already wary, and handled it in an okay way, but could have communicated much better.
followups.speaker: Jay Jo

blocks.speaker: Jay Jo

blocks.question: Why did Jay leave to start something of Jay's own?
answer: Jay says Silicon Valley respects founders more than celebrities, so starting a company felt normal. The Kleiner Perkins fellowship, taken at age 21, made it seem accessible because many fellows had founded companies or were considering it. In 2019 Jay and a co-founder began building an AWS cost-management startup on nights and weekends.

followups.question: Why did that first startup not work out?
answer: Jay says cost management is a dull market, since fast-growing companies do not need to cut costs and stalling ones make poor customers. The startup found little traction, and Jay is glad not to have spent years on it. In 2021 the pair turned to crypto, aiming to build something like Robinhood in a decentralized way. They first built an on-chain order-book exchange, then realized the infrastructure underneath was the better thing to build.
followups.speaker: Jay Jo

blocks.speaker: Jay Jo

blocks.question: What did Jay need to see before going all in on the new company?
answer: Jay says a small team willing to work part-time, a good working relationship with the co-founder, and early excitement about the product were enough. Jay's bar was low because the IPO had just happened and Jay was near the end of a four-year grant, so there was little downside. Jay now calls it a fantastic time to make the move.

followups.question: Would Jay still have left with a middling pay package?
answer: Jay says it would have been even easier to leave, since the six months of equity given up was still a high dollar value to Jay. Jay thinks people are much too scared of leaving jobs. A competent person usually finds work again, and Jay does not know anyone who was good at one job and could not find another.
followups.speaker: Jay Jo

followups.question: If a startup fails, can someone simply go back?
answer: Jay says the main cost is opportunity cost. Building a product teaches validation, design, engineering, marketing and business development, which makes a person more valuable to employers. Seed-stage startups often value a former founder more than a typical engineer, since that person can have more impact in the zero-to-one phase. Jay adds that founders who fail often look at smaller companies next, partly by choice, and has seen people leave big tech, fail at a startup, and return to big tech.
followups.speaker: Jay Jo

blocks.speaker: Jay Jo

blocks.question: How did fundraising go for the company?
answer: Jay says the company raised about $35 million in total, starting with a $5 million seed round, followed by strategic rounds. The seed raise began about three weeks after the collapse of Terra, which Jay calls one of the worst times in crypto to raise money. Most investors said no, and Jay learned the full cycle: intro calls, partner meetings, and talks about the team, product and vision.

Jay says it was less frightening than expected. Investors start out skeptical, and once one fund is excited, others become easier to convince. Many stay on the sidelines to keep options open, giving reasons such as still doing diligence.

followups.question: How did Jay land a lead investor?
answer: Jay says a tier-one lead makes everything else easier. The team was introduced to top crypto investors, and Multicoin, which Jay says was the biggest early Solana investor, invested after good conversations. That credibility opened doors for business development, later fundraising and the launch.
followups.speaker: Jay Jo

followups.question: How is crypto fundraising different from traditional venture?
answer: Jay says crypto projects typically raise a seed round and a Series A, then hold a token launch, and seldom raise institutional rounds afterward. Web2 companies are judged on revenue and ARR, while crypto projects are judged on softer measures such as excitement and the number of teams building. Jay compares this to internet investing in about 1995 to 1997, when metrics like eyeball counts stood in for revenue.
followups.speaker: Jay Jo

blocks.speaker: Jay Jo

blocks.question: Is crypto mostly grift, and what is the clear case for its value?
answer: Jay argues that any early industry attracts grift, and that the early internet had plenty of its own, with adult content arguably one of its biggest early uses. Jay expects grift to fade as regulation gives clearer rules and as social pressure makes investors wary of bad actors. Jay says AI is showing similar hype, with some companies raising money without building anything meaningful.

followups.question: Where does crypto deliver real value, in Jay's view?
answer: Jay says crypto has been strongest at payments and trading. A distributed ledger is expensive, because many machines repeat the same work, but it offers verifiability, which matters when real money is at stake. Jay points to stablecoins for international remittances, and to people in countries with rapidly inflating currencies who hold USDC or USDT, especially in Southeast Asia and Latin America. Jay expects verifiable computation between parties who do not trust each other to matter for many financial uses.
followups.speaker: Jay Jo

blocks.speaker: Jay Jo

blocks.question: Which period of Jay's career brought the most growth?
answer: Jay says 2022, the year Jay started the company, brought the most growth. Building alone means working through every problem without the support a job provides, and Jay says every year since has taught more than any earlier job.

followups.question: Are the most important lessons non-engineering ones?
answer: Jay says so. Engineering is generally the easier part of building a company, since most businesses solve fairly mundane problems rather than the scaling challenges of a company like Meta. Jay says a competent L4 engineer can do well as a founder in most engineering settings. Jay's main lessons were about starting a business and raising money.
followups.speaker: Jay Jo

followups.question: Should a new graduate stay until technically competent before starting something?
answer: Jay says that if you know what you want to build, you should just go for it. Technical competence can be built or, more likely, hired for, and a good idea makes fundraising easier, which in turn makes it straightforward to grow a team.
followups.speaker: Jay Jo

blocks.speaker: Jay Jo

blocks.question: How has the company's team grown since it started?
answer: Jay says the company started in 2022 with five to seven people and now has around 60 full-time staff across its entities. Jay calls that lean growth relative to places like Robinhood and says it was the right decision, because slow growth keeps the culture intact and avoids bureaucracy and confusion about what to do.
blocks.speaker: Jay Jo

blocks.question: What would Jay tell a UCLA graduate, knowing what Jay knows now?
answer: Jay would say not to be so scared. Jay describes being naturally risk-averse and hesitant to take big leaps, unlike some people Jay knows. The best approach, Jay says, is to think through a decision and then pull the trigger quickly. Looking back, Jay should not have been so scared of leaving Robinhood, potentially even earlier.

followups.question: So in a perfect world, would Jay have left Robinhood sooner?
answer: Jay says yes in a perfect world, but is not sure things would have played out the same. Leaving earlier might have meant not starting the crypto company, and a cost-management startup would not have led to the same outcome.
followups.speaker: Jay Jo

sections.title: Sash: A Career Built Through Prototypes and Team Changes
sections.deck: A staff engineer explains the appeal and risks of broad exploration, from design delight and hardware to blockchain, Threads and early AI demonstrations.

blocks.question: How did you choose your first team at Meta?
answer: An initial London-based option lost its appeal when code review across locations took days. Sash then met someone who saw his mix of design and engineering experience as a fit for a team that would turn designers’ unused prototypes into shipped experiences.

That News Feed delight team prioritized animations, playful interactions and other small moments of enjoyment without a clear metrics requirement at the outset. He loved it, but the team lasted only about half a year. Looking back, he recognizes that an enjoyable proposition without a durable impact story was unlikely to survive scrutiny in that organization.
blocks.speaker: Sash

blocks.question: How could a design-oriented team prove its work was successful?
answer: Sash retrospectively sees the need for an executive sponsor with a credible theory of value. He recalls a survey measure asking whether people felt Facebook cared about them, which supplied a possible connection for delight work. The measure was subjective and open to interpretation.

He thinks it is harder to defend such teams when the company is intensely focused on efficiency. This explains a tension in his choices: he sought work he found compelling even when its measurable payoff was uncertain.
blocks.speaker: Sash

blocks.question: What were you optimizing for when choosing teams?
answer: Initially, fun. He followed people, intuition and opportunities that seemed interesting, then made sense of the resulting path afterward. Over time he became somewhat more deliberate but still preferred risky zero-to-one work.

He noticed that many strong engineers wanted a clear product definition, diagram or design before beginning. His comfort working without those gave him a useful niche. Breadth accumulated tools, relationships and knowledge that could become valuable on later projects, although that does not guarantee a successful outcome for every move.
blocks.speaker: Sash

blocks.question: What makes a designer especially good to work with?
answer: A willingness to collaborate continuously. An initial design need not anticipate every engineering constraint, but the team eventually has to resolve missing data, network failure and other real-world conditions. Engineering can also introduce possibilities the designer may not have considered, such as sensors affecting an interaction.

He values short feedback loops. On an unreleased hardware project, he worked on a makeshift pipeline that showed Figma designs on the device quickly so designers could change them and immediately see the result. Both sides listening and adjusting produces a stronger product than handing off a supposedly finished idea.
blocks.speaker: Sash

followups.question: Is the key both rapid iteration and two-way communication?
answer: Yes. He likes beginning with an ambitious picture rather than rejecting it immediately through constraints, then jointly adapting it to processing power, heat or other limits. The constraints still matter; delaying premature dismissal gives the collaboration more room to discover a good solution.

blocks.question: Why leave iOS work for experimental hardware and Android?
answer: He was looking for interesting work in New York and found a new hardware team’s opening more appealing than the available iOS options. The project used Android’s open-source platform. He had no hardware or Android experience, but wanted to try it.

The new domain was unfamiliar rather than a carefully planned career optimization. Once involved, he enjoyed the exploration. His first six months produced only about two committed diffs because much of the work was prototyping, sourcing hardware and learning what an eventual product could do.

One investigation used a Raspberry Pi to emulate a car’s Bluetooth messaging integration and inspect its communication with an iPhone. The throwaway code was not intended for the main repository: it helped establish the best experience the protocol might support before production implementation. Exploring that upper bound became a recurring part of his work.
blocks.speaker: Sash

blocks.question: How was your performance judged when you committed so little code?
answer: The early team’s expectations centered on reducing uncertainty, not simply landing production code. It was staffed with senior people who understood that a risky project needed that kind of work. Sash describes this as one way a large company can encourage exploration without promising a promotion.

He also sees a tension in review cadence: frequent feedback is useful, but a short cycle can discourage bets whose outcome takes multiple cycles. He does not claim there is a review process that perfectly serves everyone. The important point in his example is that expected contribution was aligned with the project’s exploratory stage.
blocks.speaker: Sash

blocks.question: What differed most between hardware and software teams?
answer: Timelines. A physical device must eventually have software flashed onto it and enter a manufacturing process. Moving that deadline can disrupt a much larger chain of commitments. A day-one update is possible but does not eliminate the need to put something usable in the box.

Compared with continuous software delivery, that makes the late project period more unforgiving. Work can feel relaxed early and become a crunch near the manufacturing date. He likens it to an earlier software era when a product had to be finalized and shipped on a physical disc.
blocks.speaker: Sash

blocks.question: Why move from hardware back to software prototyping?
answer: He wanted to try living in London. Staying on the hardware team from abroad was not workable in the situation he encountered. He speculates that unreleased technology and cross-border complexity could have contributed, but does not claim to know the precise regulatory cause.

Instagram was opening a London office with a blockchain team, offering another exploratory opportunity. He helped ship an NFT feature and then became interested in a broader question inspired by leadership: could following a creator exist outside a single platform?

Translating that idea into a product required both technical experiments and partnerships. What would onboarding look like? How could another platform recognize the relationship? Would a wallet or token participate? More difficult still, why would advertising, subscription and merchant-service businesses all want the same system?

Working with partners gave him a view of business incentives he had not usually encountered as an engineer. The project ended as the crypto environment deteriorated, but the experience showed him that technical feasibility alone does not make a multi-company product viable.
blocks.speaker: Sash

blocks.question: How did you get involved in the early Threads project?
answer: As the blockchain effort wound down, he worked on more conventional Instagram features. People then contacted him about ActivityPub and decentralized social networking. He is uncertain exactly why they approached him, but suspects a reputation for sharing prototypes played a part.

During the holiday period, he connected internal Instagram and Mastodon instances with crude experimental code so that a user search could resolve an Instagram account. The technical possibility was not particularly surprising, but a concrete working example generated excitement more effectively than another presentation.

Next, he stripped images from an Instagram client, enlarged captions and worked with a deeply experienced back-end colleague to build text-only posting and feeds. The early experience lived behind internal gates inside Instagram. It was a progressive carving-out of a product, not an isolated application built without an existing platform.

Working from London, he often repaired broken experimental builds before US teammates came online. The early team grew around a leadership-backed opportunity to release a text product amid Twitter’s turmoil. Support for privacy, integrity and performance arrived as needed. He remembers roughly five or six months from prototype to public launch, while emphasizing the benefit of Instagram’s mature primitives and infrastructure.
blocks.speaker: Sash

blocks.question: What made the senior back-end engineer on that project so effective?
answer: Deep familiarity with the existing system. The colleague knew how to create a feed, make a post work without an image and understand consequences elsewhere in the application. Their conversations rapidly became working front-end/back-end changes that Sash could test.

Large, mature primitives also helped. A high-level operation could provide defaults and integrations without each engineer rebuilding lower layers. The knowledgeable partner knew how to use those facilities appropriately. Sash’s playful comparison with a copilot emphasizes accurate context and judgment, rather than a literal substitute for the person.
blocks.speaker: Sash

blocks.question: Did sharing prototypes build the reputation that led to new opportunities?
answer: He cannot know exactly what others thought, but believes repeated internal demonstrations made people associate him with fast, exploratory work. Prototypes using company technology could not be shared publicly, so internal posts were an important venue even when immediate engagement was modest.

Responding to an ambiguous inquiry with something working also showed initiative. Early projects benefit from people who can move without a fully assigned checklist. He thinks that behavior stands out amid the meetings and alignment work common in a large company.
blocks.speaker: Sash

blocks.question: Which AI prototype stands out from the later part of your work?
answer: He built an early conversational assistant over public account-safety and support information using retrieval-augmented generation. It still hallucinated substantially, but it made a possible direction for support tangible. Sharing it produced many messages from people in other parts of the company.

He does not claim to have invented the approach or solved support. The value was bringing an outside technical possibility into a familiar corporate context and showing how it might interact with the company’s own data and products. Colleagues focused on their jobs may not follow every new industry development; a situated demonstration can make the opportunity visible.
blocks.speaker: Sash

blocks.question: Why does a prototype communicate better than a written proposal?
answer: A written description depends on everyone constructing the same mental model. An image narrows that ambiguity; a video narrows it further. An interactive prototype lets people experience the behavior directly and talk about a specific interaction.

Sash has seen meetings progress for some time before participants discover they imagined different products. A prototype can expose that disagreement early and shorten the ambiguous part of a project. Its fidelity helps alignment, not merely publicity.
blocks.speaker: Sash

blocks.title: What a prototype contributes before production
blocks.caption: An editor-assembled sequence across Sash’s examples; arrows show a possible collaboration process, not a guarantee that a prototype will ship.

steps.title: Explore the upper bound
steps.text: Use rough code to discover the experience that might be possible.

steps.title: Make the idea tangible
steps.text: Give partners something they can inspect or interact with.

steps.title: Resolve different mental models
steps.text: Discuss concrete behavior instead of assuming everyone read a proposal the same way.

steps.title: Learn constraints and incentives
steps.text: Adapt the design to hardware, software and business realities.

steps.title: Decide what to productionize
steps.text: Turn selected learning into a durable product, or stop when the case is weak.

blocks.question: How do you assess your growth from IC4 to IC6 despite frequent team switches?
answer: Staying in one space usually makes leveling easier: expertise, goodwill and relationships compound around a known problem. He saw that in a colleague who remained on the original team for years. He often found that kind of continuity less interesting for himself.

His choices favored enjoyable projects and breadth over maximizing promotion speed. They accumulated connections and knowledge, with some wrong turns along the way. Because he worked long hours, enjoyment mattered to sustaining the effort.

He explicitly resists turning his path into universal advice. The right strategy depends on the career and life a person wants. His eventual promotion does not prove that repeated switching is the fastest route, only that the route can develop a useful niche for someone with his preferences.
blocks.speaker: Sash

blocks.question: How did your path compare with people from your original bootcamp group?
answer: He remembers peers becoming managers or remaining in the same application or domain, generally doing well. They preferred vertical growth more than his broad exploration. The comparison is a small anecdotal sample, not evidence that one strategy wins.

When leaving, he found it difficult to identify a replacement for a role centered almost entirely on prototyping. He thinks large-company incentives naturally direct most people toward predictable impact. Yet a company also needs some people prepared to test uncertain directions. That balance may help it discover options beyond its established work.
blocks.speaker: Sash

blocks.question: What are the limits of optimizing only for a metric?
answer: Sash invokes the familiar problem that a measure can become less informative once it becomes a target: people learn to game it. He also thinks important parts of product quality are difficult to measure and require taste.

A relentlessly increasing local measure can obscure opportunities that require a temporary setback or a different direction. He recognizes the difficulty of translating that insight into a scalable framework, because large organizations also need repeatable processes. His preference for experimentation is a response to that tension, not a fully specified replacement for metrics.
blocks.speaker: Sash

blocks.question: Do you regret any of the ten team switches?
answer: Some paid off less than he hoped, but he learned from them and built relationships. Trying to be a good teammate made those connections useful in both directions: someone could invite him to a later project, or he could bring them along.

The size of that network became particularly visible after he left Meta, when people offered introductions or expressed interest in what he might build next. He values the adventure and people as outcomes, rather than evaluating every move only by title progression.
blocks.speaker: Sash

blocks.question: Why leave Meta instead of switching teams again?
answer: After a long period, he wanted to return to a startup-like environment where his preferred pace felt natural. He wanted to test his own ideas close to the outcome, without attributing failure to a meeting or another team.

He acknowledges greater financial and practical risk. He views a return to a larger company as a possible fallback, while recognizing that it is a hope rather than a guaranteed future offer. His circumstances allowed him to take the experiment, and the choice reflected that personal capacity.
blocks.speaker: Sash

followups.question: Did it help to think of the decision as a two-way door?
answer: Yes. He distinguishes decisions that are difficult to reverse from ones that appear reversible. A perceived fallback can justify taking a risk while circumstances permit, although it still calls for care. His language is a decision framework, not proof that any job transition will be reversible.

blocks.question: What advice would you give yourself at the beginning of your career?
answer: Address weaknesses enough that they do not obstruct the work, then invest in the strengths that make the contribution distinctive. A manager helped him see that fixing every shortcoming was not necessarily the highest-value development plan.

For Sash, that means choosing a setting where his comfort with ambiguity, design collaboration and rapid prototyping can be useful. The advice asks a person to understand their own strengths and fit, rather than copy his specific team choices.
blocks.speaker: Sash

sections.title: A learning project becomes a community of engineering stories
sections.deck: Ryan Peterman explains how the podcast grew from deliberate speaking practice into a way to surface engineers whose work is better known inside companies than outside them.

blocks.question: Why create a podcast about senior engineers’ careers?
answer: Ryan wanted to become a better speaker, a skill he believes affects careers, relationships, and how others perceive someone. Toastmasters supplied useful practice, but he found that recordings often went unreviewed amid other priorities. Publishing created a stronger commitment: because people would listen, he examined every word during editing. The content became both practice and a feedback loop.

He chose an initially modest goal of one episode per month because he already had substantial responsibilities. The process turned out to be enjoyable in its own right: he could have conversations he wanted to have with engineers he admired. Internal Facebook career narratives had earlier absorbed him with their accounts of impressive work and growth. The podcast sought to bring those otherwise little-known stories to a wider industry audience.
blocks.speaker: Ryan Peterman

blocks.question: What surprised you behind the scenes of successful episodes?
answer: Ryan remembers being unusually absorbed while recording with Philip Su, whose writing he had admired inside Meta. Strong engagement during the conversation and rapid audience growth afterward suggested that other engineers valued these career stories too. He felt similar energy with Ethan Evans and especially admired the guest’s ability to speak clearly.

Trailers created a separate challenge. Established shows can rely on reputation, but a new show may need to explain quickly why an unfamiliar guest is worth hearing. An especially aggressive trailer thrilled him at first, then audience feedback pushed him to balance attention-grabbing excerpts with taste and ease of listening. He considers shorter or absent trailers for recurring audio-podcast listeners while keeping a carefully edited introduction for discovery on YouTube. These are his plans at the time, rather than a promise about the current distribution format.
blocks.speaker: Ryan Peterman

blocks.question: Which future guests are you trying to find?
answer: His ideal guests are highly accomplished engineers known within their company or organization but not necessarily famous publicly. They may have substantial technical and career stories without being active on social media. Standard searches do not reliably reveal that group.

His own big-tech network supplied early guests. Audience recommendations then became a way to find admired senior ICs at other companies. He describes viewers’ suggestions leading to planned conversations at Apple, Google, and Microsoft. The sourcing challenge explains why community participation matters to the show’s editorial direction.
blocks.speaker: Ryan Peterman

blocks.question: What was harder about podcasting than ordinary conversation?
answer: Natural verbal acknowledgments—short agreements and listening noises—can obscure a guest’s answer in an audio recording. Ryan had to learn to express engagement with nods while holding back interruptions. Producing something pleasant to hear calls for a different listening habit than an unrecorded conversation.
blocks.speaker: Ryan Peterman

blocks.question: How do you balance a full-time engineering job with publishing?
answer: He finds it difficult and rejects an effortless side-project picture. For roughly two years he often stayed up until about four in the morning on Thursdays to finish a newsletter. A fellow newsletter writer cautioned him about burning the candle at both ends, and experience convinced him the warning was justified.

Content work pushes out other parts of life when meeting the day job’s expectations already takes substantial effort. He believes additional family or time commitments would have made the arrangement much harder. The account is an honest cost description, not a recommended sustainable schedule.
blocks.speaker: Ryan Peterman
